title: R for Social Science
text:
Preface
Welcome to R for Social Science! This book introduces R, tidystata, and the tidyverse through practical examples from social-science research. You will learn how to organize your work, explore datasets, transform variables, and summarize data using R. Tidystata supplies the main tools for routine recoding, tabulation, and numerical summaries; the tidyverse supplies general table operations and graphics.
The goal is not simply to teach R commands, but to help you develop the skills and habits needed for clear, efficient, and reproducible social-science research.

title: R for Social Science
text:
Who this book is for
This book is written for students and researchers in sociology, political science, economics, education, and related fields who want to learn R for data analysis.
No prior programming experience is required. Basic familiarity with variables, averages, and percentages is sufficient. We introduce R syntax from the beginning and explain statistical concepts as they become relevant.
If you have used Stata, SPSS, or another statistical package, you may find some concepts familiar. However, the book assumes no experience with statistical software.

title: R for Social Science
text:
Learning with real data
Social-science research involves more than writing code. Understanding what observations represent, how variables are measured, and how results should be interpreted is equally important.
Basic syntax examples use small numbers, strings, and logical values so that you can follow each operation directly. Data-handling and analysis lessons use real datasets, especially World Bank country indicators in lifeexp and the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS). Each chapter normally keeps one main dataset, and adjacent lessons reuse it where possible. Other datasets are introduced when they supply a needed feature, such as genuine dates.
For these data examples, the book explains the relevant sources, units of measurement, and transformations so that you can understand both the code and the underlying data.

title: R for Social Science
text:
How to use this book
The book is designed to be read progressively, with each chapter building on the skills introduced earlier.
Begin with Get started with R, then read 2  Objects in R for an overview of R objects and the reasons this book centers on tibbles. Enter Manipulate tables next. 3  Select columns introduces the packaged country data and the shared selection language. Sorting, the pipe, and observation selection then show how to work with one table and connect operations.
6  Select observations continues with the same country data. 8  Tabulate data introduces the 2024 GSS for tabulation, summaries, descriptive plots, and variable manipulation. Follow the one-time preparation recipe in Appendix A: GSS data at that point; later survey chapters reuse the saved extract.
Explore variables follows. 7  Inspect a dataset examines records and variable descriptions, then teaches a CSV download, import, and export. Continue to 8  Tabulate data, 9  Summarize data, and 11  Visualize data to describe categories, numerical distributions, and graphical patterns. Return to these inspection tools whenever a transformation needs checking.
Manipulate variables starts with 12  Create variables, then develops numeric and logical transformations in 14  Logicals and numbers, factors and questionnaire scores in 15  Strings and factors, and strings and dates in 16  Dates and times. Return to frequency tables and summaries after a transformation to check what changed.
Manage datasets covers 18  Import and export, 19  Group and reshape, and 20  Combine datasets: bring files into R, reorganize observations, and connect tables through checked identifiers. Analyze variables then uses 22  ggplot2 to build and refine figures, 23  Statistical tests to compare groups and test associations, 24  OLS regression for OLS models, and 25  Logit and probit for binary-outcome models.
The final part, Programming, is optional. It explains basic expressions, vectors, and other R data structures in more detail. Read it when you want to understand the machinery behind an operation; it is not a prerequisite for the practical chapters. Each practical chapter explains the syntax needed for its own tasks.
A few suggestions will help you get the most out of the book:

Run the examples yourself. Follow the examples in order, beginning with the package and data setup provided in each chapter.
Work with the data. Experiment with the code, inspect the results, and consider what the output means.
Complete the exercises. Try solving problems independently before consulting the worked answers or an AI assistant.
Keep your work organized. Save your scripts and data files so that you can return to previous exercises and reproduce your results.

Before working with the GSS examples, follow the instructions in Appendix A: GSS data to prepare and save the required data extract. Subsequent chapters will use this saved file.

title: R for Social Science
text:
Reading conventions
Throughout the book, a few conventions help distinguish essential material from supplementary information.

Optional references provide additional explanations or resources. You can skip them on a first reading without missing the main lesson. The GSS applications state their data setup explicitly.
Previews illustrate techniques that will be explained in greater detail later. Focus on understanding their purpose rather than memorizing every command.
Installation instructions generally need to be run only once when setting up your environment. Other code blocks may demonstrate operations on your own files or optional software rather than code executed automatically by the book.

You do not need to understand every detail on your first reading. The most effective way to learn R is to practice regularly and return to earlier examples as your skills develop.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.1 Downloading R and Positron
R is a programming language designed by statisticians.
Your first goal is to run a saved script, then open a real dataset. This chapter introduces the setup and code you need, then considers where R fits into social-science research: what it asks you to learn and what it makes possible. The final discussion of learning with AI is optional.
Install two separate programs: R, which runs your code, and an integrated development environment (IDE), which helps you write code, inspect data, and view results. This book uses Positron as its main IDE.
Start by downloading R from the R website. Follow the CRAN link and choose the installer for your operating system. Install R before opening Positron.
Next, download and install Positron. Choose the installer for your operating system and processor. The website may show a different recommended download on your computer. Positron requires R 4.2 or later; its download page lists any additional system requirements.
Positron includes support for running R code, exploring data, viewing plots, and reading help. Posit recommends it for new R users. We use one main IDE so that beginners can follow a consistent set of instructions. RStudio remains supported and is a useful alternative if your course already uses it. VS Code also supports R, but its setup requires an R extension and the languageserver package. Readers already comfortable with either editor can continue using it for the R examples in this book.
In the layout shown here, the file explorer is on the left, the editor is in the center, and the console is below the editor. The right sidebar contains variables and plots, with tabs for help and other tools. The layout can be customized, so your screen may differ. Open an R script, select an R interpreter if prompted, and use the console to run code. The screenshot is an orientation example from the official documentation; you do not need its example files, packages, or R version.
For now, remember one shortcut: Ctrl + Enter on Windows or Linux, or Cmd + Enter on macOS, runs the selected code in the editor. If no code is selected, Positron runs the current statement.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
Figure 1.2: The R website, with links to download R through CRAN.










Figure 1.3: The Positron download page, shown on Windows.










Figure 1.4: The main regions of Positron, illustrated in Posit’s documentation. Source: Posit Software, PBC.






1.1.1 Keeping your work
Create a folder called r4ss in a location you can find again, such as your Documents folder. Use Positron’s Open Folder command to open it. This is your project folder: keep this book’s scripts, downloaded examples, and saved results together here.
Create a new text file in the editor and save it inside that folder as first.R. The .R extension identifies an R script. Type the examples in the next section into this file, save it, and run statements from top to bottom with the shortcut above. The editor keeps your instructions; the console runs them and displays results. Saving the file keeps the instructions on disk. Running a line creates or changes objects in the current R session.
Reopen this folder and the saved first.R file whenever you resume your work. Saving a script does not preserve the running session’s objects; running its statements in order recreates them. You can also select all the code in a script and run the selection when every line is intended to run. We will check where R reads and writes files when we export our first table in Section 5.5.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.2 Trying some simple code
Once R and your IDE are installed, we can try a little code. R can perform arithmetic directly:
The shaded R blocks contain code to run; the output appears separately below them. In the console, > is R’s prompt for new input. Do not type that prompt or copy output back as code. An output marker such as [1] identifies the position of the first printed value; it is not part of the answer. Text after # on a code line is a comment for the reader and is ignored by R.

1 + 1

[1] 2

# Make 24 using 3, 4, 5, and 9
(4 + 9 - 5) * 3

[1] 24


In R, quotation marks enclose text:

# Use straight single quotes '' or double quotes "" to represent text
"Hello, R!"

[1] "Hello, R!"


A function performs an operation on supplied inputs and returns a result. Write its name followed by parentheses containing the input. For example, sqrt() takes a number and returns its square root:

# Use sqrt() to calculate a square root
sqrt(25)

[1] 5


The result is 5: five multiplied by itself gives 25. The parentheses make this a function call. The name sqrt refers to the function itself; sqrt(25) calls it on the number 25.
For text, nchar() returns the number of characters. Quotation marks identify the text input:

# Use nchar() to count characters
nchar("hello")

[1] 5


The result is also 5, because hello contains five characters. The two functions perform different operations even though these calls return the same number.
If the console shows + instead of >, R is waiting for the rest of an incomplete expression. For example, typing sqrt(25 leaves its opening parenthesis unmatched:
> sqrt(25
+
The + here is a continuation prompt, not an instruction to add something. Check that parentheses and quotation marks have matching partners. To cancel this unfinished input in Positron, press Ctrl+C with the console focused and no text selected. When the normal prompt returns, enter the complete sqrt(25) again.
For information about a function, enter help("sqrt") in the console. Positron displays its documentation in the Help pane. Find Arguments to see what inputs the function accepts and Examples to see calls you can try. Read the input description before changing a call; help explains the function, while your question determines which input is appropriate.
We can store results for later use:
The arrow <- assigns the result on its right to the name on its left. Assignment is normally silent: a <- 123 stores a value without displaying it. Typing a displays that stored value. a * 2 displays a calculation without changing a, while b <- a * 2 stores that calculation under a second name:

# Assign 123 to a
a <- 123
# Inspect the value of a
a

[1] 123

# Multiply a by 2
a * 2

[1] 246

# Assign the result of a * 2 to b
b <- a * 2
# Inspect the value of b
b

[1] 246


Here, b stores 246. It is a calculated value, not a spreadsheet formula that stays linked to a. If you change a, rerun b <- a * 2 to update b. After restarting R, run a <- 123 before b <- a * 2; running the second line alone in an empty session gives an object-not-found error.
Object names must match exactly, including capital letters: a and A are different names. Creating a does not create A; looking up A gives an object-not-found error unless you have separately assigned it. Prefer short, descriptive lower-case names, with underscores between words, such as income_total. This is a naming convention that helps you read and retype code consistently.
Later chapters deliberately reuse example names such as countries. Running a chapter’s setup replaces an older object with that name in the session. Keep each chapter’s setup with its examples in your saved script, and run the setup before the examples that depend on it.

1.2.1 Values and functions
Store a number under the name x, then display it:

# Store a number
x <- 2.75
x

[1] 2.75


The next line displays the saved value, 2.75. R stores even one number as a vector of length one.
An expression is something R can evaluate to produce a result: a number, a calculation, or a function call. The inputs to a function are called arguments. A comma separates arguments, and = names an argument. round() takes a number and returns a rounded value; its digits argument sets the number of decimal places:

round(x, digits = 1)

[1] 2.8

x

[1] 2.75


The first argument supplies the value and digits = 1 requests one decimal place. The result is 2.8, while x remains 2.75.
Here = supplies an input setting; <- stores a returned result. Later, == will test equality. To keep the rounded result, assign it separately:

rounded_x <- round(x, digits = 1)
rounded_x

[1] 2.8


rounded_x stores 2.8. The original x still holds 2.75.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.3 Installing R packages
This book mainly uses the tidyverse and tidystata packages. A package adds functions to R. Installing puts a package in a library on your computer; normally you do this once, then install again only when you want an update. Loading with library() makes its functions available in the current session, so repeat that step after restarting R. Installing a package does not load it.
Before continuing, install these two packages. install.packages() downloads from a package repository; pak provides another installer. In pak::pak(), the part before :: names the package and the part after it names the function. This notation calls a function from an installed package without loading the whole package:

# Install tidyverse
install.packages("tidyverse")
# Install the pak installer
install.packages("pak")

Now call pak to install the tested tidystata revision from GitHub:

pak::pak("socimh/tidystata@fd6ef6b9080a7527e870a4bbc5c9c1ff13c7fa46")

These lessons were tested with tidystata 0.4.1 and dplyr 1.2.1. The GitHub revision above fixes the tidystata version used in the examples; installing the current tidyverse supplies dplyr.
When you later run library(tidyverse), attachment messages list the loaded packages. A conflict notice means that two packages supply the same function name; package::function() selects the one you intend. These notices are informational. A message beginning with Error, such as a report that a package is missing, means the requested operation failed and needs attention.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.4 Data and functions
To understand a line of R code, ask two questions: what data are we supplying, and what do we want to do with them? In the earlier calls, sqrt() received a number and calculated its square root; nchar() received text and counted its characters. Both returned results that we could save with assignment. Data can record information about people, places, and activities; functions let us work with the values representing that information.
Code that contains only data usually does very little. Think of data as nouns and functions as verbs. “Students, scores, average” is a list of words. “Calculate the average of the students’ scores” describes an action. In the same way, a function tells R what to do with data.






NoteNote



In R, data usually act like nouns, while functions usually act like verbs.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.5 Asking for help
A useful help request lets someone reproduce the problem without your current session. Before sending it:

Keep the smallest input and code that still show the problem. Plain values from this chapter are enough for many questions; do not send private respondent records.
Include the assignments that create needed objects and any package-loading calls. For round(x, digits = 1), include the preceding x <- 2.75.
Copy the exact error message and say what you expected. Here, a successful call should return 2.8.
Start a fresh R session and run just the code you intend to share, from the beginning. Check that it reproduces the same problem.

These details help another reader distinguish a missing input, a mistyped name, and an unexpected result.
You have now used functions to calculate results and saved instructions that you can run again. These small examples introduce a way of working that can extend to an entire analysis. Before we open a dataset, consider where that approach is useful and what it requires of you.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.6 Where R falls short
Writing instructions makes an analysis repeatable, but you must learn the syntax and keep track of the objects those instructions use. In the examples above, running a calculation before creating its input produces an error; changing an input does not automatically update a saved result. Learning to recognize and resolve these problems takes practice.
R also need not replace every tool you already use. If Stata already handles your data, statistical methods, and outputs well, you may have little immediate reason to switch. A useful starting question is whether a recurring research task is becoming difficult to express, repeat, or extend in your current software.






Figure 1.5: Common workflows and the tools often used for them. R is highlighted as this book’s focus.



Different tools have their own comfortable areas of use. Stata provides a familiar environment for survey analysis and econometrics. Python is widely used for general programming, web applications, and scientific computing; a project built around a framework such as PyTorch may give you a reason to learn Python. These areas overlap. Choose a language with attention to your research question, collaborators, and the tools you need.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.7 Where R shines
The same features that take practice can become useful as a project grows. Your saved script already records how to recreate a result, and named objects let you keep inputs and results available together. For many social scientists, the first reasons to develop these habits arise before model fitting. You may need to combine survey files with administrative records, read spreadsheets and data from online services, keep several datasets and intermediate results available, or repeat complicated cleaning across many survey waves. R lets you organize these as named objects and reusable functions. Stata also supports multiple datasets through frames; R’s appeal grows when you want to connect data preparation with a wider range of research tools.






Figure 1.6: Many sources, reusable R code, and different research outputs.



Visualization is another common reason. ggplot2 provides a consistent way to build and refine figures, from a quick check of a distribution to a comparison across groups. The tidyverse connects importing, cleaning, reshaping, and plotting data through related conventions. Learning those conventions can make an entire analysis easier to adapt as your question changes.
See Figure 1.1 for an example of a ggplot2 figure.
As research needs expand, R offers packages for text, spatial, and network data, as well as causal inference, machine learning, simulation, and Bayesian analysis. The CRAN Task Views organize packages by these areas. R can also connect analysis to interactive displays and reports. You can add specialized tools as your work requires them; this book begins with the data preparation, description, and visualization skills that support many such applications.
Some extensions require additional infrastructure. For example, Arrow lets R work with multi-file and larger-than-memory datasets, but installing R alone does not remove memory or computing limits. The value of learning R depends on the workflow it makes possible for you. Its free, open-source ecosystem gives you room to extend that workflow as new needs arise.
We will build on these ideas by comparing ways to organize data in Chapter 2, then choosing columns from a real table in Chapter 3. First, the exercises let you practise calculating with R, storing a value, and using a function. The following discussion of AI is optional; you can go directly to those exercises.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.8 Learning R with AI [Optional]
You may know what you want to find out before you know the R commands to use. An AI assistant can help you turn that intention into code, explain unfamiliar functions, and get past errors. You can then run the code in R and inspect what it actually does. AI assistance is optional; you can follow this book without it.

1.8.1 Understanding unfamiliar code
Consider five countries from tidystata::lifeexp: Albania, Poland, Canada, Cuba, and Argentina. Their life expectancy at birth is recorded in years. These are rounded World Bank World Development Indicators observations for 1998, distributed with tidystata. We transcribe the five named rows below so that you can inspect every input. The World Bank data are available under CC BY 4.0.

library(tidyverse)
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

countries <- tibble(
  country = c("Albania", "Poland", "Canada", "Cuba", "Argentina"),
  lexp = c(74, 73, 79, 75, 73)
)
countries
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  country    lexp
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Albania      74
2 Poland       73
3 Canada       79
4 Cuba         75
5 Argentina    73


Ask for an explanation. The exchanges here are illustrative; a chatbot or coding assistant may reply differently.

You: Explain this code to a beginner. What does each row represent, and what are the units?
Assistant: library(tidyverse) loads the packages. tibble() creates a table with two columns, country and lexp; c() combines the entries in each column. The arrow <- stores the table as countries. Each row connects a named country with its life expectancy at birth, measured in years.

Typing countries displays the table. Compare Canada’s row with the transcribed code: its recorded value is 79 years. Keeping country names attached to their measurements lets you check which observation an output describes.


1.8.2 From a question to a figure
Describe the result you want. Continue with the same table:

You: Use ggplot2 to compare life expectancy in these five countries in a bar chart. Put countries on the horizontal axis and years on the vertical axis. Explain the code.
Assistant: ggplot() uses the countries table. Inside aes(), country supplies the horizontal positions and lexp supplies the heights. geom_col() draws the bars; labs() sets the axis titles. The + signs add these parts to the plot.


ggplot(countries, aes(x = country, y = lexp)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Country", y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)")







Figure 1.7: Life expectancy at birth in five countries, 1998. Source: World Bank WDI, as distributed in tidystata::lifeexp; rounded years.





Ask about a specific error. If you accidentally type lepx in place of lexp, the plot fails. Include your code and the error when asking for help. Use the help-request checklist in Section 1.5 to make the problem reproducible.

You: My code uses aes(x = country, y = lepx). The error says object 'lepx' not found. The table above has a column called lexp. What is the smallest correction?
Assistant: Change y = lepx to y = lexp. Column names must match exactly.

Run the corrected code and check Canada’s bar against its recorded 79 years. The default display puts country names in alphabetical order, so compare names rather than assuming that the third bar is the third input row. This connects the assistant’s suggestion to a result you can verify.


1.8.3 Checking AI’s suggestions
Check the answer and its meaning. For the same five countries, ask the assistant to calculate the average using dplyr:

summarise(countries, average = mean(lexp))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  average
    <dbl>
1    74.8


Here, summarise() produces a summary table, mean(lexp) calculates the arithmetic average, and average names the result column. The result is 74.8 years: the five values sum to 374, and 374 divided by 5 is 74.8. Each country contributes equally; this calculation does not weight countries by their population size.

You: Can I conclude that people worldwide had a life expectancy of 74.8 years in 1998?
Assistant: This calculation describes the five selected countries. They were chosen for this teaching example, so their average is not a worldwide estimate. A population-weighted average would also require population counts and a different calculation.

Try the task yourself first. When you need help, ask for a hint or explanation, read the suggested code, predict its result, and run it. AI can help write the commands; knowing the source, units, and selection of observations helps you judge the conclusion.


1.8.4 AI tools [Optional]
You can ask questions in a chatbot or use an assistant alongside your code. These tools are optional. The tabs show examples from official documentation; their code illustrates the interfaces rather than the country comparison. Select a tab and click its image to enlarge it. Your editor and version may look different.

GitHub CopilotClaude CodeOpenAI Codex


GitHub Copilot offers code suggestions and chat, depending on the editor. In this RStudio example, a comment describes the task and lighter text shows suggested code. Read a suggestion before accepting it. For our country example, a comment could ask for a ggplot2 bar chart.






Figure 1.8: Copilot suggests code inside RStudio’s editor. Source: Posit Software, PBC, RStudio User Guide.





Claude Code lets you discuss code and request changes. Here, selected code is on the left and a question and explanation appear on the right. You could select the life-expectancy plotting code and ask, “Explain what each line does.”






Figure 1.9: Claude Code explains selected code in VS Code. Source: Anthropic, Claude Code documentation.





OpenAI Codex can work with project files and propose edits. Here, the conversation is on the right and changed lines are visible on the left. You could ask it to fix lepx in the country plotting script, then review the change and rerun the code.






Figure 1.10: Codex presents file changes for review beside its conversation. Source: OpenAI, Codex IDE documentation.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.9 Review

<- stores a result under a name; saving a script keeps the instructions for another session.
sqrt() calculates square roots, nchar() counts characters, and round() rounds numbers.
help() opens function documentation; include setup, code, and the exact problem when asking for help.
install.packages() installs packages from CRAN; pak::pak() can install tidystata from GitHub.
library() loads an installed package for the current session.

Next, Chapter 2 introduces the structures that hold our data and explains why this book mainly uses tibbles.

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
1.10 Exercises
Practise calculating, saving results, and rebuilding a session from your script. Predict each result before running the code. After trying a question, open the answer with the same number under Worked answers.

Calculate with R. In Section 1.2, + adds numbers and * multiplies them. Run these two lines, one at a time. What answer does each line give?
8 + 2
8 * 2
Saved values and names. Run a <- 10 and b <- a * 2. Predict b after running a <- 12. What must you rerun to update b? Explain why typing A cannot retrieve the value stored as a.
Change a function’s input. The function round() rounds a number. Its digits argument tells R how many decimal places to keep, as in Section 1.2.1. Run the line below. Then change digits = 1 to digits = 2 and run it again. What result do you get each time?
round(2.75, digits = 1)
Reconstruct a session. Save these lines in first.R. Restart R with your IDE’s restart command, then run only the last line. Explain the error. Now run the saved script from the beginning and report both values. What did saving the script preserve?
starting_value <- 10
doubled_value <- starting_value * 2
doubled_value

title: 1  Get started with R
text:
Worked answers






NoteCalculate with R






8 + 2

[1] 10

8 * 2

[1] 16


The first answer is 10: R adds 8 and 2. The second is 16: R multiplies 8 by 2. Changing the symbol changes the calculation.









NoteSaved values and names






a <- 10
b <- a * 2
a <- 12
b

[1] 20

b <- a * 2
b

[1] 24


The first printed b is 20. It stores the earlier calculation; changing a does not recalculate it. Rerunning the assignment to b produces 24. Names are case-sensitive: A is a different name and, unless separately created, gives an object-not-found error. Use the lower-case a to retrieve 12.









NoteChange a function’s input






round(2.75, digits = 1)

[1] 2.8

round(2.75, digits = 2)

[1] 2.75


With digits = 1, the answer is 2.8, rounded to one decimal place. With digits = 2, the answer is 2.75, which already has two decimal places. The number being rounded stays the same; the named argument changes how many decimal places we request.









NoteReconstruct a session





In a fresh session, the last line alone fails because doubled_value has not been created. Run all three saved lines in order:

starting_value <- 10
doubled_value <- starting_value * 2
doubled_value

[1] 20

starting_value

[1] 10


The results are 20 and 10. The script preserved instructions on disk, not the previous session’s objects. Replaying those instructions creates the inputs before they are needed.



Continue to Chapter 2 for a short tour of R objects and a comparison of data-frame and tibble output.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
2.1 Different ways to hold information
We have used R to calculate with numbers, work with text, and store results under names. A research project brings these pieces together: observations, measurements, summaries, and fitted models. How should we organize them so that one step can build on another?
R supports several kinds of objects. This chapter gives a short tour, then explains why this book mainly works with tibbles, a form of data frame. You only need the skills from the first chapter: running code, loading packages, and assigning results with <-.
By the end, you will be able to:
An object is something R can work with, such as a number, a table, or a function. A name lets us refer to a stored object again. Its structure determines how its pieces fit together; a function determines what operation we perform on it.
A single value, such as 1, is the smallest starting point in our picture. We can think of it as zero-dimensional (0D) information. R stores it as a vector of length one. A vector extends that picture to an ordered sequence of values. An ordinary numeric vector might contain the life expectancies of several countries; a character vector might contain their names.
A data frame keeps columns together in a table. Each column can have a different type: names can be text while life expectancy is numeric. Columns have the same number of entries, so each row can keep one country’s measurements together. A tibble is a form of data frame, with conventions that make these tables convenient to inspect and work with.
A list can hold different kinds of objects together, including objects of different sizes. A matrix is a rectangular structure whose values share one type; an array can extend that regular structure to more dimensions. Nested lists hold objects inside other lists. Nesting describes a hierarchy, rather than the fixed dimensions of an array.
Figure 2.1 provides a map of these possibilities. Read it as an orientation, not a set of definitions to memorize. The examples 1, "A", and TRUE represent numeric, character, and logical values. For the next several chapters, our main concern is the table and its columns. The optional Programming part returns to these structures with construction and extraction examples in Chapter 28.

title: 2  Objects in R
text: Figure 2.1: Common R data structures, from a single value to sequences, tables, and nested collections.

title: 2  Objects in R
section: 2.2 Read the same data in two forms
text:
2.2 Read the same data in two forms
A wide table can be awkward to read even when it contains only a few observations. We will compare the same ten counties in two forms, keeping all 28 variables. Load the tidyverse packages installed in the first chapter:

library(tidyverse)

For this printing example, we use midwest, a packaged dataset supplied by ggplot2, one of the tidyverse packages. It contains 437 counties and 28 variables. No download or preparation is needed. ggplot2::midwest names the dataset in that package; head() takes its first ten rows because we supply 10 as its second argument, keeping every column.
The package notes incomplete variable documentation. We use these records only to compare printing, not to interpret their measures or draw substantive conclusions.
First save and inspect the ten-row tibble returned by head():

midwest_ten <- head(ggplot2::midwest, 10)
midwest_ten

The heading reports ten rows and 28 columns. All ten counties appear together. At this width, the body shows the first nine columns; the footer identifies the other 19 variables and their types. The tibble abbreviates the display rather than removing data.
Type cues appear below the column names. <int> identifies integer values, <dbl> identifies double-precision numbers, and <chr> identifies text. Some county names are abbreviated, and some numbers display fewer digits. Their full stored values remain unchanged.
A tibble is still a data frame. Its compact display trades some visible detail for an overview that is easier to scan. To read an abbreviated label in full, use the viewer introduced later in Chapter 7. Both displays contain the same data; consistent table structure and reusable operations provide a further reason to use tibbles, beyond their printing style.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
2.3 Why this book uses tibbles
Readable printing is one benefit. Another is continuity: we can organize both data and results as tables, then use familiar table tools on them.
Suppose we study how country income and life expectancy vary together. A statistical model describes that relationship. We do not need to understand the calculation yet; in Figure 2.2, focus on the objects we work with.
The left route moves through a data frame, a fitted model, a model summary, and a matrix of numerical results. These objects have different structures, so accessing their contents requires different operations. The right route brings the model’s results into a tibble. We can then add a column of significance stars and choose the columns to report, using ordinary table operations. Each displayed result on the right is a tibble.
On a narrow screen, scroll sideways to compare both routes.







Figure 2.2: From country data to model results: different objects on the left, tibbles ready for further work on the right.




Both routes fit the same relationship and give the same estimates. The advantage illustrated on the right is what we can do next: add information, rearrange columns, or export results with the same kinds of tools used on the original data. This is the habit the book develops: work with tables and keep results in a form that supports the next step.
The first transition on the right combines fitting the model and converting its results to a tibble. A model object is still created along the way; the figure shows the tables we keep working with. The stars are reporting labels based on p-values, not a measure of an effect’s size or importance. Their interpretation belongs in the later analysis chapters.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
2.4 Where we go next
Most of the book works with tables. Their columns are vectors, so working with a table often means working with the values in one or more vectors. The following parts approach these objects at different levels:

Manipulate tables begins with selecting columns, then sorting and selecting rows within a single table. The pipe connects these operations.
Explore variables uses printed previews, a viewer, frequency tables, numerical summaries, and plots to examine a dataset. The selection language and pipe are already familiar when we need them here.
Manipulate variables works inside the columns. We calculate with numeric vectors, test conditions, and work with text, categories, and dates while keeping values aligned with their observations.
Manage datasets covers reading and saving tables, changing a table’s shape, and combining multiple tables by matching records.
Analyze variables uses prepared tables to make plots, conduct tests, and fit models. Models create other kinds of objects; their results can often be organized into tables for interpretation and reporting.
Programming, an optional part, returns to vectors, lists, matrices, and other structures in more detail.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
2.5 Review

Objects organize information in different ways; tables keep related column values together.
A tibble is a form of data frame, with a compact preview and visible type cues.
A preview can omit rows from the display without removing them from the data.
Many table operations work together, letting us build an analysis from familiar steps.

Next, Chapter 3 introduces the country dataset and shows how to choose the columns needed for a task.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
2.6 Exercises
Use the objects created in Section 2.2. These questions ask you to read the displays and explain what the structures allow; no new commands are needed.

Follow a printed block. Find the row for ADAMS county in Illinois in midwest_df. Explain why its row number appears in several blocks. Does each block add another county?
Read the tibble. Use the header, column type cues, and footer of midwest_tb to report its dimensions and explain where the undisplayed variables are. Did converting it remove counties or columns?
Reuse table operations. In Figure 2.2, suppose we want fewer report columns and a different reading order. Which objects on the right can use ordinary table operations? Explain why we cannot assume that the same operations work directly on every object on the left.

title: 2  Objects in R
text:
Worked answers






TipFollow a printed block





ADAMS in Illinois is row 1. The same row number recurs because the 28 variables are printed in blocks at the normal width. Match row 1 across blocks to follow that county’s attributes. There are still ten counties; another block supplies more variables for the same records.









TipRead the tibble





The header reports ten rows and 28 columns. Type cues such as <int>, <dbl>, and <chr> describe the displayed columns. At the book’s normal width, the body shows nine variables and the footer lists the other 19. The compact display does not delete their values. Both converted objects retain the same ten counties, 28 columns, and stored measurements.









TipReuse table operations





Every checkpoint on the right is a tibble, so table operations can choose and rearrange its columns. The left contains a data frame, a fitted model, a model summary, and a matrix. Their different structures require appropriate operations. The figure’s right route converts the model results into a table before continuing; it does not claim that the fitted model itself is a tibble.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.1 Keep the columns you need
Suppose we want to compare countries’ life expectancy and water coverage. The source has six variables, but we can make a more convenient table containing the three columns we need. Selecting columns keeps the same observations; moving columns changes their reading order.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to select columns by name, position, or name pattern; move them with relocate(); and save a result while preserving its source. We will use lifeexp, a country dataset included with tidystata. Load the packages in your current session:
Typing the dataset name prints the table, just as in Chapter 2:
The header reports 68 countries and six variables. Each row describes one country, and each column records one attribute. country identifies countries; region contains labelled region codes; popgrowth measures annual population growth in percent; lexp is life expectancy at birth in years; gnppc is income per person in current US dollars; and safewater is safe-water access in percent. NA marks an unavailable measurement. Most indicators refer to 1998; safe water refers to 2000. The dataset notes document the sources and units.
We can begin by choosing columns from this table. Later, Chapter 7 examines its individual records and variable descriptions more closely.
select() takes the data first, followed by the columns to retain. In this function, write column names directly, without quotation marks. Save the result as country_view, then type its name to inspect it:
country_view <- select(lifeexp, country, lexp, safewater)
country_view
# A tibble: 68 × 3
   country                 lexp safewater
   <chr>                  <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74        49
 2 Armenia                   70        83
 3 Austria                   78        97
 4 Azerbaijan                64        49
 5 Belarus                   68        82
 6 Belgium                   77       100
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina    74        87
 8 Bulgaria                  71        90
 9 Croatia                   72        85
10 Czechia                   75        95
# ℹ 58 more rows
country_view contains all 68 countries and three columns, in the order requested. Values, missing measurements, and row order are unchanged. <- stores this result under a new name. lifeexp still has all six columns. Selection does not erase columns from the original object.
The first argument is a table name; the remaining arguments identify its columns. country identifies observations, lexp measures life expectancy in years, and safewater measures water coverage in percent. Choosing fewer variables is different from choosing fewer countries.
We can check the number of observations directly. nrow() takes a table and returns its row count:
nrow(country_view)

[1] 68
The result is 68: all countries remain in the selected table. To count its columns, use ncol():
ncol(country_view)

[1] 3
The result is 3, matching the three names supplied to select(). These counting functions leave the table unchanged.
We can request a different reading order simply by changing the order of the selected names:
select(lifeexp, country, safewater, lexp)
# A tibble: 68 × 3
   country                safewater  lexp
   <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Albania                       49    74
 2 Armenia                       83    70
 3 Austria                       97    78
 4 Azerbaijan                    49    64
 5 Belarus                       82    68
 6 Belgium                      100    77
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina        87    74
 8 Bulgaria                      90    71
 9 Croatia                       85    72
10 Czechia                       95    75
# ℹ 58 more rows
Water coverage now precedes life expectancy. This command prints a result but does not replace country_view or lifeexp. Assign a result when you want to use it again.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.2 Check column names
Sometimes we want to check the column names without reading the country records. Tidystata’s ds() takes a table and returns its column names as text, in their current order:

ds(lifeexp)

[1] "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"


The six names follow the order in the original table. Quotation marks show that the result contains text. select() returns a table containing data; ds() returns the names of its columns. Neither call changes the source unless we assign its result back to that name. We will reuse ds() to check column order below.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.3 Tidyselect: ways to choose columns
Tidyselect is the shared selection language used inside select(), relocate(), and other functions that choose columns. It combines column names, operators, and helper functions. You do not need another package-loading command: the tidyverse setup above makes these helpers available.
We will first use : for a consecutive range and - to exclude columns. Then we will work through three helpers for matching text in column names, one at a time. Each method identifies columns; it does not select observations.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.4 Select ranges and exclude columns
Whole-number positions identify columns in their current order. A range made with : includes both endpoints and every column between them:

select(lifeexp, 1:3)
# A tibble: 68 × 3
       region country                popgrowth
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                      <dbl>
 1          1 Albania                     -0.6
 2          1 Armenia                     -1.2
 3          1 Austria                      0.1
 4          1 Azerbaijan                   0.9
 5          1 Belarus                     -0.5
 6          1 Belgium                      0.2
 7          1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8
 8          1 Bulgaria                    -0.7
 9          1 Croatia                     -0.1
10          1 Czechia                     -0.1
# ℹ 58 more rows

select(lifeexp, region:popgrowth)
# A tibble: 68 × 3
       region country                popgrowth
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                      <dbl>
 1          1 Albania                     -0.6
 2          1 Armenia                     -1.2
 3          1 Austria                      0.1
 4          1 Azerbaijan                   0.9
 5          1 Belarus                     -0.5
 6          1 Belgium                      0.2
 7          1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8
 8          1 Bulgaria                    -0.7
 9          1 Croatia                     -0.1
10          1 Czechia                     -0.1
# ℹ 58 more rows


Both results contain region, country, and popgrowth. A name range follows the table’s current order, not alphabetical order. Names are usually easier to check against a codebook than positions.
Separate arguments combine selections. Here we keep the country identifier and the range from life expectancy through water coverage:

select(lifeexp, country, lexp:safewater)
# A tibble: 68 × 4
   country                 lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74   870        49
 2 Armenia                   70   570        83
 3 Austria                   78 27810        97
 4 Azerbaijan                64   510        49

 8 Bulgaria                  71  1440        90

10 Czechia                   75  6140        95

The result has country, lexp, gnppc, and safewater, with all 68 rows. A minus sign before a selection excludes those columns; it does not make their values negative:

select(lifeexp, -region)
# A tibble: 68 × 5
   country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater

 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87

 9 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95

select(lifeexp, -region, -popgrowth)
# A tibble: 68 × 4
   country                 lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74   870        49
 2 Armenia                   70   570        83
 3 Austria                   78 27810        97
 4 Azerbaijan                64   510        49

10 Czechia                   75  6140        95

The first result omits the regional code; the second also omits population growth. All countries and the missing values in retained columns remain. Give each excluded column its own minus sign as shown.
To exclude a whole consecutive range, group it in parentheses and put the minus sign before the group:

select(lifeexp, -(region:popgrowth))
# A tibble: 68 × 3
    lexp gnppc safewater
   <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1    74   870        49
 2    70   570        83
 3    78 27810        97
 4    64   510        49
 5    68  1540        82
 6    77 26530       100
 7    74  1230        87
 8    71  1440        90
 9    72    NA        85
10    75  6140        95

The parentheses make region:popgrowth one selection to exclude. The result keeps lexp, gnppc, and safewater, still with 68 countries. The range includes country, so this particular demonstration also removes the identifier.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.5 Select by name patterns
When column names share some text, a helper can spare us from typing each name. starts_with() matches text at the beginning of a column name. Supply that text in quotation marks inside the helper:

select(lifeexp, starts_with("pop"))
# A tibble: 68 × 1
   popgrowth
       <dbl>
 1      -0.6
 2      -1.2
 3       0.1
 4       0.9
 5      -0.5
 6       0.2
 7       1.8
 8      -0.7
 9      -0.1
10      -0.1
# ℹ 58 more rows


This selects popgrowth, whose name begins with pop. The result still contains all 68 countries.
To match the end of a name, use ends_with():

select(lifeexp, ends_with("water"))
# A tibble: 68 × 1
   safewater
       <dbl>
 1        49
 2        83
 3        97
 4        49
 5        82
 6       100
 7        87
 8        90
 9        85
10        95
# ℹ 58 more rows


This selects safewater, whose name ends in water. Again, only the set of columns changes.
To match text anywhere in a name, use contains():

select(lifeexp, contains("p"))
# A tibble: 68 × 3
   popgrowth  lexp gnppc
       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1      -0.6    74   870
 2      -1.2    70   570
 3       0.1    78 27810
 4       0.9    64   510
 5      -0.5    68  1540
 6       0.2    77 26530
 7       1.8    74  1230
 8      -0.7    71  1440
 9      -0.1    72    NA
10      -0.1    75  6140
# ℹ 58 more rows


This selects popgrowth, lexp, and gnppc, because each name contains the letter p. All 68 countries remain. The three helpers ignore letter case by default. They match spelling, not meaning: the three names containing p measure different things.
We can combine a named identifier with a helper, or exclude the helper’s selection:

select(lifeexp, country, starts_with("pop"))
# A tibble: 68 × 2
   country                popgrowth
   <chr>                      <dbl>
 1 Albania                     -0.6
 2 Armenia                     -1.2
 3 Austria                      0.1
 4 Azerbaijan                   0.9
 5 Belarus                     -0.5
 6 Belgium                      0.2
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8
 8 Bulgaria                    -0.7
 9 Croatia                     -0.1
10 Czechia                     -0.1
# ℹ 58 more rows

select(lifeexp, -contains("p"))
# A tibble: 68 × 3
       region country                safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                      <dbl>
 1          1 Albania                       49
 2          1 Armenia                       83
 3          1 Austria                       97
 4          1 Azerbaijan                    49
 5          1 Belarus                       82
 6          1 Belgium                      100
 7          1 Bosnia and Herzegovina        87
 8          1 Bulgaria                      90
 9          1 Croatia                       85
10          1 Czechia                       95
# ℹ 58 more rows


The first table pairs country names with population growth. The second keeps region, country, and safewater. The minus sign applies to all columns identified by the helper. Neither call changes lifeexp.
An exact name is a request for a particular variable. If we write select(lifeexp, income), R reports that income does not exist; the income column here is gnppc. A pattern can legitimately match no names. For example:

select(lifeexp, starts_with("income"))
# A tibble: 68 × 0


This returns a table with 68 rows and zero columns, without an error. No names begin with income; the helper does not know that we meant income per person. A successful call can therefore still be unsuitable for our question. Check the header and the selected names, then correct the spelling or selection rule.
A shared spelling need not identify a shared measurement. Check the selected names before interpreting the result; choosing columns is a research decision as well as a coding operation.

title: 3  Select columns
section: 3.6 Move a column without dropping others
text:
3.6 Move a column without dropping others



relocate() also takes the table first, but moves named columns while keeping the rest. Its default places the selected column at the front. Use the familiar ds() check to compare the result with the original:

country_front <- relocate(lifeexp, safewater)
ds(country_front)

[1] "safewater" "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"    

ds(lifeexp)

[1] "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"


All six columns remain. Water coverage is first in country_front; the original names show that lifeexp has not changed. No country has moved to another row.
Use .after or .before to choose a more precise location. These are argument names, including their leading dots:

country_reading <- relocate(lifeexp, safewater, .after = country)
ds(country_reading)

[1] "region"    "country"   "safewater" "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"    

relocate(country_view, safewater, .before = lexp)

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.7 Review

select() keeps columns by name, range, or position; exclusions remove columns without removing observations.
starts_with(), ends_with(), and contains() match literal parts of column names.
Name patterns match spelling rather than meaning; check that the selected columns answer the research question.
relocate() moves columns while retaining the others; .before and .after specify their destination.
ds(), nrow(), and ncol() check the result; use <- to save it without replacing the source.

Next, Chapter 4 changes the order of whole rows.

title: 3  Select columns
text:
3.8 Exercises

Save a table named income_view containing country, gnppc, and lexp, in that order. Check its row and column counts.
Move lexp immediately after country in the full dataset, saving the result as life_first. Predict its column order before checking it. Explain why this differs from selecting only these two columns. Then predict region:popgrowth after moving country to the end, as in Section 3.6.

Predict the names selected by contains("p") and ends_with("water"), then run both calls. Diagnose the difference between select(lifeexp, income) and select(lifeexp, starts_with("income")). Which error or header would alert you that neither request supplies the recorded income variable? Correct the selection to keep country and income per person.

title: 4  Sort observations
text:
4.1 Prepare ranking columns
Which countries have the highest recorded life expectancy? Sorting makes the order useful for inspection without separating a country’s values from its name. Moving columns in Chapter 3 changed the reading order of variables; here we change the reading order of observations.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to prepare columns from stored names or numeric storage, sort rows, reverse a sorting direction, resolve ties, and locate missing sorting values. Start with the unchanged package data:
Before ranking countries, we can prepare a table containing the identifier and measurements we need. The preceding chapter chose columns directly. Sometimes we want to save their names for reuse, for example when producing several versions of a ranking. We will store quoted names, then tell select() how to interpret them. None of these preparation steps sorts rows or changes lifeexp.
c() combines its inputs into a vector, an ordered sequence of values. Here we use it only to store column names as text. Put each name in quotation marks and separate the names with commas:
ranking_names <- c("country", "lexp", "gnppc")
ranking_names

[1] "country" "lexp"    "gnppc"
The result contains three character values in the order supplied. ranking_names holds names, not the corresponding country measurements. Quoted "lexp" is text in this vector; the unquoted lexp in our earlier selection identified a column directly.
Inside the familiar select(), all_of() reads a character vector as required column names:
ranking_table <- select(lifeexp, all_of(ranking_names))
ranking_table
# A tibble: 68 × 3
   country                 lexp gnppc
   <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74   870
 2 Armenia                   70   570
 3 Austria                   78 27810
 4 Azerbaijan                64   510
 5 Belarus                   68  1540
 6 Belgium                   77 26530
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina    74  1230
 8 Bulgaria                  71  1440
 9 Croatia                   72    NA
10 Czechia                   75  6140
# ℹ 58 more rows
The table has 68 countries and three columns, following the vector’s order. all_of() requires every name to exist. If we replaced "gnppc" with "income", the call would fail because that name is absent. This check protects a ranking that depends on particular variables: a missing required column should stop the task so we can correct it.
For genuinely optional columns, any_of() keeps whichever requested names exist. Save the optional request separately, then use it alongside explicitly required columns:
optional_names <- c("safewater", "income")
select(lifeexp, country, lexp, gnppc, any_of(optional_names))
# A tibble: 68 × 4
   country                 lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74   870        49
 2 Armenia                   70   570        83
 3 Austria                   78 27810        97
 4 Azerbaijan                64   510        49
 5 Belarus                   68  1540        82
 6 Belgium                   77 26530       100
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina    74  1230        87
 8 Bulgaria                  71  1440        90
 9 Croatia                   72    NA        85
10 Czechia                   75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows
This returns country, lexp, gnppc, and safewater. It silently omits income; it neither creates that variable nor substitutes gnppc for it. Country names and the two intended sorting variables remain explicitly required. Use optional selection only when the task can proceed without an absent variable; using it for a needed sorting key would hide the problem until a later step.
We can also choose columns by storage type. First try is.numeric() on plain inputs. It returns a logical answer, TRUE for numeric input and FALSE otherwise:
is.numeric(25)

[1] TRUE

is.numeric("25")

[1] FALSE
The first result is TRUE; the second is FALSE. Quotation marks make the second input text even though it contains digits. These calls return answers without changing their inputs.
Inside select(), where() keeps columns that pass a predicate, a function returning one TRUE or FALSE decision for each complete column. Supply is.numeric without parentheses: where() will call that function on each column in turn.
numeric_ranking <- select(lifeexp, country, where(is.numeric))
ds(numeric_ranking)

[1] "country"   "region"    "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"
country remains explicitly selected because names identify the records we will rank. The other columns pass the numeric test, including the labelled region codes. Numeric storage does not establish quantitative meaning: a region code identifies a category, so its magnitude is not a measure of how much region a country has. Use the variable descriptions to choose meaningful sorting keys. The predicate selects whole columns, not individual cells, and leaves missing entries and all 68 countries in place. Next we will introduce row sorting and apply it to a prepared table.

title: 4  Sort observations
text:
4.2 Order whole records



arrange() takes a table and one or more sorting columns. Its default order is ascending, from smaller to larger. Use the ranking_table prepared above. Save the sorted result, then use the familiar head() to return the first six rows for inspection without replacing the full table:

life_low_first <- arrange(ranking_table, lexp)
head(life_low_first)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  country     lexp gnppc
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 Haiti         57   410
2 Bolivia       61   960
3 Tajikistan    62   170
4 Honduras      62   960
5 Kazakhstan    63  1340
6 Azerbaijan    64   510


The lowest life expectancies appear first. All three selected columns move with each country. The result still contains 68 countries; head() returns the first six rows for inspection. lifeexp remains in its original order because we saved the sorted result separately.
Put a sorting column inside desc() to reverse its direction, from larger to smaller:

arrange(lifeexp, desc(lexp))
# A tibble: 68 × 6
       region country     popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>           <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1          1 France            0.4    79 25740        97
 2          1 Italy             0      79 22270        95
 3          1 Spain             0.4    79 15410        99
 4          1 Sweden            0.1    79 31100        99
 5          1 Switzerland       0.3    79 46650        97
 6          2 Canada            0.8    79 20900        99
 7          1 Austria           0.1    78 27810        97
 8          1 Greece            0.6    78 13540        99
 9          1 Netherlands       0.6    78 27840       100
10          1 Norway            0.6    78 36120       100
# ℹ 58 more rows


This specifies an order; it does not replace life expectancy with a negative measurement. For numeric keys, you may also encounter arrange(lifeexp, -lexp), which sorts on temporary negative values but returns the original measurements. desc() states the direction directly and also works with text.

title: 4  Sort observations
text:
4.3 Resolve ties with additional keys
When countries share a life expectancy, sorting by that key alone keeps their previous relative order. Supply country as a second key to make the order within ties explicit:

life_high_first <- arrange(lifeexp, desc(lexp), country)
head(life_high_first)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
      region country     popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
  <hvn_lbll> <chr>           <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1          2 Canada            0.8    79 20900        99
2          1 France            0.4    79 25740        97
3          1 Italy             0      79 22270        95
4          1 Spain             0.4    79 15410        99
5          1 Sweden            0.1    79 31100        99
6          1 Switzerland       0.3    79 46650        97


The highest recorded life expectancy is 79 years. Some countries share a recorded value. The second key, country, orders names within each tied life expectancy. The first key has priority: the entire dataset is not sorted alphabetically. For example, country name decides the order only after life expectancy is tied. Reversing the keys to arrange(lifeexp, country, desc(lexp)) would make country name the primary order, answering a different question. These historical measurements describe the countries and years in the source, not current rankings.

title: 4  Sort observations
section: 4.4 Interpret text order and missing values
text:
4.4 Interpret text order and missing values
A text key can also determine the entire ordering:

arrange(lifeexp, country)
# A tibble: 68 × 6
       region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1          1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2          3 Argentina                    1.2    73  7960        NA
 3          1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 4          1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 5          1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 6          1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 7          1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 8          3 Bolivia                      1.8    61   960        NA
 9          1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
10          3 Brazil                       1.5    69  4980        76
# ℹ 58 more rows


Country names follow dplyr’s default C locale text order for data in memory. This is a reproducible character order, but not necessarily language-sensitive dictionary order for every writing system. The country key above follows the same rule within tied life expectancies.
Water coverage is unavailable for some countries. Missing sorting values appear after known ones, including when the known values are sorted in descending order. Tidystata’s print_headtail() previews rows from both ends, so we can inspect high known values and missing keys together. It returns the complete input table unchanged; only the display is shortened:

water_high_first <- arrange(lifeexp, desc(safewater), country)
print_headtail(water_high_first)
# A tibble: 68 × 6
       region country             popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1          1 Belgium                   0.2    77 26530       100
 2          1 Germany                   0      77 28070       100
 3          1 Netherlands               0.6    78 27840       100
 4          1 Norway                    0.6    78 36120       100
 5          1 United Kingdom            0.3    77 27040       100
 ⋮          ⋮          ⋮                 ⋮      ⋮     ⋮         ⋮
64          2 Trinidad and Tobago       0.3    68  4450        NA
65          1 Turkiye                   1.4    71  4150        NA
66          2 United States             1.2    77 32040        NA
67          3 Uruguay                   0.5    74  7360        NA
68          3 Venezuela, RB             2      72  3380        NA
# ... 58 rows omitted in the middle; use print(x, n = Inf) to show all rows.

nrow(water_high_first)

[1] 68


The first five displayed rows are at the high end of known water coverage. The last five have NA, not exceptionally low coverage. All 68 countries remain in the returned table. A preview from both ends is not a representative sample or a selection of just the highest values.
To inspect positions throughout the sorted table, use print_interval() from tidystata. It displays approximately evenly spaced rows, including the first and last:

print_interval(water_high_first)
# A tibble: 68 × 6
       region country       popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1          1 Belgium             0.2    77 26530       100
 8          1 Spain               0.4    79 15410        99
16          1 Finland             0.3    77 25810        94
23          1 Bulgaria           -0.7    71  1440        90
31          3 Brazil              1.5    69  4980        76
38          3 Colombia            1.8    71  2600        68
46          1 Albania            -0.6    74   870        49
53          1 Moldova             0      67   580        40
61          2 Nicaragua           1.5    64   890        NA
68          3 Venezuela, RB       2      72  3380        NA
# ... 58 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to
# show all rows.


Both helpers display ten data rows by default. print_headtail() divides them between the beginning and end; print_interval() spreads them through the table. Read the row numbers to see their positions. Here, the interval view lets us inspect water coverage between the high end and the missing values at the bottom. Evenly spaced positions need not have evenly spaced measurements.
Choose the view that fits the question: head/tail for boundaries, interval for coverage across the current order. Both helpers return the complete input table unchanged and invisibly, so R prints the preview without automatically printing the returned table again. They do not select a subset for later calculations. Section 7.7.3 shows why interval previews are also useful when nearby rows belong to the same place.

title: 4  Sort observations
text:
4.5 Review

c() stores quoted names; all_of() requires them and any_of() tolerates absent optional names.
where() applies a column predicate such as is.numeric(); numeric storage alone does not justify a quantitative interpretation.
arrange() sorts whole records while keeping each observation’s values together.
desc() reverses a sorting key; missing keys still follow known values in these local tables.
Additional sorting keys resolve ties, with priority from left to right.
print_headtail() displays both ends; print_interval() displays positions throughout the ordered table. Both return the complete table.
<- saves the sorted result; sorting alone neither replaces the source nor removes observations.

Next, Chapter 5 connects these operations in reading order.

text:

Does including region establish that its codes are quantities? Does the selection remove missing water measurements? Describe where those missing keys appear after descending water sorting.

Each country’s life expectancy remains attached to it, and both previews retain the complete table. Neither selection nor sorting modifies lifeexp.

title: 5  Pipe
text:
5.1 Read the pipe as “and then”
We can now choose columns, move them, and order rows. A research task often needs several of these operations. The pipe, |>, connects them so that the code follows the order in which we describe the work.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to read a pipeline, save its result, and inspect a step when the result is unexpected. The operations themselves come from Chapter 3 and Chapter 4.
Imagine making French fries: wash the potatoes, cut them into sticks, dry them, fry them, and season. The following blocks use imaginary functions to illustrate the syntax, so read them as a recipe rather than code to run. We could nest the steps inside one another:
To follow the steps, we must read from the inside outward. The pipe, written |>, puts them in the order we would naturally describe them:
Read |> as “and then”: each step passes its result to the next. In fry(oil = TRUE), the pipe supplies the potatoes, while oil = TRUE specifies an option. The function calls describe the operations; the pipes pass each result onward.
The native pipe |> is part of R (since R 4.1). For the calls in this chapter, it supplies the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. Other arguments, such as oil = TRUE in the recipe, stay inside that function’s parentheses.
Data preparation follows the same pattern. We can connect the table operations from the preceding chapters, passing a whole table from one step to the next.

title: 5  Pipe
5  Pipe
text:
5.2 Connect familiar table operations
Load the packages to work with the same lifeexp country data as before:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)

Suppose we want country names, life expectancy, and water coverage, with water beside the name and high life expectancy first. We can retain each intermediate table:

country_view <- select(lifeexp, country, lexp, safewater)
water_beside_name <- relocate(country_view, safewater, .after = country)
country_ranked <- arrange(water_beside_name, desc(lexp), country)
head(country_ranked)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  country     safewater  lexp
  <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
1 Canada             99    79
2 France             97    79
3 Italy              95    79
4 Spain              99    79
5 Sweden             99    79
6 Switzerland        97    79


These functions take a table and return another table. That shared structure lets one operation use the result of the previous operation, like pieces with compatible connectors. The columns and row order can change while the result remains a tibble.
Each line uses the result from the preceding line. Every stored table remains available with all 68 countries; head() returns six rows for inspection. These intermediate names are useful when checking the work.
As in the nested French fries recipe, we can supply one function’s result directly as another’s argument:

country_nested <- arrange(
  relocate(select(lifeexp, country, lexp, safewater), safewater, .after = country),
  desc(lexp), country
)
head(country_nested)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  country     safewater  lexp
  <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
1 Canada             99    79
2 France             97    79
3 Italy              95    79
4 Spain              99    79
5 Sweden             99    79
6 Switzerland        97    79


Read this from the inside outward, just as with the nested recipe: select, move, then sort. It returns the same table as the named steps, but the order of operations is less visible.
Apply the first-argument rule to a familiar selection. These calls mean the same thing:

select(lifeexp, country, lexp)
# A tibble: 68 × 2
   country                 lexp
   <chr>                  <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74
 2 Armenia                   70
 3 Austria                   78
 4 Azerbaijan                64
 5 Belarus                   68
 6 Belgium                   77
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina    74
 8 Bulgaria                  71
 9 Croatia                   72
10 Czechia                   75
# ℹ 58 more rows

lifeexp |>
  select(country, lexp)
# A tibble: 68 × 2
   country                 lexp
   <chr>                  <dbl>
 1 Albania                   74
 2 Armenia                   70
 3 Austria                   78
 4 Azerbaijan                64
 5 Belarus                   68
 6 Belgium                   77
 7 Bosnia and Herzegovina    74
 8 Bulgaria                  71
 9 Croatia                   72
10 Czechia                   75
# ℹ 58 more rows


In the second form, the pipe supplies lifeexp, so we do not write that argument again inside select(). Column names still identify the variables to keep. Use this connection to express our three steps as one pipeline:

country_pipeline <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, lexp, safewater) |>
  relocate(safewater, .after = country) |>
  arrange(desc(lexp), country)
head(country_pipeline)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  country     safewater  lexp
  <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>
1 Canada             99    79
2 France             97    79
3 Italy              95    79
4 Spain              99    79
5 Sweden             99    79
6 Switzerland        97    79


Read this as: start with lifeexp, keep these columns, move water coverage, and then sort the rows. It returns the same table as the named steps. <- saves the final result; the source stays unchanged. The function calls do the work, while the pipes pass their results onward.

5.2.1 Keep a needed column until its work is done
Compatible table structure is only part of the requirement: the next step also needs particular columns. Suppose we want country names ordered by income but do not want income in the final table. Sort while gnppc is available, then drop it:

ranked_names <- lifeexp |>
  arrange(desc(gnppc), country) |>
  select(country, lexp)
head(ranked_names)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  country        lexp
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 Switzerland      79
2 Norway           78
3 Denmark          76
4 United States    77
5 Sweden           79
6 Germany          77


The result is ordered by income, even though the final display contains only names and life expectancy. Selecting columns preserves that row order. Reversing the steps below intentionally fails:

lifeexp |>
  select(country, lexp) |>
  arrange(desc(gnppc), country)
Error in `arrange()`:
ℹ In argument: `..1 = gnppc`.
Caused by error:
! object 'gnppc' not found


The first result is still a tibble, but it no longer contains gnppc. The later sorting call cannot find its key. Restore that column to the selection, or sort before dropping it, as in the successful version. Moving operations can change whether a pipeline can run even when each step expects a table.

title: 5  Pipe
text:
5.3 Save and check results
If the result is unexpected, run only the first part and inspect it. Saving an intermediate table gives us something concrete to check:

first_step <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, lexp, safewater)
ds(first_step)

[1] "country"   "lexp"      "safewater"

nrow(first_step)

[1] 68


There should be three named columns and 68 countries. If those are correct, add the next operation. ds() returns column names as text, not another country table. The next operation must accept the object it receives.



Now suppose we want to put lexp first, but insert ds() before relocate(). The following pipeline intentionally produces an error:

lifeexp |>
  ds() |>
  relocate(lexp)
Error in `UseMethod()`:
! no applicable method for 'relocate' applied to an object of class "character"


The message says that no relocate() method applies to an object of class "character": this function cannot move columns in the text returned by ds(). To find the problem, stop before the failing call and save the result under a name. This gives us something we can inspect separately:

column_names <- lifeexp |>
  ds()
column_names

[1] "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"


The result contains the six column names as text. To check what kind of object we now have, use tidystata’s var_type(). It takes one object and returns a description of its type, without changing it:

var_type(column_names)

[1] "character"


The type is "character". These are text values, not a table with a lexp column. relocate() needs a table, so it cannot continue from this result. To move life expectancy first, use lifeexp |> relocate(lexp) without inserting ds().
We can also pipe the names directly into the type check we just used:

lifeexp |>
  ds() |>
  var_type()

[1] "character"


This returns "character" again. If our goal is instead to count the variables, keep ds() and choose a function that counts text entries. length() counts the elements of a vector; here that means the number of column names:

lifeexp |>
  ds() |>
  length()

[1] 6
