The result is 6, one entry per column name. A pipeline can continue after it leaves a tibble, provided the next function accepts the returned object. The pipe passes a result along; it does not convert that result into whatever the next function needs.
When a pipeline fails, run it up to the step before the error, save that result, and inspect it. Check both its type and its contents against what the next function requires. The intermediate objects from the table workflow are useful for exactly this purpose.






NoteRecognizing older pipes



Older tidyverse code often uses %>%, supplied by magrittr and available after loading tidyverse. For these first-argument calls, lifeexp %>% select(country, lexp) gives the same result as lifeexp |> select(country, lexp). Their advanced rules differ, so check unfamiliar code before replacing one with the other. This book uses |>.

title: 5  Pipe
section: 5.4 Optional: a table or a vector?
text:
5.4 Optional: a table or a vector?
select() keeps table structure. pull() takes a table and a column name and returns that column as a vector. Compare the same water measurements in both forms:

water_table <- select(lifeexp, safewater)
water_vector <- pull(lifeexp, safewater)
var_type(water_table)

[1] "tibble"

var_type(water_vector)

[1] "double"


The results are "tibble" and "double". Both objects contain the same 68 measurements, with the same order and missing values. Their structures differ: water_table has rows and a named column; water_vector is a sequence of values. The $ syntax is another way to extract one column: write the table name, $, and the column name. Thus lifeexp$safewater returns the same vector as pull(lifeexp, safewater). Neither changes lifeexp. This distinction matters when the next function requires a table, as in Chapter 5.

title: 5  Pipe
text:
5.5 Export the finished table
Assignment retained country_pipeline in the R session. To keep its values outside that session, we will write a file in the r4ss project folder created in Section 1.1.1. First check where R will resolve the filename. getwd() takes no input and returns the current working directory:

getwd()

The result should be the full path to your r4ss folder. If it differs, use setwd() with the full path to your own folder in quotation marks. For example, on Windows:

setwd("C:/Users/you/Documents/r4ss")

Replace that example path with the actual location of your folder before running it. Use forward slashes in R paths, including on Windows. On macOS or Linux, a full path will usually begin with /. setwd() changes this session’s working directory; it does not create a folder or move files. Run getwd() again to confirm the change. Check this whenever you start a file workflow in a new session.
A relative path, such as "country-ranked.csv", is resolved from the working directory. Here it names a file directly inside that folder. A full path identifies the location without relying on the working directory.
write_csv() takes a table and a quoted file path, and writes a comma-separated-values (CSV) file. It overwrites an existing file at that path; choose another name if you want to keep an earlier result. Run:

write_csv(country_pipeline, "country-ranked.csv")

Writing normally produces no printed table. To check whether a file exists at the path, file.exists() takes that path and returns TRUE or FALSE:

file.exists("country-ranked.csv")

Expect TRUE. If the result is FALSE, check the write error, spelling, and working directory. Existence alone does not establish that the contents are correct. read_csv() reads the file and returns a table; save that result under a new name:

saved_countries <- read_csv("country-ranked.csv")

The import message reports the detected column types. The names should be text and the two measurements numeric. Now inspect the returned table with familiar checks:

head(saved_countries)
ds(saved_countries)
nrow(saved_countries)

Expect 68 rows, with country, safewater, and lexp in that order, and the same country ordering as country_pipeline. The preview alone shows only the first six rows; the row count checks the full result. CSV preserves values, column names, and missing entries, but not the variable labels attached to the original columns. The later file lesson in Section 7.8 develops this distinction further.
The same workflow applies to your own data: import a file into a named table, inspect it, select and order the relevant columns and rows, and export the result under a new filename. Use your file’s variable names in place of the ones shown here. Keep the import and transformation commands in your script so that the saved result can be reproduced.

title: 5  Pipe
text:
5.6 Review

|> passes a result to the next function; <- saves a result under a name.
select(), relocate(), and arrange() can be connected through named steps, nested calls, or pipes to express the same procedure.
ds() and nrow() check intermediate tables; retain required columns until their operations are complete.
var_type() identifies an object’s kind and length() counts vector entries; each function must accept the preceding result.
Optional: pull() extracts a vector, while select() keeps a table.
getwd() and setwd() locate the file workflow; relative paths begin at the working directory.
write_csv() exports, file.exists() checks the path, and read_csv() imports for inspection.

Next, Chapter 6 selects rows, beginning with the same country data. The GSS survey and its one-time preparation are introduced later in Chapter 8.

title: 5  Pipe
text:
5.7 Exercises

Rewrite the income workflow from Chapter 4 as one pipeline: keep country, gnppc, and lexp, then order by descending income and country name. Save it as income_pipeline.
Inspect the column names and row count after just its selection step. Diagnose two failures: inserting ds() before arrange(), and selecting only country and lexp before sorting by gnppc. Explain how the problems differ and correct each one.
Export income_pipeline to "income-ranked.csv" in your checked project folder, check that the file exists, read it as saved_income, and inspect its first rows, column names, and total row count. What would you check if existence returned FALSE? Why does TRUE still require inspection of the contents?
Optional: A table or a vector? Run select(lifeexp, lexp) and pull(lifeexp, lexp). Use var_type() on each result. Which result keeps table structure? Which is the same kind of object as lifeexp$lexp?

title: 5  Pipe
text:
Worked answers
Run the chapter package setup first.






TipConnect the income workflow






income_pipeline <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, gnppc, lexp) |>
  arrange(desc(gnppc), country)
head(income_pipeline)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  country       gnppc  lexp
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 Switzerland   46650    79
2 Norway        36120    78
3 Denmark       33440    76
4 United States 32040    77
5 Sweden        31100    79
6 Germany       28070    77


All 68 countries remain. The last row has unavailable income; saving the result does not change lifeexp.









TipInspect an intermediate result






income_columns <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, gnppc, lexp)
ds(income_columns)

[1] "country" "gnppc"   "lexp"   

nrow(income_columns)

[1] 68


The names are country, gnppc, and lexp; the row count is 68. A name listing is character data with no country records to sort, so remove ds() from the table pipeline and inspect names separately. A table containing only country and lexp has the right structure but lacks the gnppc key. Keep that key until after sorting:

income_names <- lifeexp |>
  arrange(desc(gnppc), country) |>
  select(country, lexp)
head(income_names)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  country        lexp
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 Switzerland      79
2 Norway           78
3 Denmark          76
4 United States    77
5 Sweden           79
6 Germany          77


This returns names and life expectancy in income order. The two failures concern different requirements: object type and available columns.









TipExport and read back





Recreate income_pipeline if needed, then check your working directory. Change it using your actual project path if necessary, as taught above. These commands write a file, so choose a new filename if this one already contains work you want to retain.

income_pipeline <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, gnppc, lexp) |>
  arrange(desc(gnppc), country)
getwd()
write_csv(income_pipeline, "income-ranked.csv")
file.exists("income-ranked.csv")
saved_income <- read_csv("income-ranked.csv")
head(saved_income)
ds(saved_income)
nrow(saved_income)

Expect TRUE, the three names country, gnppc, and lexp, and 68 rows in income order. If the check returns FALSE, inspect any write error, the filename, and the working directory. A TRUE result establishes only existence; reading and inspecting the file checks whether it contains the intended table. Missing income remains missing and sorts after known values.









NoteA table or a vector?






life_table <- select(lifeexp, lexp)
life_vector <- pull(lifeexp, lexp)
var_type(life_table)

[1] "tibble"

var_type(life_vector)

[1] "double"

var_type(lifeexp$lexp)

[1] "double"


The results are "tibble", "double", and "double". select() keeps a table with the named column lexp. pull() and $ return the same numeric vector, with one entry per country. None of these operations changes lifeexp.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.1 First rows
Which observations belong in an analysis? Selecting variables keeps columns; selecting observations keeps rows. In either case, keeping some of the data also excludes the rest. Here we will distinguish selecting by a row’s current position from selecting by its recorded values.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
This chapter builds on selecting columns, sorting observations, and the pipe. We continue with the familiar country table throughout, selecting observations by their positions and recorded measurements. Comparisons and missing-value checks are introduced here as we need them. No optional programming chapter is required.
Continue with the packaged country data used in the preceding chapters. Keep the country name, region, life expectancy, income per person, and safe-water coverage:
Each row is one country. region contains the labelled region codes introduced in Chapter 3; lexp records life expectancy in years, gnppc records income per person in current US dollars, and safewater records safe-water access in percent. Most measurements refer to 1998; water coverage refers to 2000. Missing measurements remain NA. All 68 countries remain. A row position tells us where a record currently appears; the country name identifies it when the order changes.
To inspect the beginning of the records, pass the table to the familiar head(). Its default result contains the first six rows:
head(countries)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  country        region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>      <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania             1    74   870        49
2 Armenia             1    70   570        83
3 Austria             1    78 27810        97
4 Azerbaijan          1    64   510        49
5 Belarus             1    68  1540        82
6 Belgium             1    77 26530       100
The result contains six countries and the same five columns, showing the beginning of the current order. These positions do not identify typical countries. The original countries still contains all 68 rows.
head() accepts n, the number of rows to return. We can store the first three records separately:
first_three <- head(countries, n = 3)
first_three
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania          1    74   870        49
2 Armenia          1    70   570        83
3 Austria          1    78 27810        97

nrow(first_three)

[1] 3

nrow(countries)

[1] 68
first_three has three rows; countries has 68. The printing helpers in Chapter 4 display selected rows while returning the complete object. head() selects data. Later calculations on first_three would use only those three countries.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.2 Row positions
Suppose we need the fifth record in the current table. slice() selects rows by position:

countries |> slice(5)
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Belarus          1    68  1540        82

countries |> slice(1:5)
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  country        region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>      <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania             1    74   870        49
2 Armenia             1    70   570        83
3 Austria             1    78 27810        97
4 Azerbaijan          1    64   510        49
5 Belarus             1    68  1540        82

countries |> slice(-5)
# A tibble: 67 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                         1    74   870        49
 2 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 3 Austria                         1    78 27810        97
 4 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 5 Belgium                         1    77 26530       100
 6 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 7 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 8 Croatia                         1    72    NA        85
 9 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
10 Denmark                         1    76 33440        95
# ℹ 57 more rows


The first result is country Belarus, which currently occupies row 5. In the second call, 1:5 supplies the sequence of positions 1 through 5, so five records remain. The negative position in the last call excludes row 5 and keeps the other 67 countries. It does not change any recorded life expectancy. Use positive positions to keep rows or negative positions to exclude them; do not mix the two in one selection.
The c() function stored quoted column names in Section 4.1. It can also combine several numeric row positions. Their order determines the returned order:

countries |> slice(c(5, 1))
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Belarus          1    68  1540        82
2 Albania          1    74   870        49


Country Belarus appears before country Albania. Repeating a position would repeat its row. This flexibility is useful, but a position is not a permanent identity. For example, sorting by life expectancy before selecting position 1 changes the result:

countries |>
  arrange(lexp) |>
  slice(1)
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Haiti            2    57   410        NA


The result is the first country among those tied at the lowest recorded life expectancy. Without another sorting key, a tie retains the previous row order. All columns moved together during sorting. To select a particular country regardless of order, use a condition on the country name, following the equality examples below.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.3 Conditions

6.3.1 Read a condition
A comparison asks whether a condition holds. Store a number to use in the following comparisons:

x <- 8

Is x at least 5, greater than 8, or equal to 8?

x >= 5

[1] TRUE

x > 8

[1] FALSE

x == 8

[1] TRUE


The results are TRUE, FALSE, and TRUE. These answers are logical values: var_type(TRUE) returns "logical". Write TRUE and FALSE in full without quotation marks; "TRUE" is text.
Table 6.1 collects all six comparison operators using x <- 8.




Table 6.1: Comparison operators with x equal to 8.





Operator
Question
Example
Result




<
Less than?
x < 8
FALSE


<=
Less than or equal to?
x <= 8
TRUE


>
Greater than?
x > 8
FALSE


>=
Greater than or equal to?
x >= 8
TRUE


==
Equal to?
x == 8
TRUE


!=
Different from?
x != 8
FALSE







The two equals signs in == ask about equality. They neither assign a value nor name an argument. Text comparisons are case-sensitive:

text <- "hello"
text == "hello"

[1] TRUE

text == "Hello"

[1] FALSE


Only the first comparison is TRUE. The capital letter changes the string.


6.3.2 Combine simple conditions
To check whether x falls between 5 and 10, inclusive, combine two conditions with &, meaning and:

(x >= 5) & (x <= 10)

[1] TRUE


Both comparisons hold for 8, so the result is TRUE. Parentheses separate the two comparisons. Use |, a vertical bar, for or:

(x == 2) | (x == 8)

[1] TRUE


This is TRUE because the second comparison holds. This is inclusive “or”: at least one condition must hold; both may hold when the conditions allow it.
%in% asks whether a value matches any member of a collection:

x %in% c(2, 8)

[1] TRUE


c() combines these two numbers into a vector, preserving their order. Commas separate the inputs. The membership condition gives the same TRUE result as the preceding example. The ! operator means not:

!(x %in% c(2, 8))

[1] FALSE


The parentheses group the membership test. Its result was true, so negating it returns FALSE. A single function call can also follow ! directly, as in !is.na() later.


6.3.3 One comparison per value
Compare two numbers with the same threshold:

c(2, 8) >= 5

[1] FALSE  TRUE


R returns FALSE and TRUE, in that order. It compares each value with 5. This is an elementwise operation: one result for each input, in the same position. Table columns work on this principle, which lets filter() decide whether to retain each row.


6.3.4 Apply conditions to rows
We now apply these comparisons to countries. Positions describe where rows are; conditions describe which recorded values meet our question. filter() takes a table and retains the rows for which a condition is TRUE. Inside it, a column name refers to the whole column. We do not need to write countries$gnppc.
< means less than. The comparison returns TRUE when a recorded income meets the rule, FALSE when it does not, and NA when income is unknown. Which countries have recorded income per person below $10,000?

countries |>
  filter(gnppc < 10000)
# A tibble: 48 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                         1    74   870        49
 2 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 3 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 4 Belarus                         1    68  1540        82
 5 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 6 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 7 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 8 Estonia                         1    69  3820        92
 9 Georgia                         1    70   870        59
10 Hungary                         1    71  4420        83
# ℹ 38 more rows


The result contains 48 countries, with their original columns and values. The comparison applies to each income. The 1 country with unknown income does not appear: an unknown income is not known to be below $10,000.
For a country name, use == to test equality and quote it exactly as recorded:

countries |>
  filter(country == "Canada")
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Canada           2    79 20900        99

countries |> filter(gnppc == 870)
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania          1    74   870        49
2 Georgia          1    70   870        59


The first result locates Canada independently of its row position. The second finds countries with recorded income per person of $870. That measurement is numeric, so its value is unquoted. Two countries share this value; income is not a country identifier. Text comparisons are case-sensitive: "Canada" differs from "canada". These calls return selected tables; neither changes countries.


6.3.5 Combining conditions
To retain countries with life expectancy from 70 through 75 years inclusive, both bounds must hold. Use & for and. >= means greater than or equal to, and <= means less than or equal to:

countries |>
  filter((lexp >= 70) & (lexp <= 75))
# A tibble: 28 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                         1    74   870        49
 2 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 3 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 4 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 5 Croatia                         1    72    NA        85
 6 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 7 Georgia                         1    70   870        59
 8 Hungary                         1    71  4420        83
 9 Lithuania                       1    71  2870        70
10 North Macedonia                 1    72  2010        80
# ℹ 18 more rows

countries |>
  filter(lexp >= 70, lexp <= 75)
# A tibble: 28 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania                         1    74   870        49
 2 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 3 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 4 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 5 Croatia                         1    72    NA        85
 6 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 7 Georgia                         1    70   870        59
 8 Hungary                         1    71  4420        83
 9 Lithuania                       1    71  2870        70
10 North Macedonia                 1    72  2010        80
# ℹ 18 more rows


Both commands retain 28 countries. In filter(), separate conditions divided by commas also mean that all must hold. The parentheses in the first version make the two comparisons clear. If a required measurement were unknown, the row would be excluded unless the combined condition could still be known to be true.
Use | for inclusive or. To keep Poland or countries with safe-water coverage of at least 95 percent:

countries |>
  filter((country == "Poland") | (safewater >= 95))
# A tibble: 16 × 5
   country            region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>          <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Austria                 1    78 27810        97
 2 Belgium                 1    77 26530       100
 3 Czechia                 1    75  6140        95
 4 Denmark                 1    76 33440        95
 5 France                  1    79 25740        97
 6 Germany                 1    77 28070       100
 7 Greece                  1    78 13540        99
 8 Italy                   1    79 22270        95
 9 Netherlands             1    78 27840       100
10 Norway                  1    78 36120       100
11 Poland                  1    73  4390        NA
12 Spain                   1    79 15410        99
13 Sweden                  1    79 31100        99
14 Switzerland             1    79 46650        97
15 United Kingdom          1    77 27040       100
16 Canada                  2    79 20900        99


A country qualifies if either condition is true. Poland is retained because its name meets the first condition, even though its water coverage is unknown. Cuba, whose water coverage is also unknown, does not qualify: one condition is false and the other is unknown. The vertical bar | combines conditions; the pipe |> passes a result to another function. They serve different purposes.
When several exact values are acceptable, %in% asks whether each value matches one of the supplied alternatives. c() combines those alternatives, with commas between them:

countries |>
  filter(country %in% c("Canada", "Albania", "Armenia"))
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania          1    74   870        49
2 Armenia          1    70   570        83
3 Canada           2    79 20900        99

countries |>
  filter(gnppc %in% c(960, 870))
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  country      region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>    <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania           1    74   870        49
2 Georgia           1    70   870        59
3 Honduras          2    62   960        42
4 Bolivia           3    61   960        NA


The first result contains those three countries in their original row order. Unlike slice(c(5, 1)), the order of alternatives inside c() does not rearrange the rows. The second selects four countries whose recorded income is exactly $960 or $870, again retaining their original order. Membership can test text or numerical values. Use & and | for column conditions; the similar-looking && and || are intended for single logical decisions rather than these elementwise comparisons.
A condition can run without an error and still select the wrong countries. Suppose we want the same recorded incomes, $960 or $870, but omit the second comparison. Compare the row counts:

income_alternatives_wrong <- countries |>
  filter(gnppc == 960 | 870)
income_alternatives_checked <- countries |>
  filter(gnppc %in% c(960, 870))
nrow(income_alternatives_wrong)

[1] 68

nrow(income_alternatives_checked)

[1] 4


The first result keeps all 68 countries; the second keeps 4. In the first condition, R interprets the bare nonzero number 870 as TRUE. The OR therefore succeeds for every row, even Croatia’s unknown income. Write a complete comparison on both sides, gnppc == 960 | gnppc == 870, or use the membership test shown above. Check whether the selected records answer the question, rather than treating the absence of an error as evidence that the condition is correct.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.4 Unknown conditions
filter() keeps only TRUE. It excludes both FALSE and NA, but those conditions convey different information. To examine a column outside a table operation, write the table name, $, and the column name. countries$gnppc returns the income vector in the same country order, including missing values. It neither removes the column nor changes countries. This extraction is useful even if you skipped the optional extraction example in Chapter 5.
We can see the distinction before selecting:

(countries$gnppc >= 10000) |>
  head()

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE


The comparison creates one logical result per country; head() selects the first six results for inspection. Known incomes at least $10,000 return TRUE, lower incomes return FALSE, and unknown incomes return NA. Croatia, farther down the table, has the missing income measurement.
is.na() takes values and returns one logical result per input: TRUE for an unavailable value and FALSE otherwise. First follow it on plain inputs:

is.na(c(870, NA, 960))

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE


Only the second result is TRUE. The function tests whether a value is missing; comparing with == NA would ask for equality with an unknown value and would itself be unknown. We can use this test alone to find the country whose income is unavailable:

countries |>
  filter(is.na(gnppc))
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Croatia          1    72    NA        85


The result contains Croatia and its other recorded measurements. We have selected the missing record without assigning an income to it. To keep countries with income of at least $10,000 and also retain unknown incomes for inspection, state both possibilities:

high_or_unknown <- countries |>
  filter((gnppc >= 10000) | is.na(gnppc))
high_or_unknown
# A tibble: 20 × 5
   country            region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>          <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Austria                 1    78 27810        97
 2 Belgium                 1    77 26530       100
 3 Croatia                 1    72    NA        85
 4 Denmark                 1    76 33440        95
 5 Finland                 1    77 25810        94
 6 France                  1    79 25740        97
 7 Germany                 1    77 28070       100
 8 Greece                  1    78 13540        99
 9 Ireland                 1    76 21430        75
10 Italy                   1    79 22270        95
11 Netherlands             1    78 27840       100
12 Norway                  1    78 36120       100
13 Portugal                1    76 12190        94
14 Slovenia                1    75 10970        92
15 Spain                   1    79 15410        99
16 Sweden                  1    79 31100        99
17 Switzerland             1    79 46650        97
18 United Kingdom          1    77 27040       100
19 Canada                  2    79 20900        99
20 United States           2    77 32040        NA


This result retains countries with recorded income of at least $10,000, together with Croatia, whose income is unknown. It is a table of high or unknown incomes, not a table in which every country is known to have high income. To retain only known incomes, filter(!is.na(gnppc)) explicitly excludes missing measurements.
Use != for not equal to. To negate membership, put ! before the parenthesized %in% test. ! reverses true and false, but an unknown comparison stays unknown:

countries |>
  filter(gnppc != 870)
# A tibble: 65 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 2 Austria                         1    78 27810        97
 3 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 4 Belarus                         1    68  1540        82
 5 Belgium                         1    77 26530       100
 6 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 7 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 8 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 9 Denmark                         1    76 33440        95
10 Estonia                         1    69  3820        92
# ℹ 55 more rows

countries |>
  filter(!(gnppc %in% 870))
# A tibble: 66 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 2 Austria                         1    78 27810        97
 3 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 4 Belarus                         1    68  1540        82
 5 Belgium                         1    77 26530       100
 6 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 7 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 8 Croatia                         1    72    NA        85
 9 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
10 Denmark                         1    76 33440        95
# ℹ 56 more rows


The first result contains countries with a known income other than $870. It excludes Croatia’s missing measurement. The second also keeps Croatia: %in% returns FALSE for NA when the alternatives contain only 870, and negation makes that result TRUE. Neither operation has discovered Croatia’s income.
If the intended rule is “known income other than $870,” make the missingness decision explicit:

countries |>
  filter(!is.na(gnppc), !(gnppc %in% 870))
# A tibble: 65 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 2 Austria                         1    78 27810        97
 3 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 4 Belarus                         1    68  1540        82
 5 Belgium                         1    77 26530       100
 6 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 7 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 8 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 9 Denmark                         1    76 33440        95
10 Estonia                         1    69  3820        92
# ℹ 55 more rows


Only countries with a recorded income other than $870 remain. Selecting an analysis subset therefore requires more than a convenient expression: we need to decide how unknown measurements affect inclusion.
For the next abstract checks, set x <- NA; c() combines the stated alternatives.

x <- NA

%in% tests membership and never returns NA. Compare:

x == 2

[1] NA

x %in% c(2, 6)

[1] FALSE


The comparison returns NA; the membership test returns FALSE because the stored value NA does not match either alternative. This does not establish what the missing number would have been.
Sometimes the known part of a combined condition settles the result even when another part is missing:

FALSE & NA

[1] FALSE

TRUE | NA

[1] TRUE


The first is FALSE: both parts cannot be true if one is already false. The second is TRUE: at least one part is true regardless of the unknown part. An expression containing NA can therefore have a known result.
In the next chapter, Section 7.3, na.rm = TRUE asks summary functions to omit missing inputs from a calculation. It does not fill in missing values or delete them from the original object.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.5 A country analysis subset
Suppose our next analysis will compare income and water coverage among countries with life expectancy of at least 75 years. Life expectancy alone defines this subset; we are not yet requiring reported income or water coverage.
Use a condition, then the familiar select() to keep the country identifier and measurements needed for this question. Assign the result a new name:

high_lifeexp <- countries |>
  filter(lexp >= 75) |>
  select(country, lexp, gnppc, safewater)

head(high_lifeexp)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  country  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Austria    78 27810        97
2 Belgium    77 26530       100
3 Czechia    75  6140        95
4 Denmark    76 33440        95
5 Finland    77 25810        94
6 France     79 25740        97

nrow(countries)

[1] 68

nrow(high_lifeexp)

[1] 23


The original has 68 countries; high_lifeexp contains 23. Each retained row has life expectancy of at least 75 years. Missing water measurements remain, and head() displays only the first six rows. The rule defines the countries available for the proposed comparison; it does not require a measurement for every variable or establish why life expectancy differs. The original countries is unchanged.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.6 Optional selection tools
The following tools are useful for particular tasks. They are not prerequisites for the exercises.

6.6.1 Display or select rows?
The printing helpers discussed in Chapter 4 and later in Section 8.1.1 display rows from both ends or at intervals while returning the full table unchanged. They do not select a smaller dataset. Use the slice() positions taught above when you need to retain particular rows for a later calculation. Evenly spaced display positions are not a probability sample.


6.6.2 A random subset
slice_sample() is a variant of slice() for selecting rows at random rather than by stated positions. Here n = 3 requests three different records: sampling is without replacement by default. It returns the selected rows with all original columns; assignment keeps that subset separately.
For a reproducible illustration, first use set.seed() to set the random-number generator’s starting state. Its numeric argument is a chosen starting value, not a requested country or sample size:

set.seed(2026)

Now select the records:

random_three <- countries |>
  slice_sample(n = 3)
random_three
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  country        region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>      <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Tajikistan          1    62   170        36
2 Canada              2    79 20900        99
3 Sweden              1    79 31100        99


The output has three rows and the original five columns. Rerunning the seed command followed by the selection in the same software environment reproduces it. It is a random subset of the countries in this table. Randomly selecting records from a dataset does not by itself make them representative of a wider population.


6.6.3 Distinct values and records
distinct() returns non-repeated combinations of the columns supplied. With just region, it returns the three observed region codes:

countries |>
  distinct(region)
# A tibble: 3 × 1
      region
  <hvn_lbll>
1          1
2          2
3          3


The result has one column and one row for each observed region code. Its rows describe distinct recorded values, not distinct countries. If the supplied column contained missing values, one missing value would also remain.
Two different countries can have the same life expectancy and region. We can inspect the combinations without treating them as duplicate countries:

combinations <- countries |>
  select(lexp, region)
combinations |>
  distinct()
# A tibble: 38 × 2
    lexp     region
   <dbl> <hvn_lbll>
 1    74          1
 2    70          1
 3    78          1
 4    64          1
 5    68          1
 6    77          1
 7    71          1
 8    72          1
 9    75          1
10    76          1
# ℹ 28 more rows

countries |>
  distinct(lexp, region, .keep_all = TRUE)
# A tibble: 38 × 5
   country        region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>      <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Albania             1    74   870        49
 2 Armenia             1    70   570        83
 3 Austria             1    78 27810        97
 4 Azerbaijan          1    64   510        49
 5 Belarus             1    68  1540        82
 6 Belgium             1    77 26530       100
 7 Bulgaria            1    71  1440        90
 8 Croatia             1    72    NA        85
 9 Czechia             1    75  6140        95
10 Denmark             1    76 33440        95
# ℹ 28 more rows


With no columns specified, distinct() compares all columns in combinations. It returns one row per different life-expectancy–region combination, treating repeated missing values as the same value for this purpose. The second command also keeps one row per combination, but .keep_all = TRUE retains the country name, income, and water coverage. Those values belong to the first country encountered with each combination; they do not describe every country sharing it.
These commands discard repeated combinations for a particular inspection task; they do not establish that a country was entered twice. Selecting by country name would answer a different question. Repeated country names can be legitimate in data observed across years, so investigate the observation unit before removing records.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.7 Review

head() returns the first rows; slice() selects rows by their current positions.
filter() retains rows whose conditions are TRUE, excluding both FALSE and NA conditions.
& requires both conditions, | requires either, %in% tests membership, and ! negates a result.
is.na() identifies unknown values; decide explicitly whether they should remain, especially when negating membership.
nrow() checks how many observations remain; assign the subset separately to preserve the source.
Optional: slice_sample() selects random rows, set.seed() makes that selection reproducible in the same environment, and distinct() returns unique values or combinations.

The next part begins with Chapter 7. We continue with the country table and use the selection skills learned here to inspect and describe its contents.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
6.8 Exercises

Keep country, region, lexp, gnppc, and safewater from lifeexp as countries. Select positions 5 and 1, in that order, then repeat after sorting by life expectancy and country name. Explain why the countries can change while their measurements remain correctly aligned.
First set x <- 4. Test whether it lies between 5 and 10, inclusive, and whether it belongs to c(2, 4, 6). Set x <- NA and repeat the interval test. Explain all three answers. Then keep countries with life expectancy from 70 through 75 years inclusive and income per person below $5,000. Report how many remain. Explain why Croatia is excluded and whether that establishes its income.
Compare filter(gnppc != 870) with filter(!(gnppc %in% 870)). Count the additional countries retained by the second rule. Write a rule requiring known income other than $870.
Using lifeexp, create long_lived containing country, lexp, and safewater for countries with life expectancy of at least 75 years. Report its row count and explain whether missing water measurements have been removed. Check that the original row count is unchanged.

title: 6  Select observations
text:
Worked answers






NotePositions and order





Each answer can start in a fresh session with the packaged country data:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
countries <- select(lifeexp, country, region, lexp, gnppc, safewater)
countries |> slice(c(5, 1))
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  country     region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>   <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Belarus          1    68  1540        82
2 Albania          1    74   870        49

countries |>
  arrange(lexp, country) |>
  slice(c(5, 1))
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  country        region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>      <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Kazakhstan          1    63  1340        63
2 Haiti               2    57   410        NA


The first result contains the countries at the fifth and first positions in the original table. Sorting moves whole records, so the second draws from the low end of the life-expectancy distribution. Country name resolves tied life expectancies explicitly. Row positions change; a country’s measurements move together.









NoteConditions and two requirements






x <- 4
(x >= 5) & (x <= 10)

[1] FALSE

x %in% c(2, 4, 6)

[1] TRUE

x <- NA
(x >= 5) & (x <= 10)

[1] NA


The first is FALSE because 4 is below 5. Membership is TRUE because 4 is one of the alternatives. The last condition is NA: we cannot place an unknown value inside or outside the interval.
Now apply the conditions to the country records:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
selected_countries <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, region, lexp, gnppc, safewater) |>
  filter(lexp >= 70, lexp <= 75, gnppc < 5000)
head(selected_countries)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
  <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Albania                         1    74   870        49
2 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
3 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
4 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
5 Georgia                         1    70   870        59
6 Hungary                         1    71  4420        83

nrow(selected_countries)

[1] 21


The result contains 21 countries. All three comparisons must be true. Croatia’s life expectancy is in the requested range, but its income is unknown, so the combined condition is unknown and the country is excluded. That does not establish whether its income is below or above $5,000.









NoteNegating an unknown value






library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
countries <- select(lifeexp, country, region, lexp, gnppc, safewater)
comparison <- countries |>
  filter(gnppc != 870)
membership <- countries |>
  filter(!(gnppc %in% 870))
nrow(membership) - nrow(comparison)

[1] 1

countries |>
  filter(!is.na(gnppc), !(gnppc %in% 870))
# A tibble: 65 × 5
   country                    region  lexp gnppc safewater
   <chr>                  <hvn_lbll> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 Armenia                         1    70   570        83
 2 Austria                         1    78 27810        97
 3 Azerbaijan                      1    64   510        49
 4 Belarus                         1    68  1540        82
 5 Belgium                         1    77 26530       100
 6 Bosnia and Herzegovina          1    74  1230        87
 7 Bulgaria                        1    71  1440        90
 8 Czechia                         1    75  6140        95
 9 Denmark                         1    76 33440        95
10 Estonia                         1    69  3820        92
# ℹ 55 more rows


The difference is 1, exactly the number of missing income measurements. The inequality comparison is unknown for Croatia; membership against the supplied value is false, so negating membership retains it. The final rule explicitly excludes unknown incomes.









NoteCountries with longer life expectancy






library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
original_rows <- nrow(lifeexp)
long_lived <- lifeexp |>
  filter(lexp >= 75) |>
  select(country, lexp, safewater)
nrow(long_lived)

[1] 23

nrow(lifeexp) == original_rows

[1] TRUE


The subset contains 23 countries with life expectancy of at least 75 years. The final check is TRUE: the original still has 68 rows. Missing safewater values remain because no condition required known water coverage. The result describes these countries at the recorded dates; it does not show change over time.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.1 Preview the table
Which countries are in our data, and what can their measurements tell us? We have selected columns and rows from the country table. Now we return to it for a closer look at individual records, variable descriptions, and missing measurements, using the same data supplied by tidystata.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to preview and browse a table, read a first numerical summary, find variable names and descriptions, check available measurements, and download, import, and save a data file. Begin with the package-loading commands from Section 1.2; for the file examples, reopen the project folder from Section 1.1.1.
Chapter 2 introduced tibbles and their printed previews. Here we inspect what the country table contains and what its measurements mean.
Load the packages in your current session. We will use lifeexp, a dataset included with tidystata. No download, file import, or survey preparation is needed.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
library() makes a package available in this session. Run these package-loading lines again after restarting R.
Start with the printing method from Chapter 2. A short preview lets us check column names and see a few actual records. It does not tell us the distribution of values across the full dataset.
Typing the table name prints it in the console without opening a viewer or assigning a new object:
lifeexp
# A tibble: 68 × 6
       region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
   <hvn_lbll> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1          1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2          1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 3          1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 4          1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 5          1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 6          1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 7          1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
 8          1 Bulgaria                    -0.7    71  1440        90
 9          1 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10          1 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows
A tibble prints only the rows and columns that fit, but its header reports the full dimensions: 68 rows and six columns here. The far-left numbers give row positions. The omitted records remain stored in lifeexp.
nrow() counts rows and ncol() counts columns in the complete table:
nrow(lifeexp)

[1] 68

ncol(lifeexp)

[1] 6
The counts are still 68 rows and six columns, even though the console displays only a preview. Type cues such as <chr> for text and <dbl> for numbers help read the display. There is no need to memorize a catalogue of R types before working with these columns.
A narrow console may also omit columns from a tibble printout. The footer lists columns that did not fit; they remain stored in the table. The viewer introduced next lets us inspect these columns and the rows beyond the preview. Printed values may also be shortened or rounded to fit the display. A preview does not select a smaller dataset or make its countries representative of the whole table.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.2 Browse the table
The printed preview gives us a first look. To examine individual values throughout the full dataset, we can open a data viewer. If you have used a spreadsheet, this offers a familiar way to inspect a table. You can scroll down through rows and across columns to examine individual cells. The viewer lets you inspect the data without editing the stored values.
Tidystata’s browse() opens a table in the data viewer supplied by your editor. Supply the table name inside the parentheses. The command opens the complete dataset without changing it or assigning a new object. Run it in your editor:

browse(lifeexp)

Figure 7.1 illustrates the table view opened by browse(lifeexp). The window and controls may differ between editors. Nine rows are shown in this schematic view; the full table still contains 68 countries and six variables. The far-left number is the row position, while country identifies the observation. Missing measurements appear as NA, meaning unavailable rather than zero, and region retains its attached value labels. Scroll to inspect countries beyond those visible at the top; all 68 remain available.






Figure 7.1: Illustration of the table view opened by browse(lifeexp).



As Chapter 2 explained, a tibble keeps columns together in a table. Here, each row keeps the values belonging to one country together. The table contains 68 countries and six variables. The country column identifies the countries.
The data contain historical World Bank indicators. lexp is life expectancy at birth in years; popgrowth is annual population growth in percent; gnppc is GNI per capita in current US dollars, Atlas method. These refer to 1998. safewater is the percentage using safely managed drinking water services in 2000. The dataset does not cover every country in the world. The dataset notes document its source and units.
To read the rows and columns more closely, Table 7.1 presents a smaller view of the same data. It shows the first five countries in lifeexp and three of its variables. The headings give each variable’s meaning and the short name that R uses. For now, focus on how the information fits together.





Table 7.1: A preview of lifeexp. The complete dataset contains 68 countries and six variables.











Country (country)
Life expectancy in years (lexp)
Safe water, percent (safewater)




Albania
74
49


Armenia
70
83


Austria
78
97


Azerbaijan
64
49


Belarus
68
82









Read the first row from left to right. Albania has a recorded life expectancy of 74 years and safe-water access of 49 percent. These values belong together because they describe the same country. Now read down the life-expectancy column: each number measures the same attribute for a different country.
This gives us three useful terms:

An observation is the unit described by a row. Here, one observation is one country.
A variable is an attribute recorded in a column, such as country name or life expectancy.
A value is one entry in the table, such as Albania’s life expectancy of 74 years.

When each observation has its own row, each variable has its own column, and each cell contains one value, we call the arrangement tidy data. Table 7.1 follows that arrangement: reading across keeps one country’s information together; reading down lets us compare the same variable across countries.
A column is a sequence of values, called a vector. A country-name column contains text; a life-expectancy column contains numbers. Columns in the same table have the same number of entries, so their positions keep each country’s measurements together. We can use these tables without first learning every other structure R supports.
A tibble is a storage format; tidy data describe the arrangement of information. Converting an object to a tibble does not by itself make its organization appropriate for a research question.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.3 From records to summaries
Browsing helps us inspect individual observations. We can find a country and read its measurements across a row. But with thousands of rows, we could scroll to row 1,000 and still struggle to describe a column as a whole. Summary statistics give compact numerical descriptions of recorded values, such as their average and their minimum and maximum.

7.3.1 Follow a mean and a standard deviation
Before reading a summary table, we can follow its two central calculations on short abstract inputs. c() combines values in their written order. These numbers are a syntax demonstration, with no claim about respondents or countries:

x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)

mean() takes a numeric vector and returns its arithmetic mean: add the values and divide by their number. It returns one value without changing the input:

mean(x)

[1] 6


The result is 6: the five values add to 30, and 30 divided by 5 is 6. An average can describe the center without being an observed value.
The standard deviation, calculated by sd(), describes spread around that mean. It takes a numeric vector and returns one value in the input’s units:

sd(x)

[1] 3.162278


The result is about 3.16. Standard deviation uses squared distances from the mean, divides their sum by the number of values minus one, and takes the square root. It is neither the largest minus the smallest value nor a guarantee that every value lies within one standard deviation of the mean.
Compare the same five values with a second, more concentrated vector:

y <- c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
mean(x)

[1] 6

mean(y)

[1] 6

sd(x)

[1] 3.162278

sd(y)

[1] 1.581139


Both means are 6, but the values in y lie closer to that center. Its standard deviation is about 1.58, compared with 3.16 for x. The mean and standard deviation answer different questions about the same values.


7.3.2 Missing inputs to a calculation
An unavailable input changes what can be calculated. Store a short vector containing a missing value, then calculate its mean:

with_missing <- c(2, 4, NA, 8, 10)
mean(with_missing)

[1] NA


The result is NA: by default, an unknown input makes the mean unknown. The named argument na.rm = TRUE asks mean() to exclude missing inputs from this calculation:

mean(with_missing, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 6


The four recorded values add to 24, so their mean is 6. This is the mean of the available values; it does not establish what the omitted value would have been. The saved vector still contains five entries, including NA.
sd() also returns NA by default when an input is missing. Give it the same exclusion instruction separately:

sd(with_missing)

[1] NA

sd(with_missing, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 3.651484


The second result describes spread among the four recorded values. Exclusion belongs to this call: setting na.rm for mean() does not set it for sd() or for later calls. Neither operation fills in missing data or deletes rows from a table.


7.3.3 Apply the calculations to countries
Recall $ from Section 6.4: the table name on the left and column name on the right extract that column. What is average life expectancy across these countries, in years?

mean(lifeexp$lexp)

[1] 71.66176


All 68 countries have a recorded life expectancy, so all contribute equally to the average of about 71.7 years. A country with a larger population has no extra influence in this calculation. It is a country average, not a population-weighted average across people.
Water coverage has missing measurements. Compare the default mean with the explicit available-measurement calculation, then count the countries that contribute:

mean(lifeexp$safewater)

[1] NA

mean(lifeexp$safewater, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 77.16667

lifeexp |>
  filter(!is.na(safewater)) |>
  nrow()

[1] 54


The first mean is NA; the second is about 77.2 percent across the 54 countries with measurements. The filtered table is used only for the count; lifeexp retains all 68 countries and its missing values. The average alone does not tell us why 14 water measurements are unavailable.


7.3.4 Read a summary table
For a first look, summ() from tidystata takes a table followed by the numeric columns to summarize. Here we request life expectancy and safe-water access, writing the column names without quotation marks:

summ(lifeexp, lexp, safewater)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name      type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr>     <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 lexp      dbl      68     20    57  71.7  5.16    79
2 safewater dbl      54     32    36  77.2 20.6    100


Each output row describes one variable, rather than one country. name identifies the variable and type describes its storage type (dbl means numeric here). n counts non-missing values; unique counts distinct non-missing values. min and max are the smallest and largest values, mean is the arithmetic mean, and sd is the standard deviation just demonstrated. Both retain the measurement’s units. Unlike the default mean() and sd() calls, summ() excludes missing values automatically and reports the contributing count in n.
Life expectancy averages about 71.7 years across the 68 countries, with recorded values from 57 to 79 years. Its standard deviation is about 5.2 years. Safe-water coverage averages about 77.2 percent among the 54 countries with measurements; its standard deviation is about 20.6 percentage points. Fourteen countries lack that measurement. These describe the countries with recorded values in this dataset, not every country in the world.
The calculations use all non-missing values in each requested column, not just the rows visible in the viewer. The result is a new summary table; lifeexp is unchanged. We return to the choice and interpretation of statistics in Chapter 9.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.4 Inspect names and labels



Recall ds() from Section 3.2. It lists the exact column names that we can use in code:

ds(lifeexp)

[1] "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"


The names are useful for writing commands, but abbreviations can be hard to interpret. Tidystata’s variables() takes the table and returns a list of its column names with variable labels where available. Each row of this result describes one variable:

variables(lifeexp)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  name      label                   
  <chr>     <chr>                   
1 region    Region                  
2 country   Country                 
3 popgrowth Avg. annual % growth    
4 lexp      Life expectancy at birth
5 gnppc     GNP per capita          
6 safewater Safe water              


The name column contains the names used in code; label contains their descriptions. For example, lexp is paired with “Life expectancy at birth”. Neither entry is an individual country’s value. variables() leaves all country records unchanged. Labels help us identify a measure; the dataset notes supply its source and units.
Variable labels describe columns. Value labels attach meanings to recorded codes, such as region names attached to numeric codes. The <hvn_lbll> cue marks this metadata in region; numeric storage does not make its categories quantities to average.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.5 Inspect values and missingness



codebook() reports names, labels, types, observed counts (n), and counts of distinct observed values (unique). Additional column names limit its report:

codebook(lifeexp, lexp, safewater)
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  variable  label                    type       n unique
  <chr>     <chr>                    <chr>  <int>  <int>
1 lexp      Life expectancy at birth double    68     20
2 safewater Safe water               double    54     32


Life expectancy has 68 observed values and 20 distinct observed values; water coverage has 54. The remaining 14 water measurements are missing. An observed count tells us how much information is recorded, not whether the measurements are correct or why others are unavailable. The region codes describe categories, not quantities to average. Always connect the printed values to their definitions.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.6 Inspect and sort a view
We can focus the view on a few variables. Bare column names after the table specify columns in the supplied order. Here country identifies the country, lexp gives life expectancy in years, and safewater gives the water percentage:

browse(lifeexp, country, lexp, safewater)

Figure 7.2 displays three columns from the same 68-country table. The illustration shows the same nine rows as the full-table view. Choosing columns does not choose observations. Both calls leave lifeexp unchanged. This recalls the column selection learned in Chapter 3.






Figure 7.2: Illustration of browse(lifeexp, country, lexp, safewater): the same observations with three selected variables.



Return to the full-table view from browse(lifeexp). Use your viewer’s sorting control to order lexp from highest to lowest. The control’s name and location depend on your editor. Figure 7.3 shows the descending sort; the downward arrow beside lexp marks its direction. Across the complete dataset, life expectancy runs from 79 down to 57 years. All six variables move together with their countries; sorting does not attach one country’s water measurement to another country.






Figure 7.3: The view opened by browse(lifeexp), after sorting by descending life expectancy in the viewer.



Sorting within the viewer changes its display, not the stored order of lifeexp. Chapter 4 shows how to create and retain a reordered table in code.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
section: 7.7 Download and open a data file
text:
7.7 Download and open a data file
Your own survey will usually arrive as a file, rather than a dataset supplied by an R package. Downloading saves a file on your computer. Importing reads that file into an object in the current R session. We will use a second life-expectancy dataset to practice both steps.
Our World in Data’s life-expectancy page presents estimates in years, compiled from historical sources and the United Nations World Population Prospects. Read the source description before downloading: these are period life-expectancy estimates, which summarize mortality conditions in a particular year, rather than the eventual lifespans of people born that year.

7.7.1 Download the CSV
A CSV is a plain-text table: the first line usually contains column names, and commas separate the fields. For this lesson:

Open your r4ss project folder from Section 1.1.1. Inside it, create a folder named examples using your file manager.
Open the CSV download. Your browser may download it or display its text; if it displays text, use Save As to save the file. Keep the .csv extension.
Move the downloaded file into examples and name it life-expectancy.csv. Downloading to your browser’s Downloads folder does not put the file in your project.

The online data can change. To reproduce this edition exactly, use the book’s saved CSV, downloaded on 29 October 2026, and save it in the same location. Both links supply data from Our World in Data; the book copy preserves the downloaded file without changing its values. Source notes record the attribution and the saved version.
Check the working directory and file location before importing. getwd() reports the folder from which R resolves relative paths. file.exists() takes a path in quotation marks and returns TRUE when it finds that file. First inspect your location, then check the input:

getwd()

Use that location to interpret the relative path:

file.exists("examples/life-expectancy.csv")

The first result should be your r4ss folder; the second should be TRUE. If it is FALSE, check the folder and exact filename, including a possible extra .txt extension or a suffix such as (1). In an R path, use forward slashes even on Windows. The path starts in the working directory, enters examples, and identifies the file.


7.7.2 Read and inspect the table
read_csv(), loaded with tidyverse, reads a comma-separated file and returns a tibble. Its first argument is the path in quotation marks. Assignment stores that tibble as life_expectancy:

life_expectancy <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

life_expectancy
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
   Entity      Code   Year `Life expectancy`
   <chr>       <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan AFG    1950              28.2
 2 Afghanistan AFG    1951              28.6
 3 Afghanistan AFG    1952              29.0
 4 Afghanistan AFG    1953              29.5
 5 Afghanistan AFG    1954              29.7
 6 Afghanistan AFG    1955              30.4
 7 Afghanistan AFG    1956              30.8
 8 Afghanistan AFG    1957              31.3
 9 Afghanistan AFG    1958              31.8
10 Afghanistan AFG    1959              32.3
# ℹ 21,555 more rows

nrow(life_expectancy)

[1] 21565

ncol(life_expectancy)

[1] 4


The import message reports the dimensions and inferred column types; it is not an error. In the saved file, the table has 21565 rows and 4 columns. Entity identifies a country, territory, or aggregate region; Code contains a geographic code where supplied; Year identifies the year; and Life expectancy is measured in years. A row represents one place in one year. The first displayed rows describe Afghanistan in successive years; they are not different countries in every row.
Reuse the inspection tools from this chapter:

ds(life_expectancy)

[1] "Entity"          "Code"            "Year"            "Life expectancy"


Check that place names and codes were read as text, and years and life expectancy as numbers. Blank codes can appear as NA; this does not by itself mean that the life-expectancy measurement is missing. If R reports parsing problems, investigate them before analysis. The file-reading checks in Section 18.3 show how to inspect parsing problems, identify the affected entries, and check their intended types before continuing. A successful import establishes that R could read the file, not that every value is appropriate for your question.
life_expectancy is separate from the package’s lifeexp: it has different sources, years, and rows. Importing it does not replace lifeexp, and the country examples in this chapter continue to use lifeexp. The next chapter introduces GSS for a continuous sequence of survey lessons. You can inspect your own imported table in the same way, using its actual column names and documentation.
For your own data, choose a reader that matches the file format. Chapter 18 develops Stata, SPSS, and other formats, including the treatment of labels and missing-value codes.


7.7.3 Preview clustered rows
Does the beginning of this file show the range of places it contains? Nearby rows describe successive years for the same place. A short run of rows can therefore show many years but few places.
read_csv() returns a tibble with an additional import-specific class. The printing helpers need an ordinary tibble. Use as_tibble(), introduced in Section 2.2, to create life_table with the same rows, columns, order, and values. The original import remains available as life_expectancy:

life_table <- as_tibble(life_expectancy)

Compare the two printing helpers from Section 4.4 on this table:

print_headtail(life_table)
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
      Entity      Code   Year `Life expectancy`
      <chr>       <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
    1 Afghanistan AFG    1950              28.2
    2 Afghanistan AFG    1951              28.6
    3 Afghanistan AFG    1952              29.0
    4 Afghanistan AFG    1953              29.5
    5 Afghanistan AFG    1954              29.7
    ⋮      ⋮       ⋮        ⋮                ⋮ 
21561 Zimbabwe    ZWE    2019              61.1
21562 Zimbabwe    ZWE    2020              61.5
21563 Zimbabwe    ZWE    2021              60.1
21564 Zimbabwe    ZWE    2022              62.4
21565 Zimbabwe    ZWE    2023              62.8
# ... 21,555 rows omitted in the middle; use print(x, n = Inf) to show all
# rows.


In the book’s saved CSV, the first five rows describe Afghanistan and the last five describe Zimbabwe. This view is useful for checking the file’s boundaries, but it shows only two entities because each place occupies a block of adjacent rows.

print_interval(life_table)
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
      Entity                 Code   Year `Life expectancy`
      <chr>                  <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
    1 Afghanistan            AFG    1950              28.2
 2397 Bosnia and Herzegovina BIH    2011              77.0
 4793 Djibouti               DJI    1959              43.1
 7189 Greenland              GRL    1964              60.7
 9585 Kazakhstan             KAZ    1963              58.6
11981 Malta                  MLT    2007              79.7
14377 North Macedonia        MKD    2015              75.6
16773 San Marino             SMR    2004              81.6
19169 Thailand               THA    1962              51.4
21565 Zimbabwe               ZWE    2023              62.8
# ... 21,555 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to
# show all rows.


The interval preview reaches 10 different entities across the file. Its row numbers show the positions inspected. With the same ten-row display budget, it gives broader coverage of this table than the head/tail view. This is especially useful when records are ordered in blocks by country, school, or another group.
The spacing is by row position, not by entity or year. Larger blocks can occupy more displayed positions, so interval previews do not guarantee equal coverage of groups. They are deterministic inspection views, not random samples; a repeating pattern in the row order can also be missed. Use the full data for summaries and analysis.
Both helpers return all 21565 rows unchanged. The display does not shorten the stored table or alter the place-year observations.






TipOptional: Keep a preview style





If you repeatedly inspect the same table, tidystata’s preview() can store a preferred console display on a returned object. Its first argument is the table. The named argument style = "interval" requests evenly spaced positions; omitting it gives a head/tail display. Assignment keeps the result under a new name:

life_preview <- preview(life_table, style = "interval")
life_preview
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
      Entity                 Code   Year `Life expectancy`
      <chr>                  <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
    1 Afghanistan            AFG    1950              28.2
 2397 Bosnia and Herzegovina BIH    2011              77.0
 4793 Djibouti               DJI    1959              43.1
 7189 Greenland              GRL    1964              60.7
 9585 Kazakhstan             KAZ    1963              58.6
11981 Malta                  MLT    2007              79.7
14377 North Macedonia        MKD    2015              75.6
16773 San Marino             SMR    2004              81.6
19169 Thailand               THA    1962              51.4
21565 Zimbabwe               ZWE    2023              62.8
# ... 21,555 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to
# show all rows.

nrow(life_preview)

[1] 21565


Typing life_preview now uses the interval style, while its row count remains 21565. All columns and stored values are retained. The original life_table keeps its ordinary printing, and the viewer is unaffected by these console preferences.
Use unpreview() to return an object with ordinary printing restored. Save and print that result:

life_plain <- unpreview(life_preview)
life_plain
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
   Entity      Code   Year `Life expectancy`
   <chr>       <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan AFG    1950              28.2
 2 Afghanistan AFG    1951              28.6
 3 Afghanistan AFG    1952              29.0
 4 Afghanistan AFG    1953              29.5
 5 Afghanistan AFG    1954              29.7
 6 Afghanistan AFG    1955              30.4
 7 Afghanistan AFG    1956              30.8
 8 Afghanistan AFG    1957              31.3
 9 Afghanistan AFG    1958              31.8
10 Afghanistan AFG    1959              32.3
# ℹ 21,555 more rows


Removing the preference changes the display while retaining the complete data. For a single inspection, use print_headtail() or print_interval() directly.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
section: 7.8 Save a table to a file
text:
7.8 Save a table to a file
The imported table exists in the running R session. Saving your script keeps the instructions, while exporting saves the table’s values to a file. write_csv() takes the table first and an output path second. Run this command in your project folder to save a separate copy:

write_csv(life_expectancy, "examples/life-expectancy-copy.csv")
file.exists("examples/life-expectancy-copy.csv")

The write command normally prints no table; the check should return TRUE. The new file is inside examples. write_csv() replaces an existing file with the same name, so choose a new name when you want to keep an earlier version. This command leaves the original download and the object life_expectancy unchanged.
Open the saved copy to check that it is readable:

saved_life <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy-copy.csv")
saved_life
nrow(saved_life)
ncol(saved_life)
ds(saved_life)

Its first rows and row count should agree with the imported table. Also check its column names with ds(saved_life) and compare ncol(saved_life) with ncol(life_expectancy). A TRUE file-existence check only establishes that a file is present: a different row count, missing column, or unexpected type after readback is a reason to check which object was written and which path was read. Recheck the working directory before overwriting or re-exporting anything. CSV preserves a plain table of values, but it does not preserve R’s full type information or the variable and value labels that statistical files can contain. Keep the original download and its documentation. Section 18.4 explains other export choices.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.9 Review

A tibble prints a preview naturally; nrow() and ncol() report its full dimensions.
print_headtail() checks boundaries; print_interval() reaches across ordered or clustered rows. Both retain the full table.
Optional: preview() stores a console display preference; unpreview() restores ordinary printing.
browse() opens a table in the viewer without changing the stored data.
ds() lists column names, and variables() connects them to available labels. codebook() checks types and recorded coverage.
mean() describes center and sd() describes spread in the measurement’s units; each call needs its own missing-input decision.
summ() describes numeric columns using available measurements and reports their contributing counts.
getwd() and file.exists() check location; read_csv() imports and write_csv() exports. Inspect the readback and preserve the original.

Next, Chapter 8 uses frequency tables to describe which categories are common and how missing answers affect a percentage. Numerical summaries and graphs follow in the same exploration part.

title: 7  Inspect a dataset
text:
7.10 Exercises

Display lifeexp in the console, browse it in the viewer, and summarize lexp and safewater with summ(). Which display helps you inspect one country, and which describes a whole column? Check whether the full row count has changed. Predict why mean(lifeexp$safewater) returns NA, correct the calculation, and report its contributing country count and units. Does the correction change the source table?
List the column names, then use their variable labels to identify population growth. Inspect the observed count for gnppc with the codebook. Does every country have this measurement?
Import the saved life-expectancy CSV as downloaded_life. Compare head/tail and interval previews, and report what one row represents. Why do the previews show different sets of places? Check that the full row count is unchanged. Save a separate file named life-expectancy-practice.csv inside examples, then read it back and check the dimensions and column names. If the file exists but has a different row count, what would you check before exporting again? Does saving this copy change the original download?

text:
Worked answers
Run the package setup at the start of this chapter first.

Run browse(lifeexp) in your editor to inspect an individual country’s row. Typing lifeexp gives a preview of the table; summ() describes each requested column using its non-missing values across the full table. The summary has two rows, one per variable, but there are still 68 countries in lifeexp. None of these calls replaces the source table.

mean(lifeexp$safewater)

[1] NA

mean(lifeexp$safewater, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 77.16667

lifeexp |>
  filter(!is.na(safewater)) |>
  nrow()

[1] 54

nrow(lifeexp)

[1] 68


The default mean is unknown because 14 inputs are missing. The corrected mean describes water coverage, in percent, across the 54 countries with measurements. There are still 68 countries in the original table; excluding inputs from one calculation does not replace unknown measurements.









TipFind and inspect






ds(lifeexp)

[1] "region"    "country"   "popgrowth" "lexp"      "gnppc"     "safewater"

variables(lifeexp)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  name      label
