1 gnppc    GNP per capita double    67     64


The label “Avg. annual % growth” identifies popgrowth as population growth; the dataset notes explain its units. The income column has 67 observed values, so one country lacks this measurement. This result alone does not explain why it is missing.









TipOpen and save a downloaded table





Place the downloaded file in examples as instructed in Section 7.7, then run:

downloaded_life <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
downloaded_life
downloaded_table <- as_tibble(downloaded_life)
print_headtail(downloaded_table)
print_interval(downloaded_table)
nrow(downloaded_life)
write_csv(downloaded_life, "examples/life-expectancy-practice.csv")
file.exists("examples/life-expectancy-practice.csv")
practice_readback <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy-practice.csv")
nrow(practice_readback)
ncol(practice_readback)
ds(practice_readback)

The first displayed rows describe Afghanistan in successive years. A row identifies a place and year, not a different country in every row. The head/tail preview shows Afghanistan and Zimbabwe; the interval preview reaches places throughout the file because it spreads its positions across the intervening blocks. Neither preview changes the full count of 21565 rows or guarantees balanced coverage of entities. The file check returns TRUE, and the readback has the same dimensions and names. If the count differs, check the working directory, input and output filenames, and whether a subset was exported. The new filename preserves the original download; exporting does not alter downloaded_life either.

title: 8  Tabulate data
text:
8.1 Read frequency tables with tab(), tab1(), and tab2()
How common is a response, and how does its distribution differ across groups? A frequency table describes the distribution of categories, such as happiness or educational qualifications. It can also count each distinct recorded value of a numeric variable. Every percentage requires us to be clear about who contributes to the calculation.
tab() counts cases and reports percentages and cumulative percentages, tab1() produces a separate distribution for each selected variable, and tab2() cross-tabulates each pair of selected variables. fre() adds total rows to a frequency table.
These tabulation functions come from tidystata and return new tables without changing the data we give them.
The examples build on inspecting a dataset in Chapter 7. We supply the dataset as the first argument, followed by column names without quotation marks: for example, tab(gss24, happy). Commas separate the arguments inside the parentheses. The pipe learned in Chapter 5 gives an equivalent form: gss24 |> tab(happy). We use direct calls when a single operation is enough. A named argument such as .by = sex sets an option; the = here supplies an argument value rather than saving an object. Grouped percentages are explained where they first appear.
After installing the packages (see Section 1.3), load them at the start of your session:
We now move from country records to individual survey respondents, using one survey extract throughout this chapter and the following numerical-summary lessons. The 2024 General Social Survey (GSS) records adults’ demographic characteristics and answers about their families, work, education, and attitudes. The GSS has interviewed adults in the United States since 1972.
The one-time recipe in Appendix A explains how to obtain the freely available source data, prepare the variables, and save the gss24 extract as gss24.rds. Complete that recipe before running the examples below. If that file is in your working directory, load it with:
readRDS() restores the saved R object, and <- stores it under the name gss24. You only need to load it once per session. Each row is one respondent; id is the respondent identifier. A row position or printed line number is not a permanent identity. Unknown answers remain missing rather than becoming response categories. The appendix prepares categorical columns with defined levels so we can tabulate them here without constructing factors ourselves.
Our extract contains 3,986 respondents and 25 variables. The main examples use full gss24. A final application creates a working-age subset and identifies its different percentage denominators explicitly.

title: 8  Tabulate data
text:
8.1.1 Start with numeric frequencies
Frequency tables help us inspect numeric measurements. Are recorded values repeated, and how far apart are the low and high values? In gss24, age records respondents’ ages in years. It measures a quantity rather than a named category, but tab() can still count every distinct recorded value. Store that result so we can inspect it in two ways:

age_freq <- tab(gss24, age)

Assignment with <- saves the full table under age_freq without printing it. Read the values and counts first; the next examples explain the percentage columns. Each row represents an exact recorded age, or a missing value, and n counts respondents with that value. These rows are not age brackets. The counts describe stored values: ages recorded in whole years are shared by many respondents.
There are many distinct values, so use the complementary previews from Section 4.4: head/tail to inspect the boundaries, and interval to inspect positions across the interior. Start with print_headtail():

print_headtail(age_freq)
# A tibble: 73 × 6
     age     n percent     cum   valid valid_cum
   <dbl> <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>

The header reports 73 rows, although only ten are displayed. Recorded ages run from 18 to 89. Each non-missing row counts respondents sharing a recorded age. The final NA row counts the 127 respondents with unknown age, not the oldest respondents. The omission message marks the undisplayed middle of the table.
For coverage through the middle, use print_interval() with the same default budget of ten data rows. It displays approximately evenly spaced positions through the table, including the first and last:

print_interval(age_freq)

49    66    70   1.76   77.4    1.81     79.9  
57    74    57   1.43   89.2    1.48     92.1  
65    82    18   0.452  94.6    0.466    97.7  
73    NA   127   3.19  100     NA        NA    
# ... 63 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to
# show all rows.


The row numbers show where those ages occur in the complete table. The selected positions are evenly spaced through distinct recorded values, not through individual respondents. This preview does not produce age brackets, population quantiles, or a random sample. Repeated ages represent multiple respondents, and the missing category still comes last.
Both printing helpers return the entire age_freq table unchanged and invisibly, meaning that R displays the preview without automatically printing the returned object again. They do not remove rows, combine values into bins, or recalculate percentages. In particular, cum and valid_cum still include the categories skipped in the display; adding only the displayed percentages does not reconstruct the distribution. Exact-value frequencies are useful for inspection, while the numerical summaries in Chapter 9 give more compact descriptions of location and spread.


8.1.2 Count response categories
The GSS asks respondents how happy they are, all things considered: very happy, pretty happy, or not too happy. Which answer is most common? Tidystata’s tab() takes a table and the column to describe, returning one row per response category. Start by reading n, the number of respondents in each category:

tab(gss24, happy)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  happy             n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 very happy      797  20.0    20.0  20.2      20.2
2 pretty happy   2303  57.8    77.8  58.2      78.4
3 not too happy   854  21.4    99.2  21.6     100  
4 NA               32   0.803 100    NA        NA  


Each output row represents a category rather than a respondent. The most common answer is “pretty happy,” with 2,303 respondents. The last row, <NA>, counts the 32 respondents with no recorded answer; they are still part of the dataset. Adding n across all rows gives the original 3,986 respondents.
The result is a new tibble; gss24 is unchanged. Counts tell us how many people gave each answer. The other columns express their relative sizes and make the denominator visible.


8.1.3 Read percentages
Besides the count n, tab() reports:

percent: the percentage of all respondents in each category.
cum: the running total of percent down the displayed rows.
valid: the percentage among respondents with a recorded answer, excluding missing answers from the denominator.
valid_cum: the running total of valid across the non-missing categories.

For “pretty happy,” percent divides its count by all 3,986 respondents, while valid divides by the 3,954 who answered. The valid percentage is 58.2%: more than half of those with a recorded answer chose this category. Missing answers have a count and an all-case percentage, but no valid percentage of their own.
Read cumulative percentages in the displayed category order. At “pretty happy,” valid_cum combines “very happy” and “pretty happy”: 78.4% of valid answers fall in those first two categories. Cumulative percentages depend on order and are useful only when combining successive categories answers a meaningful question. They are usually less informative for unordered categories such as marital status.
The appendix prepares happy as a factor, a column with a defined set of category levels. Those levels retain the source-code order: “very happy,” “pretty happy,” then “not too happy.” That is why these categories appear in this order rather than alphabetically. Cumulative totals follow that level order; preparation has not ranked respondents by how happy they are.
Because only 32 happiness answers are missing, percent and valid differ slightly. Section 8.2 returns to the choice of denominator.


8.1.4 Questions not asked of everyone
An unavailable answer need not be a refusal. The GSS uses ballots, different versions of the questionnaire assigned to parts of the sample. The institutional-confidence questions were asked on only two of the 2024 ballots. We therefore expect substantial missingness in conpress, confidence in the press:

tab(gss24, conpress)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  conpress         n percent    cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>        <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 a great deal   225    5.64   5.64  8.68      8.68
2 only some     1045   26.2   31.9  40.3      49.0 
3 hardly any    1321   33.1   65.0  51.0     100   
4 NA            1395   35.0  100    NA        NA   


The missing row counts about a third of the sample. percent includes all respondents, including people never assigned this question, in its denominator. valid describes the distribution among people with recorded confidence answers. That denominator excludes missing answers both by design and for other reasons; it is not the number of everyone who was assigned the question. A frequency table alone cannot distinguish these reasons. Consult the questionnaire and source documentation before describing missingness as refusal or lack of confidence.


8.1.5 Cross-tabulate two variables
Does happiness differ with self-rated health? Start by counting each combination of the two answers:

# Two variables: one row for each combination
tab(gss24, happy, health)
# A tibble: 20 × 7
   happy         health        n percent    cum  valid valid_cum
   <fct>         <fct>     <int>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 very happy    excellent   246  6.17     6.17  6.24       6.24
 2 very happy    good        438 11.0     17.2  11.1       17.4 
 3 very happy    fair         96  2.41    19.6   2.44      19.8 
 4 very happy    poor         15  0.376   19.9   0.381     20.2 
 5 pretty happy  excellent   323  8.10    28.0   8.19      28.4 
 6 pretty happy  good       1338 33.6     61.6  33.9       62.3 
 7 pretty happy  fair        565 14.2     75.8  14.3       76.6 
 8 pretty happy  poor         69  1.73    77.5   1.75      78.4 
 9 not too happy excellent    94  2.36    79.9   2.38      80.8 
10 not too happy good        360  9.03    88.9   9.13      89.9 
11 not too happy fair        311  7.80    96.7   7.89      97.8 
12 not too happy poor         87  2.18    98.9   2.21     100   
13 very happy    NA            2  0.0502  98.9  NA         NA   
14 pretty happy  NA            8  0.201   99.1  NA         NA   
15 not too happy NA            2  0.0502  99.2  NA         NA   
16 NA            excellent     2  0.0502  99.2  NA         NA   
17 NA            good         15  0.376   99.6  NA         NA   
18 NA            fair          3  0.0753  99.7  NA         NA   
19 NA            poor          2  0.0502  99.7  NA         NA   
20 NA            NA           10  0.251  100    NA         NA   


Each row represents a pair of categories. The first row describes respondents who are both very happy and in excellent health. Here, percent is a percentage of the entire sample, and valid uses respondents with answers to both questions. Neither column is a percentage within the excellent-health group.
To compare the counts across health groups more easily, arrange the same combinations as a contingency table with tab2():

tab2(gss24, happy, health)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  `happy \\ health` excellent  good  fair  poor  `NA`
  <fct>                 <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>
1 very happy              246   438    96    15     2
2 pretty happy            323  1338   565    69     8
3 not too happy            94   360   311    87     2
4 NA                        2    15     3     2    10


Happiness categories form the rows and health categories the columns. Each cell is a count, not a percentage. For example, 246 respondents are very happy and report excellent health. The NA row and column retain missing answers; the bottom-right cell counts respondents missing both answers.
For a comparison within excellent health, divide the very-happy count by the sum of the three non-missing happiness counts in that column: 246 / (246 + 323 + 94). This gives about 37%. The corresponding share among respondents in poor health is 9%. These percentages describe those with recorded happiness answers in each health group; they are calculated from the counts, not printed by tab2() above. They show an association in this sample, not that health causes happiness. Section 8.2 shows how to request within-group percentages directly.


8.1.6 Tabulate several variables separately
Sometimes we want a separate distribution for each of several questions, rather than a table of their combinations. tab1(gss24, happy, health, marital) produces three one-way tables:

# Tabulate several variables at once with tab1()
tab1(gss24, happy, health, marital)
$happy
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  value             n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 very happy      797  20.0    20.0  20.2      20.2
2 pretty happy   2303  57.8    77.8  58.2      78.4
3 not too happy   854  21.4    99.2  21.6     100  
4 NA               32   0.803 100    NA        NA  

$health
# A tibble: 5 × 6
  value         n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 excellent   665  16.7    16.7 16.8       16.8
2 good       2151  54.0    70.6 54.3       71.0
3 fair        975  24.5    95.1 24.6       95.6
4 poor        173   4.34   99.4  4.36     100  
5 NA           22   0.552 100   NA         NA  

$marital
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  value             n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 married        1659  41.6    41.6 41.8       41.8
2 widowed         269   6.75   48.4  6.77      48.6
3 divorced        579  14.5    62.9 14.6       63.1
4 separated       130   3.26   66.2  3.27      66.4
5 never married  1334  33.5    99.6 33.6      100  
6 NA               15   0.376 100   NA         NA  


By default, the result is a named list: one object containing three separate tables. Its printed headings, $happy, $health, and $marital, identify those tables. Within each, value holds that variable’s categories; the remaining columns have the same meanings as in tab(). Each table has its own denominator, so do not add counts across the three tables: the same respondents contribute to each distribution.
For a single rectangular result, set .type = "tibble":

tab1(gss24, happy, health, marital, .type = "tibble")
# A tibble: 15 × 7
   variable value             n percent   cum valid valid_cum
   <chr>    <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 happy    very happy      797  20.0    20.0 20.2       20.2
 2 happy    pretty happy   2303  57.8    77.8 58.2       78.4
 3 happy    not too happy   854  21.4    99.2 21.6      100  
 4 happy    NA               32   0.803 100   NA         NA  
 5 health   excellent       665  16.7    16.7 16.8       16.8
 6 health   good           2151  54.0    70.6 54.3       71.0
 7 health   fair            975  24.5    95.1 24.6       95.6
 8 health   poor            173   4.34   99.4  4.36     100  
 9 health   NA               22   0.552 100   NA         NA  
10 marital  married        1659  41.6    41.6 41.8       41.8
11 marital  widowed         269   6.75   48.4  6.77      48.6
12 marital  divorced        579  14.5    62.9 14.6       63.1
13 marital  separated       130   3.26   66.2  3.27      66.4
14 marital  never married  1334  33.5    99.6 33.6      100  
15 marital  NA               15   0.376 100   NA         NA  


This argument changes the output format, not the calculation. The tables are stacked into one tibble, and the variable column identifies which question each row describes. Read variable and value together: “good” is a health answer, whereas “married” is a marital-status answer. Each row is now a category within a particular variable, rather than a combination of happiness, health, and marital status.
The happiness rows have exactly the same counts and percentages as the $happy table above; the same holds for health and marital status. Within each block, percent adds to 100 across all categories, and valid adds to 100 across non-missing answers. Each block’s counts add to 3,986, so summing n over the whole stacked result would count the same respondents three times. Stacking makes several distributions convenient to inspect together; it does not turn them into one distribution with a shared denominator.


8.1.7 Cross-tabulate several variable pairs
How are happiness, health, and marital status related to one another? We can inspect all three pairs without writing three separate calls. Give tab2() the same variables we just passed to tab1() and save its result. Typing its name displays the list at the normal console width:

pair_tables <- tab2(gss24, happy, health, marital)
pair_tables
$`happy x health`
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  `happy \\ health` excellent  good  fair  poor  `NA`
  <fct>                 <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>
1 very happy              246   438    96    15     2
2 pretty happy            323  1338   565    69     8
3 not too happy            94   360   311    87     2
4 NA                        2    15     3     2    10

$`happy x marital`
# A tibble: 4 × 7
  `happy \\ marital` married widowed divorced separated `never married`  `NA`
  <fct>                <int>   <int>    <int>     <int>           <int> <int>
1 very happy             473      42       94        13             172     3
2 pretty happy           965     160      329        67             774     8
3 not too happy          209      64      152        47             379     3
4 NA                      12       3        4         3               9     1

$`health x marital`
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  `health \\ marital` married widowed divorced separated `never married`  `NA`
  <fct>                 <int>   <int>    <int>     <int>           <int> <int>
1 excellent               295      29       97        13             228     3
2 good                    953     156      285        65             685     7
3 fair                    355      61      161        43             353     2
4 poor                     48      22       34         8              60     1
5 NA                        8       1        2         1               8     2


The result is a list of three cross-tabulations. A narrow display may omit columns and name them in its footer; those columns remain in the returned tables. Inspect the result in your editor’s viewer when necessary. The list names identify the pairs:

happy x health: happiness in the rows and health in the columns, repeating our earlier two-variable table.
happy x marital: happiness in the rows and marital status in the columns.
health x marital: health in the rows and marital status in the columns.

Each cell counts respondents with that pair of answers, and NA rows or columns retain missing answers. Each table uses only its two named variables: someone with missing marital status can still contribute to a recorded happiness-health combination in the first table. Across all cells, including missing categories, each table counts the full sample once.
In the happiness-marital-status table, very-happy answers are more common among married respondents than among those who have never married. Divide the very-happy count in each column by that column’s total across the three recorded happiness categories. The resulting shares are 28.7% for married respondents and 13.0% for never-married respondents. These denominators exclude missing happiness answers within each marital-status group. The comparison describes an association, not an effect of marriage on happiness.
The three functions answer different questions even when given the same variables. tab1(gss24, happy, health, marital) describes each variable separately. tab2(gss24, happy, health, marital) describes each pair separately. By contrast, tab(gss24, happy, health, marital) would count joint combinations of all three, such as very happy, excellent health, and married. Three pairwise tables do not show how the happiness-health relationship varies within marital-status groups; that requires an additional grouping step, planned for a later chapter beyond this chapter.


8.1.8 Include totals with fre()
fre() works like tab() but adds total rows. These make the two denominators visible in the output:

fre(gss24, happy)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  happy             n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <chr>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 very happy      797  20.0    20.0  20.2      20.2
2 pretty happy   2303  57.8    77.8  58.2      78.4
3 not too happy   854  21.4    99.2  21.6     100  
4 Valid Total    3954  99.2    NA   100        NA  
5 NA               32   0.803 100    NA        NA  
6 Total          3986 100      NA    NA        NA  


Valid Total counts the 3,954 non-missing answers; Total counts all 3,986 respondents. The missing-answer count bridges the difference. These are summary rows, not additional response categories or additional respondents.


8.1.9 Optional reference: preserve the input table class
You can continue using tibbles throughout this chapter. If you work with other table classes, tidystata normally returns newly calculated tables in the same container as the input: a base data.frame, tibble, or data.table. This preserves the kind of table, not its original rows or columns.
as.data.frame() converts our tibble to a base data frame. Save the converted table separately:

gss_base <- as.data.frame(gss24)

class() takes an object and reports its class names. Compare the same tabulation with the two inputs:

class(tab(gss24, happy))

[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

class(tab(gss_base, happy))

[1] "data.frame"


The tibble result has classes "tbl_df", "tbl", and "data.frame"; the base result has class "data.frame". A tibble is also a kind of data frame, which is why its class listing contains all three names. The category counts and percentages agree; only the container differs.
To try a data.table input, install the optional package once if needed:

install.packages("data.table")

data.table::as.data.table() converts the input without attaching the package. The :: notation names the package that supplies the function:

gss_dt <- data.table::as.data.table(gss24)

class(tab(gss_dt, happy))

[1] "data.table" "data.frame"


The result has classes "data.table" and "data.frame", so a data.table input produces a data.table frequency table. These calls return new results without changing gss24 or its converted copies.
For functions that return several tables, distinguish the outer list from the tables inside it. Store the default tab1() result as tables_dt. Double brackets, [[1]], extract the first table from that list:

tables_dt <- tab1(gss_dt, happy, health, marital)

class(tables_dt)

[1] "list"

class(tables_dt[[1]])

[1] "data.table" "data.frame"


The outer object is a "list"; its first table is a data.table. The other two tables preserve the same class. The three-variable tab2() result follows this pattern too: a list of cross-tabulations, each in the input’s table class.
An explicit output request can override this default. As we saw above, .type = "tibble" in tab1() both stacks the one-way tables and requests a tibble, including when the input is a data.table:

class(tab1(gss_dt, happy, health, marital, .type = "tibble"))

[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"


The class names are now "tbl_df", "tbl", and "data.frame". The distributions remain the same. When deciding how to use a result, check both its structure, one table or a list, and the class of the tables it contains.

title: 8  Tabulate data
section: 8.2 Application: educational qualifications in the 2024 GSS
text:
8.2 Application: educational qualifications in the 2024 GSS
This section puts the tools together to describe education in the 2024 GSS, and shows why every percentage needs a clearly stated denominator.

8.2.1 Who has which degree?
What is the distribution of respondents’ highest educational qualifications? Each category of degree represents a highest degree, so someone with a graduate degree is not counted again under bachelor’s or high school:

tab(gss24, degree)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  degree                       n percent    cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>                    <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 less than high school      362   9.08    9.08  9.10      9.10
2 high school               1817  45.6    54.7  45.7      54.8 
3 associate/junior college   360   9.03   63.7   9.05     63.8 
4 bachelor's                 863  21.7    85.3  21.7      85.5 
5 graduate                   577  14.5    99.8  14.5     100   
6 NA                           7   0.176 100    NA        NA   


The last row shows that 7 respondents did not report a degree. That is why the two kinds of percentages differ:

percent divides by all 3,986 respondents.
valid divides by the 3,979 respondents who answered.

Here the difference is tiny. Among those who answered, 45.7% have a high school diploma as their highest degree, and 36.2% hold a bachelor’s or graduate degree.
For questions with more missing answers, the choice of denominator matters a great deal (see Exercise 2).


8.2.2 Comparing groups: which denominator?
To compare women and men, we need a distribution of degrees within each category of sex. The argument .by = sex asks tab() to perform its calculation separately for those groups, for this operation only.
tab() retains missing values, including a separate group for the 30 respondents whose sex is missing. This does not change the denominators within the recorded male and female groups. First save and display the returned table:

degrees_by_sex <- tab(gss24, degree, .by = sex)
degrees_by_sex
# A tibble: 17 × 7
   sex    degree                       n percent    cum valid valid_cum
   <fct>  <fct>                    <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 male   less than high school      135  7.55     7.55  7.57      7.57
 2 male   high school                860 48.1     55.7  48.2      55.8 
 3 male   associate/junior college   141  7.89    63.6   7.90     63.7 
 4 male   bachelor's                 395 22.1     85.7  22.1      85.8 
 5 male   graduate                   253 14.2     99.8  14.2     100   
 6 male   NA                           3  0.168  100    NA        NA   
 7 female less than high school      208  9.59     9.59  9.60      9.60
 8 female high school                952 43.9     53.5  43.9      53.5 
 9 female associate/junior college   219 10.1     63.6  10.1      63.6 
10 female bachelor's                 466 21.5     85.1  21.5      85.1 
11 female graduate                   322 14.8     99.9  14.9     100   
12 female NA                           2  0.0922 100    NA        NA   
13 NA     less than high school       19 63.3     63.3  67.9      67.9 
14 NA     high school                  5 16.7     80    17.9      85.7 
15 NA     bachelor's                   2  6.67    86.7   7.14     92.9 
16 NA     graduate                     2  6.67    93.3   7.14    100   
17 NA     NA                           2  6.67   100    NA        NA   


Each output row is now a combination of sex and degree. The normal preview may omit some combinations. For this interpretation, deliberately display every row with print(). The named argument n = Inf removes the finite row limit for this call; it changes the display without selecting or recalculating the data:

print(degrees_by_sex, n = Inf)
# A tibble: 17 × 7
   sex    degree                       n percent    cum valid valid_cum
   <fct>  <fct>                    <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 male   less than high school      135  7.55     7.55  7.57      7.57
 2 male   high school                860 48.1     55.7  48.2      55.8 
 3 male   associate/junior college   141  7.89    63.6   7.90     63.7 
 4 male   bachelor's                 395 22.1     85.7  22.1      85.8 
 5 male   graduate                   253 14.2     99.8  14.2     100   
 6 male   NA                           3  0.168  100    NA        NA   
 7 female less than high school      208  9.59     9.59  9.60      9.60
 8 female high school                952 43.9     53.5  43.9      53.5 
 9 female associate/junior college   219 10.1     63.6  10.1      63.6 
10 female bachelor's                 466 21.5     85.1  21.5      85.1 
11 female graduate                   322 14.8     99.9  14.9     100   
12 female NA                           2  0.0922 100    NA        NA   
13 NA     less than high school       19 63.3     63.3  67.9      67.9 
14 NA     high school                  5 16.7     80    17.9      85.7 
15 NA     bachelor's                   2  6.67    86.7   7.14     92.9 
16 NA     graduate                     2  6.67    93.3   7.14    100   
17 NA     NA                           2  6.67   100    NA        NA   


Read the group and category columns together. Within each sex, percent adds to 100 across all degree rows, including any missing answers. valid adds to 100 across recorded degrees only. To answer “What share of women who reported a degree hold a graduate degree?”, find the female/graduate row and read valid. Its denominator is women with a recorded degree, not all degree holders in the sample.
We can combine categories within the same denominator. Adding the valid percentages for bachelor’s and graduate degrees gives 36.4% of women and 36.3% of men. This comparison describes the degree distribution within each sex among those who reported it.
A different question, “What share of graduate-degree holders are women?”, needs a different denominator. Swap the roles of the two variables and read valid within each recorded degree group:

sex_by_degree <- tab(gss24, sex, .by = degree)
print(sex_by_degree, n = Inf)
# A tibble: 17 × 7
   degree                   sex        n percent   cum valid valid_cum
   <fct>                    <fct>  <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 less than high school    male     135  37.3    37.3  39.4      39.4
 2 less than high school    female   208  57.5    94.8  60.6     100  
 3 less than high school    NA        19   5.25  100    NA        NA  
 4 high school              male     860  47.3    47.3  47.5      47.5
 5 high school              female   952  52.4    99.7  52.5     100  
 6 high school              NA         5   0.275 100    NA        NA  
 7 associate/junior college male     141  39.2    39.2  39.2      39.2
 8 associate/junior college female   219  60.8   100    60.8     100  
 9 bachelor's               male     395  45.8    45.8  45.9      45.9
10 bachelor's               female   466  54.0    99.8  54.1     100  
11 bachelor's               NA         2   0.232 100    NA        NA  
12 graduate                 male     253  43.8    43.8  44        44  
13 graduate                 female   322  55.8    99.7  56       100  
14 graduate                 NA         2   0.347 100    NA        NA  
15 NA                       male       3  42.9    42.9  60        60  
16 NA                       female     2  28.6    71.4  40       100  
17 NA                       NA         2  28.6   100    NA        NA  


Now percentages add to 100 within each degree category. The female/graduate row’s valid uses all graduate-degree holders with recorded sex as its denominator. Its percent also includes graduate-degree holders whose sex is missing, so the columns can differ. The missing-degree group is shown separately and is not part of the graduate denominator. Swapping the variables has changed the question, not the respondents’ qualifications.
For the respondents with both answers, the underlying cell counts are the same whichever distribution we calculate. tab2() arranges those counts in rows and columns, retaining missing-answer cells at the edges:

tab2(gss24, degree, sex)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  `degree \\ sex`           male female  `NA`
  <fct>                    <int>  <int> <int>
1 less than high school      135    208    19
2 high school                860    952     5
3 associate/junior college   141    219     0
4 bachelor's                 395    466     2
5 graduate                   253    322     2
6 NA                           3      2     2


With degree in the rows and sex in the columns, dividing a graduate cell by its column total across recorded degrees asks about degrees within a sex; dividing it by its row total across recorded sexes asks about sex within that degree. Exclude the missing-answer row or column from these valid-answer totals. Before reporting a percentage, state its denominator: all respondents or valid answers, and which group. None of these commands overwrites gss24.
These are unweighted sample descriptions: each respondent contributes equally. They describe associations, not causal effects. Survey weighting is beyond this edition.

title: 8  Tabulate data
text:
8.3 Application: a GSS analysis subset
Suppose our next analysis will concern schooling and working hours among GSS respondents aged 18 through 64. Age alone defines this subset; we are not yet requiring a reported schooling value or working-hours answer.
Use the two inclusive bounds, then the familiar select() to keep the ID and variables needed for this question. Assign the result a new name:

working_age <- gss24 |>
  filter(age >= 18, age <= 64) |>
  select(id, age, educ, hrs1)

title: 8  Tabulate data
text:
8.4 Chapter review

tab() counts records by category and reports percentages, retaining missing answers.
percent uses all observations and valid uses complete answers; fre() adds explicit total rows.
tab1() tabulates variables separately; tab2() produces a count matrix for each selected pair.
.by requests within-group distributions; check the grouping and missingness rules before interpreting a percentage.
print_headtail() and print_interval() preview a long frequency table without changing its contents or recalculating percentages.
Optional: class() checks the returned container; supported input classes are preserved by default, while .type can request tibbles explicitly.

Always identify a percentage’s denominator. Next, Chapter 9 describes numerical center and spread.

title: 8  Tabulate data
text:
8.5 Exercises
1. Syntax and meaning. Tabulate marital in gss24 with tab() and then with fre(). Identify the total rows. Which column of tab() gives the share of each marital status among respondents who answered the question?
2. Interpretation. Tabulate conpress (confidence in the press). Use the questionnaire-version explanation to say why percent and valid differ. Which would you report to describe recorded confidence answers, and whose answers does that denominator include?
3. Adapt the comparison. Within each recorded category of race, what percentage of respondents who answered the degree question hold a graduate degree? Keep missing answers visible in the table, but exclude them from the percentage denominator and explain how you did so. State why this differs from asking what share of graduate-degree holders belong to each racial category.
4. Predict and diagnose. Predict how many separate distributions or pairwise tables tab1(gss24, happy, health, marital) and tab2(gss24, happy, health, marital) produce. Compare them with tab(gss24, happy, health, marital). A colleague adds n over the entire stacked tab1() result and reports a sample three times too large. Diagnose that claim, and explain why adding only the percentages shown in an interval preview is also incorrect.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
9.1 Summarize variables with summ()
What does a typical value look like, and how widely do values vary? Numerical summaries describe quantities such as age, years of schooling, and income through measures of center and spread. As with the percentages in Chapter 8, we must identify which observations contribute to each calculation.
summ() from tidystata produces common statistics for one or more variables. Its companion tabstat() compares selected statistics across groups. We use individual calculations to explain the statistics, then briefly show summarise() for a custom summary.
This chapter builds on inspecting a dataset and reading frequency tables in Chapter 8. We continue with the same 2024 GSS respondents. As in tab(), the dataset is the first argument and column names follow without quotation marks: summ(gss24, age). Commas separate arguments. A named argument, such as .by = degree, sets an option for that call. Each new summary statistic is explained before we interpret it.
After installing the packages (see Section 1.3), load them at the start of your session:
Use Appendix A to create the gss24 extract and save it as gss24.rds. If that file is in your working directory, load it with:
readRDS() restores the saved R object, and <- stores it under the name gss24. You only need to load it once per session.
gss24 comes from the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS), which has interviewed adults in the United States since 1972 about their families, work, education, and attitudes. Our extract has 3,986 respondents and 25 variables. Its degree categories are already prepared; factor construction is not required here. We begin with age, recorded in years, before comparing schooling, working hours, and family income.
In Section 7.3, summ() described complete columns without requiring us to inspect every record. We now use its output to ask what a typical value looks like and how widely values differ. Supply a table and the numeric variable to summarize:
# The type, number of non-missing values, number of distinct values,
# minimum, mean, standard deviation, and maximum of age
summ(gss24, age)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3859     72    18  49.0  17.7    89
Read its columns as follows:
Here, 3859 respondents share 72 distinct recorded ages. Repeated ages are not missing observations. Finer measurement, such as recording age in months rather than whole years, allows more distinct values, but the observed count also depends on the sample. A high unique does not by itself make a variable continuous or substantively informative: even an identifier can be unique for every case.
The statistics describe recorded ages in years, with each respondent contributing equally. These are unweighted sample summaries, rather than estimates adjusted for how the sample represents the population. The n column makes the number of contributing respondents explicit. This one-variable result does not need a name column.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
type: the type of the variable (or its unit, if the variable has one).
n: the number of non-missing values.
unique: the number of distinct non-missing values, which cannot exceed n.
min: the minimum.
mean: the arithmetic mean, the sum of observed values divided by their number.
sd: the standard deviation.
max: the maximum.




9.1.1 Extract a column
Chapter 7 explains observations, variables, tidy data, and table previews. Recall that a tibble is a form of data frame: it stores columns together, but its class alone does not determine what an observation means. Each row of gss24 represents a respondent.
The $ operator extracts a column by name. Put the table on the left and the column name on the right. length() counts entries, including missing values; var_type() identifies the object’s type:

age_vector <- gss24$age


length(age_vector)

[1] 3986

var_type(age_vector)

[1] "double"


The extracted vector has 3,986 entries, stored as doubles, in the same respondent order as the table. Its length includes missing ages. Extracting a column does not remove it from its source.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
9.2 Understand center and spread

9.2.1 Ordered positions
The mean and standard deviation introduced in Section 7.3.1 describe average level and spread. A median or quartile answers a different question: where does a value lie among the ordered observations? We first use abstract numbers so every position is visible. c() combines the values in their written order.
sort() takes a vector and returns its values in increasing order. It does not change the saved input:

x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
sort(x)

[1]  2  4  6  8 10


These five values are already ordered. If their written order changed, sort() would still return the same increasing sequence.
median() returns the middle value after ordering the observations:

median(x)

[1] 6


The median is 6: two entries lie below it and two above it. With an even number of values, two occupy the middle. median() averages them:

four_values <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
median(four_values)

[1] 5


The two middle values are 4 and 6, so the median is (4 + 6) / 2, or 5. Here + adds the middle values, parentheses make that addition happen first, and / 2 divides the sum by two. A median need not be an input value.
quantile() takes a numerical vector and probabilities specifying positions. Probabilities run from zero to one; .25 requests the lower quartile and .75 the upper quartile. Supply both in one c() value:

quantile(x, c(.25, .75))

25% 75% 
  4   8 


The 25% and 75% headings identify the requested positions. Here the quartiles are 4 and 8, the second and fourth values. Quartiles locate one quarter and three quarters of the way through an ordered distribution. They are not 25% and 75% of the largest number. With other inputs, interpolation can place a cutpoint between recorded values.


9.2.2 Summarize a recorded column
The familiar extraction gss24$age supplies all recorded and missing ages. As with mean() and sd() in Section 7.3.1, an unavailable input requires a decision about the calculation. median() supports its own na.rm argument. Its default is FALSE; TRUE excludes missing ages from this calculation:

median(gss24$age)

[1] NA

median(gss24$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 48


The first result is NA; the second locates the middle among the 3,859 recorded ages. Neither command fills missing ages or changes gss24.
quantile() also supports na.rm = TRUE. Without it, missing inputs produce an error rather than defined quartiles. Apply the explicit exclusion when requesting the two age cutpoints:

quantile(gss24$age, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)

25% 75% 
 34  64 


The 25% and 75% cutpoints are both in years. Recall that sd() uses the same unit as the original measurements:

sd(gss24$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 17.66311


Recorded age ranges from 18 to 89 years. Its median is 48 years, and its standard deviation is about 17.7 years. These describe location and spread among the same respondents with recorded ages. summ() excludes missing measured values automatically and reports the contributing count.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
9.3 Summarize several variables
When we summarize several variables, name identifies the variable in each output row:

# Summarize several variables at once
summ(gss24, age, educ, hrs1:realinc)
# A tibble: 4 × 8
  name    type      n unique   min    mean       sd     max
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     72   18     49.0    17.7      89 
2 educ    dbl    3952     21    0     14.2     2.92     20 
3 hrs1    dbl    2201     76    0     39.3    13.6      89 
4 realinc dbl    3563     26  182. 34252.  34697.   117565.


Using the tidyselect range introduced in Section 3.3, hrs1:realinc selects the columns from hrs1 through realinc in their dataset order. Here those two columns are adjacent. It is a column range, not a sequence of numeric values. age and educ are selected separately. Each output row describes one variable, not one respondent.
educ records completed years of schooling; hrs1 records hours worked last week and is generally available for respondents who were working. realinc measures family income in constant 1986 dollars, adjusted to the purchasing power of dollars in 1986. It is based on income brackets rather than exact amounts. Compare statistics only with their units in mind: a standard deviation in dollars is not directly comparable with one in years or hours.
summ() calculates these statistics from non-missing values. The n column reveals that working hours are missing for 1,785 respondents and family income for 423. Their means therefore describe different sets of respondents. A missing work-hours value need not mean a refusal: some respondents were not asked because they were not working. The coverage diagnostics in Section 10.2 will examine these different contributing samples more closely.
The income example also shows why we compare a mean with a median. Some families have much higher recorded incomes than others. The .stat argument requests statistics by name. c() combines the quoted names into one argument value; here c("n", "mean", "median") asks for the observed count and two measures of center on the same recorded incomes:

summ(gss24, realinc, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  type      n   mean median
  <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 dbl    3563 34252. 24502.


The mean of $34,252 exceeds the median of $24,502: high family incomes pull the mean upward. The median locates the middle recorded income among respondents who reported it. Both statistics are in constant 1986 dollars and give each respondent equal influence. Neither describes individual earnings or a survey-weighted population estimate.

9.3.1 Optional reference: detailed statistics
You can skip the detailed output on a first reading. The argument .detail = TRUE requests the full set of available statistics. print(width = Inf) allows all columns to be printed, even when they need several blocks of output:

# Show all available statistics
detailed_gss <- summ(gss24, age, educ, hrs1:realinc, .detail = TRUE)
print(detailed_gss, width = Inf)
# A tibble: 4 × 19
  name    type      n unique miss_n valid_pct   min    q1 median    mean
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int>  <int>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     72    127     0.968   18    34     48     49.0
2 educ    dbl    3952     21     34     0.991    0    12     14     14.2
3 hrs1    dbl    2201     76   1785     0.552    0    35     40     39.3
4 realinc dbl    3563     26    423     0.894  182. 9982. 24502. 34252. 
       mad       sd    q3     max    iqr    skew kurtosis       se        sum
     <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
1    22.2     17.7     64     89     30   0.158      2.00   0.284     189223 
2     2.97     2.92    16     20      4  -0.655      5.38   0.0464     56270 
3     7.41    13.6     45     89     10  -0.0694     4.69   0.289      86468 
4 21527.   34697.   43560 117565. 33578.  1.55       4.30 581.     122040909.


Alongside the familiar columns, miss_n counts missing values and valid_pct gives the non-missing proportion. q1, median, and q3 locate the quartiles; iqr is q3 - q1, the width of the middle half of the distribution. mad is a scaled median absolute deviation, another measure of spread. skew describes asymmetry, while kurtosis describes tail weight relative to the distribution’s spread. se is the standard error of the mean, discussed below, and sum adds the observed values. Not every available statistic is useful for every variable: summing respondents’ ages, for example, does not describe a typical respondent.
summ() uses Stata’s percentile rule, so its quartiles can differ from those produced by R’s default quantile(). A small difference in q1 between the two outputs need not be a calculation error. Two patterns in the detailed output help us describe the distributions:

For realinc, the mean ($34,252) is above the median ($24,502), and skewness (skew) is positive. High recorded family incomes extend the upper tail and pull the mean upward. The median locates the middle recorded income, following the comparison in the core lesson.
For educ, skewness is negative: respondents cluster around high-school and college schooling, with a longer tail toward few completed years. Its observed range is 0 to 20 years. Skewness describes the distribution’s asymmetry; it does not judge the people whose answers produce it.



9.3.2 Choose statistics
Instead of displaying every statistic, .stat requests a few by name. c("n", "valid_pct", "mean") combines three names into a character vector. The name and type columns still identify each variable:

# Choose summaries that show how many respondents contribute
summ(gss24, age, educ, hrs1:realinc, .stat = c("n", "valid_pct", "mean"))
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  name    type      n valid_pct    mean
  <chr>   <chr> <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     0.968    49.0
2 educ    dbl    3952     0.991    14.2
3 hrs1    dbl    2201     0.552    39.3
4 realinc dbl    3563     0.894 34252. 


n counts the non-missing observations. Despite its name, valid_pct is displayed on a 0–1 scale: 1 means complete coverage, and 0.894 means about 89.4% of respondents have a recorded family income. The income mean describes those respondents, not all 3,986 respondents.
Counts alone do not explain why answers are missing. Section 10.2 compares income coverage across degree categories before we use the joint availability of measurements in graphs.


9.3.3 Optional reference: custom calculations
For a custom calculation, first identify the quantities it needs. min() receives a numeric vector and returns its smallest value. Its own na.rm = TRUE option excludes missing inputs from this calculation:

min(gss24$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 18


This is the youngest recorded age, in years. max() instead returns the largest value, with its own missing-input instruction:

max(gss24$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 89


This is the oldest recorded age. The range is the distance between these extremes: subtract the minimum from the maximum. It differs from standard deviation, which uses distances around the mean.
For a calculation outside the standard summary choices, dplyr’s summarise() lets us write each expression ourselves. It takes a table and returns summary columns. Here we request the mean and range. In the range expression, - subtracts the smallest recorded age from the largest:

summarise(
  gss24,
  mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
  range_years = max(age, na.rm = TRUE) - min(age, na.rm = TRUE)
)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_age range_years
     <dbl>       <dbl>
1     49.0          71


The output has one row and two columns, both in years. A name on the left of = supplies the output heading; the expression on the right supplies its value. The mean agrees with summ(), while the range describes the distance between the extremes rather than the spread around the mean. Neither command changes gss24. All calculations use respondents with recorded ages.


9.3.4 Optional reference: standard error
You can skip this section and continue to the application. Standard deviation describes differences among observations. A standard error concerns how an estimated mean would vary across repeated samples: imagine repeatedly drawing independent random samples of the same size from one population and calculating a mean each time. Those sample means would differ. Their standard deviation is the standard error of the mean.
Under the simple independent-sampling model, we estimate it as sd / sqrt(n), where n counts non-missing observations and sqrt() takes the square root. A larger sample can make a mean more stable without making individual observations less spread out. To inspect that calculation in the teaching data, request n, sd, and se together:

summ(gss24, age, .stat = c("n", "sd", "se"))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  type      n    sd    se
  <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3859  17.7 0.284


The two spread measures have the variable’s units, here years, but describe different things. The printed se uses the simple formula above. It does not account for the GSS sampling design and weights or correct systematic missingness, so it should not be treated as a design-adjusted measure of population precision. Inference and survey-design methods require later teaching beyond this chapter.


9.3.5 Check whether a summary is meaningful
With only the dataset argument, summ() examines all columns rather than requiring us to name them individually. This is convenient, but it makes us responsible for deciding which results make sense:

# Select all variables at once
summ(gss24)
sex, race, ... are factors (**).

# A tibble: 25 × 8
   name      type      n unique   min    mean       sd   max
   <chr>     <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
 1 id        int    3986   3986     1 1994.   1151.     3986
 2 age       dbl    3859     72    18   49.0    17.7      89
 3 **sex     fct    3956      2     1    1.55    0.498     2
 4 **race    fct    3906      3     1    1.54    0.764     3
 5 **region  fct    3986      4     1    2.68    0.987     4
 6 **degree  fct    3979      5     1    2.87    1.27      5
 7 educ      dbl    3952     21     0   14.2     2.92     20
 8 paeduc    dbl    2866     21     0   12.5     3.88     20
 9 maeduc    dbl    3445     21     0   12.5     3.48     20
10 **marital fct    3971      5     1    2.80    1.75      5
# ℹ 15 more rows


summ() marks categorical factors with ** and prints a message. Their numerical summaries describe internal category codes, not meaningful measurements; use tab() to describe the categories. It also summarizes id, whose numbers identify respondents. Its mean of 1993.5 is mathematically defined but has no substantive interpretation: assigning different ID numbers would change it without changing anyone’s age, schooling, or income. Numeric storage alone does not make an average meaningful.

title: 9  Summarize data
section: 9.4 Application: age, schooling, and income in the 2024 GSS
text:
9.4 Application: age, schooling, and income in the 2024 GSS
How old are the respondents, how much schooling have they completed, and how many children have they had? How does family income vary? These quantities use different units, so first identify the variables:

age is in years.
educ is the number of years of schooling completed.
childs is the number of children the respondent has ever had.
realinc is family income in constant 1986 dollars: amounts adjusted for price changes to the purchasing power of dollars in 1986. The GSS asks about income in brackets, meaning ranges of amounts rather than exact dollar answers, so realinc has only 26 distinct recorded values.

Use summ() to inspect the distributions together:

summ(gss24, age, educ, childs, realinc)
# A tibble: 4 × 8
  name    type      n unique   min     mean       sd     max
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     72   18     49.0     17.7      89 
2 educ    dbl    3952     21    0     14.2      2.92     20 
3 childs  dbl    3944      9    0      1.72     1.65      8 
4 realinc dbl    3563     26  182. 34252.   34697.   117565.


Each output row describes one variable and uses its non-missing observations, so n differs across rows. For example, the mean of childs can be fractional even though each observed number of children is a whole number: an average need not be an observed value. The mean of realinc is in 1986 dollars, not current dollars or individual earnings. A common output layout does not make the variables interchangeable.
tabstat() returns a table of statistics for a numerical variable. Begin with the table and variable, before choosing options:

tabstat(gss24, realinc)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  type    mean
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 dbl   34252.


This describes the recorded family incomes together. Unlike summ()’s variable-oriented layout, tabstat() arranges selected statistics in columns, making it convenient for the group comparison that follows. The source remains unchanged.
Its .stat option requests statistics by quoted names, as in summ(). First choose the non-missing count, mean, and median without dividing the data into groups:

tabstat(gss24, realinc, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  type      n   mean median
  <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 dbl    3563 34252. 24502.


Those measures use the same recorded incomes. Now add .by = degree to request a separate row for each degree category:

tabstat(gss24, realinc, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"), .by = degree)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  degree                   type      n   mean median
  <fct>                    <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 less than high school    dbl     287 13210.  7714.
2 high school              dbl    1621 24308. 16335 
3 associate/junior college dbl     336 31510. 19965 
4 bachelor's               dbl     783 46575. 36300 
5 graduate                 dbl     530 59746. 43560 
6 NA                       dbl       6 20842. 18513 


A missing degree is included as a separate group by default. That group’s summary describes respondents whose degree is unavailable. To compare only the five recorded categories, add .missing = FALSE. This excludes the unknown-degree group; missing income is still excluded separately within every remaining group:

tabstat(gss24, realinc, .by = degree,
        .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"), .missing = FALSE)
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  degree                   type      n   mean median
  <fct>                    <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 less than high school    dbl     287 13210.  7714.
2 high school              dbl    1621 24308. 16335 
3 associate/junior college dbl     336 31510. 19965 
4 bachelor's               dbl     783 46575. 36300 
5 graduate                 dbl     530 59746. 43560 


Each row now describes an educational group rather than a variable. Its n counts group members with reported income; a recorded degree does not guarantee a recorded income. Median family income rises at every step of education, from $7,714 among respondents without a high school diploma to $43,560 among those with a graduate degree. In every group, the mean is above the median, consistent with high incomes pulling the mean upward. Comparing the two measures helps show why a mean alone can give an incomplete description.
Two cautions apply to these descriptions:

They describe associations in a sample. They do not show that a degree causes higher income.
They are unweighted sample statistics: each respondent contributes equally. A survey weight changes a record’s contribution to account for how the sample represents the population. The GSS provides such weights; using them is beyond this edition and planned for later teaching.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
9.5 Chapter review

summ() describes variables and reports the number of observed values contributing to each calculation.
mean() and median() describe center, while sd() describes spread in the variable’s units.
min() and max() identify extremes; quantile() locates positions such as the lower and upper quartiles.
Check each statistic’s contributing count; excluding missing inputs changes a calculation without replacing missing answers.
tabstat() compares selected statistics across groups; .by identifies groups and .stat chooses the reported statistics.
Optional: summarise() defines custom calculations; .detail requests additional statistics from summ(), and print() can widen the display.

Check units, column types, and non-missing counts before interpreting these unweighted sample summaries. Next, Chapter 10 examines item and joint coverage. Graphs in Chapter 11 then explore distributions and relationships.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
9.6 Exercises

Explain why mean(gss24$age) returns NA, correct the calculation, and compare its result and contributing sample with summ(gss24, age). Then compare mean and median family income. Choose a measure for a description of typical income, and report its count, units, and interpretation.
Use the abstract values c(2, 4, 6, 8) to predict the median before running the code. Find the lower and upper quartiles separately from the median. Why need a cutpoint not equal a recorded value? Then calculate the median and quartiles of recorded GSS schooling in years.
Compare family income across recorded marital-status categories with tabstat(). Report counts, means, and medians. Explain why a row counts income reporters within a category rather than all its members, and why neither the largest mean nor the largest count establishes a causal relationship.
A researcher compares the standard deviation of age with the standard deviation of income and concludes that income is more variable because its number is larger. Another averages id to describe a typical respondent. Diagnose both claims using the meanings of the columns. If you read the optional standard-error section, explain why a smaller standard error does not imply that respondents have more similar ages.

title: 9  Summarize data
text:
Worked answers






NoteDiagnose and interpret





Start a fresh session, load the packages, and restore the prepared GSS extract:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


mean(answer_gss24$age)

[1] NA

mean(answer_gss24$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 49.03421

summ(answer_gss24, age)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3859     72    18  49.0  17.7    89

summ(answer_gss24, realinc, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  type      n   mean median
  <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 dbl    3563 34252. 24502.


Missing ages make the first mean NA. The corrected mean agrees with summ() and uses its reported non-missing count; neither replaces missing ages. For income, the median describes the middle recorded family income because high values pull the mean upward. Among 3,563 income reporters, the median is $24,502, compared with the mean of $34,252. Both use constant 1986 dollars and describe unweighted reported family income. A mean remains appropriate when the question explicitly concerns the arithmetic average.









NoteLocate ordered positions





Start a fresh session, load the packages, and restore the prepared GSS extract:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_values <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
sort(answer_values)

[1] 2 4 6 8

median(answer_values)

[1] 5

quantile(answer_values, c(.25, .75))

25% 75% 
3.5 6.5 

median(answer_gss24$educ, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 14

quantile(answer_gss24$educ, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)

25% 75% 
 12  16 

summ(answer_gss24, educ)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3952     21     0  14.2  2.92    20


The abstract median is 5, midway between 4 and 6. The quartiles are 3.5 and 6.5 under R’s default interpolation, so neither needs to be an input value. GSS schooling cutpoints describe positions among respondents with recorded completed years; n supplies their contributing count. A lower quartile of schooling is a position in that distribution, not one quarter of its largest recorded years. Default quantile() cutpoints can differ from summ()’s Stata percentile rule.









NoteAdapt a group comparison





Start a fresh session, load the packages, and restore the prepared GSS extract:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


tabstat(answer_gss24, realinc, .by = marital,
        .stat = c("n", "mean", "median"), .missing = FALSE)
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  marital       type      n   mean median
  <fct>         <chr> <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 married       dbl    1492 49107. 36300 
2 widowed       dbl     227 21084. 13612.
3 divorced      dbl     537 23857. 16335 
4 separated     dbl     118 21644. 14974.
5 never married dbl    1181 23974. 16335 

tab(answer_gss24, marital)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  marital           n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 married        1659  41.6    41.6 41.8       41.8
2 widowed         269   6.75   48.4  6.77      48.6
3 divorced        579  14.5    62.9 14.6       63.1
4 separated       130   3.26   66.2  3.27      66.4
5 never married  1334  33.5    99.6 33.6      100  
6 NA               15   0.376 100   NA         NA  


Each summary row identifies a recorded marital-status category. Its n counts people in that category who also reported income; the frequency table counts everyone in the category. Income means and medians are in constant 1986 dollars. Group size describes how many observations contribute, and the summaries describe the observed distribution. Neither establishes that changing marital status would cause income to change. Differences in ages and other circumstances may also matter.









NoteCheck meaning before magnitude





Start a fresh session, load the packages, and restore the prepared GSS extract:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


summ(answer_gss24, age, realinc)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name    type      n unique   min    mean      sd     max
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     72   18     49.0    17.7     89 
2 realinc dbl    3563     26  182. 34252.  34697.  117565.

summ(answer_gss24, id)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 int    3986   3986     1 1994. 1151.  3986


Age is measured in years and income in constant 1986 dollars. Their standard deviations retain those units, so comparing the printed magnitudes does not give a unit-free ranking of variation. An ID identifies a record; its arithmetic average changes if we renumber respondents and has no substantive interpretation. In the optional section, standard deviation describes differences among individual ages, while standard error describes the sampling variability of an estimated mean under a stated model. More observations can reduce standard error while leaving individual variation unchanged.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.1 Recognize an unknown value
A missing answer is not a known zero or a negative answer. This lesson explains the NA values encountered in summaries and revisits the explicit selection decisions introduced in Section 6.4. We begin with plain values, then inspect missing questionnaire answers using the prepared GSS extract.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
The first examples use base R and need no packages. The survey application uses selection, filtering, and the tabulations and summaries already taught; creating new variables is not a prerequisite.
Use NA to represent a missing value. In the next example, >= asks whether a value is at least 5, and / divides it by 2. A known comparison returns TRUE or FALSE; an unknown answer is NA:
x <- NA
x >= 5

[1] NA

x / 2

[1] NA
Both results are NA. We cannot determine whether an unknown value is at least 5 or calculate half of it. Missing is different from FALSE, which says a condition is known not to hold, and from zero, which is a known number.
Use is.na() to ask whether a value is missing. The comparison operator == tests equality; it does not assign a value:
is.na(x)

[1] TRUE

x == NA

[1] NA

is.na("NA")

[1] FALSE
is.na(x) returns TRUE. Comparing a value with NA using == returns NA, because equality with an unknown value cannot be established. The literal string "NA" has two known characters, so its missingness test is FALSE.
c() combines values in their written order. A vector can contain both known and missing values:
c(2, NA, 6) >= 5

[1] FALSE    NA  TRUE
The results are FALSE, NA, and TRUE. The middle position retains an unknown answer.
As Section 7.3.1 and Chapter 9 showed, na.rm = TRUE excludes missing inputs from a calculation. It does not fill in missing values or delete rows from the source. Report the number of observed answers alongside a summary.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.2 Inspect questionnaire coverage
Does each summary describe the same respondents? Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


10.2.1 Begin with one measurement
Family income is unavailable for some respondents. misstable() from tidystata takes a table and selected columns and returns a coverage report. Begin with one variable, realinc, family income in constant 1986 dollars:

misstable(gss24, realinc)
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 realinc     423     10.6    3563


valid_n counts recorded incomes and miss_n counts missing incomes. They add to the total number of respondents. miss_pct divides the missing count by all respondents and expresses it on a 0–100 scale. The report does not fill values or change gss24. By default, misstable() displays selected variables that have missing values.


10.2.2 Compare groups
An overall missing percentage can conceal unequal coverage. Add .by = degree to report missing and observed incomes separately within each educational group:

misstable(gss24, realinc, .by = degree)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  degree                   variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <fct>                    <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 less than high school    realinc      75    20.7      287
2 high school              realinc     196    10.8     1621
3 associate/junior college realinc      24     6.67     336
4 bachelor's               realinc      80     9.27     783
5 graduate                 realinc      47     8.15     530
6 NA                       realinc       1    14.3        6


Each row now describes income coverage in a degree category. Its miss_pct uses all respondents in that category as its denominator. A missing degree is a separate group. These percentages therefore answer a within-group question, rather than using everyone in the extract as a common denominator.
The .all = TRUE option keeps every requested variable in each group, including groups without missing measurements. It controls which report rows appear, not which respondents are in the data. Save the complete report for comparison:

income_by_degree <- misstable(gss24, realinc, .by = degree, .all = TRUE)
income_by_degree
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  degree                   variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <fct>                    <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 less than high school    realinc      75    20.7      287
2 high school              realinc     196    10.8     1621
3 associate/junior college realinc      24     6.67     336
4 bachelor's               realinc      80     9.27     783
5 graduate                 realinc      47     8.15     530
6 NA                       realinc       1    14.3        6


For every row, valid_n + miss_n gives the group’s total, including people whose income is unavailable. These 0–100 missing percentages differ from the 0–1 valid_pct proportions shown by summ(). The original gss24 remains unchanged.
Income is missing more often among respondents without a high school diploma (20.7%) than among those with a graduate degree (8.1%). The income comparisons in Section 9.4 describe income reporters within each group. Unequal coverage does not establish why answers are missing or what unreported incomes would have been.


10.2.3 Check the confidence items
Keep ID and the three confidence items used again in the variable-manipulation lessons. The same misstable() reports their missingness without changing the source:

confidence_coverage <- gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
misstable(confidence_coverage, conbus:conmedic)
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 conbus     1398     35.1    2588
2 coneduc    1372     34.4    2614
3 conmedic   1376     34.5    2610

tab(confidence_coverage, conbus)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  conbus           n percent    cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>        <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 a great deal   372    9.33   9.33  14.4      14.4
2 only some     1555   39.0   48.3   60.1      74.5
3 hardly any     661   16.6   64.9   25.5     100  
4 NA            1398   35.1  100     NA        NA  


The missing row in the frequency table is separate from every recorded response, including “hardly any” confidence. The percent column uses all 3986 respondents. The valid column excludes missing answers and describes those with a recorded response to that item. Items with different coverage can therefore have different valid-response denominators.
Inspect recorded and missing answers separately using the familiar filter():

observed_business <- confidence_coverage |>
  filter(!is.na(conbus))
missing_business <- confidence_coverage |>
  filter(is.na(conbus))
head(missing_business)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id conbus coneduc conmedic
  <int> <fct>  <fct>   <fct>   
1     4 NA     NA      NA      
2    10 NA     NA      NA      
3    15 NA     NA      NA      
4    16 NA     NA      NA      
5    18 NA     NA      NA      
6    20 NA     NA      NA      

nrow(observed_business)

[1] 2588

nrow(missing_business)

[1] 1398

nrow(observed_business) + nrow(missing_business)

[1] 3986


There are 2588 recorded answers and 1398 missing answers, together accounting for all respondents. A missing business-confidence answer does not determine whether education or medicine was answered. Read those columns alongside it. Selecting recorded business answers changes who remains; it does not recover the unavailable answers.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.3 Check joint coverage
The graph in Chapter 11 will place each respondent using schooling and family income. Having either answer alone is insufficient: both coordinates must be known. summ() reports each variable’s recorded count separately:

nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986

summ(gss24, educ, realinc)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name    type      n unique   min    mean       sd     max
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 educ    dbl    3952     21    0     14.2     2.92     20 
2 realinc dbl    3563     26  182. 34252.  34697.   117565.


Schooling is recorded for 3952 respondents and income for 3563. These marginal counts do not identify how many respondents have both. Even the smaller count could include people missing the other measurement.
Use the familiar filter() with two conditions separated by a comma to require both recorded answers. $ is unnecessary inside filter() because column names refer to its input table:

schooling_income <- gss24 |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(realinc))
nrow(schooling_income)

[1] 3551


There are 3551 respondents with both measurements. The selection retains their original IDs and columns. It does not change gss24, replace a missing income with zero, or make a claim about the excluded people’s income.
To account for everyone else, select respondents missing schooling or income. | includes either condition and also those missing both. The two selections do not overlap:

incomplete_schooling_income <- gss24 |>
  filter(is.na(educ) | is.na(realinc))
nrow(incomplete_schooling_income)

[1] 435

nrow(schooling_income) + nrow(incomplete_schooling_income)

[1] 3986

nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986


The 435 respondents missing at least one measurement and the 3551 complete pairs together account for every respondent. The count applies to this pair of variables. A different pair, such as age and income, can have a different set of complete observations.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.4 Interpret source missingness
Survey files may distinguish “don’t know”, refusal, questions not asked, and other unavailable responses with designated codes or labelled missing values. Their meanings come from the questionnaire and codebook, not from whether the stored number is negative. A negative number can be a valid measurement in another variable.
The appendix preparation converts the GSS source missing values to NA. The saved extract does not retain every original reason, so this table cannot separate refusal from a question absent on a respondent’s questionnaire. Consult the original documentation and preparation recipe when the reason matters. Do not invent numeric missing codes in the prepared extract or reinterpret unavailable answers as “hardly any” confidence.
Replacing missing values with zero asserts a known quantity or a known negative response. That requires evidence from the question’s recording rules. It is not a general data-cleaning step. Likewise, na.rm = TRUE excludes unavailable measurements from a calculation; it does not explain why they are missing or establish that the observed answers represent everyone.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.5 Review

NA represents an unknown value, distinct from zero, FALSE, and the text "NA".
is.na() tests for missingness; equality with NA does not.
Calculations and comparisons can preserve unknown inputs as unknown results.
misstable() describes overall and grouped coverage; frequency tables distinguish missing answers from recorded categories.
Separate recorded counts do not establish joint availability. Select both required measurements explicitly before counting complete pairs.
State whether a denominator includes everyone or only recorded answers. Source documentation determines what designated missing codes mean.

Section 6.4 provided the selection conditions used here. The next chapter, Chapter 11, uses joint availability to identify its plotting sample. Chapter 13 later checks missingness across a block of items.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
10.6 Exercises

Explain the results of is.na(NA), NA == NA, and is.na("NA"). Why are zero and FALSE different from a missing value?
Reload the GSS extract, select ID and the three confidence items, and inspect missingness. For confidence in education, count recorded and missing answers separately. Which denominator does the frequency table’s valid column use?
A researcher replaces every missing confidence answer with “hardly any”, saying this simply cleans the data. Explain the substantive change.
