Can the saved extract identify which missing answers were refusals? Then inspect income coverage by degree. Why can two degree groups have different coverage percentages even if they have the same missing count?
Adapt the joint-coverage check to age and family income. Save complete and incomplete selections, count them, and verify that they account for every respondent. Explain why the separate summary counts alone do not supply the complete-pair count.

title: 10  Missing values
text:
Worked answers






NoteUnknown values and literal text






is.na(NA)

[1] TRUE

NA == NA

[1] NA

is.na("NA")

[1] FALSE


The results are TRUE, NA, and FALSE. The middle comparison cannot establish equality with an unknown value. The last input is known text. Zero is a known number and FALSE is a known logical result; neither means that the answer is unavailable.









NoteCount recorded and missing answers





Load the packages and saved extract in a fresh session:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_items <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
misstable(answer_items, conbus:conmedic)
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 conbus     1398     35.1    2588
2 coneduc    1372     34.4    2614
3 conmedic   1376     34.5    2610

answer_recorded <- answer_items |>
  filter(!is.na(coneduc))
answer_missing <- answer_items |>
  filter(is.na(coneduc))
nrow(answer_recorded)

[1] 2614

nrow(answer_missing)

[1] 1372

nrow(answer_recorded) + nrow(answer_missing) == nrow(answer_items)

[1] TRUE

tab(answer_items, coneduc)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  coneduc          n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>        <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 a great deal   513    12.9  12.9  19.6      19.6
2 only some     1479    37.1  50.0  56.6      76.2
3 hardly any     622    15.6  65.6  23.8     100  
4 NA            1372    34.4 100    NA        NA  


The final equality is TRUE. Valid percentages use the 2614 recorded education-confidence answers, whereas overall percentages include all 3986 respondents. Excluding missing answers changes the denominator without filling any response.









NoteDistinguish cleaning from an assumption





The replacement assigns the lowest confidence category to people whose answer is unavailable. It changes both category counts and the set treated as having answered. The prepared extract does not retain every original missing-value reason, so it cannot identify refusals from NA alone. The questionnaire and original source coding must justify any treatment of those reasons.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


misstable(answer_gss24, realinc, .by = degree, .all = TRUE)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  degree                   variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
  <fct>                    <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
1 less than high school    realinc      75    20.7      287
2 high school              realinc     196    10.8     1621
3 associate/junior college realinc      24     6.67     336
4 bachelor's               realinc      80     9.27     783
5 graduate                 realinc      47     8.15     530
6 NA                       realinc       1    14.3        6


Each group’s denominator is its own total. The same missing count produces a larger missing percentage in a smaller group. A coverage difference alone cannot tell us what caused missing answers or what their values would have been.









NoteAccount for a pair of measurements





Restore the source independently before selecting the two sets:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_complete <- answer_gss24 |>
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(realinc))
answer_incomplete <- answer_gss24 |>
  filter(is.na(age) | is.na(realinc))
nrow(answer_complete)

[1] 3496

nrow(answer_incomplete)

[1] 490

nrow(answer_complete) + nrow(answer_incomplete) == nrow(answer_gss24)

[1] TRUE

summ(answer_gss24, age, realinc)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name    type      n unique   min    mean      sd     max
  <chr>   <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 age     dbl    3859     72   18     49.0    17.7     89 
2 realinc dbl    3563     26  182. 34252.  34697.  117565.


The final equality is TRUE: complete pairs and respondents missing at least one answer partition the source. Separate n values in summ() do not say which people provided both answers. Each selection retains original source values in respondent order; neither changes answer_gss24 or recovers an unavailable measurement.

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
11.1 Schooling and family income
A graph can reveal a pattern that a mean or percentage alone does not show. A scatterplot shows how two numerical variables vary together; a histogram shows the distribution of a numerical variable; a bar chart compares categories. Begin with a question about the observations, then choose marks that represent the quantities you want to compare.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
The examples build on inspecting datasets, frequency tables from Chapter 8, and numerical summaries from Chapter 9. We introduce the plotting syntax here, using complete datasets as inputs. The introductory illustration is not a prerequisite. Later, Chapter 22 develops grouped figures, annual trends, presentation choices, and export.
Load tidyverse, which includes ggplot2, and tidystata, which supplies summ() and tab(). All examples use the prepared GSS extract introduced in Chapter 8. With gss24.rds saved in your project folder, readRDS() restores that saved R object; <- assigns it the name gss24. Appendix A gives the preparation recipe.
Do respondents with more schooling tend to report higher family incomes? In the same gss24 extract used for tables and summaries, educ records completed years of schooling and realinc records family income in constant 1986 dollars. Family income is based on brackets rather than exact dollar answers. Each point will represent a respondent with both coordinates recorded. Reuse the joint-coverage check from Section 10.3:
schooling_income <- gss24 |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(realinc))
nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986

nrow(schooling_income)

[1] 3551
The plot can position 3551 of 3986 respondents. We will supply the full source to the layer and explicitly omit unavailable coordinates; this has the same contributing sample as the checked selection. Missing income remains unknown.
A mapping connects a variable to a graphical role. aes() creates those instructions. Here x = educ means that horizontal positions use schooling, and y = realinc means that vertical positions use family income. The unquoted names identify columns that the plot will find in its dataset:
survey_mapping <- aes(x = educ, y = realinc)
Assignment saves the two mapping instructions. They do not calculate income differences, modify the table, or draw a graph.
ggplot() receives the dataset and those mappings and returns a plot object. It establishes the plot’s inputs before choosing how to draw observations:
survey_plot <- ggplot(gss24, survey_mapping)
The saved object has data and axis instructions, but no marks yet. A geometric layer chooses those marks. geom_point() adds one point for each row with both coordinates available. The + operator adds a layer to a plot; put it at the end of a continued line. Assign the updated result to keep the addition.
Set na.rm = TRUE in this layer to omit respondents that cannot be positioned because a coordinate is missing. This avoids a warning about that explained omission without changing gss24. color outside aes() sets one appearance for all points; the hexadecimal value specifies the book’s blue:
survey_plot <- survey_plot +
  geom_point(color = "#2B6487", na.rm = TRUE)
The plot now has points, but assignment keeps it from displaying before its labels are ready. Only the variables in aes() determine positions here; the fixed color does not represent another variable.
labs() supplies readable labels: its x and y arguments name the axes. Adding these labels to the saved object returns an updated plot, which we assign again. Type the object’s name only after this last step to display the labelled graph. Its caption identifies the survey and contributing sample.
survey_plot <- survey_plot +
  labs(
    x = "Completed years of schooling",
    y = "Family income (constant 1986 dollars)"
  )
survey_plot







Figure 11.1: Schooling and family income among GSS 2024 respondents with both measurements. Each point represents a respondent; repeated values overlap. Family income is in constant 1986 dollars.
Figure 11.1 shows substantial income variation at the same schooling level. A horizontal distance measures years of schooling; a vertical distance measures constant-dollar family income. Schooling is recorded in whole years and income has only 26 recorded values, so multiple respondents occupy the same coordinates. The visible dots therefore understate the number of respondents: a dot’s darkness or size does not count how many overlap. The grouped summaries in Section 9.4 make the income differences across educational groups easier to assess; this simple scatterplot does not display the frequency at each position.
This graph describes an unweighted association in the observed sample. It does not show that schooling causes a particular income increase, describe individual earnings, or establish the relationship in the population. We retain the same GSS extract for the age distributions and marital-status comparison below. The contributing respondents can differ because each plot uses the answers recorded for its own variables.

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
11.2 A distribution of ages
How are ages distributed among the GSS respondents with a recorded age? A histogram groups a numerical variable into adjacent intervals and counts observations in each interval. geom_histogram() supplies those counts, so we map only x = age. Its binwidth argument chooses the interval width in the units of age, here years. boundary = 0 aligns interval boundaries with multiples of that width. A boundary observation is assigned to one interval rather than counted twice.
First check how many ages are recorded. nrow() counts all respondents in the extract, while the summary’s n counts non-missing ages.

nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986

summ(gss24, age)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3859     72    18  49.0  17.7    89


The histograms will use 3859 of 3986 respondents, leaving out 127 whose age is missing. Both layers use na.rm = TRUE, so they omit the same missing ages from their counts. This does not change the saved extract.
Begin with five-year intervals. fill sets the interior color of the bars and color their outlines; both are constants outside aes(). We reuse the familiar one-variable mapping and plot construction, then add the new geom_histogram() layer:

age_plot_5 <- ggplot(gss24, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, na.rm = TRUE,
    fill = "#E3EDF5", color = "#2B6487"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Respondents")

Each bar will count recorded ages in a five-year interval, with boundaries aligned to multiples of five. With these defaults, a shared boundary belongs to the interval ending there: age 20 goes in the interval above 15 through 20, while age 21 goes in the next interval. Adjacent intervals therefore do not count age 20 twice. Assignment saves the labelled plot for the captioned comparison below.
Now change only binwidth to 10. With boundary = 0 unchanged, the new intervals follow multiples of ten. The data, missing-age rule, and axis labels stay the same:

age_plot_10 <- ggplot(gss24, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, na.rm = TRUE,
    fill = "#E3EDF5", color = "#2B6487"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Respondents")

A ten-year interval spans two adjacent five-year intervals. Predict how combining those counts changes bar heights before reading the two panels. Both finished objects remain available for reuse.
age_plot_5
age_plot_10












(a) Five-year intervals.













(b) Ten-year intervals.








Figure 11.2: Age among GSS 2024 respondents with a recorded age: five-year intervals in panel (a) and ten-year intervals in panel (b). Both histograms use the same unweighted respondents.



Both panels describe the same 3859 respondents. The ten-year bars generally contain more respondents because they span wider intervals, not because the second graph has a larger sample. The narrower intervals reveal more local variation; the wider intervals make broader patterns easier to see. Neither choice recovers information about people outside the sample or resolves missing ages.
The y-axis shows counts, not percentages. These are unweighted sample distributions. When presenting one version, state the interval width and keep it appropriate to the question. Do not change the width simply to make a distribution look smoother or more uneven without explaining the comparison.

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
11.3 Income across degrees [Optional]
How much income variation lies behind the educational-group summaries in Section 9.4? A boxplot compares numerical distributions across categories. Keep respondents with both income and degree recorded, then check each group’s contributing count with the familiar tabstat():

income_degree <- gss24 |>
  filter(!is.na(degree), !is.na(realinc))
tabstat(income_degree, realinc, .by = degree,
        .stat = "n", .missing = FALSE)
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  degree                   type      n
  <fct>                    <chr> <int>
1 less than high school    dbl     287
2 high school              dbl    1621
3 associate/junior college dbl     336
4 bachelor's               dbl     783
5 graduate                 dbl     530


The plot uses 3557 of 3986 respondents. The five degree categories already have readable labels and their source order; no category construction is needed. Group sizes differ, so equally wide boxes will not mean equally many respondents.
Map income horizontally and degree vertically. geom_boxplot() calculates a separate box for each degree. Its line marks the median; its ends mark the lower and upper quartiles, locating the middle half by ordered positions. The interquartile range (IQR) is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile. Each whisker reaches the furthest observed value within 1.5 IQR below the lower quartile or above the upper quartile. Whiskers need not reach those limits exactly. Values beyond them appear as separate points.

income_degree_plot <- ggplot(income_degree, aes(x = realinc, y = degree)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#E3EDF5", color = "#2B6487") +
  labs(x = "Family income (constant 1986 dollars)", y = "Highest degree")
income_degree_plot







Figure 11.3: Recorded family income by highest degree among GSS 2024 respondents with both answers. Boxes and points describe unweighted respondents; income is in constant 1986 dollars.





Figure 11.3 shows higher medians alongside overlapping income ranges. Income comes from brackets, producing repeated values; the plot cannot recover variation within a bracket. Ties can place more than half the observations inside a box, and repeated points can overlap. Graduate respondents have no points beyond their whiskers, although their recorded incomes extend high. These points follow a group-specific rule; they are not automatic errors or a list of everyone with high income. The comparison describes this unweighted sample, not a causal effect of education.

title: 11  Visualize data
section: 11.4 Turn a frequency table into bars
text:
11.4 Turn a frequency table into bars
What proportion of respondents with a recorded marital-status answer belong to each category? Begin with the familiar tab(). Supply gss24 and marital directly, then store the returned frequency table as marital_table.

marital_table <- tab(gss24, marital)
marital_table
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  marital           n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 married        1659  41.6    41.6 41.8       41.8
2 widowed         269   6.75   48.4  6.77      48.6
3 divorced        579  14.5    62.9 14.6       63.1
4 separated       130   3.26   66.2  3.27      66.4
5 never married  1334  33.5    99.6 33.6      100  
6 NA               15   0.376 100   NA         NA  


Each row represents a marital-status category, rather than an individual respondent. As in Chapter 8, percent uses every respondent as its denominator; valid uses only recorded answers. We want valid, whose denominator is 3971 respondents. The missing row counts the other 15 respondents, but its valid value is NA because it is not a recorded marital-status answer.
geom_col() draws bars whose lengths are already in the data. Map x = valid for bar length and y = marital for the category label. This horizontal arrangement gives the words room. By contrast, geom_histogram() calculated counts from individual numerical observations. Here the frequency table has already calculated the percentages.
Set na.rm = TRUE in geom_col() to omit the missing row’s undefined bar length. The missing label retains an empty position on the category axis, but has no bar. The valid percentages already exclude these respondents from their denominator; omitting the undefined bar does not recalculate the table.

marital_plot <- ggplot(marital_table, aes(x = valid, y = marital)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#236862", na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Percent of valid answers", y = "Marital status")
marital_plot







Figure 11.4: Marital status among GSS 2024 respondents with a recorded answer. Bar lengths are unweighted percentages of valid answers; the missing row has no valid percentage and no bar.





Figure 11.4 shows that married and never-married respondents make up the two largest categories among valid answers. Their percentages, together with those of the other recorded categories, add to 100 apart from rounding. They describe this sample without survey weights. Mapping percent instead would answer a different question because its denominator includes missing answers.
Do not count the rows of marital_table to estimate how many respondents are married. One table row can summarize many people. Supplying category counts to a layer that counts rows again would discard the work already done by the frequency table. Check that the axis names the quantity actually mapped, whether count or percentage.

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
11.5 Review

ggplot() receives data, aes() maps variables, and geometric layers determine how observations are drawn.
geom_point() shows relationships, while geom_histogram() counts numerical observations within chosen intervals.
geom_col() draws precomputed values, so a percentage chart inherits its table’s denominator.
Optional: geom_boxplot() compares distributions using medians, quartiles, whiskers, and points beyond whiskers.
labs() supplies readable labels, and constants outside aes() set a shared appearance.
na.rm = TRUE omits missing values needed by a layer; it does not replace them or change the source dataset.
A graph’s interpretation depends on its observations, units, interval widths, and denominators.

We can now inspect, tabulate, summarize, and graph a dataset. The next part begins with Chapter 12, which creates and changes columns within a table. Chapter 22 later builds on these first plots to construct grouped figures and export them.

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
11.6 Exercises

Read Figure 11.1. What do its horizontal and vertical distances mean? Can one visible point stand for several respondents? State the contributing sample and explain why the graph cannot establish a causal effect or identify individual earnings.
Recreate the GSS age summaries and two histogram objects, using widths of five and ten years. Predict which plot will use more respondents and why its bar heights can differ. Retain the same interval boundary in both, then compare your predictions with the figures.
Recreate the marital-status frequency table and valid-percentage bar object from a fresh GSS import. Identify its denominator. Predict what changes if you map percent instead of valid, including the missing row, then create that alternative with a matching axis label.
A researcher counts rows in marital_table and reports that count as the number of married respondents. Another adds geom_histogram() to this table to plot its already calculated percentages. Diagnose both errors. Which object supplies respondents, which supplies categories, and which taught layer should draw precomputed percentages?

title: 11  Visualize data
text:
Worked answers






NoteInterpret the plotted observations





Horizontal differences represent completed years of schooling; vertical differences represent family income in constant 1986 dollars. Repeated schooling and bracket-based income values put multiple respondents at exactly the same location, so visible dots do not count respondents. The graph uses people with both measurements recorded, as checked in Section 10.3. It describes an unweighted sample association in reported family income. It does not isolate a schooling effect from other differences, represent individual earnings, or supply a survey-weighted population relationship.









NoteChange intervals, retain people





Load the prepared extract independently from the saved file in your project folder.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


summ(answer_gss24, age)
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 dbl    3859     72    18  49.0  17.7    89

answer_age_5 <- ggplot(answer_gss24, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, na.rm = TRUE,
                 fill = "#E3EDF5", color = "#2B6487") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Respondents")
answer_age_10 <- ggplot(answer_gss24, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, na.rm = TRUE,
                 fill = "#E3EDF5", color = "#2B6487") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Respondents")

Both use all 3859 respondents with a recorded age. A wider interval collects more ages into each bar and uses fewer bars. The interval choice changes how those same respondents are grouped; it does not add people. Compare shape with that changed grouping in mind.
answer_age_5
answer_age_10











(a) Five-year intervals.











(b) Ten-year intervals.







Figure 11.5: The same recorded GSS ages grouped into five-year and ten-year intervals.












NotePredict a denominator change





Use a fresh GSS import and load the package supplying tab().

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_marital <- tab(answer_gss24, marital)
answer_marital
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  marital           n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 married        1659  41.6    41.6 41.8       41.8
2 widowed         269   6.75   48.4  6.77      48.6
3 divorced        579  14.5    62.9 14.6       63.1
4 separated       130   3.26   66.2  3.27      66.4
5 never married  1334  33.5    99.6 33.6      100  
6 NA               15   0.376 100   NA         NA  

nrow(answer_gss24)

[1] 3986

nrow(answer_marital)

[1] 6

answer_marital_plot <- ggplot(answer_marital, aes(x = valid, y = marital)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#236862", na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Percent of valid answers", y = "Marital status")

For a comparison that uses all respondents, map percent instead, and change the axis label to state that denominator:

answer_overall_plot <- ggplot(answer_marital, aes(x = percent, y = marital)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#236862", na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Percent of all respondents", y = "Marital status")

The recorded categories’ overall percentages sum to less than 100 because missing answers occupy the remaining share. The missing row now has a known overall percentage and receives a bar. The source frequency table is unchanged.
The denominator for valid is 3971 respondents with a recorded marital-status answer. The table has 6 rows: five recorded categories and one missing row. Each row summarizes a different number of respondents. Counting those rows describes categories, not people. geom_col() preserves the valid percentages; its missing-value argument omits the undefined bar, leaving its category position empty.
answer_marital_plot
answer_overall_plot











(a) Recorded answers.











(b) All respondents, including missing answers.







Figure 11.6: Marital-status percentages using recorded answers and all respondents as denominators.












NoteDiagnose the observation unit and layer





A row in gss24 represents one respondent; a row in marital_table summarizes a marital-status category. nrow(marital_table) therefore counts category rows, including the missing row, rather than married people. Read the married category’s n column in the frequency table for its respondent count.
geom_histogram() groups a numerical variable into intervals and counts input observations. The frequency table has already calculated the percentages we want to draw. Use geom_col() with x = valid and y = marital, as in Answer 3, and label the axis as percent of valid answers. That layer draws the precomputed values without counting category rows again. Changing layers alone does not choose a denominator; the mapped table column does.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.1 Renaming variables
A survey’s recorded answers are often the starting point for an analysis. Before calculating a new measure, we need to know how to name a column, add one, and retain the returned table. These operations should preserve the connection between a respondent and their answers.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We build on selecting columns and observations, sorting, and the pipe. Our data are the prepared 2024 GSS respondents. This chapter establishes the mechanics of changing columns and text. Chapter 13 next applies an operation to several columns, before Chapter 14 develops calculations and conditions. The optional programming chapters are not prerequisites.
Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:
Keep the ID, hours worked last week, and years of schooling. These are observed answers, including their original missing values:
There are 3986 respondents in work; only six are displayed. hrs1 refers to the previous week, not a respondent’s usual schedule or commuting time. Its missing values do not imply zero working hours. The examples below change table structure without changing the recorded answers.
The abbreviation hrs1 is concise but gives little information outside the codebook. rename() returns a table with changed column names. Write the new name on the left of = and the existing name on the right:
work |>
  rename(hours_last_week = hrs1)
# A tibble: 3,986 × 3
      id hours_last_week  educ
   <int>           <dbl> <dbl>
 1     1              43    16
 2     2              NA    16
 3     3              NA    14
 4     4              20    12
 5     5              NA    13
 6     6              NA    14
 7     7              80    13
 8     8              NA    14
 9     9              50    14
10    10              NA    12
# ℹ 3,976 more rows
The result replaces the heading hrs1 with hours_last_week. Values, row order, and dimensions are unchanged. work itself still uses hrs1, because we have not assigned the result back to it.
We can rename several columns in one call and save the returned table:
work_named <- work |>
  rename(hours_last_week = hrs1, schooling_years = educ)
work_named
# A tibble: 3,986 × 3
      id hours_last_week schooling_years
   <int>           <dbl>           <dbl>
 1     1              43              16
 2     2              NA              16
 3     3              NA              14
 4     4              20              12
 5     5              NA              13
 6     6              NA              14
 7     7              80              13
 8     8              NA              14
 9     9              50              14
10    10              NA              12
# ℹ 3,976 more rows
Both new names describe the existing quantities; renaming has not converted their units or changed any answer. The original ID remains alongside each respondent’s measurements.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.2 Creating and changing columns
mutate() takes a table and returns a table containing new or replaced columns. Bare names refer to existing columns. The expression to the right of = supplies values; the name on the left names the result. First copy the recorded hours into a separate column so that we can inspect the operation without changing the measurement:

work_copy <- work_named |>
  mutate(hours_copy = hours_last_week)
head(work_copy)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id hours_last_week schooling_years hours_copy
  <int>           <dbl>           <dbl>      <dbl>
1     1              43              16         43
2     2              NA              16         NA
3     3              NA              14         NA
4     4              20              12         20
5     5              NA              13         NA
6     6              NA              14         NA

ncol(work_copy)

[1] 4


The returned table has the same respondents and one additional column, hours_copy. Each copied value belongs to the respondent on that row. Missing hours remain missing, and the ID, original hours, and schooling values stay alongside the copy. mutate() does not sort or remove respondents. The copy demonstrates column creation; it is not a new measure for analysis.
Using an existing name replaces that column in the returned table rather than adding another column. Repeat the copy using the name that now exists:

work_copy |>
  mutate(hours_copy = hours_last_week)
# A tibble: 3,986 × 4
      id hours_last_week schooling_years hours_copy
   <int>           <dbl>           <dbl>      <dbl>
 1     1              43              16         43
 2     2              NA              16         NA
 3     3              NA              14         NA
 4     4              20              12         20
 5     5              NA              13         NA
 6     6              NA              14         NA
 7     7              80              13         80
 8     8              NA              14         NA
 9     9              50              14         50
10    10              NA              12         NA
# ℹ 3,976 more rows


The result still has four columns, because hours_copy already exists. Its values are unchanged in this particular demonstration because we copied the same source again. In an applied transformation, a different expression would supply replacement values. Check the meaning and unit of a replacement before saving it; Chapter 14 works through that decision with hours and minutes.
Assignment and column naming do different jobs. In work_copy <-, <- saves the entire returned table under an object name. Inside mutate(), hours_copy = names one column in that table. Neither call changes work_named: it still contains only the renamed original columns. Likewise, a pipeline that is printed without assignment returns a result but does not save it over its input.
Keep calculations inside the table whose rows supply their inputs. A column copied or calculated there stays aligned with its respondent. A separately sorted or filtered column may no longer have the same rows in the same order, even if its length looks plausible.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.3 Text
Quotation marks tell R to treat their contents as text, also called a character value or string. Even digits become text inside quotation marks:

12

[1] 12

"12"

[1] "12"


The first is numeric and the second is character. Printed quotation marks help distinguish them. A string may contain digits, spaces, or punctuation; it need not be a single letter. Use straight quotation marks in code, either single or double.
var_type() takes one object and returns its type without changing it:

var_type(12)

[1] "double"

var_type("12")

[1] "character"


The results are "double" and "character". A double is R’s usual numeric type, including fractional values such as 2.75. Quoted digits remain character values even when they look numeric.
paste() joins its inputs, inserting a space by default:

text <- "hello"
greeting <- paste(text, "R")
greeting

[1] "hello R"

text

[1] "hello"


The result is "hello R". The original text remains "hello"; the joined string is stored separately as greeting.
Joining text can change how missingness appears. Consider an abstract label whose second component is unknown:

missing_component <- NA_character_
missing_label <- paste("Label:", missing_component)
missing_label

[1] "Label: NA"

is.na(missing_component)

[1] TRUE

is.na(missing_label)

[1] FALSE


NA_character_ is a missing character value. The input check returns TRUE, but the joined label is the non-missing string "Label: NA", so its check returns FALSE. paste() has inserted visible text representing the unknown component. Checking only the finished label would miss that unavailable input. If a label requires every component, check their missingness before joining them; a readable string does not establish that all its information was recorded.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.4 Convert text and numbers
To convert numeric text explicitly, use as.numeric():

number_text <- "12"
number <- as.numeric(number_text)
number

[1] 12

var_type(number_text)

[1] "character"


The returned number is 12. Assignment stores it in number; the original number_text remains character. as.character() makes the reverse conversion:

as.character(number)

[1] "12"


It returns "12" without changing the numeric input. A string with no numeric representation cannot be converted successfully:

converted_text <- as.numeric("hello")

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

converted_text

[1] NA

is.na(converted_text)

[1] TRUE


R warns that NAs were introduced by coercion, its term for conversion. The output is NA, and is.na() returns TRUE. The failed conversion does not produce zero.
A conversion can succeed while losing part of the text:

code <- "01"
as.numeric(code)

[1] 1

code

[1] "01"


The converted result is 1, losing the leading zero. The original remains "01" because we did not overwrite it. Keep identifiers as text when their formatting matters. Keep a field’s meaning in view: numeric-looking identifiers and category codes are not automatically quantities to average. Chapter 15 develops factor levels and labelled survey scores later.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.5 Prepare descriptive text
Extra spaces can prevent two otherwise identical labels from matching. str_squish() receives character values and returns character values with surrounding whitespace removed and repeated internal whitespace reduced to one space. It does not change an object unless we assign its result. Use a plain phrase to make the spacing rule visible:

spacing_example <- "  A   short phrase  "
spacing_example

[1] "  A   short phrase  "

str_squish(spacing_example)

[1] "A short phrase"


The quotation marks show where the original spaces occur. The returned phrase keeps the words and their order. This is a syntax demonstration with plain text. Spaces can be meaningful in identifiers, so inspecting the source and understanding its coding rules should precede any automatic cleaning.
Case is another feature of text. str_to_lower() returns a lowercase version without changing the supplied object:

case_example <- "A Short Phrase"
str_to_lower(case_example)

[1] "a short phrase"

case_example

[1] "A Short Phrase"


The result is "a short phrase"; the original retains its capitals. Lowercasing can provide a consistent search form. Neither spacing changes nor a consistent case establishes that two records identify the same person.

12.5.1 Labels from recorded answers
Can we describe respondents by their recorded sex and highest degree without changing those source answers? Select the three columns together so their rows remain aligned:

respondent_labels <- gss24 |>
  select(id, sex, degree)
head(respondent_labels)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id sex    degree                  
  <int> <fct>  <fct>                   
1     1 male   bachelor's              
2     2 male   graduate                
3     3 female associate/junior college
4     4 male   high school             
5     5 female high school             
6     6 male   associate/junior college


id identifies the respondent. sex and degree are the prepared category columns already encountered in the GSS tables. Use as.character() to obtain their displayed category text. Convert one column first and keep its source:

respondent_labels <- respondent_labels |>
  mutate(sex_text = as.character(sex))
head(respondent_labels)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id sex    degree                   sex_text
  <int> <fct>  <fct>                    <chr>   
1     1 male   bachelor's               male    
2     2 male   graduate                 male    
3     3 female associate/junior college female  
4     4 male   high school              male    
5     5 female high school              female  
6     6 male   associate/junior college male    


The new column contains the sex category names. Unknown answers remain missing. Repeat the same explicit conversion for degree:

respondent_labels <- respondent_labels |>
  mutate(degree_text = as.character(degree))
head(respondent_labels)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
     id sex    degree                   sex_text degree_text             
  <int> <fct>  <fct>                    <chr>    <chr>                   
1     1 male   bachelor's               male     bachelor's              
2     2 male   graduate                 male     graduate                
3     3 female associate/junior college female   associate/junior college
4     4 male   high school              male     high school             
5     5 female high school              female   high school             
6     6 male   associate/junior college male     associate/junior college


Both text columns have one value for every respondent, in the same order. We can therefore join these equal-length inputs row by row. sep = " / " replaces paste()’s default separating space with the supplied separator:

respondent_labels <- respondent_labels |>
  mutate(description = paste(sex_text, degree_text, sep = " / "))
head(respondent_labels)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
     id sex    degree                   sex_text degree_text         description
  <int> <fct>  <fct>                    <chr>    <chr>               <chr>      
1     1 male   bachelor's               male     bachelor's          male / bac…
2     2 male   graduate                 male     graduate            male / gra…
3     3 female associate/junior college female   associate/junior c… female / a…
4     4 male   high school              male     high school         male / hig…
5     5 female high school              female   high school         female / h…
6     6 male   associate/junior college male     associate/junior c… male / ass…


Each description combines the two answers belonging to that row. A label containing "NA" still has an unknown source component, as the plain-input example showed. Inspect the source answers when either component is required:

respondent_labels |>
  filter(is.na(sex) | is.na(degree)) |>
  head()
# A tibble: 6 × 6
     id sex   degree                sex_text degree_text           description  
  <int> <fct> <fct>                 <chr>    <chr>                 <chr>        
1    18 NA    high school           NA       high school           NA / high sc…
2   202 NA    graduate              NA       graduate              NA / graduate
3   307 NA    less than high school NA       less than high school NA / less th…
4   705 NA    less than high school NA       less than high school NA / less th…
5   954 male  NA                    male     NA                    male / NA    
6   998 NA    high school           NA       high school           NA / high sc…


The preview selects respondents with at least one unavailable input. It does not establish that the joined label itself is missing. We have retained every source answer so that this distinction remains checkable.
Do descriptions uniquely identify respondents? Use a familiar frequency table:

tab(respondent_labels, description)
# A tibble: 17 × 6

   <chr>                             <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>

Several respondents share each common sex-degree description. A category combination describes an observation; it does not replace id. Keep the recorded identifier and source categories alongside any description.
We can also prepare a separate search form using the two text operations just learned. Show each step before combining it with another operation:

respondent_labels <- respondent_labels |>
  mutate(description_search = str_squish(description))

This supplies a spacing rule; it does not claim that the recorded GSS categories contain a spacing error. Now lowercase only that derived search column:

respondent_labels <- respondent_labels |>
  mutate(description_search = str_to_lower(description_search))
head(respondent_labels)
# A tibble: 6 × 7

description remains available for display, and description_search follows a consistent search convention. Neither field establishes identity or resolves conflicting records. Chapter 15 later uses these tools with original country names and codes.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.6 Review

rename() changes column names without changing their values or row order.
mutate() adds a column when its output name is new and replaces a column when that name already exists.
A column expression uses values from the same row; preserve the connection to the observation’s ID.
Assignment saves the returned table. Printing a result leaves the input object unchanged.
as.numeric() and as.character() return explicit conversions; check failed conversions and formatting losses.
paste() joins aligned text inputs; a visible label can conceal a missing component and need not identify a respondent.
str_squish() and str_to_lower() prepare derived text while source values remain available.

Chapter 13 next applies an operation to several selected variables. Chapter 14 then uses these mechanics for calculations, indicators, and numeric recoding.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
12.7 Exercises

Keep ID and hours worked, then rename the hours column to hours_last_week. Save the result under a new object name. Explain whether this changes the recorded hours or the original table.
Copy hours_last_week into hours_copy in a saved result. Repeat that operation on the result. Explain why the first call adds a column, the second replaces one, and both preserve respondent order and unknown hours.
Diagnose conversions and joins. Convert "hello" to numeric and inspect the result. Convert "01" to numeric and compare it with the source string. Join "Label:" to a missing character input, then compare missingness checks on the input and output. Explain the warning, the lost zero, and the concealed missing component.
Keep id, sex, and degree; convert the two category columns to text separately and join their equal-length values into a descriptive label. Tabulate the labels and create a separate lowercase search form. Which columns must remain available to diagnose missing inputs? Explain why repeated descriptions cannot replace id.

title: 12  Create variables
text:
Worked answers






NoteRename and save





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_work <- gss24 |>
  select(id, hrs1)
answer_named <- answer_work |>
  rename(hours_last_week = hrs1)
head(answer_named)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
     id hours_last_week
  <int>           <dbl>
1     1              43
2     2              NA
3     3              NA
4     4              20
5     5              NA
6     6              NA

ds(answer_work)

[1] "id"   "hrs1"


answer_named contains the same IDs and hours under the clearer heading. answer_work still has the original hrs1 name. Renaming changes neither the reference period nor the values, including missing answers.









NoteNew and existing column names





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_named <- gss24 |>
  select(id, hrs1) |>
  rename(hours_last_week = hrs1)
answer_copy <- answer_named |>
  mutate(hours_copy = hours_last_week)
answer_replaced <- answer_copy |>
  mutate(hours_copy = hours_last_week)
head(answer_replaced)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id hours_last_week hours_copy
  <int>           <dbl>      <dbl>
1     1              43         43
2     2              NA         NA
3     3              NA         NA
4     4              20         20
5     5              NA         NA
6     6              NA         NA

ncol(answer_named)

[1] 2

ncol(answer_copy)

[1] 3

ncol(answer_replaced)

[1] 3


The column counts are two, three, and three. The first mutate() adds hours_copy; the second uses that existing name and therefore replaces it. Here both copies contain exactly the same source hours, so replacement changes no values. IDs and row order remain aligned, and unknown hours remain unknown in both columns. Saving each returned table makes it available without changing its input.









NoteDiagnose conversions and joins






converted_text <- as.numeric("hello")

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

converted_text

[1] NA

is.na(converted_text)

[1] TRUE

code <- "01"
as.numeric(code)

[1] 1

code

[1] "01"


The first conversion warns and returns NA, confirmed by TRUE from is.na(). The string has no numeric representation, so the conversion cannot return a known number such as zero. Converting "01" succeeds but returns 1, discarding its leading zero. The original text remains "01".

missing_component <- NA_character_
missing_label <- paste("Label:", missing_component)
missing_label

[1] "Label: NA"

is.na(missing_component)

[1] TRUE

is.na(missing_label)

[1] FALSE


The missing input gives TRUE, but "Label: NA" is a non-missing string, giving FALSE. Inspect the inputs before using a joined label as evidence of complete information.









NoteA description and an identifier





Load the saved extract in a fresh session:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_labels <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, sex, degree) |>
  mutate(sex_text = as.character(sex)) |>
  mutate(degree_text = as.character(degree)) |>
  mutate(description = paste(sex_text, degree_text, sep = " / ")) |>
  mutate(description_search = str_squish(description)) |>
  mutate(description_search = str_to_lower(description_search))
