title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.1 Begin with separate operations
A questionnaire often asks several questions with the same response format. We may need to inspect the same feature of each answer. Writing the operation once reduces repetition, but choosing the columns remains a research decision: similar names alone do not establish that questions belong together.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We use mutate() from Chapter 12, column selection from Chapter 3, and the familiar is.na() missingness test. Numeric recoding and factor construction are not prerequisites. Prepare the GSS extract following Appendix A, then restore it:
Which confidence answers are missing for each respondent? Select confidence in major companies, education, and medicine. Each row continues to represent one respondent:
confidence <- gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
head(confidence)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id conbus       coneduc      conmedic    
  <int> <fct>        <fct>        <fct>       
1     1 a great deal a great deal a great deal
2     2 only some    only some    a great deal
3     3 only some    a great deal a great deal
4     4 NA           NA           NA          
5     5 only some    hardly any   only some   
6     6 hardly any   only some    only some
First create one missingness flag per item using familiar commands. A flag is TRUE when the answer is missing and FALSE when it is recorded:
separate_flags <- confidence |>
  mutate(
    conbus_missing = is.na(conbus),
    coneduc_missing = is.na(coneduc),
    conmedic_missing = is.na(conmedic)
  )
head(separate_flags)
# A tibble: 6 × 7
     id conbus  coneduc conmedic conbus_missing coneduc_missing conmedic_missing
  <int> <fct>   <fct>   <fct>    <lgl>          <lgl>           <lgl>           
1     1 a grea… a grea… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
2     2 only s… only s… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
3     3 only s… a grea… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
4     4 NA      NA      NA       TRUE           TRUE            TRUE            
5     5 only s… hardly… only so… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
6     6 hardly… only s… only so… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE
The source answers remain beside three new logical columns. A flag describes whether an answer is available; it does not say why it is missing or whether the respondent has confidence in that institution. Some GSS items were not asked on every questionnaire.

title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.2 Apply one operation across columns
Inside mutate(), across() selects columns and applies the supplied function to each one. Its first argument uses the same column-selection rules as select(). The range conbus:conmedic contains exactly the three adjacent items selected above. As with the predicate supplied to where() in Section 4.1, pass the function itself without parentheses. Here across() calls is.na separately on each column and returns a missingness flag for every entry. Unlike column selection, this transforms the selected columns rather than deciding which complete columns to retain.
Before running the block operation, choose names for the results. The .names argument supplies a naming pattern. In "{.col}_missing", {.col} stands for each source column name and _missing adds a descriptive suffix. This creates new columns beside the source answers. Without this new naming pattern, mutate(across()) would replace the selected answers with flags:

confidence_flags <- confidence |>
  mutate(across(
    conbus:conmedic,
    is.na,
    .names = "{.col}_missing"
  ))
head(confidence_flags)
# A tibble: 6 × 7
     id conbus  coneduc conmedic conbus_missing coneduc_missing conmedic_missing
  <int> <fct>   <fct>   <fct>    <lgl>          <lgl>           <lgl>           
1     1 a grea… a grea… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
2     2 only s… only s… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
3     3 only s… a grea… a great… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
4     4 NA      NA      NA       TRUE           TRUE            TRUE            
5     5 only s… hardly… only so… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           
6     6 hardly… only s… only so… FALSE          FALSE           FALSE           


The three added columns have the same meanings as the separate flags above. Their sources remain available alongside them. A six-row preview cannot show that every entry agrees. identical() receives two objects and returns one logical result: TRUE requires agreement of the complete objects, including values, row and column order, types, and attributes such as labels.

identical(confidence_flags, separate_flags)

[1] TRUE


The check returns TRUE, so both methods produced the same complete table. A FALSE result would require checking more than the first few printed values.
There are still 3986 respondents. We grouped variables for an operation; we did not collect respondents into regions or reduce them to group summaries. Grouping observations is developed in Chapter 19.

13.2.1 Supply an unnamed function
Sometimes an operation needs an expression rather than a function name alone. \(x) defines a function without assigning it a name. The name x represents the input that the function will receive; the expression after it gives the returned result. Begin with the familiar missingness operation:

confidence_flags_function <- confidence |>
  mutate(across(
    conbus:conmedic,
    \(x) is.na(x),
    .names = "{.col}_missing"
  ))
identical(confidence_flags_function, confidence_flags)

[1] TRUE


For each selected column, across() supplies that entire column as x. is.na(x) returns one flag per entry, so this function has exactly the same result as supplying is.na directly. The comparison is TRUE. The function argument and its input are local to this expression; writing x here does not refer to a column called x. Chapter 15 later uses the same syntax for a two-step scoring operation.

title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.3 Count recorded answers
How many of the three confidence answers are recorded for each respondent? Tidystata’s row_non_miss() counts non-missing values across its supplied columns within each row. Name the three items explicitly so that id cannot contribute to the count:

confidence_coverage <- confidence |>
  mutate(n_answered = row_non_miss(conbus, coneduc, conmedic))
tab(confidence_coverage, n_answered)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  n_answered     n percent   cum  valid valid_cum
       <int> <int>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1          0  1351  33.9    33.9 33.9        33.9
2          1    10   0.251  34.1  0.251      34.1
3          2    73   1.83   36.0  1.83       36.0
4          3  2552  64.0   100   64.0       100  


n_answered ranges from 0 through 3. Each frequency counts respondents with that many available answers; its percentage denominator includes all 3986 respondents because every row receives a count. Zero means none of these answers is recorded. It is not a confidence score of zero and does not identify refusal. A count of 3 marks complete responses. The item values remain unchanged; counting their availability does not require converting the categories to scores.

title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.4 Conditions across several columns
To inspect respondents with at least one missing confidence answer, use if_any() inside filter(). It applies a condition to each selected column, then returns one logical result per row. With is.na, the result is TRUE if any selected answer is missing:

any_missing <- confidence |>
  filter(if_any(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
head(any_missing)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id conbus coneduc conmedic
  <int> <fct>  <fct>   <fct>   
1     4 NA     NA      NA      
2    10 NA     NA      NA      
3    15 NA     NA      NA      
4    16 NA     NA      NA      
5    18 NA     NA      NA      
6    20 NA     NA      NA      

nrow(any_missing)

[1] 1434


if_all() instead requires every selected column to meet the condition:

all_missing <- confidence |>
  filter(if_all(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
head(all_missing)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id conbus coneduc conmedic
  <int> <fct>  <fct>   <fct>   
1     4 NA     NA      NA      
2    10 NA     NA      NA      
3    15 NA     NA      NA      
4    16 NA     NA      NA      
5    18 NA     NA      NA      
6    20 NA     NA      NA      

nrow(all_missing)

[1] 1351


The first selection contains 1434 respondents; the second contains 1351. Every respondent in the second also belongs to the first. Neither result establishes refusal: the prepared extract records unavailable answers as NA without retaining every source reason.
To select complete responses, negate the result of if_any() with !:

complete_confidence <- confidence |>
  filter(!if_any(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
nrow(complete_confidence)

[1] 2552

nrow(complete_confidence) + nrow(any_missing)

[1] 3986


The complete and any-missing selections partition all 3986 respondents. This is a check of coverage, not an instruction to discard incomplete records for every analysis. Later, Section 15.4 explicitly chooses a complete-response rule for a teaching score.

title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.5 Review

across() applies one function to selected columns inside a table operation.
.names gives derived columns informative names while retaining their sources.
An unnamed function supplies an expression for each selected column.
row_non_miss() counts available answers in each row; exclude identifiers and unrelated columns.
if_any() and if_all() combine column conditions into one result per observation.
Check a block operation against separate operations before extending it.
A block of variables differs from groups of observations; missingness flags do not explain missingness.

Chapter 14 next develops arithmetic and numeric recoding. Chapter 15 later applies a shared scoring rule to a questionnaire battery.

title: 13  Group variables
text:
13.6 Exercises

Create missingness flags for the three confidence items with separate operations and with across(). Verify exact agreement and confirm that the original answers remain.
Select respondents with any missing answer, all three missing, and no missing answer. Explain the difference between the selections and check that the first and third cover the entire source. Count recorded answers per row, excluding id, and tabulate these counts. Which count identifies each of the all-missing and complete selections? Does zero mean zero confidence?
A researcher writes mutate(across(conbus:conmedic, is.na)) and then treats the results as confidence responses. Diagnose the problem and repair the command. Would using starts_with("con") on the full GSS extract select the same three items?

title: 13  Group variables
text:
Worked answers






NoteCompare the complete tables





Load the packages and saved extract in a fresh session:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_items <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
answer_separate <- answer_items |>
  mutate(
    conbus_missing = is.na(conbus),
    coneduc_missing = is.na(coneduc),
    conmedic_missing = is.na(conmedic)
  )
answer_block <- answer_items |>
  mutate(across(conbus:conmedic, \(x) is.na(x), .names = "{.col}_missing"))
identical(answer_separate, answer_block)

[1] TRUE

identical(select(answer_block, id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic), answer_items)

[1] TRUE


Both checks return TRUE, covering all rows rather than just the displayed preview. The original factors and their missing answers remain intact. The unnamed function receives each item column as x and returns its missingness flags, so it agrees with the named is.na operation.









NoteDistinguish coverage rules






library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_items <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
answer_any <- answer_items |>
  filter(if_any(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
answer_all <- answer_items |>
  filter(if_all(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
answer_complete <- answer_items |>
  filter(!if_any(conbus:conmedic, is.na))
nrow(answer_any)

[1] 1434

nrow(answer_all)

[1] 1351

nrow(answer_complete)

[1] 2552

nrow(answer_any) + nrow(answer_complete) == nrow(answer_items)

[1] TRUE

answer_coverage <- answer_items |>
  mutate(n_answered = row_non_miss(conbus, coneduc, conmedic))
tab(answer_coverage, n_answered)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  n_answered     n percent   cum  valid valid_cum
       <int> <int>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1          0  1351  33.9    33.9 33.9        33.9
2          1    10   0.251  34.1  0.251      34.1
3          2    73   1.83   36.0  1.83       36.0
4          3  2552  64.0   100   64.0       100  


The final check is TRUE. All-missing records are part of the any-missing selection, so adding those two counts would double-count some respondents. These counts describe answer availability. n_answered == 0 identifies all three missing; n_answered == 3 identifies complete responses. Counts below 3 identify the any-missing selection. Zero available answers supplies no information about a person’s confidence level.









NotePreserve answers and choose the block






library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_flags <- answer_gss24 |>
  mutate(across(conbus:conmedic, is.na, .names = "{.col}_missing"))
answer_gss24 |>
  select(starts_with("con")) |>
  ds()

[1] "conbus"   "coneduc"  "conmedic" "conpress" "consci"   "conlegis"

identical(answer_flags$conbus, answer_gss24$conbus)

[1] TRUE


New names keep the original responses. The prefix selects six confidence items in the full extract, including confidence in the press, science, and the legislature. A convenient name pattern is not a substitute for specifying the intended battery.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.1 Numbers
A recorded number may need a different unit, a comparison with another answer, or a category chosen for a research question. These transformations do different jobs. We will calculate them in new columns, retain the source measurements, and check what happens when an answer is unknown.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We use mutate() and rename() from Chapter 12, the conditions from Chapter 6, and the summaries from Chapter 9. Some GSS answers are factors, columns with a defined set of categories. We can use their existing names in conditions without changing the categories; Chapter 15 develops their construction and labels. The optional programming chapters are not prerequisites. All calculations describe the sample without survey weights.
Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:
Keep ID, hours worked last week, and years of schooling, using the clearer names from Chapter 12:
There are 3986 respondents; only six are displayed. hours_last_week refers to the previous week, not a respondent’s usual schedule or commuting time. Missing hours do not imply zero work.
Use + for addition and - for subtraction:
8 + 2

[1] 10

8 - 2

[1] 6
The results are 10 and 6. Use * for multiplication and / for division:
8 * 2

[1] 16

8 / 2

[1] 4
These return 16 and 4. To calculate the average of 8 and 2, add them and divide the sum by two:
(8 + 2) / 2

[1] 5
The result is 5. Parentheses make R calculate the sum first.
Use ^ for a power. For example, 2 ^ 3 multiplies three copies of 2:
2 ^ 3

[1] 8
The result is 8. Powers are evaluated before multiplication and division, which in turn come before addition and subtraction. Compare:
8 + 2 / 2

[1] 9

(8 + 2) / 2

[1] 5
The first result is 9: R divides 2 by two before adding 8. The second is 5 because the sum is calculated first. Only the second expression computes the average of the two numbers.
We can pass a calculation directly to a function:
round(8 / 3, digits = 1)

[1] 2.7
R calculates 8 / 3, then rounds the result to one decimal place, giving 2.7.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
NoteOptional: calculated decimals



Two calculations can print alike without storing exactly the same number. R represents many decimal fractions approximately. Subtract two fractions, then compare the result with a tenth:

calculated_tenth <- 7 / 10 - 6 / 10
calculated_tenth

[1] 0.1

calculated_tenth == 1 / 10

[1] FALSE

near(calculated_tenth, 1 / 10)

[1] TRUE


The printed result looks like 0.1, but exact comparison returns FALSE. Dplyr’s near() receives the two numbers and returns TRUE when their difference is within a small computational tolerance. Here it accommodates approximation in the calculation. This does not establish that two measured quantities are substantively equivalent. Keep exact comparisons for identifiers, category codes, and the age boundaries used later in this chapter.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.2 Calculate numeric columns
How many minutes correspond to the recorded hours? Use the column-creation method from Section 12.2. Multiplication by 60 converts each recorded hour into minutes:

work_minutes <- work_named |>
  mutate(minutes_last_week = hours_last_week * 60)
head(work_minutes)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id hours_last_week schooling_years minutes_last_week
  <int>           <dbl>           <dbl>             <dbl>
1     1              43              16              2580
2     2              NA              16                NA
3     3              NA              14                NA
4     4              20              12              1200
5     5              NA              13                NA
6     6              NA              14                NA


The returned table has the same respondents and one additional column. The number 60 applies the same hours-to-minutes conversion to every row. Both units remain available. Missing hours produce missing minutes, and expressing an answer in minutes does not make the original hour measurement more precise.
Using an existing name replaces that column in the returned table:

work_named |>
  mutate(hours_last_week = hours_last_week * 60)
# A tibble: 3,986 × 3
      id hours_last_week schooling_years
   <int>           <dbl>           <dbl>
 1     1            2580              16
 2     2              NA              16
 3     3              NA              14
 4     4            1200              12
 5     5              NA              13
 6     6              NA              14
 7     7            4800              13
 8     8              NA              14
 9     9            3000              14
10    10              NA              12
# ℹ 3,976 more rows


The calculation returns minutes under a heading that still says hours. This illustrates why a replacement needs a suitable name. Prefer the additional column above, or rename a replacement to match its new unit. Neither command alters work_named unless its result is assigned back.
A calculation can also combine two recorded columns. To inspect educational differences between respondents and their fathers, subtract father’s schooling from respondent’s schooling:

schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, paeduc)
schooling_changes <- schooling |>
  mutate(schooling_difference = educ - paeduc)
head(schooling_changes)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id  educ paeduc schooling_difference
  <int> <dbl>  <dbl>                <dbl>
1     1    16     NA                   NA
2     2    16     NA                   NA
3     3    14     12                    2
4     4    12     NA                   NA
5     5    13     11                    2
6     6    14      5                    9


A positive difference means that the respondent reports more completed years than their father; zero means the reported years agree. If either answer is missing, the difference is missing. The appendix explains the parental-variable definition, including its treatment of same-sex parents. This arithmetic describes paired reported schooling, not an effect of parental education.






NoteOptional: standardize a measure



How far is a respondent’s schooling from the sample average? Tidystata’s std() subtracts the mean of the recorded values and divides by their sample standard deviation. This expresses differences in standard-deviation units. Keep schooling in years alongside the new column:

schooling_standardized <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ) |>
  mutate(schooling_z = std(educ))
head(schooling_standardized)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id  educ schooling_z
  <int> <dbl>       <dbl>
1     1    16      0.603 
2     2    16      0.603 
3     3    14     -0.0816
4     4    12     -0.767 
5     5    13     -0.424 
6     6    14     -0.0816


Each row still represents the same respondent. A positive schooling_z indicates schooling above this sample’s mean, a negative value indicates schooling below it, and zero corresponds to the mean. A value of 1 is one sample standard deviation above the mean. Missing schooling remains missing; the mean and standard deviation use respondents with recorded schooling.
Compare the original and transformed units with the familiar summary command:

summ(schooling_standardized, educ, schooling_z)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name        type      n unique   min      mean    sd   max
  <chr>       <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 educ        dbl    3952     21  0     1.42e+ 1  2.92 20   
2 schooling_z dbl    3952     21 -4.88 -2.16e-16  1     1.97


educ remains in completed years. schooling_z has a mean approximately zero and a standard deviation of one; a tiny printed difference from zero can arise from computer arithmetic. These reference values come from this sample, so the same schooling value can receive a different standardized value in another sample. Standardization does not make the distribution normal. If there is no variation or fewer than two recorded values, std() returns missing values because the required standard deviation is zero or undefined.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.3 Calculate with aligned values
c() combines supplied values in their written order. Start with two short vectors whose calculations we can read in full:

x <- c(2, 4, 6)
y <- c(1, 2, 3)
x - y

[1] 1 2 3

x * 2

[1]  4  8 12


Subtraction pairs values at the same position: 2 - 1, 4 - 2, and 6 - 3, returning 1, 2, and 3. Multiplication applies the single value 2 to every element of x, returning 4, 8, and 12. Adding, dividing, taking powers, and rounding also act element by element:

round(x / 3, digits = 2)

[1] 0.67 1.33 2.00


The result is 0.67, 1.33, and 2. Division happens first, then round() rounds each result to two decimal places. Printing may omit trailing zeros. We use equal-length vectors or a single shared value; more general recycling rules are beyond this example.
The same rule applies to recorded columns. To revisit the schooling comparison in Section 14.2, select the respondent’s and father’s years of education from the GSS extract loaded above. Keeping both columns in one table preserves their pairing:

schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, paeduc)

Extract the two columns and subtract:

respondent_years <- schooling$educ
father_years <- schooling$paeduc
length(respondent_years)

[1] 3986

length(father_years)

[1] 3986

var_type(respondent_years)

[1] "double"

(respondent_years - father_years) |>
  head()

[1] NA NA  2 NA  2  9


Both vectors have 3986 elements. Their positions refer to the same respondents; subtraction returns one schooling difference per respondent. A missing input produces a missing difference. Equal lengths alone do not guarantee correct alignment: sorting only one vector would break these pairs. Keeping related columns in one table helps preserve those connections.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.4 Conditions and recoding
mutate() can store a logical condition as a new column. The comparison produces one result per respondent:

people <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age)
people |>
  mutate(older = age >= 65)
# A tibble: 3,986 × 3
      id   age older
   <int> <dbl> <lgl>
 1     1    33 FALSE
 2     2    64 FALSE
 3     3    69 TRUE 
 4     4    19 FALSE
 5     5    70 TRUE 
 6     6    53 FALSE
 7     7    48 FALSE
 8     8    30 FALSE
 9     9    60 FALSE
10    10    25 FALSE
# ℹ 3,976 more rows


Every respondent remains. Known ages at least 65 produce TRUE, younger ages produce FALSE, and unknown ages produce NA. This differs from filter(), which uses a condition to decide which rows remain.

14.4.1 One result per value
A logical vector records TRUE, FALSE, or NA for each element:

x <- c(2, 4, NA, 8)
x >= 4

[1] FALSE  TRUE    NA  TRUE

(x >= 4) & (x <= 6)

[1] FALSE  TRUE    NA FALSE

var_type(x >= 4)

[1] "logical"


The first comparison returns FALSE, TRUE, NA, and TRUE. Adding the upper bound changes the last answer to FALSE; 8 is greater than 6. & combines conditions at each position, while | asks whether at least one holds. The results are logical vectors with the same length as x.
The next examples use conditions inside mutate() to retain a logical column without selecting rows.


14.4.2 Two outcomes
if_else() receives a condition, an output for true cases, and an output for false cases. Here 1 identifies respondents aged at least 65 and 0 identifies younger respondents. An unknown condition produces a missing result by default:

age_indicators <- people |>
  mutate(older = if_else(age >= 65, 1, 0))
head(age_indicators)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id   age older
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1    33     0
2     2    64     0
3     3    69     1
4     4    19     0
5     5    70     1
6     6    53     0


The rule creates an indicator without changing recorded ages. Its true and false outputs must have compatible types: both are numeric here. A missing age is not evidence that a respondent is younger than 65.


14.4.3 Several categories
stata_recode() from tidystata maps numeric values to new codes. Supply the input column first, then rules with the old values to the left of ~ and the new code to the right. Inside a rule, 18:34 means the closed interval from 18 through 34, including both endpoints. The special upper bound max in 65:max means any value at least 65. Rules use the original values, and the first matching rule wins. .default = NA makes unmatched values missing:

age_groups <- people |>
  mutate(age_group = stata_recode(
    age,
    18:34 ~ 1,
    35:64 ~ 2,
    65:max ~ 3,
    .default = NA
  ))
head(age_groups)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id   age age_group
  <int> <dbl>     <dbl>
1     1    33         1
2     2    64         2
3     3    69         3
4     4    19         1
5     5    70         3
6     6    53         2


The new column uses 1 for ages 18-34, 2 for ages 35-64, and 3 for ages 65 and above, retaining every row and the original age. Unknown ages and values outside the stated ranges remain missing. Without .default = NA, stata_recode() would keep unmatched input values, which could mix ages with category codes. A broad range placed first would capture values before a later, narrower rule could apply. Categories are analytical choices, not replacements for the original ages.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.5 Compare ways to form groups
Age bands can represent a substantive threshold or a position within this particular sample. Those are different definitions. Tidystata’s cut_breaks() places numeric values into intervals at specified break points. Supply the numeric column and breaks, a vector of internal boundaries:

age_cuts <- people |>
  mutate(age_bands = cut_breaks(age, breaks = c(35, 65)))
tab(age_cuts, age_bands)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  age_bands     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <ord>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 [18,35)     983   24.7   24.7  25.5      25.5
2 [35,65)    1964   49.3   73.9  50.9      76.4
3 [65,89]     912   22.9   96.8  23.6     100  
4 NA          127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


With its default right = FALSE, cut_breaks() includes the lower boundary of each interval. Here 35 enters the middle band and 65 enters the oldest band. The outer limits shown in the output are the observed minimum and maximum. The final bracket includes the maximum, so the oldest recorded age remains classified. The default labels reflect this sample’s observed limits; they are not definitions of every possible age in another sample. The new category column leaves the source ages unchanged.
cut_quantile() instead uses sample quantiles, dividing the recorded distribution into four groups by default. Apply it to the same source ages and retain both definitions:

age_cuts <- age_cuts |>
  mutate(age_quartiles = cut_quantile(age))
tab(age_cuts, age_quartiles)
# A tibble: 5 × 6
  age_quartiles     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <ord>         <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 [18,34]         983   24.7   24.7  25.5      25.5
2 (34,48]        1000   25.1   49.7  25.9      51.4
3 (48,64]         964   24.2   73.9  25.0      76.4
4 (64,89]         912   22.9   96.8  23.6     100  
5 NA              127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


Quantile groups instead describe relative position among the recorded ages. In the displayed labels, ( excludes an endpoint and ] includes it. The first interval also includes the observed minimum. Equal ages stay together under the default quantile method, so ties can prevent exactly equal group sizes; a variable with too few distinct values may not support the requested split. The same age can occupy a different quantile group in another sample. Do not choose this method merely to make substantive categories look balanced.
Check known boundaries against their source ages:

age_cuts |>
  filter(age %in% c(34, 35, 64, 65) | is.na(age)) |>
  select(id, age, age_bands, age_quartiles)
# A tibble: 424 × 4
      id   age age_bands age_quartiles
   <int> <dbl> <ord>     <ord>        
 1     2    64 [35,65)   (48,64]      
 2    17    64 [35,65)   (48,64]      
 3    18    NA NA        NA           
 4    42    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 5    49    NA NA        NA           
 6    50    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 7    57    NA NA        NA           
 8    83    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 9    89    34 [18,35)   [18,34]      
10    98    34 [18,35)   [18,34]      
# ℹ 414 more rows


count() receives a table and the columns defining groups. It returns one row per observed group and a column n giving its row count. Here that is the number of respondents in each age category, with missing categories counted separately. It retains no individual respondent rows in this returned summary and does not change age_cuts:

count(age_cuts, age_bands)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  age_bands     n
  <ord>     <int>
1 [18,35)     983
2 [35,65)    1964
3 [65,89]     912
4 NA          127

count(age_cuts, age_quartiles)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  age_quartiles     n
  <ord>         <int>
1 [18,34]         983
2 (34,48]        1000
3 (48,64]         964
4 (64,89]         912
5 NA              127


Both methods retain all 3986 respondents and preserve unknown ages as missing groups. Among recorded ages, the smallest fixed band contains 23.6 percent and the smallest quantile group contains 23.6 percent. Neither split produces a group below 15 percent here. In another sample, inspect small groups before proceeding and reconsider cut points only with a substantive justification. Keep continuous age available: either grouping loses differences within its intervals.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.6 Review

Arithmetic operates element by element; parentheses control grouping and round() controls rounding.
Numeric calculations preserve row alignment; check the meaning and units of each result.
Missing inputs normally produce missing calculated values. A missing value is not zero or a negative answer.
Logical comparisons return TRUE, FALSE, or NA; if_else() supplies two outcomes while preserving unknown conditions.
stata_recode() maps original numeric values and ranges to codes. Check endpoints, rule order, and unmatched values.
cut_breaks() forms intervals at chosen boundaries; cut_quantile() forms sample-relative groups. Check ties, group sizes, and missingness.
Preserve original measurements alongside transformations. Numeric category codes do not establish meaningful distances.
Optional: std() expresses a numeric measure in sample standard-deviation units; near() compares calculated decimals with a small computational tolerance.

Next, Chapter 15 gives codes readable category labels, controls their display order, and develops an explicit questionnaire-scoring rule.

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
14.7 Exercises

Keep ID and hours worked, rename the hours column, and create minutes worked as a separate column. Check the dimensions and explain what happens to unknown hours.
Apply the age-group rule to respondents aged 34, 35, 64, or 65, and to those with unknown ages. Explain which category each known boundary enters and why unknown ages stay missing. Compare the membership with cut_breaks() at 35 and 65. Would quantile groups answer the same substantive question? Diagnose a rule that puts 18:max ~ 1 before the three age-band rules. Then explain what omitting .default = NA would do to an unmatched plain input of 16. Check both predictions.
Use the selection and transformation skills from this part of the book to compare years of schooling for respondents with and without a bachelor’s or graduate degree. Keep only degree and educ, exclude missing degrees, create a logical indicator of those two degree categories, and summarize schooling separately for its TRUE and FALSE groups. Report the number of non-missing schooling values and the mean in years. Explain why a missing degree must not be silently treated as no college degree, and why averaging the stored category codes would not answer this question. Do not invent a new numeric missing code for the prepared GSS file.
Predict and explain. What do 8 + 2 / 2 and (8 + 2) / 2 return? Which computes the average of 8 and 2? Check the types of 12 and "12" with var_type(). Then store "12" as text, convert it to numeric, subtract 4, and divide the difference by 2. Save the result. What happens if the 4 is replaced by NA? If you later change the numeric input, will the saved result update automatically?

title: 14  Logicals and numbers
text:
Worked answers






NoteA new unit in a new column





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


work <- gss24 |>
  select(id, hrs1)
result <- work |>
  rename(hours_last_week = hrs1) |>
  mutate(minutes_last_week = hours_last_week * 60)
head(result)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id hours_last_week minutes_last_week
  <int>           <dbl>             <dbl>
1     1              43              2580
2     2              NA                NA
3     3              NA                NA
4     4              20              1200
5     5              NA                NA
6     6              NA                NA

nrow(result)

[1] 3986

ncol(result)

[1] 3

ds(work)

[1] "id"   "hrs1"


The result has 3986 rows and three columns. Hours and minutes remain aligned with ID; unknown hours produce unknown minutes. The original work still has ID and its hrs1 heading. Changing units does not change the reference period or precision of the recorded answer.









NoteAge boundaries and missingness





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


people <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age) |>
  filter(age %in% c(34, 35, 64, 65) | is.na(age))
result <- people |>
  mutate(age_group = stata_recode(
    age,
    18:34 ~ 1,
    35:64 ~ 2,
    65:max ~ 3,
    .default = NA
  ))
head(result)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id   age age_group
  <int> <dbl>     <dbl>
1     2    64         2
2    17    64         2
3    18    NA        NA
4    42    65         3
5    49    NA        NA
6    50    65         3


Age 34 receives code 1 (18-34), 35 and 64 receive code 2 (35-64), and 65 receives code 3 (65+). An unknown age remains missing. The preview contains actual respondents, including repeated ages; it is not a list of distinct age-category pairs. A default oldest category would assert information that is absent.
Use plain numeric inputs to inspect rule order and unmatched values directly. These are syntax checks, not fabricated respondents:

stata_recode(c(34, 35, 64, 65), 18:max ~ 1, 35:64 ~ 2, 65:max ~ 3,
             .default = NA)

[1] 1 1 1 1

stata_recode(16, 18:34 ~ 1, 35:64 ~ 2, 65:max ~ 3)

[1] 16

stata_recode(16, 18:34 ~ 1, 35:64 ~ 2, 65:max ~ 3, .default = NA)

[1] NA


The broad first rule assigns all four boundary values to code 1 before later rules can apply. With no explicit default, an unmatched 16 remains 16 and could be confused with a category code. The explicit default instead makes it missing. Repair the first command by restoring the non-overlapping age ranges taught above.
Form both alternative groupings from all respondents before inspecting boundary cases. Quantiles calculated on only the boundary subset would describe a different distribution:

answer_cuts <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age) |>
  mutate(
    age_bands = cut_breaks(age, breaks = c(35, 65)),
    age_quartiles = cut_quantile(age)
  )
answer_cuts |>
  filter(age %in% c(34, 35, 64, 65) | is.na(age))
# A tibble: 424 × 4
      id   age age_bands age_quartiles
   <int> <dbl> <ord>     <ord>        
 1     2    64 [35,65)   (48,64]      
 2    17    64 [35,65)   (48,64]      
 3    18    NA NA        NA           
 4    42    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 5    49    NA NA        NA           
 6    50    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 7    57    NA NA        NA           
 8    83    65 [65,89]   (64,89]      
 9    89    34 [18,35)   [18,34]      
10    98    34 [18,35)   [18,34]      
# ℹ 414 more rows

count(answer_cuts, age_bands)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  age_bands     n
  <ord>     <int>
1 [18,35)     983
2 [35,65)    1964
3 [65,89]     912
4 NA          127

count(answer_cuts, age_quartiles)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  age_quartiles     n
  <ord>         <int>
1 [18,34]         983
2 (34,48]        1000
3 (48,64]         964
4 (64,89]         912
5 NA              127


The fixed breaks agree with the earlier age-group membership, including missing ages. Quantile boundaries depend on the recorded sample and need not coincide with these thresholds; they answer a relative-position question. Both methods retain the measured ages for later checks and analyses.









NoteSchooling by degree group





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


gss24 |>
  select(degree, educ) |>
  filter(!is.na(degree)) |>
  mutate(college = degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate")) |>
  tabstat(educ, .by = college, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  college type      n  mean
  <lgl>   <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 FALSE   dbl    2505  12.6
2 TRUE    dbl    1440  17.0


degree is categorical, educ is a numeric quantity in completed years, and college is a logical condition. %in% tests membership in the two named categories; the prior filter ensures that an unknown degree is not classified as FALSE. No source-specific missing codes remain after the appendix’s preparation, so we handle ordinary NA values here. The summary has one row per logical group. Its n counts that group’s recorded schooling values, matching the observations used by mean(). Respondents in the TRUE group have more completed schooling on average; this comparison describes the sample and does not establish a causal effect of a degree. The race exercise in Section 8.5 uses a within-race percentage denominator, whereas this exercise averages years within each degree group.









NotePredict and explain






library(tidystata)
8 + 2 / 2

[1] 9

(8 + 2) / 2

[1] 5

var_type(12)

[1] "double"

var_type("12")

[1] "character"


The first expression gives 9 because division precedes addition. Parentheses make the second expression add first and return the average, 5. The types are "double" and "character".

number_text <- "12"
x <- as.numeric(number_text)
result <- (x - 4) / 2
result

[1] 4


Subtraction gives 8; division gives 4. An unknown input makes the calculation unknown:

(x - NA) / 2

[1] NA


The result is NA. Changing x does not update the previously saved result; rerun result <- (x - 4) / 2 to calculate with a new input.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.1 Create factors
Survey answers such as marital status and confidence in institutions describe categories. A table needs readable category names and a useful display order. A questionnaire score needs a separate decision about which numbers represent which answers. This chapter distinguishes those tasks so that changing a label does not silently change an analysis.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We use the prepared 2024 GSS extract, the column-creation method from Chapter 12, and the numeric recoding from Chapter 14. Frequency tables from Chapter 8 help us check each change. The GSS examples describe the sample without survey weights. A separate, contiguous text application reuses the captured aggregate country data because its names are character fields.
Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:
A factor represents categories with a defined set of possible values, called levels. A character column stores text; a factor also records which categories are allowed and their order. The prepared GSS already uses factors for categorical answers.
First, recreate the numeric age groups from Section 14.4. This chapter starts from the saved extract rather than depending on objects left in your session:
people <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age)
age_groups <- people |>
  mutate(age_group = stata_recode(
    age,
    18:34 ~ 1,
    35:64 ~ 2,
    65:max ~ 3,
    .default = NA
  ))
The codes 1, 2, and 3 identify age bands, not ages in years. Now give these codes readable category labels by making a factor. The levels argument lists the codes in display order; labels supplies their corresponding text. Here c() combines each set of three values:
gss_ages <- age_groups |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(
    age_group, levels = c(1, 2, 3), labels = c("18-34", "35-64", "65+")
  ))
head(gss_ages)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id   age age_group
  <int> <dbl> <fct>    
1     1    33 18-34    
2     2    64 35-64    
3     3    69 65+      
4     4    19 18-34    
5     5    70 65+      
6     6    53 35-64    

nrow(gss_ages)

[1] 3986
factor() returns the categorical values. All 3986 respondents remain in their original order. Changing a level order does not move rows or change anyone’s age. A missing age remains missing rather than becoming a fourth category.
levels() receives a factor and returns its category names in level order. Extract the new factor with the familiar $:
levels(gss_ages$age_group)

[1] "18-34" "35-64" "65+"
The three labels appear in the order we supplied. This list describes the factor’s categories, rather than the order in which respondents appear.
An explicitly supplied level list must cover the known input codes: a non-missing value absent from that list becomes missing. Check the codes and the correspondence between levels and labels. The order controls display and sorting; it does not establish equal distances between categories or turn category codes into years of schooling.
To see the categories alongside their frequencies, use the familiar tab():
gss_ages |>
  tab(age_group)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  age_group     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 18-34       983   24.7   24.7  25.5      25.5
2 35-64      1964   49.3   73.9  50.9      76.4
3 65+         912   22.9   96.8  23.6     100  
4 NA          127    3.19 100    NA        NA
The age bands appear in their level order. The missing row represents unavailable ages; it is not an age band. Cumulative percentages follow the displayed order, so that order should make substantive sense.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.2 Change category order
Suppose a presentation needs the oldest age band first. fct_relevel() from forcats, loaded by tidyverse, moves the named levels to the beginning in the order supplied. Levels not named follow in their existing order. Save its result in a new column so that the original ordering remains available:

age_display <- gss_ages |>
  mutate(age_group_oldest_first = fct_relevel(age_group, "65+", "35-64"))
levels(age_display$age_group_oldest_first)

[1] "65+"   "35-64" "18-34"

age_display |>
  tab(age_group_oldest_first)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  age_group_oldest_first     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>                  <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 65+                      912   22.9   22.9  23.6      23.6
2 35-64                   1964   49.3   72.2  50.9      74.5
3 18-34                    983   24.7   96.8  25.5     100  
4 NA                       127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


The new order is 65+, 35-64, then 18-34. Each band still contains the same respondents, and the rows of age_display remain in their original order. arrange() sorts whole observations; fct_relevel() changes category order within a column. A factor with deliberately arranged levels is still an ordinary factor. R also has an ordered-factor class, which has additional consequences for comparisons and modeling; changing the display order here does not create that class.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.3 Relabel and combine categories
A publication may need a fuller label than “65+”. fct_recode() changes level names. Write the new name on the left of = and the existing name on the right. Levels not named remain unchanged:

age_labels <- gss_ages |>
  mutate(age_group_label = fct_recode(age_group, "65 and older" = "65+"))
age_labels |>
  tab(age_group_label)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  age_group_label     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>           <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 18-34             983   24.7   24.7  25.5      25.5
2 35-64            1964   49.3   73.9  50.9      76.4
3 65 and older      912   22.9   96.8  23.6     100  
4 NA                127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


Only the label changes. The age-band membership and frequencies agree with the original factor, including its missing answers. A clearer label does not create a more precise measurement.
Combining categories changes their membership. fct_collapse() takes a new category name on the left and the old levels to combine on the right. Here c() supplies the two younger age bands:

age_bands <- gss_ages |>
  mutate(age_band = fct_collapse(age_group, "Under 65" = c("18-34", "35-64")))
age_bands |>
  tab(age_band)
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  age_band     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>    <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Under 65  2947   73.9   73.9  76.4      76.4
2 65+        912   22.9   96.8  23.6     100  
3 NA         127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


“Under 65” now includes everyone previously in either younger band; the unnamed “65+” level remains. Unknown ages remain missing. We retain the original age_group column because the broader grouping discards the distinction between the two younger bands. Choose categories for the research question, and avoid combining substantively different answers merely to shorten a table.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.4 Combine questionnaire items
The GSS asks about confidence in major companies, education, and medicine. We use these three items to demonstrate a score, without claiming they form a validated scale. A common spelling in variable names does not establish that questions belong together. Select these items because their meanings suit the teaching question:

confidence <- gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
confidence
# A tibble: 3,986 × 4
      id conbus       coneduc      conmedic    
   <int> <fct>        <fct>        <fct>       
 1     1 a great deal a great deal a great deal
 2     2 only some    only some    a great deal
 3     3 only some    a great deal a great deal
 4     4 NA           NA           NA          
 5     5 only some    hardly any   only some   
 6     6 hardly any   only some    only some   
 7     7 only some    only some    a great deal
 8     8 hardly any   hardly any   hardly any  
 9     9 only some    only some    only some   
10    10 NA           NA           NA          
# ℹ 3,976 more rows


The answers are factors. Define numeric scores explicitly: hardly any confidence is 1, only some is 2, and a great deal is 3. Higher values then mean greater confidence. Store the category names in the intended order, and apply that order to one item before converting any scores:

score_levels <- c("hardly any", "only some", "a great deal")
business_ordered <- factor(confidence$conbus, levels = score_levels)
levels(business_ordered)

[1] "hardly any"   "only some"    "a great deal"


The result lists hardly any, only some, then a great deal. The original conbus factor puts a great deal first, so its original order does not match the score direction we chose. The level list must cover all recorded answers: a value absent from it would become missing in factor().
Tidystata’s encode() receives a factor and returns labelled integer codes. The first supplied level receives 1, the second 2, and the third 3; the level text remains attached as value labels. It uses the factor order rather than choosing a score direction. Encode just the ordered business item:

business_score <- encode(business_ordered)
head(business_score)

<labelled<integer>[6]>
[1]  3  2  2 NA  2  1

Labels:
 value        label
     1   hardly any
     2    only some
     3 a great deal


Recorded answers now have numeric scores with their meanings attached. Unknown answers remain missing. Neither assignment changes the original factor in confidence or gss24.
Apply these checked ordering and encoding steps separately to all three items:

confidence_scores <- confidence |>
  mutate(
    conbus = encode(factor(conbus, levels = score_levels)),
    coneduc = encode(factor(coneduc, levels = score_levels)),
    conmedic = encode(factor(conmedic, levels = score_levels))
  )
head(confidence_scores)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id conbus            coneduc           conmedic         
  <int> <int+lbl>         <int+lbl>         <int+lbl>        
1     1  3 [a great deal]  3 [a great deal]  3 [a great deal]
2     2  2 [only some]     2 [only some]     3 [a great deal]
3     3  2 [only some]     3 [a great deal]  3 [a great deal]
4     4 NA                NA                NA               
5     5  2 [only some]     1 [hardly any]    2 [only some]   
6     6  1 [hardly any]    2 [only some]     2 [only some]   


The returned table keeps the same respondents and replaces the three factors with their scores. The source factors remain in confidence. Some questions were not asked on every ballot, so an unavailable answer need not indicate refusal.

15.4.1 Apply the same scoring rule to the battery
The three calls above use the same level order and conversion. After checking them separately, we can use across() from Chapter 13 to express the shared rule once:

confidence_scores_block <- confidence |>
  mutate(across(
    conbus:conmedic,
    \(x) encode(factor(x, levels = score_levels))
  ))
identical(confidence_scores_block, confidence_scores)

[1] TRUE


As in Section 13.2.1, \(x) supplies an unnamed function. For each selected column, across() supplies that column as x; the function orders its categories and encodes the result. It returns one score per original response. The comparison returns TRUE, including values, missingness, and value labels. The scores replace columns in the returned scoring table, while confidence retains the original answers. The common rule is justified by the three items’ shared response scale, not merely by their names. Do not reuse it for a battery containing differently worded or reverse-scored items without inspecting those definitions.


15.4.2 Require complete responses
Use row_non_miss() from Chapter 13 to count recorded answers before calculating a score. As before, count just the three items and exclude id:

confidence_coverage <- confidence_scores |>
  mutate(n_answered = row_non_miss(conbus, coneduc, conmedic))
tab(confidence_coverage, n_answered)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  n_answered     n percent   cum  valid valid_cum
       <int> <int>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1          0  1351  33.9    33.9 33.9        33.9
2          1    10   0.251  34.1  0.251      34.1
3          2    73   1.83   36.0  1.83       36.0
4          3  2552  64.0   100   64.0       100  


Every respondent has a count from 0 through 3; 3 identifies complete responses. Zero available answers is not a confidence score of zero and does not establish why answers are unavailable. The scores and source respondents remain unchanged by this count.
For this demonstration, require all three answers. Tidystata’s row_mean() calculates one arithmetic mean per respondent across the supplied columns. It omits missing answers by default; na.rm = FALSE instead makes the score missing whenever any of the three answers is missing:

scored_confidence <- confidence_coverage |>
  mutate(mean_score = row_mean(conbus, coneduc, conmedic, na.rm = FALSE))
scored_confidence |>
  select(id, n_answered, mean_score) |>
  head()
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id n_answered mean_score
  <int>      <int>      <dbl>
1     1          3       3   
2     2          3       2.33
3     3          3       2.67
4     4          0      NA   
5     5          3       1.67
6     6          3       1.67


The function combines values belonging to the same respondent, giving each item equal weight. With na.rm = FALSE, a missing item makes the score missing; we do not average two answers as though they were three. Complete scores run from 1 to 3. This complete-response rule is a teaching choice, not a recommendation for a validated confidence scale. The calculation neither fills source answers nor establishes equal spacing or measurement validity.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.5 Work with recorded text
The GSS factor examples above concern fixed response categories. To work with names stored as character text, we reuse the captured Our World in Data (OWID) life-expectancy file from Chapter 7. Its rows describe aggregate entity-year statistics, not workshop participants. Keep this text application together; it does not change the source of the GSS scoring lesson.
Copy the book’s captured life-expectancy CSV into an examples folder inside your project. read_csv() returns a tibble and reports the types it inferred. We retain the original column names and measurements:

owid <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

owid
# A tibble: 21,565 × 4
   Entity      Code   Year `Life expectancy`
   <chr>       <chr> <dbl>             <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan AFG    1950              28.2
 2 Afghanistan AFG    1951              28.6
 3 Afghanistan AFG    1952              29.0
 4 Afghanistan AFG    1953              29.5
 5 Afghanistan AFG    1954              29.7
 6 Afghanistan AFG    1955              30.4
 7 Afghanistan AFG    1956              30.8
 8 Afghanistan AFG    1957              31.3
 9 Afghanistan AFG    1958              31.8
10 Afghanistan AFG    1959              32.3
# ℹ 21,555 more rows


Each row records an entity in a year. Entity is the displayed name, Code is an identifying text field, and Year records the year. Some entities are aggregates or territories. The space in Life expectancy requires backticks when naming that column in code. The stringr functions below come from tidyverse, already loaded above.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.6 Count characters
nchar() receives text and returns the number of characters inside its quotation marks:

text <- "hello"
nchar(text)

[1] 5

nchar("01")

[1] 2


The results are 5 and 2. Both the zero and the one in "01" count; quotation marks do not. Counting characters neither converts the text to numbers nor changes the original string.
As with arithmetic in Section 14.3, text operations act element by element. c() combines strings in their written order:

words <- c("one", "two", "three")
var_type(words)

[1] "character"

nchar(words)

[1] 3 3 5

paste("Word:", words)

[1] "Word: one"   "Word: two"   "Word: three"


The type is "character", and the character counts are 3, 3, and 5. The familiar paste() returns "Word: one", "Word: two", and "Word: three". Its single prefix applies to every input value, following the single-value repetition rule from Section 14.3. Text operations on a named column likewise return one result per row.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.7 Prepare names for searching
Chapter 12 introduced numeric text, explicit conversion, paste(), spacing, and lowercase search forms. Those tools return transformed values without replacing the source unless assigned over it. Here we apply them to recorded country names. A description remains different from an identifier, and joined text can still conceal missing source components.
First select one year so that a name search does not repeat each entity across many years. Use the familiar str_squish() to supply a spacing rule in a separate column:

names_2023 <- owid |>
  filter(Year == 2023) |>
  select(Entity, Code, Year) |>
  mutate(entity_clean = str_squish(Entity))

This applies the rule without asserting that every recorded name needs correction. Now create a lowercase search form from that result:

names_2023 <- names_2023 |>
  mutate(entity_lower = str_to_lower(entity_clean))
names_2023
# A tibble: 261 × 5
   Entity              Code      Year entity_clean        entity_lower       
   <chr>               <chr>    <dbl> <chr>               <chr>              
 1 Afghanistan         AFG       2023 Afghanistan         afghanistan        
 2 Africa              OWID_AFR  2023 Africa              africa             
 3 Albania             ALB       2023 Albania             albania            
 4 Algeria             DZA       2023 Algeria             algeria            
 5 American Samoa      ASM       2023 American Samoa      american samoa     
 6 Americas            NA        2023 Americas            americas           
 7 Andorra             AND       2023 Andorra             andorra            
 8 Angola              AGO       2023 Angola              angola             
 9 Anguilla            AIA       2023 Anguilla            anguilla           
10 Antigua and Barbuda ATG       2023 Antigua and Barbuda antigua and barbuda
# ℹ 251 more rows


The new column provides a consistent search form; Entity remains suitable for display. Code remains text because its role is identification rather than arithmetic. Changing a code’s storage to a number can discard meaningful leading zeros in other datasets. Neither a digit-like appearance nor a short code makes a field a quantitative measurement.
Lowercasing is a specific transformation, not a way to reconcile different naming conventions. It cannot establish that two differently named records refer to the same entity. If names are used to combine datasets, inspect unmatched records and use an appropriate checked identifier, following Chapter 20.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.8 Search names
Which names contain the word fragment United? Begin by defining what we want to match. fixed() constructs a literal search pattern, whose characters will be matched as written rather than interpreted as special pattern symbols:

united_pattern <- fixed("United")

This saves a case-sensitive pattern; it has not yet searched any names. str_detect() receives strings and a pattern, then returns one logical result per string. Inspect that result before using it to select rows:

head(str_detect(names_2023$Entity, united_pattern))

[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE


Each displayed TRUE or FALSE refers to the corresponding entity name. Detection returns a result without changing those names. Inside the familiar filter(), its TRUE values retain matching rows:

united_names <- names_2023 |>
  filter(str_detect(Entity, united_pattern))
united_names
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Entity                       Code   Year entity_clean             entity_lower
  <chr>                        <chr> <dbl> <chr>                    <chr>       
1 United Arab Emirates         ARE    2023 United Arab Emirates     united arab…
2 United Kingdom               GBR    2023 United Kingdom           united king…
3 United States                USA    2023 United States            united stat…
4 United States Virgin Islands VIR    2023 United States Virgin Is… united stat…


The result contains 4 entity names in the selected year. Read the entire names: a shared fragment does not imply that the entities describe the same population. The original Entity, Code, and Year remain available to identify each match.
We can search the normalized column instead. The lowercase pattern must match its case:

names_2023 |>
  filter(str_detect(entity_lower, fixed("united")))
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Entity                       Code   Year entity_clean             entity_lower
  <chr>                        <chr> <dbl> <chr>                    <chr>       
1 United Arab Emirates         ARE    2023 United Arab Emirates     united arab…
2 United Kingdom               GBR    2023 United Kingdom           united king…
3 United States                USA    2023 United States            united stat…
4 United States Virgin Islands VIR    2023 United States Virgin Is… united stat…


This returns the same entities. We chose a consistent form for searching without changing the displayed names. A missing string would give an unknown detection result, NA; it would not prove that the pattern was absent. As in earlier filtering lessons, filter() retains only TRUE. Check unknown source names separately if they occur in the data you analyze, rather than replacing unknown matches with FALSE.

15.8.1 Match a position
A regular expression is a pattern whose symbols can describe positions or groups of characters. We need only a few symbols here. ^ means the start of a string, and $ means its end. Without fixed(), stringr interprets these as pattern instructions. Compare a name starting with United with a name ending in States:

starts_united <- names_2023 |>
  filter(str_detect(Entity, "^United"))
ends_states <- names_2023 |>
  filter(str_detect(Entity, "States$"))
starts_united
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Entity                       Code   Year entity_clean             entity_lower
  <chr>                        <chr> <dbl> <chr>                    <chr>       
1 United Arab Emirates         ARE    2023 United Arab Emirates     united arab…
2 United Kingdom               GBR    2023 United Kingdom           united king…
3 United States                USA    2023 United States            united stat…
4 United States Virgin Islands VIR    2023 United States Virgin Is… united stat…

ends_states
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  Entity        Code   Year entity_clean  entity_lower 
  <chr>         <chr> <dbl> <chr>         <chr>        
1 United States USA    2023 United States united states


The first result has 4 rows; the second has 1. In particular, a name containing United States can continue with other words and therefore fail the end-of-string test. These differences are consequences of the search rule, not discrepancies in the records.
Choose literal matching when you want particular characters anywhere in a name. Add a position rule only when position is part of the question. Placing ^ inside fixed() would instead search for an actual caret character. Text tools follow the instructions we supply; they cannot infer the population we meant to select.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.9 Replace and remove text
Text changes can make a search form or display label useful. str_replace_all() receives text, a search pattern, and replacement text. It returns a string with every match replaced; supplying fixed() makes the match literal. Shorten “and” to an ampersand only in a separate display column:

name_versions <- names_2023 |>
  mutate(entity_display = str_replace_all(Entity, fixed(" and "), " & "))
name_versions |>
  filter(Entity != entity_display)
# A tibble: 11 × 6
   Entity                   Code   Year entity_clean entity_lower entity_display
   <chr>                    <chr> <dbl> <chr>        <chr>        <chr>         
 1 Antigua and Barbuda      ATG    2023 Antigua and… antigua and… Antigua & Bar…
 2 Bonaire Sint Eustatius … BES    2023 Bonaire Sin… bonaire sin… Bonaire Sint …
 3 Bosnia and Herzegovina   BIH    2023 Bosnia and … bosnia and … Bosnia & Herz…
 4 Latin America and the C… NA     2023 Latin Ameri… latin ameri… Latin America…
 5 Saint Kitts and Nevis    KNA    2023 Saint Kitts… saint kitts… Saint Kitts &…

We can apply one shared text operation to several columns with the across() method from Section 13.2. Lowercase versions of both names and codes allow lowercase search queries. Choose these two character columns explicitly and retain their original spelling:

name_searches <- names_2023 |>
  mutate(across(c(Entity, Code), str_to_lower, .names = "{.col}_search"))
name_searches |>
  filter(str_detect(Entity_search, fixed("united")) | Code_search == "usa")

Entity_search and Code_search are derived search forms. The recorded codes remain uppercase in Code, and a missing code stays missing. Lowercasing already consistent text may leave it unchanged; do not describe that as repairing an observed error. Apply an operation across columns only when their meanings support the same rule. We do not apply text cleaning to the numeric year or the life-expectancy measurement.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.10 Review

factor() defines categories and their level order; levels() lists those levels.
fct_relevel() changes category order without rearranging respondents.
fct_recode() changes labels; fct_collapse() combines categories.
encode() converts explicitly ordered factor levels to labelled numeric codes; choose score direction before encoding.
row_mean() combines numeric items using an explicit missing-answer rule; count available items before interpreting the score.
across() expresses a shared conversion after individual checks; response definitions still determine whether the rule is appropriate.
str_detect(), fixed(), and anchors control searches; str_replace_all() and str_remove() produce derived text forms.
Preserve original categories and unknown answers; joined text can conceal missing inputs. Category codes do not establish equal spacing, and a calculated score is not automatically a validated scale.

The next chapter, Chapter 16, applies the same practice of retaining source values to dates and calendar components. Chapter 17 later splits these recorded entity names into word lists. Later, Chapter 19 uses categories to calculate within groups and reshape questionnaire items. The optional programming part explains values, vectors, and other R data structures in more detail; return to it when you need to examine the mechanics behind these table operations.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
15.11 Exercises

Create the age bands, then make them display in reverse order. In separate new columns, relabel “18-34” as “Ages 18 to 34” and combine “35-64” with “65+” as “35 and older”. Which operation changes membership, which loses information, and which original columns should remain? Explain what happens to row order and missing ages.
Encode the three confidence items with higher scores for greater confidence. Check that separate and block conversions agree. Count recorded answers and calculate a mean requiring all three. Inspect answer counts beside missing scores. Does zero recorded answers mean zero confidence? What would encoding the original factor order do to score direction?
Clean the abstract string "  A   short phrase  " and search the captured OWID names in 2023 for lowercase united, retaining names and codes. Create separate display names replacing ” and ” with ” & “, remove” (country)” in a search form, and add lowercase name and code columns with across(). Explain which field to display, which originals to preserve, and why the derived labels cannot be assumed to identify entities uniquely.
Compare the literal search fixed("United"), the beginning rule "^United", and the ending rule "States$" in 2023. Predict why containing United States does not guarantee an ending match. What would fixed("^United") search for? Explain what detection and filtering would do with an unavailable name.

title: 15  Strings and factors
text:
Worked answers






NoteOrder, labels, and membership





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


people <- gss24 |>
  select(id, age)
result <- people |>
  mutate(age_group = stata_recode(
    age,
    18:34 ~ 1,
    35:64 ~ 2,
    65:max ~ 3,
    .default = NA
  )) |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(
    age_group, levels = c(3, 2, 1), labels = c("65+", "35-64", "18-34")
  ))
levels(result$age_group)

[1] "65+"   "35-64" "18-34"

head(result)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id   age age_group
  <int> <dbl> <fct>    
1     1    33 18-34    
2     2    64 35-64    
3     3    69 65+      
4     4    19 18-34    
5     5    70 65+      
6     6    53 35-64    


The level list now starts with code 3, labelled 65+. The rows remain in their original respondent order, recorded ages are unchanged, and unknown ages remain missing. A display order and a row order are different things.
Relabel a separate column without changing membership:

result <- result |>
  mutate(age_group_label = fct_recode(age_group, "Ages 18 to 34" = "18-34"))
tab(result, age_group_label)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  age_group_label     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>           <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 65+               912   22.9   22.9  23.6      23.6
2 35-64            1964   49.3   72.2  50.9      74.5
3 Ages 18 to 34     983   24.7   96.8  25.5     100  
4 NA                127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


Only that category’s label changes. Its members, the other categories, and missing answers are unchanged. The original factor remains in age_group.
Combine two bands while retaining the finer grouping:

result <- result |>
  mutate(age_band = fct_collapse(age_group, "35 and older" = c("35-64", "65+")))
tab(result, age_band)
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  age_band         n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>        <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 35 and older  2876   72.2   72.2  74.5      74.5
2 18-34          983   24.7   96.8  25.5     100  
3 NA             127    3.19 100    NA        NA  


This band loses the distinction between respondents aged 35-64 and those aged 65 or older. Preserve age_group and the source age for the finer information. None of these operations rearranges respondents or assigns unknown ages to a known category. Reordering and relabelling retain membership; collapsing changes it.









NoteWho contributes to a score?





Prepare the extract following Appendix A, then restore the saved file in your project folder:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


confidence <- gss24 |>
  select(id, conbus, coneduc, conmedic)
score_levels <- c("hardly any", "only some", "a great deal")
scores <- confidence |>
  mutate(
    conbus = encode(factor(conbus, levels = score_levels)),
    coneduc = encode(factor(coneduc, levels = score_levels)),
    conmedic = encode(factor(conmedic, levels = score_levels))
  )
scores_block <- confidence |>
  mutate(across(conbus:conmedic, \(x) encode(factor(x, levels = score_levels))))
identical(scores, scores_block)

[1] TRUE

result <- scores |>
  mutate(
    n_answered = row_non_miss(conbus, coneduc, conmedic),
    mean_score = row_mean(conbus, coneduc, conmedic, na.rm = FALSE)
  )
tab(result, n_answered)
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  n_answered     n percent   cum  valid valid_cum
       <int> <int>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1          0  1351  33.9    33.9 33.9        33.9
2          1    10   0.251  34.1  0.251      34.1
3          2    73   1.83   36.0  1.83       36.0
4          3  2552  64.0   100   64.0       100  

result |>
  filter(is.na(mean_score)) |>
  select(id, n_answered, mean_score) |>
  head()
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id n_answered mean_score
  <int>      <int>      <dbl>
1     4          0         NA
2    10          0         NA
3    15          0         NA
4    16          0         NA
5    18          0         NA
6    20          0         NA


The comparison of separate and block conversions returns TRUE. Encoding the original factor order would assign the lowest code to a great deal and reverse our intended direction. The explicit level order assigns 1 to hardly any confidence, 2 to only some, and 3 to a great deal. encode() retains these meanings as value labels. row_non_miss() counts available answers, including a count of zero when all three are missing. The frequency table covers every respondent; zero recorded answers says nothing about their confidence level or the reason for missingness. Each displayed respondent has fewer than three recorded answers. row_mean() with na.rm = FALSE preserves that missingness, so the three-item mean is missing. No answer is replaced with zero, and two available answers are not treated as a complete response. The rule preserves unknown information without validating the proposed scale.









NoteKeep names for display





Start a fresh session with the saved public CSV. The new object names keep this answer independent of the main lesson.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.1 Read date text
A recorded year and a full date have different precision. We should preserve that distinction when converting date text, selecting a time window, or interpreting a measurement. This chapter uses the real monthly economics series supplied with ggplot2; it needs no external data file.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We use column creation and conversion from Chapter 12, text matching from Chapter 15, and row selection from Chapter 6. Load tidyverse and lubridate explicitly; the latter supplies year():
Annual life expectancy does not need an invented month or day. Keep the Year in the earlier Our World in Data (OWID) file as a year. To learn about full date strings, we turn to a real monthly series already supplied with ggplot2. economics contains US economic indicators, including unemploy, the number of unemployed people in thousands. Its date column is already a Date. The dataset documentation describes monthly observations; the first day shown is a representation of the month, not evidence that the entire measurement occurred on that day.
A calendar date identifies a day without a clock time. A timestamp also records a time of day, whose interpretation can depend on its time zone. This chapter works with monthly observations represented by Date values. Its parsing and comparison examples preserve that monthly precision; they do not teach timestamp conversion or time-zone handling.
We will convert those existing dates to character values and back. as.character() returns the printed text representation. Adding date_text gives us an inspectable source for parsing while keeping the original date and economic measurement.
monthly_text <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  mutate(date_text = as.character(date))
monthly_text
# A tibble: 574 × 3
   date       unemploy date_text 
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>     
 1 1967-07-01     2944 1967-07-01
 2 1967-08-01     2945 1967-08-01
 3 1967-09-01     2958 1967-09-01
 4 1967-10-01     3143 1967-10-01
 5 1967-11-01     3066 1967-11-01
 6 1967-12-01     3018 1967-12-01
 7 1968-01-01     2878 1968-01-01
 8 1968-02-01     3001 1968-02-01
 9 1968-03-01     2877 1968-03-01
10 1968-04-01     2709 1968-04-01
# ℹ 564 more rows
There are 574 monthly records. The displayed dates and strings look similar, but their column types differ. A Date supports date comparisons with known calendar meaning. A character value is a sequence of text characters until we interpret it.
For the first extraction examples, retain two existing source months so both centuries fit in a short preview. The familiar membership condition selects their exact text; it does not change the complete monthly_text table:
date_preview <- monthly_text |>
  filter(date_text %in% c("1967-07-01", "2000-07-01"))
date_preview
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  date       unemploy date_text 
  <date>        <dbl> <chr>     
1 1967-07-01     2944 1967-07-01
2 2000-07-01     5747 2000-07-01
Sometimes we want only a component of the text. str_extract() takes character values and a matching pattern. It returns the first matching part of each string, or NA when no part matches. The call returns extracted text without changing the date strings. In a pattern, ^ means the start of a string. Start by extracting the leading 2 where it occurs:
str_extract(date_preview$date_text, "^2")

[1] NA  "2"
The July 2000 string returns "2"; the July 1967 string returns NA. A missing match here does not mean the source date is missing. Our pattern simply did not ask for its first digit.
The character class [0-9] matches any one digit. Keeping ^ restricts it to the first position:
str_extract(date_preview$date_text, "^[0-9]")

[1] "1" "2"
Each ISO date now yields its first year digit. Add {4} to require four consecutive digits. The result is still character text, even though it consists of digits:
monthly_text <- monthly_text |>
  mutate(year_text = str_extract(date_text, "^[0-9]{4}"))
monthly_text
# A tibble: 574 × 4
   date       unemploy date_text  year_text
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>    
 1 1967-07-01     2944 1967-07-01 1967

 3 1967-09-01     2958 1967-09-01 1967     
 4 1967-10-01     3143 1967-10-01 1967
