 6 1967-12-01     3018 1967-12-01 1967     
 7 1968-01-01     2878 1968-01-01 1968     
 8 1968-02-01     3001 1968-02-01 1968     
 9 1968-03-01     2877 1968-03-01 1968     
10 1968-04-01     2709 1968-04-01 1968     
# ℹ 564 more rows
The new values identify the first four digits of the stored date strings. Extraction alone does not validate the rest of a date. A string could begin with four digits and still contain an invalid month later. For calendar calculations, parse the complete value and inspect the result.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.2 Parse and check dates
as.Date() converts character values into Date values. With our familiar ISO text, the default conversion recognizes the year-month-day arrangement:

as.Date(date_preview$date_text)

[1] "1967-07-01" "2000-07-01"


The result is a vector of dates. It has not replaced either column in monthly_text. Make the rule explicit before storing the result. The format argument tells R how the source string is arranged: %Y is a four-digit year, %m a numeric month, and %d a day. The hyphens in "%Y-%m-%d" match the literal separators.

monthly_dates <- monthly_text |>
  mutate(parsed_date = as.Date(date_text, format = "%Y-%m-%d"))
monthly_dates
# A tibble: 574 × 5
   date       unemploy date_text  year_text parsed_date
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <date>     
 1 1967-07-01     2944 1967-07-01 1967      1967-07-01 
 2 1967-08-01     2945 1967-08-01 1967      1967-08-01 
 3 1967-09-01     2958 1967-09-01 1967      1967-09-01 
 4 1967-10-01     3143 1967-10-01 1967      1967-10-01 
 5 1967-11-01     3066 1967-11-01 1967      1967-11-01 
 6 1967-12-01     3018 1967-12-01 1967      1967-12-01 
 7 1968-01-01     2878 1968-01-01 1968      1968-01-01 
 8 1968-02-01     3001 1968-02-01 1968      1968-02-01 
 9 1968-03-01     2877 1968-03-01 1968      1968-03-01 
10 1968-04-01     2709 1968-04-01 1968      1968-04-01

The new column has date type, while date_text remains character. We have retained the original date as a reference. Use the familiar identical() check to compare the complete columns:

identical(monthly_dates$date, monthly_dates$parsed_date)

[1] TRUE


identical() compares the complete objects, including their class and missing values, and returns one logical value. Here TRUE confirms a reversible conversion for the entire column, not just the printed rows. It verifies our representation; it does not independently validate the economic source or make its monthly measurements daily observations.
An incorrect format can produce missing dates without stopping the command. To see why checking matters, deliberately ask for slashes where the source contains hyphens. This demonstration keeps the failed result in a separate column and does not replace our successfully parsed dates.

parse_diagnosis <- monthly_text |>
  mutate(wrong_date = as.Date(date_text, format = "%Y/%m/%d"))

The last output isolates non-missing source strings whose conversions failed. All 574 monthly records fail this deliberately mismatched format. Read a source value beside the supplied format, correct the format, and repeat the check. Do not fill failed parses with a convenient date: that would turn a conversion problem into invented information.
Some wrong formats can also return plausible but incorrect dates, particularly when the order of month and day is ambiguous. Therefore, absence of NA is only one check. Retain the source strings, inspect the known date convention, and compare complete values when a reference date column is available, as it is here.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.3 Read month names
A source may write a month name instead of a month number. We need a parser that knows both the arrangement of the text and the language of its names. Readr’s parse_date() returns Date values from character input. Unlike as.Date(), it reports parsing problems in a warning when a non-missing input fails. We first use it on text whose interpretation we have already checked:

parse_date(date_preview$date_text)

[1] "1967-07-01" "2000-07-01"


Its default format is ISO year-month-day. The printed dates should agree with the earlier result. As with as.Date(), the returned vector does not alter the input. The format option makes the expected arrangement explicit:

readr_dates <- parse_date(monthly_text$date_text, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
identical(monthly_dates$date, readr_dates)

[1] TRUE


The comparison checks the complete column again. We have not gained a different time series by using a second parser.
For month names, locale() constructs a set of reading conventions. It does not read data by itself. Inspect its default specification first:

locale()

<locale>
Numbers:  123,456.78
Formats:  %AD / %AT
Timezone: UTC
Encoding: UTF-8
<date_names>
Days:   Sunday (Sun), Monday (Mon), Tuesday (Tue), Wednesday (Wed), Thursday
        (Thu), Friday (Fri), Saturday (Sat)
Months: January (Jan), February (Feb), March (Mar), April (Apr), May (May),
        June (Jun), July (Jul), August (Aug), September (Sep), October
        (Oct), November (Nov), December (Dec)
AM/PM:  AM/PM


The output describes conventions for dates, numbers, and text encoding, rather than economic observations. The default uses English date names. State that choice explicitly with the date_names option set to "en", storing the result for reuse:

english_dates <- locale(date_names = "en")
english_dates

<locale>
Numbers:  123,456.78
Formats:  %AD / %AT
Timezone: UTC
Encoding: UTF-8
<date_names>
Days:   Sunday (Sun), Monday (Mon), Tuesday (Tue), Wednesday (Wed), Thursday
        (Thu), Friday (Fri), Saturday (Sat)
Months: January (Jan), February (Feb), March (Mar), April (Apr), May (May),
        June (Jun), July (Jul), August (Aug), September (Sep), October
        (Oct), November (Nov), December (Dec)
AM/PM:  AM/PM


The printed specification includes English month names and abbreviations. It also lists other reading conventions that we do not change here. A locale determines how existing text is interpreted; it does not translate or modify the source text.
Use two real observations from economics to check an alternative representation: July 1993 and June 1999. The strings below transcribe their months using English abbreviations and two-digit years. The original date and unemploy remain alongside them. The condition in if_else() chooses the July spelling for the first date and the June spelling for the other selected date:

month_name_text <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  filter(date == as.Date("1993-07-01") | date == as.Date("1999-06-01")) |>
  mutate(month_text = if_else(date == as.Date("1993-07-01"),
                              "01 Jul.93", "01 Jun.99"))
month_name_text
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  date       unemploy month_text
  <date>        <dbl> <chr>     
1 1993-07-01     8930 01 Jul.93 
2 1999-06-01     5951 01 Jun.99 


The table has 2 source months. We have changed their text representation, not their unemployment measurements. The source dates establish the intended years as 1993 and 1999; two digits alone would not document the century.
Pass the stored locale through parse_date()’s locale option. The pattern %d %b.%y expects a day, a space, an abbreviated month, a literal period, and a two-digit year. Punctuation is part of the format, just as the hyphens were in the ISO lesson:

month_name_dates <- month_name_text |>
  mutate(parsed_month = parse_date(month_text,
                                   format = "%d %b.%y",
                                   locale = english_dates))
month_name_dates
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  date       unemploy month_text parsed_month
  <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <date>      
1 1993-07-01     8930 01 Jul.93  1993-07-01  
2 1999-06-01     5951 01 Jun.99  1999-06-01  

identical(month_name_dates$date, month_name_dates$parsed_month)

[1] TRUE


TRUE checks both transcribed strings against the real reference dates, including the century. If a documented month name does not parse, inspect both its spelling and language and the supplied pattern. An English locale cannot identify arbitrary names from another language. Do not treat an absence of missing results as proof that the year or month is right: compare against the source convention too. The day 01 continues to represent a monthly observation, not an event known to have occurred on that day.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.4 Select a time window
Once parsing is checked, year() from lubridate returns the numeric calendar year of each date. Use a new calendar_year column to make the filtering rule readable. We want the monthly observations from 2000 through 2014, including both endpoint years. The comma inside filter() requires both conditions to hold.

monthly_window <- monthly_dates |>
  mutate(calendar_year = year(parsed_date)) |>
  filter(calendar_year >= 2000, calendar_year <= 2014)
monthly_window
# A tibble: 180 × 6
   date       unemploy date_text  year_text parsed_date calendar_year
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <date>              <dbl>
 1 2000-01-01     5708 2000-01-01 2000      2000-01-01           2000
 2 2000-02-01     5858 2000-02-01 2000      2000-02-01           2000
 3 2000-03-01     5733 2000-03-01 2000      2000-03-01           2000
 4 2000-04-01     5481 2000-04-01 2000      2000-04-01           2000
 5 2000-05-01     5758 2000-05-01 2000      2000-05-01           2000
 6 2000-06-01     5651 2000-06-01 2000      2000-06-01           2000
 7 2000-07-01     5747 2000-07-01 2000      2000-07-01           2000
 8 2000-08-01     5853 2000-08-01 2000      2000-08-01           2000
 9 2000-09-01     5625 2000-09-01 2000      2000-09-01           2000
10 2000-10-01     5534 2000-10-01 2000      2000-10-01           2000
# ℹ 170 more rows

nrow(monthly_window)

[1] 180


The result retains 180 monthly observations. calendar_year repeats within each year because extraction does not aggregate observations. The unemployment measure still refers to a month and is still recorded in thousands of people. Computing one annual statistic would require a separate, explicitly chosen summary.
This distinction also protects the annual OWID data. A year can locate an annual observation on a graph without conversion into an exact date. Do not append a midyear month or day merely to satisfy a preferred storage class. Preserve what the source records and choose a representation appropriate to the comparison.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.5 Review

str_extract() returns a matching substring; extracting a year does not validate the complete date text.
as.character() and as.Date() change representation; an explicit format and a complete comparison help check conversion.
parse_date() reads dates with an explicit format; locale() specifies the language of recorded month names. Check the century against the source.
year() extracts a calendar component without changing the observation’s recorded time precision.
Retain source strings, diagnose failed conversions, and avoid inventing days for annual or monthly measurements.

Chapter 17 next develops list columns by splitting the entity names used in Section 15.7. Later, Chapter 19 uses ordered monthly records in an applied reshaping workflow.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
16.6 Exercises

Recreate date text from economics. Diagnose the slash-separated format, then parse the correct format in a new column. Check exact agreement with the original dates and explain why replacing failed dates would be inappropriate.
Before running code, predict how the number of retained months changes if the 2000–2014 window is extended through 2015. Extract the text year and calendar year independently from economics, then check the prediction. Does the first day in a displayed date establish an exact event day? Should OWID’s Year receive an added day?
Recreate the July 1993 and June 1999 source rows and their alternative month-name strings. Parse them with an English locale and verify complete equality with the source dates. Explain why "%Y-%m-%d" is unsuitable for these strings and why a format change alone would not resolve a month-name language mismatch.

title: 16  Dates and times
text:
Worked answers






NoteRepair the format





This answer uses only packaged data. The incorrect parse is retained for diagnosis beside the corrected result.

library(tidyverse)
answer_dates <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  mutate(
    date_text = as.character(date),
    wrong_date = as.Date(date_text, format = "%Y/%m/%d"),
    parsed_date = as.Date(date_text, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  )
answer_failed <- answer_dates |>
  filter(!is.na(date_text), is.na(wrong_date))
answer_failed
# A tibble: 574 × 5
   date       unemploy date_text  wrong_date parsed_date
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <date>     <date>     
 1 1967-07-01     2944 1967-07-01 NA         1967-07-01 
 2 1967-08-01     2945 1967-08-01 NA         1967-08-01 
 3 1967-09-01     2958 1967-09-01 NA         1967-09-01 
 4 1967-10-01     3143 1967-10-01 NA         1967-10-01 
 5 1967-11-01     3066 1967-11-01 NA         1967-11-01 
 6 1967-12-01     3018 1967-12-01 NA         1967-12-01 
 7 1968-01-01     2878 1968-01-01 NA         1968-01-01 
 8 1968-02-01     3001 1968-02-01 NA         1968-02-01 
 9 1968-03-01     2877 1968-03-01 NA         1968-03-01 
10 1968-04-01     2709 1968-04-01 NA         1968-04-01 
# ℹ 564 more rows

identical(answer_dates$date, answer_dates$parsed_date)

[1] TRUE


All 574 failures come from a format that expects the wrong separators. The corrected column agrees exactly with the original Date column. These are conversion failures, not evidence of unknown source months. Replacing them with arbitrary dates would conceal the cause and alter the time series.









NoteRetain monthly precision





Load the packages explicitly in a fresh session. Extract the text and calendar components after retaining the source date.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
answer_window <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  mutate(
    date_text = as.character(date),
    year_text = str_extract(date_text, "^[0-9]{4}"),
    parsed_date = as.Date(date_text, format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    calendar_year = year(parsed_date)
  ) |>
  filter(calendar_year >= 2000, calendar_year <= 2014)
answer_window
# A tibble: 180 × 6
   date       unemploy date_text  year_text parsed_date calendar_year
   <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     <date>              <dbl>
 1 2000-01-01     5708 2000-01-01 2000      2000-01-01           2000
 2 2000-02-01     5858 2000-02-01 2000      2000-02-01           2000
 3 2000-03-01     5733 2000-03-01 2000      2000-03-01           2000
 4 2000-04-01     5481 2000-04-01 2000      2000-04-01           2000
 5 2000-05-01     5758 2000-05-01 2000      2000-05-01           2000
 6 2000-06-01     5651 2000-06-01 2000      2000-06-01           2000
 7 2000-07-01     5747 2000-07-01 2000      2000-07-01           2000
 8 2000-08-01     5853 2000-08-01 2000      2000-08-01           2000
 9 2000-09-01     5625 2000-09-01 2000      2000-09-01           2000
10 2000-10-01     5534 2000-10-01 2000      2000-10-01           2000
# ℹ 170 more rows

nrow(answer_window)

[1] 180

answer_extended <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  mutate(calendar_year = year(date)) |>
  filter(calendar_year >= 2000, calendar_year <= 2015)
nrow(answer_extended)

[1] 184

nrow(answer_extended) - nrow(answer_window)

[1] 4


The original window has 180 monthly records. Extending the endpoint can add only available source months in 2015, not an assumed twelve. It adds 4 records, as the source series ends during that year. year_text is character; calendar_year is numeric. Neither reduces twelve monthly measurements to one annual measurement. The first day represents the month in this dataset; it is not an exact event day. OWID’s annual Year should remain a year, without an assumed month or day.









NoteCheck month names and the century






library(tidyverse)
answer_month_names <- economics |>
  select(date, unemploy) |>
  filter(date == as.Date("1993-07-01") | date == as.Date("1999-06-01")) |>
  mutate(month_text = if_else(date == as.Date("1993-07-01"),
                              "01 Jul.93", "01 Jun.99"))
answer_english <- locale(date_names = "en")
answer_month_names <- answer_month_names |>
  mutate(parsed_month = parse_date(month_text,
                                   format = "%d %b.%y",
                                   locale = answer_english))
answer_month_names
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  date       unemploy month_text parsed_month
  <date>        <dbl> <chr>      <date>      
1 1993-07-01     8930 01 Jul.93  1993-07-01  
2 1999-06-01     5951 01 Jun.99  1999-06-01  

identical(answer_month_names$date, answer_month_names$parsed_month)

[1] TRUE

answer_month_names |>
  filter(!is.na(month_text), is.na(parsed_month))
# A tibble: 0 × 4
# ℹ 4 variables: date <date>, unemploy <dbl>, month_text <chr>,
#   parsed_month <date>


The equality is TRUE, and the failure check has zero rows. The known dates verify July 1993 and June 1999, including the century. ISO format expects a four-digit year first and numeric month with hyphens, whereas these strings put the day first and use English month abbreviations. A language mismatch requires the documented language in the locale as well as the correct format. A plausible but incorrect century could pass a missingness check, which is why we retained reference dates. No source measurement has been replaced.

title: 17  List columns
text:
17.1 Keep different objects together
An ordinary atomic vector holds values of one basic type. A list can keep objects of different types or lengths together without converting them to a common type. A list column stores one such component for each row of a table. We will split existing entity names into words, retain the words together, then expand them while preserving their connection to the original names.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
The first example needs only base R. The application uses the public country data already used in Section 15.7, not participant information. Selection and column creation are prerequisites; the later reshaping chapter is not.
A list can hold different types together, such as a number and some text:
list(1, "a")

[[1]]
[1] 1

[[2]]
[1] "a"
The printed result has two components: the number 1 and the character value "a". Their types remain distinct. A list is useful when the pieces we want to keep together are not all the same kind of object.
A list is not necessarily a dataset with observations in rows. Tables and model results can themselves be stored as list components. The fuller comparison in Chapter 28 explains how lists relate to the other structures used in R.

title: 17  List columns
section: 17.2 Keep the words of a name together
text:
17.2 Keep the words of a name together
Our World in Data, abbreviated OWID, supplies the captured life-expectancy CSV used earlier. It contains aggregate entity-year statistics. It has no workshop participants. We reuse its entity names because names can contain different numbers of words. Copy the book’s captured CSV into your project’s examples folder:

library(tidyverse)
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

owid <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

entity_names <- owid |>
  filter(Year == 2023) |>
  select(Entity, Code, Year)
head(entity_names)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Entity         Code      Year
  <chr>          <chr>    <dbl>
1 Afghanistan    AFG       2023
2 Africa         OWID_AFR  2023
3 Albania        ALB       2023
4 Algeria        DZA       2023
5 American Samoa ASM       2023
6 Americas       NA        2023


The selected year has 261 entities. Some are territories or aggregates, so not every name denotes a sovereign country. Retaining one year avoids repeating each name across years. Code is missing for some aggregates; retain Entity and Year as well rather than assuming codes identify every row.
str_split() takes character values and a separator pattern, returning a list with one character vector for each input value. Here the familiar fixed(" ") specifies a literal space, as in Section 15.7. The captured names use single spaces between words; we are splitting their recorded form, not repairing source errors:

name_lists <- entity_names |>
  mutate(words = str_split(Entity, fixed(" ")))
head(name_lists)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  Entity         Code      Year words    
  <chr>          <chr>    <dbl> <list>   
1 Afghanistan    AFG       2023 <chr [1]>
2 Africa         OWID_AFR  2023 <chr [1]>
3 Albania        ALB       2023 <chr [1]>
4 Algeria        DZA       2023 <chr [1]>
5 American Samoa ASM       2023 <chr [2]>
6 Americas       NA        2023 <chr [1]>

name_lists |>
  filter(Entity == "United States")
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  Entity        Code   Year words    
  <chr>         <chr> <dbl> <list>   
1 United States USA    2023 <chr [2]>


The new words column is a list column. Its component for “United States” contains two strings, “United” and “States”. The printed <chr [2]> abbreviation describes a two-element character vector stored in that cell; it is not the literal cell text. Names with one word have one-element components. The table still has one row per entity in 2023, and all original name and code values remain.

title: 17  List columns
text:
17.3 Expand words into rows
When we need to inspect words separately, unnest_longer() from tidyr expands a list column. First supply the table through the pipe and select the list column words. Each component’s values become separate rows, with the other columns repeated alongside them. Assignment stores a new table; name_lists retains the complete components:

name_words_default <- name_lists |>
  unnest_longer(words)
head(name_words_default)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  Entity         Code      Year words      
  <chr>          <chr>    <dbl> <chr>      
1 Afghanistan    AFG       2023 Afghanistan
2 Africa         OWID_AFR  2023 Africa     
3 Albania        ALB       2023 Albania    
4 Algeria        DZA       2023 Algeria    
5 American Samoa ASM       2023 American   
6 American Samoa ASM       2023 Samoa      


The column is still called words, but it now contains one character value per row. The original entity, code, and year stay attached to each word. Give the expanded value column a singular name with values_to:

name_words_named <- name_lists |>
  unnest_longer(words, values_to = "word")
head(name_words_named)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  Entity         Code      Year word       
  <chr>          <chr>    <dbl> <chr>      
1 Afghanistan    AFG       2023 Afghanistan
2 Africa         OWID_AFR  2023 Africa     
3 Albania        ALB       2023 Albania    
4 Algeria        DZA       2023 Algeria    
5 American Samoa ASM       2023 American   
6 American Samoa ASM       2023 Samoa      


The option changes the output name, not the number of rows or the words. The components also have an order within each name. Add indices_to to name the column that records those positions:

name_words <- name_lists |>
  unnest_longer(
    words,
    values_to = "word",
    indices_to = "word_position"
  )
head(name_words)
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  Entity         Code      Year word_position word       
  <chr>          <chr>    <dbl>         <int> <chr>      
1 Afghanistan    AFG       2023             1 Afghanistan
2 Africa         OWID_AFR  2023             1 Africa     
3 Albania        ALB       2023             1 Albania    
4 Algeria        DZA       2023             1 Algeria    
5 American Samoa ASM       2023             1 American   
6 American Samoa ASM       2023             2 Samoa      

name_words |>
  filter(Entity == "United States")
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  Entity        Code   Year word_position word  
  <chr>         <chr> <dbl>         <int> <chr> 
1 United States USA    2023             1 United
2 United States USA    2023             2 States


The United States now contributes two rows. Each retains its original entity, code, and year, while positions 1 and 2 identify “United” and “States”. A row now represents an entity-word position. It is not an additional entity or an independent observation of life expectancy.
count() counts rows within combinations of columns, as in the age-group checks in Chapter 14. Its default result column is n. Start with the number of word positions for each entity-year:

word_counts_default <- name_words |>
  count(Entity, Year)
head(word_counts_default)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Entity          Year     n
  <chr>          <dbl> <int>
1 Afghanistan     2023     1
2 Africa          2023     1
3 Albania         2023     1
4 Algeria         2023     1
5 American Samoa  2023     2
6 Americas        2023     1


Each output row describes one entity in 2023; n counts that name’s words, not additional entities. The name option gives this count a more informative heading. It names the returned count column, rather than selecting a source variable:

word_counts <- name_words |>
  count(Entity, Year, name = "words")
head(word_counts)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Entity          Year words
  <chr>          <dbl> <int>
1 Afghanistan     2023     1
2 Africa          2023     1
3 Albania         2023     1
4 Algeria         2023     1
5 American Samoa  2023     2
6 Americas        2023     1


The values match the previous n column, but the heading now states what was counted. We can reconcile the expanded table’s row total with these component counts. sum() adds numeric input values and returns one total without changing them. Here $ extracts the numeric count column:

word_total <- sum(word_counts$words)
word_total

[1] 389

nrow(name_words)

[1] 389

word_total == nrow(name_words)

[1] TRUE


The equality returns TRUE: adding the words across names gives exactly the number of expanded rows. These counts contain no missing entries, so there is no missing-value option to set in this calculation. The total counts word positions, with repeated words counted each time they occur.
A separate check asks whether any entity-year-position combination occurs more than once. An identifying combination should occur exactly once in this example:

name_words |>
  count(Entity, Year, word_position) |>
  filter(n != 1)
# A tibble: 0 × 4
# ℹ 4 variables: Entity <chr>, Year <dbl>, word_position <int>, n <int>

nrow(name_lists)

[1] 261

nrow(word_counts)

[1] 261

nrow(name_words)

[1] 389


The duplicate-position check returns zero rows. There are still 261 entities, matching the 261 source rows, but 389 word positions. Counting rows of the expanded table would give longer names more weight. A mean of a measurement repeated across these rows would therefore answer a different question from a mean across entities.
Words are parts of names. Splitting “Trinidad and Tobago” does not create separate records for three places, and “and” is not an entity. This example teaches storage and expansion, not geographical classification. Similarly, if another source stores paired aliases and descriptions, splitting both columns requires checking that each alias still matches its own description. Expanding them independently can create incorrect combinations; this file supplies no such paired lists.

title: 17  List columns
text:
17.4 Review

list() keeps components together while allowing different types.
A component can itself be a more complex object; the list need not have a rectangular shape.
str_split() returns one list component per input string; a list column retains one component per table row.
unnest_longer() expands components into rows; retain identifiers and within-component positions.
count() names and checks component counts; sum() reconciles their total with the expanded row count.
Expanded rows need not be independent observations. Preserve the source name and interpret the new unit before calculating summaries.

The later Chapter 19 changes the layout of questionnaire and monthly data. It also checks which columns identify each resulting row.

title: 17  List columns
text:
17.5 Exercises

Explain why list(1, "a") preserves two types. What does <chr [2]> mean for a list cell containing the words of "United States"? How does it differ from literal character text?
Reload the captured CSV, keep the entity names in 2023, split them on spaces, and expand the resulting list with positions. Before running the expansion, predict how many rows “Trinidad and Tobago” contributes before and after expansion. Inspect its words and positions to check your prediction.
Name the per-entity word count words, add those counts, and reconcile the result with the expanded row count. Check that every entity-year-position combination is unique. A colleague keeps only word after expansion and calculates a mean of a measurement repeated beside those words. Diagnose the loss of identifiers and the changed weighting.

title: 17  List columns
text:
Worked answers






NoteComponents and text






library(tidyverse)
list(1, "a")

[[1]]
[1] 1

[[2]]
[1] "a"

str_split("United States", fixed(" "))

[[1]]
[1] "United" "States"


The first list retains a number and a character value as separate components. The second contains one component holding two character values. <chr [2]> describes a character vector of length two inside one list cell. It is a compact description of the cell, not literal text stored there. A literal character cell holds the complete name as one string; a list cell can hold the vector of its words without adding table rows.









NotePreserve the complete name






library(tidyverse)
answer_owid <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

answer_names <- answer_owid |>
  filter(Year == 2023) |>
  select(Entity, Code, Year) |>
  mutate(words = str_split(Entity, fixed(" ")))
answer_words <- answer_names |>
  unnest_longer(words, values_to = "word", indices_to = "word_position")
answer_names |>
  filter(Entity == "Trinidad and Tobago")
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  Entity              Code   Year words    
  <chr>               <chr> <dbl> <list>   
1 Trinidad and Tobago TTO    2023 <chr [3]>

answer_words |>
  filter(Entity == "Trinidad and Tobago")
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  Entity              Code   Year word_position word    
  <chr>               <chr> <dbl>         <int> <chr>   
1 Trinidad and Tobago TTO    2023             1 Trinidad
2 Trinidad and Tobago TTO    2023             2 and     
3 Trinidad and Tobago TTO    2023             3 Tobago  


One entity row becomes three word-position rows. Each retains the same complete name, code, and year. The three words are not three countries.









NoteCheck the new row unit






library(tidyverse)
answer_owid <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

answer_names <- answer_owid |>
  filter(Year == 2023) |>
  select(Entity, Code, Year)
answer_words <- answer_names |>
  mutate(words = str_split(Entity, fixed(" "))) |>
  unnest_longer(words, values_to = "word", indices_to = "word_position")
answer_counts <- answer_words |>
  count(Entity, Year, name = "words")
answer_total <- sum(answer_counts$words)
answer_total

[1] 389

nrow(answer_words)

[1] 389

answer_total == nrow(answer_words)

[1] TRUE

nrow(answer_counts) == nrow(answer_names)

[1] TRUE

answer_words |>
  count(Entity, Year, word_position) |>
  filter(n != 1)
# A tibble: 0 × 4
# ℹ 4 variables: Entity <chr>, Year <dbl>, word_position <int>, n <int>


Both equalities return TRUE, and the duplicate-position check returns zero rows. The same entities remain, but those with longer names contribute more rows. A row count describes word positions; a mean of repeated entity measurements would weight entities by their number of words unless we first return to one record per entity.
Keeping only word would remove the complete name, code, year, and within-name position. A repeated word could then no longer be traced to its source name. Retain these columns in the working table; select a short display separately if needed. Likewise, repeating a measurement once per word gives longer names more weight. Count or summarize at the entity level when the question concerns entities.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.1 A workflow in R
This chapter opens Manage datasets. After exploring tables and working with individual variables, we consider how to bring files into R, preserve their metadata, and save checked results. You can return here whenever a project supplies a different format.
The first download and CSV import in Section 7.7 introduced the route from a file to a table, and Section 7.8 saved a separate copy. This chapter extends that workflow to different formats, metadata, and sources. Return here when an unfamiliar file, a label, or a conversion requires more than the basic reader.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We reuse selection, conversion, missing-value checks, and column inspection from earlier chapters. All examples use the historical country data, with two six-country format excerpts and the complete package dataset. This chapter needs three files in examples: lifeexp-excerpt.dta, lifeexp-excerpt.sav, and lifeexp.csv. No GSS file is required.
So far, packaged data and a saved survey extract have supplied our tables. When a research archive supplies a file, we need to bring it into R and check what the format preserves.
My view is that learning to work comfortably with tibbles is enough to carry out most data analysis.
Files on disk and objects inside R are different things. For many tabular analyses, we can organize the work in three steps, which connect the earlier table operations to files on disk:
Imagine receiving a household survey from a research archive. The archive is the source, the downloaded Stata file is the format, and the tibble you import is an R object in your current session. Changing the format does not, by itself, change whom the survey represents or what its questions mean. A codebook describes the variables, their values, and important details of data collection. Keep it with the data: importing a file successfully does not tell you how to interpret its contents.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
Figure 18.1: Using tibbles as a bridge between input and output formats.





Import data from another format as a tibble (Section 18.2).
Process the tibble with the selection and transformation tools already learned.
Export the tibble to another format (Section 18.4).

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.2 Importing data
The same survey may be offered in several formats. Choose among those supplied by the producer before converting anything yourself: a labelled statistical file may carry information that a plain-text copy leaves to a separate codebook. Use Table 18.1 as a reference when you receive a file, rather than as a list to memorize. Functions without a prefix come from base R or from readr, readxl, and haven, which are installed with the tidyverse; a function written as package::function() comes from a package you may need to install first.




Table 18.1: Common input formats, the functions that read them, and what to check.





Format
Read with
Check




Plain text.csv, .tsv, .txt
read_csv(), read_tsv()
Identifiers such as 00123; dates such as 03/04/2025; guessed column types


Excel.xlsx, .xls
read_excel()
Title rows, merged cells, several tables on one sheet


Stata / SPSS / SAS.dta, .sav, .sas7bdat
read_dta(), read_sav(), read_sas()
Value labels; codes such as “Refused” and “Not asked”; SAS labels in a separate catalog


R data.rds, .RData, .rda
read_rds(), load()
Objects other than tables; R or package versions


Binary tables.parquet, .feather, .ftr
arrow::read_parquet(), arrow::read_feather()
Which types, labels, and documentation survived conversion


Nested and web.json, .xml, .html
jsonlite::fromJSON(), xml2::read_xml(), rvest::read_html()
Nested records or page content to rearrange into a table


Spatial.shp and its companion files, GeoTIFF .tif
sf::read_sf(), terra::rast()
A shapefile is a set of files; keep shapes with their attributes


Archives.zip, .gz, .bz2, .xz
unzip(); read_csv() also reads .csv.gz
Containers: find the data files and documentation inside


Databases and APIs(no file)
DBI::dbGetQuery(), httr2::request()
Ways of obtaining data, not formats; results are often JSON or tables


Uninformative.dat, .bin
Depends on the producer
Consult the producer’s instructions







Data can also come from inside R: datasets included with R and its packages, or values typed directly into code, as in the named-country example in Introduction to R. Folders can hold several data files at once. Text, images, and recordings may require other tools before they yield the variables needed for a particular analysis. These lists are not exhaustive. A small file is not necessarily a simple dataset.
R reads these formats with short commands. The examples below use two small files containing the same six countries: lifeexp-excerpt.dta and lifeexp-excerpt.sav. The haven package, installed with the tidyverse, reads both. In the printed tibble, the header gives rows first and columns second: 6 × 6 means six countries and six variables. Numbers at the left mark row positions, not respondent IDs. Under each column name, a cue such as <dbl> identifies its type; <dbl> means a numeric column stored as doubles:
Before running the import, open the r4ss project folder you created in Section 1.1.1 and check it with getwd(). Inside it, create a subfolder named examples using your file manager or editor. Download both linked files and move them into that subfolder, keeping their exact names. A browser may initially save them in Downloads; clicking the links alone does not place them in examples.
The relative path "examples/lifeexp-excerpt.dta" tells R to start in its working directory, enter examples, and read lifeexp-excerpt.dta. The same convention applies to the SPSS file. To check the locations before importing, file.exists() returns TRUE for each file R can find:

getwd()

[1] "D:/Agent/R4SS/en"

file.exists("examples/lifeexp-excerpt.dta")

[1] TRUE

file.exists("examples/lifeexp-excerpt.sav")

[1] TRUE


Both checks should return TRUE. If one is FALSE, check the directory, subfolder, and exact filename, including a possible extra suffix added by your browser. Keep the original downloads unchanged. Save the import commands in a script in r4ss so that you can repeat them in a new session.
Load tidyverse for table operations and haven for labelled statistical files. read_dta() takes the Stata file path and returns a tibble. Assign it to a distinct object so that importing another format will not overwrite it:

library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
countries_stata <- read_dta("examples/lifeexp-excerpt.dta")
countries_stata
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  region               country   popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
  <dbl+lbl>            <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Albania        -0.6    74   870        49
2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Poland          0      73  4390        NA
3 2 [North America]    Canada          0.8    79 20900        99
4 2 [North America]    Cuba            0.3    75  2240        NA
5 3 [South America]    Argentina       1.2    73  7960        NA
6 3 [South America]    Brazil          1.5    69  4980        76


The result has six rows and six columns. read_sav() takes an SPSS file path and also returns a tibble. Keep it separately so that the two imported excerpts remain available:

countries_spss <- read_sav("examples/lifeexp-excerpt.sav")
countries_spss
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  region               country   popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
  <dbl+lbl>            <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Albania        -0.6    74   870        49
2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Poland          0      73  4390        NA
3 2 [North America]    Canada          0.8    79 20900        99
4 2 [North America]    Cuba            0.3    75  2240        NA
5 3 [South America]    Argentina       1.2    73  7960        NA
6 3 [South America]    Brazil          1.5    69  4980        76


The same six countries appear in the same order. Neither reading function changes its file on disk. Printed equality is a useful first inspection, but labels and missing values also need checking when formats change.
The region column also prints value labels in brackets, such as 1 [Europe & C. Asia]; <dbl+lbl> indicates numeric codes with attached labels. Labels help describe those codes but do not turn them into quantities.
Each row is a country. The six rows are Albania, Poland, Canada, Cuba, Argentina, and Brazil, selected from tidystata::lifeexp. The source is the World Bank World Development Indicators, available under CC BY 4.0. The excerpt contains region, country, annual population growth in percent (popgrowth), life expectancy at birth in years (lexp), GNI per capita, Atlas method, in current U.S. dollars (gnppc), and the percentage of the population using safely managed drinking water services (safewater). Indicators refer to 1998 except safe water, which refers to 2000; values are rounded in the package. NA marks unavailable safe-water values for Poland, Cuba, and Argentina. It does not mean zero access.
These countries are a purposeful teaching selection, not a representative sample of countries. The packaged snapshot is historical; it is not a source of current country estimates. Once the data are in R, these meanings remain the same whichever file format we read.
Importing and exporting are checks at the boundaries of an analysis. A file that opens without an error can still have the wrong sheet, a misread date, or an identifier that has lost its leading zeros. Table 18.2 lists what to check at each stage.




Table 18.2: Checks at the boundaries of an analysis.









Stage
Check




Before importing
Read the documentation; identify the observations, variables, and special codes


After importing
Inspect a few records, the number of rows and columns, and the types of important variables


While cleaning
Keep the original download unchanged; clean in code; save derived files under distinct names


Before sharing
Open the export in the intended software; check identifiers, dates, missing values, and labels







For restricted data, use only the export and release procedures permitted by the provider. Changing from a statistical file to CSV does not change the conditions governing its use.

18.2.1 Where data come from
Your research question helps determine what counts as an observation. A sociologist might study people or organizations; an economist might study households, firms, or countries; a political scientist might study voters, elections, or legislative speeches. These boundaries overlap: a household survey can support questions about employment, family life, health, and political participation. Table 18.3 gives starting points, not a ranking of what each discipline uses most.




Table 18.3: Examples of data across social-science fields.









Field
Example data




Sociology
Survey responses, social ties, organizational records


Demography
Births, deaths, migration, and census records


Economics
Household income, employment, and firm records


Public policy
Program participation, benefits, and evaluation outcomes


Political science
Election results and public-opinion surveys


Psychology
Experimental responses, behavior, and psychological scales


Education
Student assessments, school records, classroom observations


Geography
Geographic boundaries, environmental measures, travel patterns


Urban studies
Housing records, land use, neighborhood indicators


Communication
Audience surveys, interviews, and communication networks


Media studies
News articles, online posts, broadcast transcripts


Anthropology
Interview transcripts, field notes, documentary photographs


Criminology
Crime reports, court records, victimization surveys


Social work
Service records, client interviews, intervention outcomes


Public health
Health surveys, disease surveillance, patient records







A subject label alone cannot tell us which file format to expect. The format depends on how the material was collected and distributed: a survey might arrive as a statistical file or CSV, election returns as a spreadsheet, online posts as JSON or text, and interviews as transcripts and recordings.






TipGetting access to data





Access follows the collection’s conditions, not the name of your discipline. Some files are openly downloadable; others require registration and an agreement, a university subscription, or a research partnership. More sensitive records may require a project application, training, and work inside a secure computing environment. “Free of charge” does not necessarily mean unrestricted reuse. Detailed locations, school records, and linked administrative records can have tighter access conditions than published summaries, and platform terms and participant consent may limit collection or reuse.
Students can use many of the same archives as established researchers, although particular collections have their own eligibility rules. The UK Data Service lets students and researchers from different disciplines and countries register; its access policy distinguishes open, safeguarded, and controlled data. IPUMS International provides census microdata without charge after an access application, subject to conditions on use. ICPSR notes that students generally need a faculty sponsor for restricted-data applications, and the Qualitative Data Repository distinguishes standard access from project-specific conditions. These are examples of access arrangements, rather than promises that any particular file will be available to every reader.
For a first project, choose a documented dataset that you can actually obtain within the time available, with a question its contents can answer.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.3 Specify the CSV import
We continue with all 68 countries and six variables in lifeexp, using countries as a working name. The assignment below retains the source’s observations, order, missing values, and labels. We keep this object for comparison with the imported copy.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
countries <- lifeexp

Research data also arrive as files. To practice importing the same observations, download lifeexp.csv and save it in the examples folder inside your r4ss project. This file contains every row and column from the supplied lifeexp, in its original order. Its dataset notes give the source, units, and missing-value convention. The Stata and SPSS examples above in Section 18.2 use a smaller excerpt; here we use the complete dataset.
Check the working directory with getwd(), as in Section 1.1.1. read_csv() reads a comma-separated file and returns a tibble. Assignment stores the import separately as countries_csv, allowing us to compare a CSV import with the labelled package object. The original file and countries stay unchanged.

countries_csv <- read_csv("examples/lifeexp.csv")
Rows: 68 Columns: 6
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (1): country
dbl (5): region, popgrowth, lexp, gnppc, safewater

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

countries_csv
# A tibble: 68 × 6
   region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
    <dbl> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1      1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2      1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 3      1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 4      1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 5      1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 6      1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 7      1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
 8      1 Bulgaria                    -0.7    71  1440        90
 9      1 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10      1 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows


Each row represents one country. lexp is life expectancy at birth in years; popgrowth is annual population growth in percent; gnppc is GNI per capita in current US dollars, using the Atlas method. These refer to 1998. safewater is the percentage using safely managed drinking water services in 2000. The import message reports inferred column types. Its optional spec() suggestion, for example spec(countries_csv), displays the column specification. Adding show_col_types = FALSE hides this informational message; it does not correct types or values.
Some water measurements are missing, including those for Poland, Cuba and Argentina. The CSV writes missing measurements as NA; this is a file token, not a reported percentage. The default read_csv() missing tokens are an empty field and "NA", so these entries are already missing after import. mean() adds a numeric vector’s values and divides by their number. Here $ extracts the water column:

mean(countries_csv$safewater)

[1] NA


The result is NA because some inputs are missing. We can state the file’s missing-value rule explicitly with na = c("", "NA"). The na argument supplies the complete set of missing tokens for this import, replacing rather than extending the default. Here it repeats the default rule. Never add a numeric code to this set without documentation: zero, for example, can be a real measurement. To average the observed water percentages, use na.rm = TRUE in the calculation:

countries_csv <- read_csv("examples/lifeexp.csv", na = c("", "NA"))
Rows: 68 Columns: 6
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (1): country
dbl (5): region, popgrowth, lexp, gnppc, safewater

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

countries_csv
# A tibble: 68 × 6
   region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
    <dbl> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1      1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2      1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 3      1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 4      1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 5      1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 6      1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 7      1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
 8      1 Bulgaria                    -0.7    71  1440        90
 9      1 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10      1 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows

mean(countries_csv$safewater, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 77.16667


na.rm = TRUE leaves missing inputs out of this calculation. It does not fill them in or remove their countries. The mean describes the 54 available country measurements and is 77.2 percent. Each contributing country receives equal weight; this is not the percentage of all people in these countries with safe water. The 14 unavailable measurements remain NA. Although this is the complete package dataset, its countries do not cover the whole world.
There is another import decision to check: the country name identifies each row. The first import correctly inferred character storage, but an explicit specification makes our expectation clear when the file is read again.
A collector specifies how readr should read a column. It is an instruction for an import, not a conversion of an existing column. Introduce the collectors separately. col_character() requests text:

col_character()

<collector_character>


The printed collector describes an expected type; it contains no country observations. Use it for country names, whose letters should remain text. col_integer() requests whole numbers:

col_integer()

<collector_integer>


Our documented region codes are whole numbers, so integer storage fits them. This does not make region a quantity: 1, 2, and 3 identify categories, and their average has no substantive meaning.
col_double() requests numeric values that can include fractional parts:

col_double()

<collector_double>


Use doubles for the measured variables. Population growth includes decimals, and the other recorded measurements are numeric quantities even where the captured values have been rounded to whole numbers.
cols() combines named collectors into one column specification. Each name identifies a CSV column; the collector on its right specifies its expected type. Begin with selected columns:

selected_types <- cols(country = col_character(), region = col_integer())
selected_types
cols(
  country = col_character(),
  region = col_integer()
)


The printout lists the two explicit instructions; unspecified columns still use guessed types. Supply this object to read_csv() through col_types, retaining the documented missing-token rule:

countries_csv <- read_csv(
  "examples/lifeexp.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  col_types = selected_types
)
var_type(countries_csv$country)

[1] "character"

var_type(countries_csv$region)

[1] "integer"


The checks report character country names and integer region codes. We have reread the unchanged file with explicit expectations, rather than repaired it after importing.
To specify every column, the .default option in cols() supplies the collector for columns not named individually. Here all remaining columns are documented numeric measurements. Keep names as character and region as integer:

country_types <- cols(
  .default = col_double(),
  country = col_character(),
  region = col_integer()
)
country_types
cols(
  .default = col_double(),
  country = col_character(),
  region = col_integer()
)


This specification covers the file’s six columns without guessing. It is appropriate to this documented file, not a rule that every unlisted column in a future dataset must be numeric. Import again with it:

countries_csv <- read_csv(
  "examples/lifeexp.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  col_types = country_types
)
countries_csv
# A tibble: 68 × 6
   region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
    <int> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1      1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2      1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 3      1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 4      1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 5      1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 6      1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 7      1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
 8      1 Bulgaria                    -0.7    71  1440        90
 9      1 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10      1 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows


The import retains 68 countries. Types now follow the specification; the next check asks whether any source entries failed those rules.
An import can return a table while reporting values it could not parse as requested. Readr’s problems() receives the imported table and returns a diagnostic table without changing its values:

problems(countries_csv)
# A tibble: 0 × 5
# ℹ 5 variables: row <int>, col <int>, expected <chr>, actual <chr>, file <chr>


Here the result has zero rows: readr recorded no parsing problems in this import. The headings show what a problem report would contain. row and col locate the source entry; expected describes what the parser required, and actual records what it encountered. file identifies the source file. If rows appear, inspect those entries in the unchanged CSV and compare them with its documentation and your type and missing-token specifications. Correct the import rule only when the source supports that correction, then import and check again.
A zero-row report does not certify that the observations, units, or identifiers are correct. Continue the type, missingness, and source comparisons below. Hiding an import message would not repair a parsing problem.
We can also inspect the whole table’s type and compare its variable descriptions with those retained by the package object. Reuse variables() from Section 7.4 to list column names and available variable labels:

var_type(countries_csv)

[1] "spc_tbl_"

variables(countries_csv)
# A tibble: 6 × 1
  name     
  <chr>    
1 region   
2 country  
3 popgrowth
4 lexp     
5 gnppc    
6 safewater

variables(countries)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  name      label                   
  <chr>     <chr>                   
1 region    Region                  
2 country   Country                 
3 popgrowth Avg. annual % growth    
4 lexp      Life expectancy at birth
5 gnppc     GNP per capita          
6 safewater Safe water              


Readr’s imported tibble carries additional import information; var_type() reports its table type. It is still a table. The CSV has names but no variable-label metadata; the package object has both. Different table metadata do not imply different observations. CSV contains values and names but does not retain the source’s variable and value labels. The original countries object still holds those labels; countries_csv lets us inspect what the file format preserves. Here region is a numeric code: 1 is Europe and Central Asia, 2 North America, and 3 South America. These codes are categories, not quantities to average.
The file opened without an error at each stage, but a useful import also follows its documented missing codes and gives important columns suitable types. Keep the original file unchanged. After checking values and metadata, we can save derived files under new names and reopen them, as the next section demonstrates.
Other formats follow a similar pattern: a reading function brings a file into R, and a writing function saves an object to a file. Table 18.4 is a reference for choosing the package and function, not a requirement to install every package now. The import and export examples in Section 18.2 explain these boundaries further.




Table 18.4: Functions for reading and writing common formats.





Format
Read
Write
Package




CSV
read_csv()
write_csv()
readr


Excel
read_excel()
write_xlsx()
readxl, writexl


Stata
read_dta()
write_dta()
haven


SPSS
read_sav()
write_sav()
haven


R data
read_rds()
write_rds()
readr


Parquet
read_parquet()
write_parquet()
arrow







library(tidyverse) loads readr. Readxl and haven are installed with tidyverse but must be loaded separately when used, for example with library(haven). Install writexl and arrow before first use of their functions.






TipOptional: a formatted table





For a report-style display, the optional flextable package supplies as_flextable(). After installing flextable, the call below converts the complete CSV import, countries_csv, to a formatting object rather than another country tibble. flextable:: identifies its package without loading that package. We use the CSV import here because it contains ordinary columns without haven value labels. This is a presentation tool; it does not replace the exploration tools above.

flextable::as_flextable(countries_csv)

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.4 Exporting results
R can write many of the formats in Table 18.1, although an exported file may not retain every feature of the original. The useful distinction is between data someone will analyze and results someone will read. A collaborator checking your analysis needs usable values and documentation; a reader of an article usually needs a clearly labelled table or figure. A screenshot of a table may be convenient for a conversation, but it is a poor substitute for the underlying values when someone needs to recalculate a result.
Table 18.5 connects common purposes to possible outputs. More than one choice can be sensible; the best depends on the recipient’s tools and the information that must survive the handover.




Table 18.5: Output choices by purpose.





Purpose
Possible output
Write with




Share an analysis table
CSV / TSV with a variable codebook
write_csv(), write_tsv()


Inspect or edit values
Excel workbook for manual review
writexl::write_xlsx()


Use other statistical software
Stata / SPSS / SAS files for analysis
write_dta(), write_sav(), write_xpt()


Resume work in R
RDS file preserving one R object
write_rds()


Exchange larger tables
Parquet file with column-oriented storage
arrow::write_parquet()


Write a report, slides, a book, or a website
Word / PDF / HTML with text and results
Quarto


Share a figure
PNG image or SVG / PDF vector graphic
ggsave()







An RDS file is a working copy for repeated work within R, not a universal exchange format. Parquet’s compression and column-oriented storage matter most when your tools can use them. A PNG stores pixels, so its export dimensions affect how readable its labels will be; SVG and PDF can preserve vector lines and text. Here, a vector graphic stores shapes and drawing instructions so that they can be resized; it does not mean an R vector of values. Whatever the output, retain the source code so that you can regenerate it.

18.4.1 Save and reopen a CSV
write_csv() takes a table first and a destination path second. It writes column names and values to a text file, returning without a console table. Use a new name to preserve the source. The output path has no folder prefix, so it is relative to the working directory:

write_csv(countries_csv, "countries-checked.csv")

A saved file remains after the R session ends. Reopen it into a separate object, using the same documented type and missing-token rules:

countries_csv_saved <- read_csv(
  "countries-checked.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  col_types = country_types
)
countries_csv_saved
# A tibble: 68 × 6
   region country                popgrowth  lexp gnppc safewater
    <int> <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
 1      1 Albania                     -0.6    74   870        49
 2      1 Armenia                     -1.2    70   570        83
 3      1 Austria                      0.1    78 27810        97
 4      1 Azerbaijan                   0.9    64   510        49
 5      1 Belarus                     -0.5    68  1540        82
 6      1 Belgium                      0.2    77 26530       100
 7      1 Bosnia and Herzegovina       1.8    74  1230        87
 8      1 Bulgaria                    -0.7    71  1440        90
 9      1 Croatia                     -0.1    72    NA        85
10      1 Czechia                     -0.1    75  6140        95
# ℹ 58 more rows

identical(countries_csv$country, countries_csv_saved$country)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries_csv$region, countries_csv_saved$region)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries_csv$popgrowth, countries_csv_saved$popgrowth)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries_csv$lexp, countries_csv_saved$lexp)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries_csv$gnppc, countries_csv_saved$gnppc)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries_csv$safewater, countries_csv_saved$safewater)

[1] TRUE


Each comparison checks one complete column, including order, type, and missing positions; all should return TRUE. Checking only a few printed rows would miss changes elsewhere. CSV does not carry the package object’s variable or value labels, so a CSV copy need not be attribute-identical to a labelled source object. Supplying the specification on readback protects the types we chose; the CSV file itself does not store those collector instructions.


18.4.2 Save and reopen a Stata file
write_dta() from haven writes a Stata file. Use the full labelled package object countries here, rather than the CSV import whose labels have already been lost:

write_dta(countries, "countries_output.dta")

Read the new file separately and compare names, measurements, and labels. as.numeric() below compares the recorded numeric values without requiring two file formats to store identical descriptive attributes:

countries_dta_saved <- read_dta("countries_output.dta")
nrow(countries_dta_saved) == nrow(countries)

[1] TRUE

identical(countries$country, countries_dta_saved$country)

[1] FALSE

identical(as.numeric(countries$region), as.numeric(countries_dta_saved$region))

18.4.3 Save and reopen an R object
write_rds() saves one R object, including its types and metadata. Save the labelled package table under a new name:

write_rds(countries, "countries-checked.rds")

read_rds() restores that object. Assign it to countries_saved; reading a file does not recreate an object name automatically:

The first TRUE checks the full restored object, including its labels. The second checks that our original working object remains identical to the packaged source. These functions use the same RDS format as base R’s saveRDS() and readRDS(). An RDS file is useful for resuming R work; it is not a universal exchange format for collaborators using other software. None of the exports changes the source download or replaces the in-memory source object.






TipOptional: a Parquet copy





The arrow package provides write_parquet() for a compact column-oriented file. Install arrow once if you need this format; installation is separate from importing or exporting data:

install.packages("arrow")

After installation, load the package and write the complete checked CSV table. This optional output does not replace the CSV, Stata, or RDS checks above:

library(arrow)
write_parquet(countries_csv, "countries_output.parquet")

The path names a new file; the table in R stays unchanged. Parquet’s support for types and metadata depends on the tools using it, so check what survives a handover rather than assuming every statistical label is retained.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.5 Check your file workflow
Use the familiar file.exists() check to locate a saved copy:

file.exists("countries-checked.csv")
getwd()

The first result should be TRUE after the CSV export. Because the path has no folder prefix, the file is directly in the directory reported by getwd(). Locate it in your file manager. Saving the script preserves instructions; exporting preserves a data file; assignment alone keeps an object only in the current R session.
Check the whole route in a fresh session: open the same project, load the required packages, rerun the import and its specification, then reopen an export into a separate object. Explain which item is a source file, which is an R object, and which is a derived file. Choose output names that do not overwrite your original downloads or another result you need to preserve.
There is no need to learn every format now. Begin with the file your project supplies, understand its rows and columns, and choose an output the next person can use. A successful conversion preserves the meaning of the information, not just the number of rows.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.6 Review

getwd() reports the working directory, and file.exists() checks a specified path.
read_csv(), read_dta(), and read_sav() import CSV, Stata, and SPSS files; inspect rows, types, missing-value codes, and labels.
col_character(), col_integer(), and col_double() specify expected column types; cols() combines those instructions.
problems() reports recorded parsing issues; a zero-row report does not validate meanings or units. var_type() and variables() help inspect types and metadata.
write_csv() and write_dta() export tables; write_rds() and read_rds() preserve and restore an R object. Reopen separate copies to check the relevant values, types, and labels.
Optional: spec() reports an import specification, write_parquet() exports a Parquet file, and as_flextable() creates a report-style formatting object.

Next, Chapter 19 develops calculations within groups and changes between long and wide tables. Chapter 20 then connects datasets through checked identifiers.

title: 18  Import and export
text:
18.7 Exercises

Locate a file. Starting from the r4ss project, check for the two excerpt files and the complete country CSV. If a check returns FALSE, what should you inspect before changing the import code? Distinguish the source file, its relative path, the script, and an assigned R object.
Check an import. Read the complete lifeexp.csv with documented missing tokens, character country names, integer region codes, and doubles for the other columns. Inspect parsing problems and the type of safewater; calculate its mean over available measurements and count the contributing countries. Explain the denominator and why integer region codes do not justify averaging region.
Compare metadata. Independently import the Stata and SPSS excerpts and load the complete packaged table. Compare their variable descriptions and region labels with a complete CSV import. Explain why a label missing from CSV need not imply a missing observation, and why a six-row excerpt must not be compared as though it contained all countries.
Save and check. Starting from the package object and a fresh checked CSV import, save new CSV, Stata, and RDS copies. Reopen them separately. Check every CSV column, Stata values and labels, and exact RDS restoration. Explain which format you would choose to resume work in R and which you might send to a collaborator using Stata.

title: 19  Group and reshape
text:
19.1 Add a regional comparison
How far is a respondent’s schooling above or below the sample average for their region? How can we compare several questionnaire items when each occupies a separate column? These questions require two different changes to a table. Grouping changes which observations enter a calculation. Reshaping changes what a row represents.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We use the column operations from Chapter 12 and factors from Chapter 15. The earlier custom summary example is optional; the grouping lesson below explains the summary syntax it needs.
The main examples use the prepared GSS extract. Prepare it following Appendix A, then put gss24.rds in your project folder. A final application uses school-to-work histories because the GSS extract has no repeated monthly observations:
Each row in gss24 represents a respondent. We will keep those rows and add a regional comparison to each one. Select respondent ID, region, schooling, and family income. The appendix already prepared region as a factor with readable categories.
respondents <- gss24 |>
  select(region, id, educ, realinc)
respondents
# A tibble: 3,986 × 4
   region       id  educ realinc
   <fct>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 northeast     1    16  43560 
 2 northeast     2    16  24502.
 3 northeast     3    14  43560 
 4 northeast     4    12  58080 
 5 northeast     5    13  24502.
 6 northeast     6    14   2722.
 7 northeast     7    13 117565.
 8 northeast     8    14   3267 
 9 northeast     9    14 117565.
10 northeast    10    12     NA 
# ℹ 3,976 more rows
educ records completed years of schooling. Its missing answers remain in the table. The regional mean uses respondents with recorded schooling and gives each equal weight; it is an unweighted description of this survey sample. na.rm = TRUE excludes missing schooling only from the mean calculation. A respondent whose schooling is missing keeps a missing deviation.
Inside mutate(), mean(educ, na.rm = TRUE) calculates a mean and the name to its left creates a column. Adding .by = region tells mutate() to calculate separately within each region. Start with that mean alone:
respondent_means <- respondents |>
  mutate(region_mean_educ = mean(educ, na.rm = TRUE), .by = region)
respondent_means
# A tibble: 3,986 × 5
   region       id  educ realinc region_mean_educ
   <fct>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>            <dbl>
 1 northeast     1    16  43560              14.4
 2 northeast     2    16  24502.             14.4
 3 northeast     3    14  43560              14.4
 4 northeast     4    12  58080              14.4
 5 northeast     5    13  24502.             14.4
 6 northeast     6    14   2722.             14.4
 7 northeast     7    13 117565.             14.4
 8 northeast     8    14   3267              14.4
 9 northeast     9    14 117565.             14.4
10 northeast    10    12     NA              14.4
# ℹ 3,976 more rows
Every respondent receives their own region’s mean. The regional value repeats because the rows still represent respondents. Now subtract that column from each person’s schooling:
respondent_comparison <- respondent_means |>
  mutate(educ_deviation = educ - region_mean_educ)
respondent_comparison
# A tibble: 3,986 × 6
   region       id  educ realinc region_mean_educ educ_deviation
   <fct>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>            <dbl>          <dbl>
 1 northeast     1    16  43560              14.4          1.56 
 2 northeast     2    16  24502.             14.4          1.56 
 3 northeast     3    14  43560              14.4         -0.442
 4 northeast     4    12  58080              14.4         -2.44 
 5 northeast     5    13  24502.             14.4         -1.44 
 6 northeast     6    14   2722.             14.4         -0.442
 7 northeast     7    13 117565.             14.4         -1.44 
 8 northeast     8    14   3267              14.4         -0.442
 9 northeast     9    14 117565.             14.4         -0.442
10 northeast    10    12     NA              14.4         -2.44 
# ℹ 3,976 more rows
The original schooling remains in educ. A positive deviation means that a respondent’s schooling is above the mean for their recorded region; a negative deviation means it is below. Both the mean and the deviation are in years. The repeated regional mean is intentional: we need it alongside each respondent, rather than in a separate summary table.
nrow() counts a table’s rows. Compare the input and output:
nrow(respondents)

[1] 3986

nrow(respondent_comparison)

[1] 3986
All 3986 respondent rows remain. Grouped mutate() adds columns without reducing the data to one row per region. The .by instruction applies only to this call; respondent_comparison carries no persistent grouping.

title: 19  Group and reshape
text:
19.2 When grouping persists
Sometimes several consecutive operations should use the same groups. group_by(region) returns a table that stores the grouping instruction. It retains all rows and columns:

respondent_groups <- respondents |>
  group_by(region)
respondent_groups

# Groups:   region [4]

Notice the Groups line above the output. Subsequent operations use those stored regions. Reuse the familiar calculation on this grouped table:

respondent_grouped <- respondent_groups |>
  mutate(
    region_mean_educ = mean(educ, na.rm = TRUE),
    educ_deviation = educ - region_mean_educ

respondent_ungrouped <- respondent_grouped |>
  ungroup()
respondent_ungrouped

   region       id  educ realinc region_mean_educ educ_deviation
   <fct>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>            <dbl>          <dbl>

10 northeast    10    12     NA              14.4         -2.44
