nested_schooling |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(region)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  region   
  <fct>    
1 northeast


The preview now shows respondent IDs and schooling values, rather than a list-column abbreviation. There are 616 respondents inside this component. The final output identifies its region using the corresponding outer row. region is absent from the inner table because it already labels the container; the same region applies to every respondent stored there.
This extraction returns an object for inspection. It does not remove the component from region_tables or alter the source records. We can therefore return to nested_schooling to work on all regions together.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
21.4 Repeat an operation
We want a respondent count beside each region. purrr::map_int() applies a function to every component of a list and collects one integer per component. Supply data as the list and nrow as the function. Write nrow without parentheses because map_int() supplies each inner table to it in turn. The _int suffix requires each call to return one integer, which a table’s row count does.
Inside mutate(), the resulting vector becomes a column aligned with the original outer rows:

region_sizes <- nested_schooling |>
  mutate(respondents = purrr::map_int(data, nrow))
region_sizes
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  region    data                 respondents
  <fct>     <list>                     <int>
1 northeast <tibble [616 × 3]>           616
2 west      <tibble [894 × 3]>           894
3 midwest   <tibble [923 × 3]>           923
4 south     <tibble [1,553 × 3]>        1553

sum(region_sizes$respondents)

[1] 3986


The outer table still has one row per region, but the new column counts the respondents inside each cell. Its sum is 3986, matching the original respondent total. nrow(region_sizes) would instead count the regional containers. Whenever a workflow contains tables within tables, say which level a row count describes.
The same distinction matters for averages. The regions contain different numbers of respondents. Averaging four regional schooling means would give each region equal weight, whereas averaging observed respondent schooling gives each recorded respondent equal weight. Nesting does not choose a statistical weighting rule for us. Here we use it to organize records and check coverage, without estimating population differences.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
21.5 Application: schooling coverage
We want the same small coverage report for every region: the number of respondents, how many have recorded schooling, and how many have recorded parent schooling. First count the rows of the already extracted first_region inside a familiar summary. n() supplies the number of rows in the current table or group. Unlike counting recorded schooling, it includes respondents with unknown schooling:

first_region |>
  summarise(respondents = n())
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  respondents
        <int>
1         616


This one-row result counts all 616 respondents in that inner table. n() is used inside table operations such as summarise(); nrow(first_region) remains the direct way to count a named table outside those operations. Here both count the same respondents.
Now give the repeated coverage calculation a name. function(x) defines a function with one input called x; braces enclose its instructions. The final expression is the returned result. Here that result is a one-row summary table:

schooling_coverage <- function(x) {
  summarise(
    x,
    respondents = n(),
    educ_recorded = sum(!is.na(educ)),
    maeduc_recorded = sum(!is.na(maeduc))
  )
}
schooling_coverage(first_region)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  respondents educ_recorded maeduc_recorded
        <int>         <int>           <int>
1         616           611             525


The function definition stores an operation; the call supplies one actual inner table as x. Test that call before repeating it. The three returned columns count all respondents, recorded respondent schooling, and recorded parent schooling. Each !is.na() condition is true for a recorded measurement, and sum() counts those true values. No respondent is removed and no unknown schooling value becomes zero.

21.5.1 Collect one numeric percentage per region
Sometimes we need just one number from each table. Define a second named function that returns the recorded-schooling percentage rather than a report table. $educ extracts the input table’s schooling column. The numerator counts recorded schooling and nrow(x) counts all respondents in that table:

schooling_percent <- function(x) {
  100 * sum(!is.na(x$educ)) / nrow(x)
}
schooling_percent(first_region)

[1] 99.18831


This test returns one numeric percentage. Its denominator includes respondents with missing schooling. The inner tables here are nonempty observed regions, so their row counts are positive.
purrr::map_dbl() applies the named function to each list component and collects one numeric value per component in a double vector. Each call must return exactly one numeric value; a respondent-length vector or a multi-column report does not meet that contract. As with map_int(), omit parentheses after the function name because the mapper supplies each table:

region_percent <- nested_schooling |>
  mutate(educ_percent = purrr::map_dbl(data, schooling_percent))
region_percent |>
  select(region, educ_percent)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  region    educ_percent
  <fct>            <dbl>
1 northeast         99.2
2 west              99.2
3 midwest           99.6
4 south             98.8


The vector aligns with the outer rows, so each displayed region receives the percentage calculated from its own respondent table. These unweighted percentages describe coverage within this sample. They are not mean years of schooling or population estimates. map_int() fits integer row counts; map_dbl() fits numeric percentages, which need not be whole numbers.


21.5.2 Keep a complete coverage report
The schooling_coverage() result has several columns. To retain both schooling measures and their counts, collect whole report tables rather than a single percentage from each call. purrr::map() applies a function to each list component and returns a list of its results. As before, supply the function’s name without parentheses:

coverage_nested <- nested_schooling |>
  mutate(coverage = purrr::map(data, schooling_coverage))
coverage_nested |>
  select(region, coverage)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  region    coverage        
  <fct>     <list>          
1 northeast <tibble [1 × 3]>
2 west      <tibble [1 × 3]>
3 midwest   <tibble [1 × 3]>
4 south     <tibble [1 × 3]>


Each coverage component holds a one-row report for the corresponding data component. The original respondent tables remain in coverage_nested$data. The displayed selection shows only the region and report containers, so we can inspect their arrangement before expanding them.
unnest() turns the rows and columns of stored tables back into ordinary table rows and columns. First select region and coverage, then ask unnest(coverage) to expand that list column. Every report has one row, so each region will still occupy one row:

coverage_report <- coverage_nested |>
  select(region, coverage) |>
  unnest(coverage)
coverage_report
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  region    respondents educ_recorded maeduc_recorded
  <fct>           <int>         <int>           <int>
1 northeast         616           611             525
2 west              894           887             779
3 midwest           923           919             814
4 south            1553          1535            1327


We can now compare availability without opening each respondent table. respondents is the denominator for each region’s coverage; educ_recorded and maeduc_recorded count recorded values separately. A respondent can contribute to one count and not the other. These are not counts of respondents with both measurements.
For a compact comparison, turn the recorded counts into percentages of all respondents in that region:

coverage_percent <- coverage_report |>
  mutate(
    educ_percent = 100 * educ_recorded / respondents,
    maeduc_percent = 100 * maeduc_recorded / respondents
  ) |>
  select(region, respondents, educ_percent, maeduc_percent)
coverage_percent
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  region    respondents educ_percent maeduc_percent
  <fct>           <int>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1 northeast         616         99.2           85.2
2 west              894         99.2           87.1
3 midwest           923         99.6           88.2
4 south            1553         98.8           85.4


The percentages include respondents with missing schooling in their denominators. Across regions, recorded respondent schooling ranges from 98.8 to 99.6 percent; recorded parent schooling ranges from 85.2 to 88.2 percent. These are unweighted descriptions of this extract’s coverage. Availability can reflect questionnaire coverage and nonresponse; it does not establish that every recorded value is valid or explain why an answer is missing.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
21.6 Return to respondent rows
The coverage report is a summary. To recover the respondent records, return to nested_schooling and expand its original data column. The outer region is repeated alongside each respondent from its container. select() then restores our starting column order:

schooling_restored <- nested_schooling |>
  unnest(data) |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc)
head(schooling_restored)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id region     educ maeduc
  <int> <fct>     <dbl>  <dbl>
1     1 northeast    16     14
2     2 northeast    16     NA
3     3 northeast    14     12
4     4 northeast    12     NA
5     5 northeast    13     11
6     6 northeast    14      5

nrow(schooling_restored)

[1] 3986

ncol(schooling_restored)

[1] 4

isid(schooling_restored, id)
Variable `id` uniquely identifies the rows.


We again have 3986 respondents and 4 columns. The ID check confirms unique, non-missing respondent identifiers. Nesting gathers each region’s records together, so expansion need not reproduce an input in which regions were interleaved. Matching dimensions and keys still do not prove that the measurements survived.
For an exact comparison, sort both tables by the unique ID. identical() checks values and attributes, including types and factor levels. We also inspect the region levels explicitly to connect that check to our categorical grouping key:

identical(
  arrange(schooling, id),
  arrange(schooling_restored, id)
)

[1] TRUE

identical(levels(schooling$region), levels(schooling_restored$region))

[1] TRUE


Both checks return TRUE. The first comparison includes every respondent’s ID, region, and both schooling values, including missing values. The second confirms that the same region levels remain in the same order. Sorting for comparison makes respondent order explicit; it does not repair altered values or missing respondents.
Our workflow has moved between two levels: regional containers on the outside and respondents on the inside. We kept the original records while adding separate reports, then verified the return to respondent rows. Use an ordinary grouped summary when only a regional report is needed. A nested table is useful when keeping and inspecting the underlying tables is part of the task.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
21.7 Review

nest() stores respondent tables in a list column, with grouping keys on the outside.
pull() extracts a list column; double square brackets extract one stored component.
map_int() requires one integer per component; map_dbl() requires one numeric value per component.
n() counts every row in the current summary table or group, including rows with missing measurements.
function() defines a reusable operation; map() collects its results in a list.
unnest() expands stored tables; the contents determine the resulting row unit.
Check dimensions, identifiers, values, and factor levels after a roundtrip, and state the respondent denominator of coverage results.

The next chapter, Chapter 22, returns to ordinary observation tables to build figures. Keep track of the row unit when carrying tables and summaries into statistical analysis.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
21.8 Exercises
Each exercise starts from the package and file-loading setup above. Recreate any objects you need; none depends on another exercise’s answer.

Count both levels. Select id, region, educ, and maeduc, then nest by region. Predict what map_int() returns before adding respondent counts. Compare the outer row count with the sum of inner row counts. What does each count represent?
Inspect one component. Recreate the nested table. Predict the object returned by pulling data and by extracting its first component, then perform both operations. Show its first respondents and identify its region from the outer table. Why is region absent from the component, and why should you not assume that component 1 always names the same region?
Report coverage and diagnose output shape. Recreate the nested table and define a numeric schooling-percentage function and schooling_coverage() locally. Test each on one inner table before mapping. Predict the double-vector result from map_dbl(), the list from map(), and the expanded report from unnest(). Retain both measures and calculate recorded parent-schooling percentages. Diagnose why mapping a function that returns a recorded-answer flag for every respondent cannot produce one numeric value per region, and repair it. State each denominator. Would nesting discard missing schooling, and what would an unknown region mean?
Check a roundtrip. Recreate the selected and nested tables. Predict the row unit and row count after expanding data, then unnest the original records and restore the selected column order. Check dimensions, unique IDs, exact equality after sorting by ID, and region levels. Explain why a correct row count is insufficient by itself.

title: 21  Nested datasets
text:
Worked answers






NoteCount both levels





Load the extract independently, retain the four requested columns, and count the respondents inside each regional container:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer1_schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc)
answer1_nested <- answer1_schooling |>
  nest(.by = region) |>
  mutate(respondents = purrr::map_int(data, nrow))
answer1_nested
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  region    data                 respondents
  <fct>     <list>                     <int>
1 northeast <tibble [616 × 3]>           616
2 west      <tibble [894 × 3]>           894
3 midwest   <tibble [923 × 3]>           923
4 south     <tibble [1,553 × 3]>        1553

nrow(answer1_nested)

[1] 4

sum(answer1_nested$respondents)

[1] 3986

sum(answer1_nested$respondents) == nrow(answer1_schooling)

[1] TRUE


map_int() returns an integer vector with one respondent count per stored table; assignment aligns it with the regions. The outer count is 4 regional containers. The inner counts sum to 3986 respondents, matching the selected input, so the equality check returns TRUE. Four containers do not imply four respondents or equally sized regional samples.









NoteInspect one component





Rebuild the nested table before extracting its first component. Use the corresponding outer row to identify the region:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer2_nested <- gss24 |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc) |>
  nest(.by = region)
answer2_tables <- answer2_nested |>
  pull(data)
answer2_first <- answer2_tables[[1]]
head(answer2_first)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id  educ maeduc
  <int> <dbl>  <dbl>
1     1    16     14
2     2    16     NA
3     3    14     12
4     4    12     NA
5     5    13     11
6     6    14      5

answer2_nested |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(region)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  region   
  <fct>    
1 northeast


Pulling returns a list; double brackets return the tibble stored in one component. The inner rows are respondents; the outer row identifies their common region. region remains outside because it is the nesting key. Component 1 is a position in this particular list, whose order follows encountered groups. A differently ordered input could place another region first. Neither extraction changes the stored records.









NoteReport coverage





Define the coverage operation independently, then repeat it for the freshly nested respondent records:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer3_coverage <- function(x) {
  summarise(
    x,
    respondents = n(),
    educ_recorded = sum(!is.na(educ)),
    maeduc_recorded = sum(!is.na(maeduc))
  )
}
answer3_schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc)
answer3_nested <- answer3_schooling |>
  nest(.by = region)
answer3_tables <- answer3_nested |>
  pull(data)
answer3_first <- answer3_tables[[1]]
answer3_coverage(answer3_first)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  respondents educ_recorded maeduc_recorded
        <int>         <int>           <int>
1         616           611             525

answer3_report <- answer3_nested |>
  mutate(coverage = purrr::map(data, answer3_coverage)) |>
  select(region, coverage) |>
  unnest(coverage) |>
  mutate(maeduc_percent = 100 * maeduc_recorded / respondents)
answer3_report
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  region    respondents educ_recorded maeduc_recorded maeduc_percent
  <fct>           <int>         <int>           <int>          <dbl>
1 northeast         616           611             525           85.2
2 west              894           887             779           87.1
3 midwest           923           919             814           88.2
4 south            1553          1535            1327           85.4


Each percentage divides the number with recorded parent schooling by all respondents in that region. Here parent schooling means the source-defined mother’s or younger parent’s schooling in maeduc. Missing schooling stays in the respondent records and contributes to the denominator. If region were unknown, nesting would retain those respondents in a separate NA container. This extract has no missing region values; no extra geographic category has been created. These coverage percentages describe the sample without survey weights.
The function test returns a one-row report. Mapping it returns a list of those report tables; expanding them gives one region per row because each component has one row. Now test and collect a scalar percentage:

answer3_percent <- function(x) {
  100 * sum(!is.na(x$educ)) / nrow(x)
}
answer3_percent(answer3_first)

[1] 99.18831

answer3_numeric <- answer3_nested |>
  mutate(educ_percent = purrr::map_dbl(data, answer3_percent))
answer3_numeric |>
  select(region, educ_percent)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  region    educ_percent
  <fct>            <dbl>
1 northeast         99.2
2 west              99.2
3 midwest           99.6
4 south             98.8


map_dbl() returns one double value per region, stored in educ_percent. This is the same recorded-respondent-schooling percentage as the report’s educ_recorded / respondents, multiplied by 100. It does not replace the report’s separate parent-schooling coverage.
For the diagnosis, define an operation returning one logical flag for every respondent:

answer3_flags <- function(x) {
  !is.na(x$educ)
}
length(answer3_flags(answer3_first))

[1] 616

nrow(answer3_first)

[1] 616


The matching lengths show why this function does not return one value per region. The following deliberate error tests that mismatch:

purrr::map_dbl(answer3_tables, answer3_flags)
Error in `purrr::map_dbl()`:
ℹ In index: 1.
Caused by error:
! Result must be length 1, not 616.


Each component result must have length one; a vector containing a flag for every respondent is too long. The repair is the tested answer3_percent() above: count the true flags and divide by that region’s respondent count before mapping. Use map() if the purpose is instead to retain the full flag vectors. Changing to map() alone would change the output shape without answering the one-percentage-per-region question.









NoteCheck a roundtrip





Use only the original data list column for the return to respondent rows. Then compare the recovered table with its selected input:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer4_schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc)
answer4_nested <- answer4_schooling |>
  nest(.by = region)
answer4_restored <- answer4_nested |>
  unnest(data) |>
  select(id, region, educ, maeduc)
nrow(answer4_schooling) == nrow(answer4_restored)

[1] TRUE

ncol(answer4_schooling) == ncol(answer4_restored)

[1] TRUE

isid(answer4_schooling, id)
Variable `id` uniquely identifies the rows.

isid(answer4_restored, id)
Variable `id` uniquely identifies the rows.

identical(
  arrange(answer4_schooling, id),
  arrange(answer4_restored, id)
)

[1] TRUE

identical(
  levels(answer4_schooling$region),
  levels(answer4_restored$region)
)

[1] TRUE


Expanding data returns respondent rows: their predicted total is the sum of the inner counts, not the number of regions. The equality checks return TRUE, and both ID checks confirm unique, non-missing identifiers. Dimensions alone could hide a duplicated respondent replacing another or a changed schooling value. The sorted exact comparison checks records and their attributes, including missing values; the final comparison explicitly checks the region levels. We restore the selected table, rather than the other columns that were never included in nesting. gss24 remains the full original extract.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.1 A relationship between countries
The first graphs in Chapter 11 helped us explore relationships, distributions, and category shares. A figure for a research paper or presentation also needs deliberate decisions about its analysis sample, group distinctions, panel scales, labels, and saved dimensions. We now use the table and variable operations learned since that chapter to prepare those comparisons explicitly.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
This chapter builds on the plotting grammar from Chapter 11, selecting observations, creating columns, and factors from Chapter 15. We use those tools to construct figures in stages. We return to the country data from the early manipulation chapters, then move to annual country records when the question requires a time series.
Load tidyverse for ggplot2 and the table operations, and tidystata for lifeexp. Copy the captured OWID file into your project’s examples folder. read_csv() restores that public table as owid. No GSS file is needed for this chapter.
Do countries with higher income tend to have higher life expectancy? In lifeexp, gnppc records GNI per capita using the Atlas method, in current US dollars in 1998. lexp records life expectancy at birth in years in 1998. Each point will represent a country, so both measurements must be recorded to locate it. Check the familiar summary’s n column before plotting:
nrow(lifeexp)

[1] 68

summ(lifeexp, gnppc, lexp)
# A tibble: 2 × 8
  name  type      n unique   min   mean       sd   max
  <chr> <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 gnppc dbl      67     64   170 9137.  11497.   46650
2 lexp  dbl      68     20    57   71.7     5.16    79
All 68 countries have life expectancy recorded, but only 67 have income recorded. Therefore, 67 countries can contribute points. The missing income is not zero.
ggplot() receives a data frame and returns a plot object. Inside it, aes() defines mappings: x = gnppc positions countries horizontally by income, and y = lexp positions them vertically by life expectancy. geom_point() adds a point for each country with both coordinates. The + operator adds a plotting layer; put it at the end of the line when continuing on the next line.
Set na.rm = TRUE in the layer to omit countries that cannot be positioned because a coordinate is missing. This choice avoids a warning about that explained omission; it neither replaces the missing value nor removes a row from lifeexp.
country_plot <- ggplot(lifeexp, aes(x = gnppc, y = lexp)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2B6487", na.rm = TRUE)
Assignment stores the plot without displaying it. The hexadecimal value specifies the book’s blue. Because color is outside aes(), it sets one appearance for every point. Only the variables inside aes() determine positions here.
labs() labelled axes in Chapter 11. Its additional subtitle argument puts a short line of context above the panel. Here it identifies the complete-pair sample. A subtitle belongs inside the plotted image; the automatic figure caption below it also records units and context when the figure is read in the book. Add the labels to the saved object, assign the updated result, then type its name to display it.
country_plot <- country_plot +
  labs(
    x = "GNI per capita (current US dollars, 1998)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years, 1998)",
    subtitle = "Countries with both measurements recorded"
  )
country_plot







Figure 22.1: GNI per capita and life expectancy in 1998. Each point is a country with both measurements; GNI uses the Atlas method in current US dollars.
Figure 22.1 suggests higher life expectancy at higher incomes, with substantial variation at the lower end of the income distribution. A horizontal distance measures a dollar difference; a vertical difference measures years. This is an association among countries in the dataset. It neither estimates an individual income effect nor shows that changing national income by itself causes a particular change in longevity.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.2 Add regional context
Do countries with higher income tend to have higher life expectancy within the recorded regions? Return to the country relationship in Figure 22.1. gnppc records GNI per capita using the Atlas method, in current US dollars in 1998; lexp records life expectancy at birth in years in 1998. This time we prepare the complete country pairs in an object before plotting and distinguish regions by point shape.
The familiar filter() retains countries with both measurements: is.na() identifies a missing value, and ! reverses that result. The comma requires both conditions to hold. mutate() then converts the labelled region column into categories with readable labels. haven::as_factor() performs that conversion; the package prefix identifies the function without loading another package. The pipe passes each result to the following operation.

country_points <- lifeexp |>
  filter(!is.na(gnppc), !is.na(lexp)) |>
  mutate(region = haven::as_factor(region))
nrow(lifeexp)

[1] 68

nrow(country_points)

[1] 67


The graph uses 67 of 68 countries, the same complete pairs as the preceding scatterplot. Saving that selection makes the analysis sample available for checking and reuse. It neither replaces the missing measurement nor changes lifeexp.

22.2.1 Map a variable, set an appearance
Map shape = region inside aes() to distinguish the recorded regions. The mapping uses each country’s category and produces a legend. All points retain the same blue because shape and the labelled legend carry the regional distinction. As in the preceding plot, the color argument outside aes() sets one appearance for every point.

region_plot <- ggplot(
  country_points,
  aes(x = gnppc, y = lexp, shape = region)
) +
  geom_point(color = "#2B6487")

Assignment stores this draft plot. We can refine it by adding layers to its name rather than rebuilding the data and mappings. labs() labels the axes, the shape legend, and a subtitle. theme_bw() supplies a white background and visible panel structure; it changes presentation without changing observations or calculations. Assign the updated result and print it.

region_plot <- region_plot +
  labs(
    x = "GNI per capita (current US dollars, 1998)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years, 1998)",
    shape = "Region",
    subtitle = "Countries with both measurements recorded"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
region_plot







Figure 22.2: GNI per capita and life expectancy in 1998. Each point is a country with both measurements; GNI uses the Atlas method in current US dollars. Shapes distinguish recorded regions.





Figure 22.2 describes an association among countries in this dataset. The points suggest higher life expectancy at higher incomes, with substantial variation at the lower end of the income distribution. A point’s horizontal distance measures a dollar difference on this scale; a vertical difference measures years. The graph neither estimates an individual income effect nor shows that changing national income by itself causes a particular change in longevity.
A quoted constant inside aes(), such as color = "blue", has a different meaning from the same argument outside it. Inside, ggplot2 treats "blue" as a category label and chooses a display color through a scale, usually with a legend. To request blue points, set color outside aes() as above. To distinguish regions by an appearance, map the unquoted variable region.






NoteOptional: compare income ratios



The linear income axis gives equal space to equal dollar differences. Much of the variation among lower-income countries occupies a small part of that axis. A logarithmic income scale offers another view of these same observations, with spacing determined by ratios instead of dollar differences.
A logarithm requires positive inputs. The recorded incomes among these complete country pairs are finite; check their minimum before changing the scale. min() returns the smallest value:

min(country_points$gnppc)

[1] 170


The minimum is 170 dollars, above zero. No further country exclusions are needed. scale_x_log10() replaces the horizontal scale with a base-ten logarithmic scale; it returns a scale to add to the existing plot object.

log_income_plot <- region_plot +
  scale_x_log10()
log_income_plot







Figure 22.3: GNI per capita and life expectancy in 1998, with a logarithmic income axis. The same complete country pairs and regional shapes are retained; income labels remain current US dollars.





The axis labels still denote dollars. Equal horizontal distances now represent equal income ratios: 100 to 1,000 dollars has the same spacing as 1,000 to 10,000 dollars. A tenfold increase is one unit on the transformed axis, although the labels display the original currency values. Life expectancy remains on its original scale in years. The new view changes spacing, not recorded incomes, the 67 contributing countries, or the limits of a country-level association. The original region_plot remains available.


To inspect countries below 10,000 dollars more closely, change the display window. coord_cartesian() sets the visible coordinates; xlim receives the lower and upper horizontal limits in a vector.

zoomed_income_plot <- region_plot +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10000))
zoomed_income_plot







Figure 22.4: The country income comparison zoomed to 0–10,000 current US dollars in 1998. Countries beyond this horizontal window are cropped; the plot retains all complete country pairs.





The plot still contains 67 country pairs, with 19 beyond the window. A cropped point remains part of the plot’s input even though it is hidden. Compare selecting rows:

income_window <- country_points |>
  filter(gnppc <= 10000)
nrow(country_points)

[1] 67

nrow(income_window)

[1] 48


Filtering returns a smaller table of 48 countries and changes the inputs to subsequent calculations. Zooming only changes what is displayed. Neither command replaces country_points; the full region_plot remains available.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.3 Compare annual trends
How did life expectancy change in China and the United States from 2000 through 2023? The cross-sectional lifeexp table cannot answer this question because it supplies one life-expectancy measurement per country. We now use the captured OWID file for annual country observations. Unlike the monthly example in Chapter 16, OWID records these observations by year. Keep Year as the annual time coordinate. Select the two names, the inclusive time window, and recorded life-expectancy values. rename() gives the outcome a short local name without changing owid.

trend_data <- owid |>
  filter(
    Entity %in% c("China", "United States"),
    Year >= 2000, Year <= 2023,
    !is.na(`Life expectancy`)
  ) |>
  rename(lexp = `Life expectancy`) |>
  arrange(Entity, Year)
trend_data
# A tibble: 48 × 4
   Entity Code   Year  lexp
   <chr>  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 China  CHN    2000  72.3
 2 China  CHN    2001  72.7
 3 China  CHN    2002  73.0
 4 China  CHN    2003  73.4
 5 China  CHN    2004  73.7
 6 China  CHN    2005  74.1
 7 China  CHN    2006  74.4
 8 China  CHN    2007  74.8
 9 China  CHN    2008  74.8
10 China  CHN    2009  75.3
# ℹ 38 more rows


Before drawing a line, check the annual coverage. count(Entity) counts the rows within each entity and returns one row per entity with the count in n. Within the selected inclusive window, each entity should have one record for each of its 24 years.

trend_coverage <- trend_data |>
  count(Entity)
trend_coverage
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Entity            n
  <chr>         <int>
1 China            24
2 United States    24


geom_line() connects observations in x-axis order. A segment helps us follow a sequence of annual values; it does not establish a continuous daily path between them. facet_wrap() puts different categories into labelled panels. Its ~ Entity formula specifies the panel variable; the tilde introduces that instruction. The default shared axis scales let us compare levels as well as changes without assigning a different color to each country.

trend_plot <- ggplot(trend_data, aes(x = Year, y = lexp)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2B6487") +
  facet_wrap(~ Entity) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)") +
  theme_bw()
trend_plot







Figure 22.5: Annual life expectancy at birth in China and the United States, 2000–2023, from the captured OWID file. Panels share the same scales; lines connect annual observations.





Figure 22.5 contains 48 entity-year observations. China starts with lower life expectancy and gains ground over most of the period. The United States shows a sharp decline in 2020–2021 followed by recovery; China has higher life expectancy in 2020–2022, but the United States is higher again in 2023. The common vertical scale preserves the size of the difference. These national annual measures summarize mortality conditions; the lines do not trace the eventual lifespan of individuals born in each year or identify a single cause of change.
Before extending a graph to another entity, check that the intended years and measurements are present. If a source year is missing and removed, connecting the remaining observations can visually bridge a gap. The present two series have all requested years. A longer uninterrupted line should never substitute for checking coverage.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.4 Save the figure
ggsave() writes a plot to a file. The filename extension selects the image format; here .png requests a raster image. Specify plot = trend_plot so the saved figure is independent of whichever plot happened to be displayed most recently. width, height, and units set its physical dimensions, and dpi specifies the raster resolution in dots per inch.

ggsave(
  "life-expectancy-trends.png",
  plot = trend_plot,
  width = 8, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300
)

The file is saved in the current project folder at eight by five inches and 300 dpi. Open the exported image and check that labels, panel headings, and units are readable at the size where it will appear. Changing output dimensions can change the space available for text even when the plotted values are unchanged. Keep the code and source data with the figure so you can reproduce or revise it.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.5 Review

Prepare a figure’s analysis sample explicitly and retain the source data unchanged.
A mapping inside aes() varies by values and can produce a legend; a constant outside it sets one appearance.
Add labels and a theme to a saved plot to refine its presentation without changing its observations.
geom_line() connects ordered observations, while facet_wrap() places groups in labelled panels.
Check annual coverage before drawing lines, and use common scales when comparing levels.
coord_cartesian() changes the display window while retaining plot inputs; filtering changes the data supplied to later calculations.
ggsave() exports a named plot with explicit dimensions and resolution.
Optional: scale_x_log10() changes income spacing from equal differences to equal ratios; check positive support first.

The next chapter, Chapter 23, uses explicit statistical comparisons to ask how sample differences relate to uncertainty. The graph remains useful for checking what those comparisons summarize.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
22.6 Exercises

A researcher writes geom_point(aes(color = "blue")) expecting every point to use that blue. Explain the result and create a corrected plot object using the complete country pairs. Then create a region-shape version. Keep both objects without changing lifeexp.
Replace China with Canada in the annual trend comparison. Retain 2000–2023, use common-scale panels, and save the explicit plot object as canada-us-trends.png, at eight by five inches and 300 dpi. Check that both entities have the requested annual coverage before interpreting the lines.

title: 22  ggplot2
text:
Worked answers






NoteSet blue and map region





Start a fresh session. These assignments create plot objects; type an object’s name in the console to display it.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_countries <- lifeexp |>
  filter(!is.na(gnppc), !is.na(lexp)) |>
  mutate(region = haven::as_factor(region))
answer_blue_plot <- ggplot(answer_countries, aes(x = gnppc, y = lexp)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2B6487") +
  labs(x = "GNI per capita (current US dollars, 1998)",
       y = "Life expectancy at birth (years, 1998)") +
  theme_bw()
answer_region_plot <- ggplot(
  answer_countries, aes(x = gnppc, y = lexp, shape = region)
) +
  geom_point(color = "#2B6487") +
  labs(x = "GNI per capita (current US dollars, 1998)",
       y = "Life expectancy at birth (years, 1998)", shape = "Region") +
  theme_bw()

Inside aes(), the quoted word would label one mapped category and could produce a legend; it would not directly set the requested color. Outside aes(), the color applies to every point. The shape mapping varies by the recorded region. Both objects use the same 67 complete country pairs.









NoteExport a new comparison





Start from the same saved public CSV in a fresh session. count(Entity) counts retained annual records within each entity, providing a coverage check for the chosen window.

library(tidyverse)
answer_owid <- read_csv("examples/life-expectancy.csv")
Rows: 21565 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): Entity, Code
dbl (2): Year, Life expectancy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

answer_trends <- answer_owid |>
  filter(
    Entity %in% c("Canada", "United States"),
    Year >= 2000, Year <= 2023,
    !is.na(`Life expectancy`)
  ) |>
  rename(lexp = `Life expectancy`) |>
  arrange(Entity, Year)
answer_coverage <- answer_trends |>
  count(Entity)
answer_coverage
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Entity            n
  <chr>         <int>
1 Canada           24
2 United States    24

answer_trend_plot <- ggplot(answer_trends, aes(x = Year, y = lexp)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2B6487") +
  facet_wrap(~ Entity) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)") +

ggsave(
  "canada-us-trends.png", plot = answer_trend_plot,
  width = 8, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300

The coverage output shows 24 annual records for Canada and 24 for the United States, covering the requested window. The shared axes permit direct comparison of levels. The exported file contains the named comparison even if another graph was displayed afterward; its annual lines do not imply exact within-year dates.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.1 Estimates, uncertainty, and samples
Do male and female respondents differ in completed schooling? Is respondents’ schooling associated with their parents’ schooling? A table or graph describes the observed respondents. A statistical test adds a comparison with a stated null hypothesis under a model of repeated sampling. We need the size of the observed difference, its uncertainty, and the respondents included before we interpret a p-value.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
We build on Chapter 6, Chapter 9, Chapter 15, and Chapter 11. Prepare the extract with Appendix A, and save gss24.rds in your project folder. Load tidyverse for table operations and plotting, and tidystata for correlation tables. The tests come from R’s stats package, which is available when R starts; stats:: makes that source explicit. Broom converts test results into tables, so we use broom:: without attaching the package.
An estimate describes a quantity using the available data: a difference in mean schooling, for example. A null hypothesis specifies a reference value or relationship, such as no mean difference. The test asks how compatible the data are with that null under its assumptions. A p-value is the probability, assuming the null and the model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A 95% confidence interval gives an interval from a procedure that would cover the target quantity in 95% of repeated samples under the assumptions. It helps us distinguish a small estimated difference from a precisely estimated difference. A large p-value does not establish equality, and a small one does not establish practical importance. We keep two-sided alternatives here: differences in either direction are relevant. Choose the question before seeing its p-value.
All examples are unweighted demonstrations using the 2024 GSS extract. They describe the included respondents. The ordinary tests below use assumptions about independent observations and sampling distributions; they do not account for the GSS sampling design or its post-stratification weights. Their intervals and p-values are model-based teaching results, rather than design-corrected population inference.
We define a separate complete-case sample for each question. A complete case has observed values for every variable needed for that calculation. Excluding an unavailable answer neither supplies that answer nor removes possible selection bias. Keep the ID so that the observations remain traceable. educ measures highest year of school completed. sex is the source’s recorded category, not a new measure of gender identity.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.2 Compare schooling between two groups
First, describe respondents with both schooling and sex recorded. The familiar filter() conditions exclude missing answers. We explicitly order the sex factor as male, then female, using factor() and its levels argument. This determines the direction of the test’s reported difference. The grouped summary uses n() for the number of respondents and mean() for their mean schooling, in years; .by = sex applies these calculations separately to each sex category.

tests_schooling <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, sex) |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(sex)) |>
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")))
tests_means <- tests_schooling |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_educ = mean(educ), .by = sex)
tests_means
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  sex        n mean_educ
  <fct>  <int>     <dbl>
1 male    1776      14.3
2 female  2158      14.2


The two rows describe 3934 respondents: 1776 male and 2158 female respondents. Their mean schooling is close: 14.29 and 14.22 years, respectively. These are unweighted group means among observed answers.
stats::t.test() compares means. In the formula educ ~ sex, the variable on the left of ~ is the numerical outcome, and the variable on the right defines the two groups. data = tests_schooling tells R where to find those columns. The default is a two-sided Welch test of a zero difference, with a 95% confidence interval. Welch’s calculation allows unequal variances in the two groups; we do not switch to an equal-variance test simply because group sizes are similar. Assignment stores a test object and leaves the data unchanged.

schooling_test <- stats::t.test(educ ~ sex, data = tests_schooling)
schooling_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  educ by sex
t = 0.67022, df = 3792.5, p-value = 0.5028
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group male and group female is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.1197879  0.2442233
sample estimates:
  mean in group male mean in group female 
            14.28604             14.22382 


The output identifies the method, test statistic t, approximate degrees of freedom df, p-value, interval, and the two sample means. The statistic expresses the mean difference relative to its estimated standard error. Degrees of freedom enter its reference distribution and can be non-integer for Welch’s test. The direction is male minus female because of the factor order.
broom::tidy() turns the stored test into a one-row tibble. estimate is the difference in years; estimate1 and estimate2 are the group means. conf.low and conf.high are its interval endpoints, and p.value repeats the test’s p-value. $ extracts a named column, and [1] selects its first value when we need a single result in prose.

schooling_tidy <- broom::tidy(schooling_test)
schooling_tidy
# A tibble: 1 × 10
  estimate estimate1 estimate2 statistic p.value parameter conf.low conf.high
     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1   0.0622      14.3      14.2     0.670   0.503     3792.   -0.120     0.244
# ℹ 2 more variables: method <chr>, alternative <chr>


The estimated male-minus-female difference is only 0.062 years. Its 95% interval extends from -0.12 to 0.244 years and includes zero. The p-value is 0.503. This example gives little evidence against a zero difference under the ordinary test assumptions. It does not demonstrate exact equality, and we keep this result rather than searching for a different specification that crosses a significance threshold.
Welch’s procedure still requires independent observations and an adequate approximation for the distribution of the estimated mean difference. Large group sizes help with that approximation, but they do not correct dependence from a survey design, coding errors, or selective missingness.

title: 23  Statistical tests
section: 23.3 Compare college attainment in a table
text:
23.3 Compare college attainment in a table
The next question concerns degrees rather than years. Define college attainment as a bachelor’s or graduate degree, using the exact prepared labels "bachelor's" and "graduate". The other recorded degree levels, including associate/junior college, form the comparison group for this particular definition. This binary measure discards differences among those levels; its meaning must accompany the result.
The %in% expression checks whether each degree matches either label. Missing degrees do not match, so that expression alone would classify unknown answers as non-college. We first test is.na(degree) with if_else() and preserve NA_character_, a missing character value. The inner if_else() then classifies known degrees. We retain the original degree column to check this decision.

tests_degree <- gss24 |>
  select(id, degree, sex) |>
  mutate(
    college = if_else(
      is.na(degree), NA_character_,
      if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"),
              "College", "Other degree")
    )
  )
tests_degree |>
  count(degree, college)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  degree                   college          n
  <fct>                    <chr>        <int>
1 less than high school    Other degree   362
2 high school              Other degree  1817
3 associate/junior college Other degree   360
4 bachelor's               College        863
5 graduate                 College        577
6 NA                       NA               7

tests_college <- tests_degree |>
  filter(!is.na(college), !is.na(sex))
tests_college |>
  summarise(n = n(), college_percent = 100 * mean(college == "College"),
            .by = sex)
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  sex        n college_percent
  <fct>  <int>           <dbl>
1 male    1784            36.3
2 female  2167            36.4


The degree check retains unknown answers as unknown. In the summary, college == "College" is a logical indicator whose mean is the proportion with college attainment. Multiplication by 100 expresses it as a percentage. Each denominator consists of respondents of that sex with known degree and sex, rather than all GSS respondents. College attainment is very similar in the two groups.
Base R’s table() counts combinations of its inputs. We supply tests_college$college first and tests_college$sex second, producing college categories in rows and sex categories in columns. It returns a count table, not a respondent-level dataset.

college_counts <- table(tests_college$college, tests_college$sex)
college_counts

              
               male female
  College       648    788
  Other degree 1136   1379


stats::chisq.test() takes that table and tests the null that row and column classifications are independent. Its usual approximation compares observed counts with expected counts calculated under independence. For this two-by-two table, R applies a continuity correction by default; the printed method names it. We retain the default. $expected retrieves the expected count table from the result, so we can inspect the approximation rather than relying on the p-value alone.

college_test <- stats::chisq.test(college_counts)
college_test


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  college_counts
X-squared = 0, df = 1, p-value = 1

college_test$expected

              
                    male    female
  College       648.3989  787.6011
  Other degree 1135.6011 1379.3989


There are 3951 respondents in this analysis. The expected counts are all comfortably above five, so sparse expected cells are not a concern here. Independence of observations and the unweighted survey limitation still matter. The observed counts are so close to the independence expectation that the default correction gives a chi-square statistic of 0 and a p-value of 1. A reported p-value of one does not prove that population proportions are identical. The small descriptive difference remains the substantive finding, under this definition and sample.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.4 Relate respondent and parent schooling
Do respondents with more educated parents tend to complete more schooling? The appendix defines maeduc as the mother’s highest year of schooling, or the younger parent’s for same-sex parents. We use that source definition throughout. This is a different coverage requirement from knowing sex or degree: retain respondents with both educ and maeduc observed.
The scatterplot uses the tools from Chapter 11. A point marks an observed pair of schooling values. Because years are recorded in whole numbers, points overlap; partial transparency with alpha = 0.15 makes repeated positions easier to see without changing their coordinates. labs() identifies the units, and the familiar theme_bw() supplies a white background.

tests_parent <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc) |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc))
nrow(tests_parent)

[1] 3432



ggplot(tests_parent, aes(x = maeduc, y = educ)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Mother/younger-parent schooling (years)",
       y = "Respondent schooling (years)") +
  theme_bw()







Figure 23.1: Respondent and mother/younger-parent schooling, in years; complete observed pairs in the 2024 GSS extract. Overlapping points share recorded coordinates.





Figure 23.1 suggests a positive association with substantial variation at each parent-schooling value. Schooling is bounded and concentrated at common completion points. A straight-line association is a useful summary, not a full account of this pattern.
Tidystata’s corr() describes Pearson’s correlation, a measure of linear association from -1 to 1. Positive values mean the variables tend to increase together; zero means no linear association, which can coexist with a curved relationship. Supply the table first, then name the two numeric columns explicitly. The ID identifies respondents and is excluded from the calculation:

parent_correlation <- corr(tests_parent, educ, maeduc)
parent_correlation
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  var1  var2       r     n
  <chr> <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 educ  maeduc 0.340  3432


The result has one row for this variable pair. var1 and var2 identify the columns, r is their Pearson coefficient, and n is the number of respondents used. corr() uses one common sample with recorded values on every selected variable; here tests_parent already contains complete pairs. The positive coefficient describes greater respondent schooling alongside greater mother/younger-parent schooling in these observed pairs. It supplies neither a p-value nor a confidence interval.
To add uncertainty, use stats::cor.test() with the same two aligned numeric columns. Its default Pearson coefficient agrees with corr(). The default two-sided test has a null correlation of zero and supplies a 95% interval. Both inputs come from the same complete-pair table so the rows remain aligned.

parent_test <- stats::cor.test(tests_parent$educ, tests_parent$maeduc)
parent_test


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  tests_parent$educ and tests_parent$maeduc
t = 21.162, df = 3430, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.3098893 0.3690858
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.3398241 

parent_tidy <- broom::tidy(parent_test)
parent_tidy
# A tibble: 1 × 8
  estimate statistic  p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method    alternative
     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <int>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     <chr>      
1    0.340      21.2 1.60e-93      3430    0.310     0.369 Pearson'… two.sided  


Respondent and mother/younger-parent schooling have a positive linear association in these 3432 observed pairs: the correlation is 0.34, with a 95% interval from 0.31 to 0.369. The very small p-value indicates incompatibility with zero correlation under the ordinary model assumptions. The coefficient is unit-free; it is not an increase in respondent schooling per year of parent schooling. Nor does it show that changing a parent’s schooling would cause a particular change in the respondent’s schooling.
The usual Pearson test and interval rely on independent pairs and distributional assumptions, commonly expressed as a bivariate normal model. The discrete, bounded measurements here make that an approximation. Extreme observations and nonlinearity can also affect Pearson’s correlation, which is why we inspect the graph before interpreting the numerical result.







NoteOptional: common or pairwise samples



What happens if we include both parent-schooling measures? The appendix defines paeduc as the father’s highest year of schooling, or the older parent’s for same-sex parents. Start from the full GSS extract and select the three schooling columns explicitly:

parent_common <- corr(gss24, educ, maeduc, paeduc)
parent_common
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  var1   var2       r     n
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 educ   maeduc 0.347  2649
2 educ   paeduc 0.375  2649
3 maeduc paeduc 0.604  2649


There is one row for each distinct pair of selected variables. All three correlations use the same 2649 respondents, those with all three schooling answers recorded. Even the educ-maeduc pair now excludes respondents whose paeduc is missing. Its coefficient changes from 0.34 to 0.347 because the included respondents changed; their recorded schooling values did not.
Tidystata’s pwcorr() instead uses the available observations for each pair by default. Call it with the same table and selected variables:

parent_pairwise <- pwcorr(gss24, educ, maeduc, paeduc)
parent_pairwise
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  var1   var2       r     n         p
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>     <dbl>
1 educ   maeduc 0.340  3432 1.60e- 93
2 educ   paeduc 0.379  2855 2.01e- 98
3 maeduc paeduc 0.606  2657 5.53e-266


The columns var1, var2, r, and n have the same meanings. Here n is specific to each pair: 3432 respondents for educ with maeduc, 2855 for educ with paeduc, and 2657 for the two parental measures. The additional column p gives a two-sided p-value for a zero Pearson correlation. These are unadjusted separate tests; several small p-values are not independent confirmations of one claim. pwcorr() does not supply confidence intervals.
Common samples hold the respondents fixed across comparisons. Pairwise samples retain more available pairs, but differences between coefficients can reflect sample composition as well as different relationships. Retaining more observations does not resolve selective missingness. Choose the sample rule for the research question rather than for a smaller p-value. The same unweighted survey and causal cautions apply to both tables.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.5 Put the evidence together
The three questions do not use the same respondents. tibble() constructs a small table from named columns, c() combines the three entries in each column, and nrow() counts each analysis sample. knitr::kable() displays this summary as a table; its Quarto caption supplies the automatic number.

test_samples <- tibble(
  Question = c("Mean schooling by sex", "College attainment by sex",
               "Respondent and mother/younger-parent schooling"),
  Required = c("educ, sex", "degree, sex", "educ, maeduc"),
  Respondents = c(nrow(tests_schooling), nrow(tests_college),
                  nrow(tests_parent))
)
knitr::kable(test_samples)



Table 23.1: Complete-case samples for the three unweighted tests in the 2024 GSS extract.











Question
Required
Respondents




Mean schooling by sex
educ, sex
3934


College attainment by sex
degree, sex
3951


Respondent and mother/younger-parent schooling
educ, maeduc
3432








Table 23.1 records the denominators needed for a conclusion. In this unweighted extract, male and female respondents have very similar mean schooling and college-attainment proportions. The Welch interval permits small differences on either side of zero, and the corrected table test gives little evidence against independence. Respondent and mother/younger-parent schooling have a positive correlation of about 0.34, with considerable variation around the pattern. These statements concern different observed-answer samples. Their model-based intervals and tests do not repair missingness, account for the complex survey design, or establish causal effects.
Review:

Define the estimate, null hypothesis, and included respondents before testing.
t.test() compares two means and returns an interval for their difference; factor order determines its direction.
Preserve unknown classifications before constructing a cross-tabulation with table().
chisq.test() compares observed counts with an independence expectation; inspect expected counts and the printed method.
corr() reports Pearson coefficients and counts on one common complete sample; cor.test() adds a test and confidence interval for a pair.
tidy() converts a test into a table, but interpretation still requires units, uncertainty, assumptions, and a denominator.
Optional: pwcorr() uses a separate available sample for each pair and reports unadjusted p-values; compare the counts before interpreting coefficients.

Chapter 24 extends the parental-schooling question by considering age and sex together on a shared analysis sample.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.6 Exercises

Repeat the Welch comparison with female before male in the sex factor. Predict what happens to the estimated difference, interval, and two-sided p-value, then verify it.
A researcher defines college with if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"), "College", "Other degree"). Diagnose the treatment of missing degrees and produce a corrected classification. Count the affected source answers.
Repeat the complete-pair correlation using paeduc, the father/older-parent variable. Use corr() to report its coefficient and count, then cor.test() for its confidence interval. Why can its difference from the maeduc result reflect coverage as well as a different parent measure? Optional: Compare corr() and pwcorr() using educ, maeduc, and paeduc from the full extract. Explain why adding the third variable changes the common-sample result for the original pair.
Country-level contrast. This exercise returns to the familiar country data to distinguish a country-level association from the respondent-level relationships above. Describe the association between lexp and gnppc in lifeexp. Give the complete-country count and Pearson coefficient. Explain why this is neither an individual-level relationship nor a population-weighted, random-sample estimate for the world’s people.

title: 23  Statistical tests
text:
23.7 Worked answers






NoteReverse the comparison





Start in a fresh session with the saved extract:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_schooling <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, sex) |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(sex)) |>
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, levels = c("female", "male")))
answer_welch <- stats::t.test(educ ~ sex, data = answer_schooling)
answer_welch_tidy <- broom::tidy(answer_welch)
answer_welch_tidy
# A tibble: 1 × 10
  estimate estimate1 estimate2 statistic p.value parameter conf.low conf.high
     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1  -0.0622      14.2      14.3    -0.670   0.503     3792.   -0.244     0.120
# ℹ 2 more variables: method <chr>, alternative <chr>


The same 3934 respondents now give a female-minus-male estimate of -0.062 years. The interval runs from -0.244 to 0.12 years. Reversing the subtraction negates the estimate and reverses the negated interval endpoints. The two-sided p-value remains 0.503 because the size of the standardized difference is unchanged. Always name the subtraction when reporting it.









NotePreserve unknown degrees





Load the packages and extract independently:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_degree <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, degree) |>
  mutate(
    college = if_else(
      is.na(degree), NA_character_,
      if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"),
              "College", "Other degree")
    )
  )
answer_degree |>
  count(degree, college)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  degree                   college          n
  <fct>                    <chr>        <int>
1 less than high school    Other degree   362
2 high school              Other degree  1817
3 associate/junior college Other degree   360
4 bachelor's               College        863
5 graduate                 College        577
6 NA                       NA               7

answer_unknown_degree <- answer_degree |>
  filter(is.na(degree))
nrow(answer_unknown_degree)

[1] 7

answer_unknown_degree
# A tibble: 7 × 3
     id degree college
  <int> <fct>  <chr>  
1   954 NA     NA     
2  1273 NA     NA     
3  1558 NA     NA     
4  3346 NA     NA     
5  3726 NA     NA     
6  3893 NA     NA     
7  3984 NA     NA     


There are 7 unknown degrees in the source. A missing degree is not in the named set, so the researcher’s expression assigns those respondents to "Other degree". The outer if_else() preserves their missing status instead. We can then exclude them for a known-degree comparison and state that denominator. Changing an unknown answer to a known non-college classification would alter the measurement.









NoteCheck father/older-parent coverage





Restore the saved extract in a new session:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_father <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, paeduc) |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(paeduc))
answer_mother <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc) |>
  filter(!is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc))
nrow(answer_father)

[1] 2855

nrow(answer_mother)

[1] 3432

answer_father_correlation <- corr(answer_father, educ, paeduc)
answer_father_correlation
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  var1  var2       r     n
  <chr> <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 educ  paeduc 0.379  2855

answer_father_test <- stats::cor.test(answer_father$educ, answer_father$paeduc)
answer_father_tidy <- broom::tidy(answer_father_test)
answer_father_tidy
# A tibble: 1 × 8
  estimate statistic  p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method    alternative
     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <int>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     <chr>      
1    0.379      21.9 2.01e-98      2853    0.348     0.410 Pearson'… two.sided  


The father/older-parent analysis includes 2855 complete pairs, compared with 3432 mother/younger-parent pairs. Its correlation is 0.379, with an interval from 0.348 to 0.41. This is a positive linear association. The two estimates concern different parent measures and different observed-answer samples. Their numerical difference alone does not establish a stronger relationship for one parent, and two separate significance tests do not test the difference between correlations.
Optional comparison. Use the full extract so that each function applies its own sample rule:

answer_common <- corr(answer_gss24, educ, maeduc, paeduc)
answer_common
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  var1   var2       r     n
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 educ   maeduc 0.347  2649
2 educ   paeduc 0.375  2649
3 maeduc paeduc 0.604  2649

answer_pairwise <- pwcorr(answer_gss24, educ, maeduc, paeduc)
answer_pairwise
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  var1   var2       r     n         p
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>     <dbl>
1 educ   maeduc 0.340  3432 1.60e- 93
2 educ   paeduc 0.379  2855 2.01e- 98
3 maeduc paeduc 0.606  2657 5.53e-266


answer_common uses respondents with all three values recorded for every coefficient. answer_pairwise uses the complete observations for each pair, so its counts differ. Adding paeduc therefore removes some otherwise complete educ-maeduc pairs from the common sample, changing the coefficient without changing any measured value. The pairwise table’s first row recovers the earlier two-variable Pearson result. More available pairs do not establish that missingness is harmless, and the printed p-values remain unadjusted model-based results.









NoteDescribe a country association





Load the packages in a fresh session. This answer uses only the packaged lifeexp table supplied by tidystata; each row represents a country:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)


answer_countries <- lifeexp |>
  select(country, lexp, gnppc) |>
  filter(!is.na(lexp), !is.na(gnppc))
nrow(answer_countries)

[1] 67

answer_country_test <- stats::cor.test(answer_countries$lexp,
                                     answer_countries$gnppc)
answer_country_tidy <- broom::tidy(answer_country_test)
answer_country_tidy
# A tibble: 1 × 8
  estimate statistic  p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method    alternative
     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <int>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     <chr>      
1    0.733      8.68 1.79e-12        65    0.598     0.827 Pearson'… two.sided  


Across 67 countries with both values observed, life expectancy in years and GNP per person in US dollars have a positive Pearson coefficient of 0.733. This describes a linear component of a country-level relationship, which can also curve. Each country contributes one pair regardless of population. These selected countries are not presented as an independent random sample of the world’s people, so the printed model-based interval and p-value do not justify that population claim. Inferring a personal income-health relationship from this country association would confuse levels of analysis.

title: 24  OLS regression
text:
24.1 Define the question and shared sample
How is parental schooling associated with respondents’ own schooling when we also consider age and sex? Chapter 23 described a pairwise association. OLS regression lets us state a model for several variables together, inspect its estimates, and check its limitations. We will use a single analysis sample so changes between models do not also change the respondents.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Use the table operations from the practical chapters, factors from Chapter 15, and graphics from Chapter 11. Prepare the saved extract using Appendix A. Load tidyverse and tidystata; stats::, broom::, and modelsummary:: identify functions from their packages without attaching them.
The reporting step adds modelsummary to the earlier package setup. Install it once before continuing: install.packages() downloads and installs the package named in quotes. You do not need to repeat this installation after restarting R.
Our first outcome, educ, is highest year of school completed. The main explanatory variable, maeduc, records the mother’s schooling or the younger parent’s schooling for same-sex parents, following the source definition. Age and sex allow a conditional comparison: the parental-schooling association among respondents of the same modeled age and sex. Adding these variables does not identify a causal effect. Family resources, institutions, cohorts, and other unmeasured circumstances can affect the association.
In Chapter 25, the outcome changes to college attainment, defined as a bachelor’s or graduate degree. To keep the OLS and binary comparisons on the same rows, select ID and all variables needed anywhere in the comparison, then exclude rows missing any of them. filter() applies the conditions together. We explicitly place male first in the sex factor: it will be the reference category, the category against which the female coefficient is expressed.
Only after excluding unknown degrees do we create college with if_else(). It is numeric 1 for "bachelor's" or "graduate", and 0 for the other known degrees, including associate/junior college. The %in% comparison is safe here because the preceding filter removed missing degree answers; it would not preserve those answers on its own.
model_data <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc, age, sex, degree) |>
  filter(!is.na(id), !is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc), !is.na(age),
         !is.na(sex), !is.na(degree)) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    college = if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"), 1, 0)
  )
nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986

nrow(model_data)

[1] 3329

summ(model_data, educ, maeduc, age)
# A tibble: 3 × 8
  name   type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
  <chr>  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 educ   dbl    3329     20     0  14.5  2.82    20
2 maeduc dbl    3329     21     0  12.5  3.44    20
3 age    dbl    3329     72    18  49.0 17.5     89

model_description <- model_data |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_educ = mean(educ),
            mean_maeduc = mean(maeduc),
            college_percent = 100 * mean(college), .by = sex)
model_description
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  sex        n mean_educ mean_maeduc college_percent
  <fct>  <int>     <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>
1 male    1484      14.5        12.7            39.8
2 female  1845      14.4        12.3            39.3
The analysis retains 3329 of the extract’s 3986 respondents. Each row remains one respondent; the summary reports schooling and age in years. The sex-specific rows show the group sizes, mean respondent and parent schooling, and college-attainment percentages within this shared sample. A mean of the 0/1 college indicator is a proportion, multiplied by 100 for a percentage. There is no need for na.rm because the required values are observed.
This restriction makes comparisons transparent, but it also excludes respondents who would be usable in an individual model. Complete-case analysis does not repair missing values or guarantee that included respondents resemble excluded ones. We retain the source table unchanged and make no population correction by restricting it.
All models below are unweighted teaching examples with ordinary model-based uncertainty. They do not account for the GSS sampling design. Its wtssps variable is a post-stratification weight; putting it into lm(weights = ...) would not, by itself, supply survey-design inference. We do not do that here.

title: 24  OLS regression
text:
24.2 Fit a simple linear model
A linear model expresses the expected outcome as an intercept plus coefficients multiplying explanatory variables. In a simple model, the fitted schooling value is an intercept plus a slope times parent schooling. The residual is an observed outcome minus its fitted value. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
stats::lm() fits this model. Its formula educ ~ maeduc places the outcome on the left of ~ and the explanatory variable on the right; data = model_data identifies their table. Assignment saves a model object rather than replacing the respondent table. Printing the object shows the fitted call and coefficients.

ols_simple <- stats::lm(educ ~ maeduc, data = model_data)
ols_simple


Call:
stats::lm(formula = educ ~ maeduc, data = model_data)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)       maeduc  
    10.9984       0.2784  


The intercept is fitted respondent schooling when parent schooling is zero. The maeduc slope is the difference in fitted respondent schooling, in years, associated with one additional year of parent schooling. It describes a comparison between respondents in this sample, not the effect of an intervention on their parents.
broom::tidy() returns one row per estimated coefficient. With conf.int = TRUE, it includes the default 95% interval as conf.low and conf.high. estimate gives the coefficient, std.error its estimated standard error, statistic its t statistic, and p.value the two-sided test of a zero coefficient. These inferential columns rely on the model’s assumptions. They do not determine whether a coefficient is substantively important.

ols_simple_tidy <- broom::tidy(ols_simple, conf.int = TRUE)
ols_simple_tidy
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   11.0      0.173       63.7 0          10.7      11.3  
2 maeduc         0.278    0.0133      20.9 4.81e-91    0.252     0.305


Respondents with more educated mothers/younger parents tend to have more schooling. One additional year of parent schooling corresponds to about 0.278 additional years of fitted respondent schooling. Its model-based interval is 0.252 to 0.305 years per parent-schooling year. The intercept describes the fitted line’s starting point, not an average for all respondents.
The fitted model and its coefficient table serve different purposes. ols_simple retains the model for later calculations, while ols_simple_tidy is a tibble that we can select, relabel, or export using the table tools already learned. The model does not become a tibble merely because its input is one. The optional comparison in Section 28.8 follows these object types through both routes.

title: 24  OLS regression
section: 24.3 Add age and a reference category
text:
24.3 Add age and a reference category
The adjusted formula adds age + sex. Within a model formula, + includes separate explanatory terms; it does not add these columns together to form a new variable. A numeric age coefficient represents a linear difference per year of age. R represents the two-level sex factor with a female indicator because male is the reference. Both models use model_data without another filter.

ols_adjusted <- stats::lm(educ ~ maeduc + age + sex, data = model_data)
ols_adjusted_tidy <- broom::tidy(ols_adjusted, conf.int = TRUE)
ols_adjusted_tidy
# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)  9.83      0.248     39.6    2.83e-281   9.35     10.3   
2 maeduc       0.299     0.0136    22.0    3.89e-100   0.272     0.326 
3 age          0.0186    0.00267    6.96   3.94e- 12   0.0134    0.0239
4 sexfemale   -0.00641   0.0919    -0.0698 9.44e-  1  -0.187     0.174 


The parental-schooling association remains positive after this adjustment: about 0.299 years of respondent schooling per parent-schooling year, holding modeled age and sex constant. Its interval is 0.272 to 0.326. Holding constant describes a comparison within the fitted equation; it does not mean we experimentally fixed those characteristics.
The age coefficient is about 0.019 schooling years per year of age at the same parent schooling and sex. This cross-sectional age pattern combines differences between people and birth cohorts; it is not a prediction that an individual gains that schooling every birthday. sexfemale is female minus male at the same age and parent schooling. Its estimate of -0.006 years is close to zero, with an interval spanning -0.187 to 0.174 years. We retain this weak evidence rather than dropping a prespecified comparison to obtain smaller p-values.
The adjusted intercept refers to a male respondent with age zero and parent schooling zero. Age zero is outside this adult sample, so the intercept mainly positions the fitted equation. A model can contain an interpretable slope without giving a substantively useful intercept at every mathematical origin.
stats::nobs() counts observations actually used by a fitted model. broom::glance() returns one row of overall model statistics. We keep only nobs and r.squared here: R-squared is the fraction of sample variation in the outcome accounted for by the fitted model, relative to an intercept-only fit.

stats::nobs(ols_simple)

[1] 3329

  select(nobs, r.squared)
