Both models use 3329 observations. Their R-squared values are about 0.116 and 0.129. Additional terms cannot lower ordinary in-sample R-squared on the same rows, so the increase alone does not establish that a model is appropriate or predicts new respondents well. The shared sample makes this comparison about specifications rather than changing coverage.

title: 24  OLS regression
text:
24.4 Inspect fitted values and residuals
OLS supplies a fitted mean, not a claim that every respondent lies on that mean. broom::augment() returns the model’s observation-level data with diagnostic columns. .fitted is fitted respondent schooling and .resid is observed minus fitted schooling, both in years. These leading dots are part of the column names. We retain the full result as ols_diagnostics and preview the two columns with familiar select() and head().

ols_diagnostics <- broom::augment(ols_adjusted)
ols_diagnostics |>
  select(.fitted, .resid) |>
  head()
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  .fitted .resid
    <dbl>  <dbl>
1    14.6  1.37 
2    14.7 -0.699
3    14.4 -1.42 
4    12.3  1.69 
5    14.3 -1.31 
6    10.9  3.06 


Plot residuals against fitted values to look for curvature, changes in spread, and unusually large discrepancies. geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") adds a dashed horizontal reference at zero residual. Point transparency reduces overplotting. Neither step changes a fitted value or removes a respondent.

ggplot(ols_diagnostics, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Fitted respondent schooling (years)",
       y = "Observed minus fitted schooling (years)") +
  theme_bw()







Figure 24.1: Residuals against fitted schooling for the adjusted OLS model; both axes are in schooling years, on the shared complete-case sample.





Figure 24.1 shows substantial variation around the fitted means and visible structure from bounded, discrete schooling. The upper schooling limit constrains possible positive residuals as fitted values increase. This is a reason to treat the linear equation as a limited summary, not a complete account of schooling attainment. The plot does not certify the model or tell us to delete inconvenient observations.
The ordinary OLS intervals above assume a correctly specified conditional mean and independent errors with constant variance; exact small-sample t inference adds normal errors. A normally distributed outcome is not itself an OLS requirement. A residual plot can reveal problems with mean shape or spread but cannot verify independence, omitted-variable assumptions, or survey-design validity. We keep these limitations alongside the estimates rather than treating a small p-value as a diagnostic.

title: 24  OLS regression
section: 24.5 Report the analysis as one argument
text:
24.5 Report the analysis as one argument
Return to the question before presenting a table. We asked how respondent schooling relates to parent schooling, defined a common sample, described its composition, fitted simple and adjusted models, and inspected residuals. A results table makes selected estimates comparable; it cannot replace those decisions or their interpretation.
modelsummary::modelsummary() accepts a named list() of models; list() holds the two model objects together and its names label the columns. statistic = "conf.int" puts the default 95% confidence interval beneath each coefficient. stars = FALSE omits significance stars so attention stays on magnitudes and intervals. gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared") limits the model-summary rows to sample size and R-squared. output = "markdown" produces a table Quarto can format. The chunk’s results: asis displays that Markdown as table content, and Quarto supplies the single caption.



Table 24.1: OLS associations with respondent schooling in years; 95% model-based confidence intervals in brackets. Male is the reference sex category, and both models use the same complete-case respondents.


modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Simple OLS" = ols_simple, "Adjusted OLS" = ols_adjusted),
  statistic = "conf.int",
  stars = FALSE,
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  output = "markdown"
)

Table 24.1 supports a modest, specific conclusion: among the 3329 included respondents, higher mother/younger-parent schooling is associated with higher respondent schooling. The adjusted estimate is about 0.3 schooling years per parent-schooling year, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 0.33. Adjusting for age and sex does not remove this association, while the conditional female-minus-male estimate is close to zero and imprecise relative to its size. Considerable schooling variation remains outside these equations, and bounded schooling limits a linear description.

title: 24  OLS regression
text:
24.6 Review

Define the question and shared complete-case sample before fitting models; exclusions do not repair missing data.
lm() fits an OLS equation; coefficients require outcome units, predictor units, and an explicit reference category.
tidy() reports coefficients and intervals, while glance() and nobs() summarize the fit and sample.
augment() supplies fitted values and residuals for diagnostic plots; a plot cannot validate every assumption.
modelsummary() presents selected model results with their limitations.

Next, Chapter 25 uses the same sample to model college attainment and compare predicted probabilities.

24.7 Exercises

text:
24.8 Worked answers






NoteReconstruct and interpret OLS





Restore the saved extract in a fresh session:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidystata)
answer_gss24 <- readRDS("gss24.rds")


answer_model_data <- answer_gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc, age, sex, degree) |>
  filter(!is.na(id), !is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc), !is.na(age),

  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    college = if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"), 1, 0)

answer_simple <- stats::lm(educ ~ maeduc, data = answer_model_data)
answer_adjusted <- stats::lm(educ ~ maeduc + age + sex, data = answer_model_data)

Both models use 3329 respondents. The adjusted parental-schooling coefficient is 0.299 schooling years per parent-schooling year, with a 95% interval from 0.272 to 0.326. At the same modeled age and sex, respondents whose mother/younger parent completed one more year of schooling have about that much more fitted schooling. This is a conditional association, with ordinary model-based uncertainty, not a causal effect or survey-adjusted population estimate.









NoteReverse the reference category

library(tidystata)

The intercept moves from the male baseline to the female baseline; the maeduc and age slopes remain the same. The fitted schooling values for every respondent remain the same, because only the representation of the same two categories changed. Reversing a reference category cannot create a stronger substantive association.

title: 25  Logit and probit
text:
25.1 Restore the shared sample
How is parental schooling associated with the probability of completing a bachelor’s or graduate degree? Chapter 24 described years of schooling with OLS. Here we retain the same respondents and model a binary outcome, then compare the two models on a probability scale.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Use the table operations from the practical chapters, factors from Chapter 15, and model formulas from Chapter 24. Prepare the saved extract using Appendix A. The setup is repeated here so the chapter runs in a fresh session. stats:: and broom:: identify functions from their packages without attaching them.
Recreate the sample from Section 24.1. Require recorded ID, schooling, parent schooling, age, sex, and degree, so these models use the same respondents as the preceding OLS comparison. The source variable educ records years of schooling; maeduc records mother’s or younger-parent schooling under the appendix’s parent definition.
The indicator college is 1 for a bachelor’s or graduate degree and 0 for another recorded degree, including associate/junior college. We exclude unknown degrees before using %in%, so an unknown answer cannot become a known zero. The sex factor lists male first to retain the same reference category. The source extract remains unchanged.
model_data <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc, age, sex, degree) |>
  filter(!is.na(id), !is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc), !is.na(age),
         !is.na(sex), !is.na(degree)) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    college = if_else(degree %in% c("bachelor's", "graduate"), 1, 0)
  )
nrow(gss24)

[1] 3986

nrow(model_data)

[1] 3329

summ(model_data, educ, maeduc, age)

  name   type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max

1 educ   dbl    3329     20     0  14.5  2.82    20
2 maeduc dbl    3329     21     0  12.5  3.44    20

model_description <- model_data |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_educ = mean(educ),
            mean_maeduc = mean(maeduc),
            college_percent = 100 * mean(college), .by = sex)
model_description
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  sex        n mean_educ mean_maeduc college_percent
  <fct>  <int>     <dbl>       <dbl>           <dbl>
1 male    1484      14.5        12.7            39.8

The analysis retains 3329 of the extract’s 3986 respondents. Each row remains one respondent; the summary reports schooling and age in years. The sex-specific rows show the group sizes, mean respondent and parent schooling, and college-attainment percentages within this shared sample. A mean of the 0/1 college indicator is a proportion, multiplied by 100 for a percentage. There is no need for na.rm because the required values are observed.
This restriction makes comparisons transparent, but it also excludes respondents who would be usable in an individual model. Complete-case analysis does not repair missing values or guarantee that included respondents resemble excluded ones. We retain the source table unchanged and make no population correction by restricting it.
All models below are unweighted teaching examples with ordinary model-based uncertainty. They do not account for the GSS sampling design. Its wtssps variable is a post-stratification weight; putting it into lm(weights = ...) would not, by itself, supply survey-design inference. We do not do that here.

title: 25  Logit and probit
section: 25.2 Model a binary outcome and predict probabilities
text:
25.2 Model a binary outcome and predict probabilities
College attainment takes values zero and one. We now model its probability on the same model_data rows. stats::glm() fits a generalized linear model. family = stats::binomial(link = "logit") specifies a binary outcome with the logit link, which relates a linear combination of the explanatory variables to the log odds of college attainment. For a probability \(p\), odds are \(p/(1-p)\), the ratio of the probability of college attainment to that of non-attainment; log odds are the natural logarithm of that ratio. A logit coefficient is a difference in log odds per unit of a predictor, conditional on the other terms. It is not a percentage-point difference.

logit_model <- stats::glm(
  college ~ maeduc + age + sex, data = model_data,
  family = stats::binomial(link = "logit")
)
logit_tidy <- broom::tidy(logit_model)
logit_tidy
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept)  -3.55     0.235     -15.1   8.92e-52
2 maeduc        0.186    0.0131     14.1   3.19e-45
3 age           0.0151   0.00219     6.86  6.67e-12
4 sexfemale     0.0499   0.0740      0.674 5.00e- 1


The positive parent-schooling coefficient means that the fitted probability increases with parent schooling at the same age and sex. The output’s statistic is a large-sample z statistic for this GLM, rather than the OLS t statistic. We have changed both the outcome and the model, so do not compare the raw schooling-year OLS coefficients with these log-odds coefficients.
A probit model uses the same binary outcome and explanatory terms with link = "probit". Its link is the inverse of the standard normal cumulative distribution, so its coefficients use a different latent scale. Coefficient magnitudes cannot be compared directly with logit magnitudes. Predictions expressed as probabilities are easier to compare.

probit_model <- stats::glm(
  college ~ maeduc + age + sex, data = model_data,
  family = stats::binomial(link = "probit")
)
probit_tidy <- broom::tidy(probit_model)
probit_tidy
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept) -2.11      0.137     -15.4   9.68e-54
2 maeduc       0.109     0.00762    14.3   1.36e-46
3 age          0.00906   0.00133     6.79  1.11e-11
4 sexfemale    0.0296    0.0454      0.653 5.14e- 1

stats::nobs(logit_model)

[1] 3329

stats::nobs(probit_model)

[1] 3329


Both binary models retain the same 3329 respondents as the OLS comparison. They assume the chosen link and additive predictor form are adequate, with independent binary observations for the ordinary model-based inference. Changing the link does not repair missingness, survey dependence, or omitted explanations.
For a concrete comparison, consider female respondents aged 50 whose mother/younger parent completed 12 or 16 years of school. Check that both complete predictor combinations occur in our sample with filter() and count(). Then construct exactly those two rows with tibble(). The two-element columns are aligned by position, and the sex factor uses the model’s level order.

prediction_support <- model_data |>
  filter(age == 50, sex == "female", maeduc %in% c(12, 16)) |>
  count(maeduc, age, sex)
prediction_support
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  maeduc   age sex        n
   <dbl> <dbl> <fct>  <int>
1     12    50 female    11
2     16    50 female     2

prediction_cases <- tibble(
  maeduc = c(12, 16),
  age = c(50, 50),
  sex = factor(c("female", "female"), levels = c("male", "female"))
)

The two combinations occur for 11 and 2 respondents, respectively. The smaller cell is a reminder that observed support can still be sparse. We are not estimating separate means from just those two cells: each fitted model uses the entire common sample.
stats::predict() takes a fitted model and newdata, the table of predictor values. For these GLMs, type = "response" returns probabilities between zero and one rather than values on the link scale. We multiply by 100 to display percentages and store a separate output table, leaving the prediction inputs unchanged. knitr::kable() formats it, with digits = 1 rounding displayed numeric values to one decimal place.

prediction_table <- prediction_cases |>
  mutate(
    logit_percent = 100 * stats::predict(
      logit_model, newdata = prediction_cases, type = "response"
    ),
    probit_percent = 100 * stats::predict(
      probit_model, newdata = prediction_cases, type = "response"
    )
  )
knitr::kable(prediction_table, digits = 1)

title: 25  Logit and probit
text:
25.3 Interpret the comparison
The binary models tell a related story for our particular degree definition: at the specified age and sex, predicted college attainment is higher at 16 than at 12 years of parent schooling. Similar logit and probit predictions are reassuring about this particular comparison, not proof that either model is correct. Complete-case selection, ordinary unweighted inference, and unmeasured circumstances limit every result. We can describe conditional associations and fitted probabilities here; we cannot claim a representative national effect or a causal return to parental schooling.

title: 25  Logit and probit
text:
25.4 Review

Define the outcome and common sample before comparing models; a missing degree is not non-attainment.
glm() fits logit or probit binary models; their coefficient scales differ.
tidy() reports model coefficients, and nobs() checks contributing observations.
predict() returns conditional probabilities with type = "response"; state the predictor values and check their support.
Compare probability predictions with their sample and model limitations, without a causal interpretation or survey-design correction.

The optional Programming part, Chapter 27 and Chapter 28, provides additional detail about R expressions and objects when you need it.

title: 25  Logit and probit
text:
25.5 Exercises

Reconstruct the shared sample, logit model, and probit model. Check support and reproduce the predicted probabilities for female respondents aged 50 at parent schooling 12 and 16. Interpret the probability differences and explain why the raw logit and probit coefficients are not directly comparable.

title: 25  Logit and probit
26  Fixed effects
text:
26.1 Compare within regions
Does the association between parent and respondent schooling persist when we compare respondents within the same region? The Chapter 24 chapter adjusted for age and sex. We now let regions have different intercepts while retaining a common parental-schooling slope. A second application uses repeated observations of the same people to explain what changes when the group is a person rather than a region.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Use the table operations from earlier chapters, factors from Chapter 15, and formulas and coefficient tables from Chapter 24. Prepare gss24.rds using the Appendix A and keep it in your working directory. The setup below is complete for a fresh session. Package prefixes such as fixest:: identify a function’s package without attaching it.
The new fitting package is fixest. The later panel application also uses data included in plm. Install both once, rather than every time you run the chapter. This installation chunk is deliberately not evaluated when the book renders.
The main outcome remains educ, the highest year of school completed. maeduc records mother’s schooling or younger-parent schooling for same-sex parents, following the source definition. Age and sex retain their earlier roles. The new variable, region, identifies the respondent’s current region. It does not necessarily describe where the respondent grew up or attended school.
A group fixed effect gives each group its own intercept. Respondents in the same region share that region’s intercept, while each respondent retains their own predictor values. In our additive model, the parent-schooling, age, and sex coefficients are shared across regions. Different intercepts do not imply different slopes. An interaction would be needed to let the parent-schooling slope vary by region; that is a different model from the one fitted here.
For this GSS comparison, fixed effects are a way to include categorical region adjustment in a linear model. They do not turn the GSS into a panel. Each row is still a different respondent observed once. The later application will use repeated observations and person fixed effects, where the available comparisons change more substantially.
First reconstruct the preceding OLS and logit chapters’ complete-case sample, adding the requirement that region is known. We retain degree even though this chapter does not model it, so the comparison preserves the earlier sample definition. Both models below use the resulting table without further filtering. Male remains the reference sex; converting region to a factor ensures that region codes are treated as categories rather than a numeric trend.
region_data <- gss24 |>
  select(id, educ, maeduc, age, sex, degree, region) |>
  filter(!is.na(id), !is.na(educ), !is.na(maeduc), !is.na(age),
         !is.na(sex), !is.na(degree), !is.na(region)) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    region = factor(region)
  )

The analysis retains 3329 respondents. The frequency table counts respondents within each of the four recorded regions; it is not a count of repeated observations of people. The numerical summary describes schooling and age in years. These checks establish the sample and units before a model comparison. Excluding unknown values makes the comparison consistent, but does not establish that retained respondents resemble those excluded.
The GSS models in this chapter are unweighted teaching examples with ordinary model-based uncertainty. They do not account for the survey’s sampling design and do not provide survey-adjusted population estimates. The available survey weight is not a substitute for specifying that design. Nor would clustering on only four broad regions provide a reliable general solution to uncertainty here.

title: 26  Fixed effects
text:
26.1.1 Include region indicators
We can fit region fixed effects with the familiar stats::lm(). Add region to the formula alongside the other explanatory terms. R represents the region factor using an omitted reference region and indicators for the other regions. In this sample, northeast is the reference region. Each displayed region coefficient is an intercept difference from the reference, conditional on the other modeled terms.

region_adjusted <- stats::lm(
  educ ~ maeduc + age + sex, data = region_data
)
region_lm <- stats::lm(
  educ ~ maeduc + age + sex + region, data = region_data
)
broom::tidy(region_lm, conf.int = TRUE)

[1] 3329


The output retains the familiar maeduc, age, and sexfemale coefficients, followed by the region contrasts. The omitted region has no separate coefficient because its intercept is already represented by (Intercept). A positive region contrast means higher fitted schooling than the reference region at the same modeled parent schooling, age, and sex. It is not a claim that moving there would increase schooling. Current residence may itself reflect earlier educational and employment choices.
Both models use 3329 observations. To focus on our question, make one coefficient table containing just the parental-schooling rows. bind_rows() stacks tables that have matching column names. Its named inputs become values in the new model column when we supply .id = "model". The familiar tidy() supplies coefficient tables; filter() and select() retain the comparison we want.

region_comparison <- bind_rows(
  "Age and sex" = broom::tidy(region_adjusted, conf.int = TRUE),
  "Age, sex, and region" = broom::tidy(region_lm, conf.int = TRUE),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  filter(term == "maeduc") |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)
region_comparison
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  model                estimate std.error conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                   <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Age and sex             0.299    0.0136    0.272     0.326
2 Age, sex, and region    0.299    0.0136    0.273     0.326


Each row is an estimate from a model, rather than a respondent. The columns contain the parental-schooling slope, its standard error, and the endpoints of its ordinary 95% confidence interval. The slope unit is respondent-schooling years per parent-schooling year.
knitr::kable() formats this small table for reading. digits = 3 rounds displayed numeric values to three decimals without changing the stored estimates. The caption identifies the sample and uncertainty; the automatic table number can be used in the text.

knitr::kable(region_comparison, digits = 3)

The parental-schooling association is essentially unchanged after allowing region intercepts. In Table 26.1, both estimates round to 0.299 additional years of respondent schooling per additional year of parent schooling. More precisely, they are 0.299025 without region and 0.299164 with region. We should report this small change rather than expect fixed effects to produce a dramatic revision.
The region-adjusted slope describes a shared within-region association, conditional on modeled age and sex. It does not hold every family circumstance constant. Broad current regions leave substantial differences within regions, and do not measure childhood institutions directly. A nearly unchanged coefficient neither proves that geography is unimportant nor establishes that the parental-schooling association is causal.


26.1.2 Absorb the intercepts
For a few groups, displaying their indicators is manageable. With hundreds of people or organizations, the group intercepts can crowd out the coefficients of interest. fixest::feols() fits a linear fixed-effects model while absorbing those intercepts: it accounts for them without listing every one among the reported slope coefficients.
In its formula, the single vertical bar separates ordinary explanatory terms from the fixed-effect grouping variable. educ ~ maeduc + age + sex | region keeps schooling as the outcome, puts the three explanatory variables before |, and places region after it. This formula separator is different from the native pipe |>, which passes an object into a function. vcov = "iid" requests ordinary independent, constant-variance model-based uncertainty for this GSS demonstration.

region_fe <- fixest::feols(
  educ ~ maeduc + age + sex | region,
  data = region_data, vcov = "iid"
)
region_fe

OLS estimation, Dep. Var.: educ
Observations: 3,329
Fixed-effects: region: 4
Standard-errors: IID 
           Estimate Std. Error   t value   Pr(>|t|)    
maeduc     0.299164   0.013591 22.011086  < 2.2e-16 ***
age        0.018409   0.002677  6.877281 7.2584e-12 ***
sexfemale -0.017525   0.092127 -0.190229 8.4914e-01

RMSE: 2.62519     Adj. R2: 0.130056
                Within R2: 0.128879


The printed model identifies region as a fixed effect and reports the nonabsorbed coefficients. The parent-schooling estimate should match the lm() model that included the region factor. Absorption changes how we obtain and present that estimate, not the underlying additive comparison.
Use the earlier coefficient-table tools to inspect that equivalence. The maeduc rows should have the same estimate apart from numerical rounding. Check the shared observation count as well. Exact reporting conventions for degrees of freedom or fit measures can differ across software; matching slope estimates is the equivalence demonstrated here.

region_equivalence <- bind_rows(
  "lm indicators" = broom::tidy(region_lm),
  "feols absorption" = broom::tidy(region_fe),
  .id = "method"
) |>
  filter(term == "maeduc") |>
  select(method, estimate)
region_equivalence
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  method           estimate
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 lm indicators       0.299
2 feols absorption    0.299

stats::nobs(region_fe)

[1] 3329


Both implementations use the same respondents and produce the same parental-schooling slope. The fixed-effect model has not estimated a separate parental-schooling slope for every region. It has estimated a common slope while permitting the baseline level of schooling to differ across regions.






NoteOptional: subtract the region means



A bounded numerical demonstration helps explain “within region.” For this demonstration only, omit age and sex and compare a simpler region-adjusted model with a model of deviations from region means. This is not a reconstruction of the full adjusted model above.
Inside mutate(), .by = region calculates each mean within a region and repeats that mean for its members. Subtracting it gives a respondent’s distance above or below the region mean. We create two new columns in a separate table, preserving the original schooling values.

region_centered <- region_data |>
  mutate(
    educ_within = educ - mean(educ),
    maeduc_within = maeduc - mean(maeduc),
    .by = region
  )
region_centered |>
  select(region, educ, educ_within, maeduc, maeduc_within) |>
  head()
# A tibble: 6 × 5
  region     educ educ_within maeduc maeduc_within
  <fct>     <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>         <dbl>
1 northeast    16       1.26      14         1.43 
2 northeast    14      -0.742     12        -0.568
3 northeast    13      -1.74      11        -1.57 
4 northeast    14      -0.742      5        -7.57 
5 northeast    13      -1.74      12        -0.568
6 northeast    14      -0.742      0       -12.6  


For example, a negative educ_within means fewer years of schooling than the sample mean in that respondent’s region. The same row’s maeduc_within gives the analogous parent-schooling deviation. These are differences in years, not standardized scores or percentages.
In an lm() formula, - 1 removes the intercept. After subtracting both region means, we fit a line through zero to the two deviation columns. The following two slopes match because both describe the simple schooling association after allowing region-specific intercepts.

region_simple <- stats::lm(educ ~ maeduc + region, data = region_data)
region_within <- stats::lm(
  educ_within ~ maeduc_within - 1, data = region_centered
)
broom::tidy(region_simple) |>
  filter(term == "maeduc")
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  term   estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 maeduc    0.279    0.0133      20.9 1.73e-91

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  term          estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 maeduc_within    0.279    0.0133      20.9 1.35e-91


This demonstrates slope equivalence only. Ordinary uncertainty from the demeaned fit does not automatically count the estimated region intercepts correctly. To reproduce the full adjusted slope by this route, we would also need to transform all the other explanatory terms appropriately. Use the full lm() or feols() fit for reporting, rather than treating this two-column illustration as a replacement.

title: 26  Fixed effects
text:
26.2 Secondary application: a panel
How are wages associated with union membership and marriage when we follow the same people over time? The GSS extract does not follow respondents annually, so this question requires a different dataset. We now use Males, a historical panel supplied by plm. Keeping the application together makes the dataset change explicit: the unit becomes one person in one year, and the outcome becomes the logarithm of hourly wages.
The installed plm help entry for Males describes observations of 545 young men over 1980–1987, with eight annual observations per person. Its source is the wage-panel application associated with Vella and Verbeek (1998), “Whose wages do unions raise? A dynamic model of unionism and wage rate determination for young men,” Journal of Applied Econometrics, 13, 163–183. This restricted historical sample should not be described as all workers or as a contemporary national workforce.
Record the package versions alongside this source reference. utils::packageVersion() takes a quoted package name and returns its installed version. The first result identifies the data package; the second identifies the fixed-effects implementation used for this application. Recording versions helps distinguish this particular reproducible example from later package updates.

utils::packageVersion("plm")

[1] '2.6.7'

utils::packageVersion("fixest")

[1] '0.14.1'


utils::data() loads a dataset distributed inside an installed package. Its first argument names the dataset and package = "plm" identifies its source. It creates Males in the session; no external file download is needed for the lesson.

utils::data("Males", package = "plm")

as_tibble() converts this data frame to the table form used throughout the book. We assign the result to a new object so the packaged source remains available unchanged.

panel_source <- as_tibble(Males)
panel_source

The source uses nr for person ID and wage for the natural logarithm of hourly wages. In particular, wage is already logged: taking its logarithm again would change the outcome incorrectly. Use familiar rename() to make these meanings visible as person_id and log_wage. year is the observation year; union and married are yes/no factors. school records schooling years, and ethn identifies the source ethnicity categories.

panel_data <- panel_source |>
  rename(person_id = nr, log_wage = wage) |>
  select(person_id, year, log_wage, union, married, school, ethn)
head(panel_data)
# A tibble: 6 × 7
  person_id  year log_wage union married school ethn 
      <int> <int>    <dbl> <fct> <fct>    <int> <fct>
1        13  1980     1.20 no    no          14 other

Each displayed row now has an explicit person identifier and year. Repeated IDs are expected in a panel; duplicate person-year combinations are not. We must check this structure before treating the observations as repeated measures.

26.2.1 Check repeated observations
count(person_id, year) creates one row per observed ID-year combination and counts its records. Filtering for n != 1 shows any combinations that occur more than once. An empty result means every observed combination is unique; it does not yet establish that every expected year exists for every person.

panel_duplicate_keys <- panel_data |>
  count(person_id, year) |>
  filter(n != 1)
panel_duplicate_keys
# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: person_id <int>, year <int>, n <int>


Next count observations per person, naming that count waves, then count how many people have each number of waves. Count years separately to verify the calendar coverage. These are familiar table operations with two different denominators: people in the first result, person-year records in the second.

panel_wave_counts <- panel_data |>
  count(person_id, name = "waves") |>
  count(waves, name = "persons")
panel_wave_counts
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  waves persons
  <int>   <int>
1     8     545

count(panel_data, year)
# A tibble: 8 × 2
   year     n
  <int> <int>
1  1980   545
2  1981   545
3  1982   545
4  1983   545
5  1984   545
6  1985   545
7  1986   545

nrow(panel_data)

[1] 4360


The results show 545 people, each with eight observations, for 4,360 person-year rows. Every year from 1980 through 1987 has 545 records. Together with the unique keys, these checks establish a balanced annual panel over this period. The 4,360 records are not 4,360 independent people.
Check missing core model values separately. This filter keeps a row if any required value is missing; | inside the filter means logical “or,” a third use distinct from |> and the feols() formula separator. nrow() counts the selected rows. We do not overwrite panel_data or silently drop records.

panel_missing <- panel_data |>
  filter(is.na(person_id) | is.na(year) | is.na(log_wage) |
           is.na(union) | is.na(married))
nrow(panel_missing)

[1] 0


Zero rows have missing values in these core variables. Both wage models can therefore use all 4,360 rows. This check concerns recorded values; it does not assess measurement accuracy or how these people entered the source panel.


26.2.2 Find within-person variation
A person fixed effect permits every person to have a different intercept. The explanatory slopes then use changes within people over time. A variable that never changes for a person cannot explain that person’s deviations from their own level.
n_distinct() counts distinct observed values. Inside summarise() with .by = person_id, it tells us how many union states, marital states, or schooling values each person has across their eight records. Because the core status variables are complete, one state means no recorded change and two states means at least one yes/no change.

panel_variation <- panel_data |>
  summarise(
    union_states = n_distinct(union),
    married_states = n_distinct(married),
    school_values = n_distinct(school),
    .by = person_id
  )
count(panel_variation, union_states)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  union_states     n
         <int> <int>
1            1   299
2            2   246

count(panel_variation, married_states)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  married_states     n
           <int> <int>
1              1   235
2              2   310

count(panel_variation, school_values)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  school_values     n
          <int> <int>
1             1   545


The first two results distinguish people who change union or marital status from those whose recorded status is constant. The last shows one schooling value for all 545 people. Person fixed effects therefore absorb schooling in this dataset: there is no within-person schooling change from which to estimate a separate schooling slope. Source ethnicity is also time invariant and is absorbed.
“Absorbed” does not mean that schooling or ethnicity is substantively unimportant. Their stable association with each person’s wage level cannot be separated from that person’s unrestricted intercept in this specification. Similarly, linear experience increases with calendar time within each person. Its linear term is collinear with person and year effects here, so we do not add it to the two-way model. Estimating a coefficient requires variation that remains after all included fixed effects are accounted for.


26.2.3 Fit person and year effects
First fit a pooled wage model with year fixed effects. It compares records across different people as well as within people, while allowing a common intercept shift for every calendar year. The union and married factors use no as their reference categories; unionyes and marriedyes are yes-minus-no contrasts. Check these categories using the familiar frequency tables before fitting.

tab(panel_data, union)
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  union     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct> <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 no     3296    75.6  75.6  75.6      75.6
2 yes    1064    24.4 100    24.4     100  

tab(panel_data, married)
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  married     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
  <fct>   <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 no       2446    56.1  56.1  56.1      56.1
2 yes      1914    43.9 100    43.9     100  


For panel uncertainty, vcov = ~ person_id requests standard errors clustered by person. The one-sided formula names the cluster identifier; it does not add a predictor. This allows errors from different years for the same person to be dependent, while treating different people as independent clusters. It changes the uncertainty calculation, not the fitted slope coefficients. We have 545 person clusters, unlike the four regions in the GSS example.

panel_year <- fixest::feols(
  log_wage ~ union + married | year,
  data = panel_data, vcov = ~ person_id
)
panel_year

Observations: 4,360
Fixed-effects: year: 8
Standard-errors: Clustered (person_id)

marriedyes 0.142476   0.027835 5.11862 4.2762e-07 ***

RMSE: 0.501477     Adj. R2: 0.111452
                 Within R2: 0.0412  


The union and marriage coefficients are positive. Because this pooled model does not allow separate person intercepts, these associations can reflect stable differences between people as well as changes in their circumstances. Year effects account for common year shifts, not for every individual wage trajectory.
Now put person_id + year after the formula separator. The plus sign includes both sets of intercepts. Person fixed effects account for stable person-level differences; year effects account for changes shared across the sample in a given year. The union and marriage coefficients use the remaining within-person variation, after those year shifts are taken into account.

panel_person_year <- fixest::feols(
  log_wage ~ union + married | person_id + year,
  data = panel_data, vcov = ~ person_id
)
panel_person_year

Both models use all 4,360 person-year records. The smaller union and marriage coefficients in the second model therefore do not result from changing the sample. Their comparison has changed from a mixture of between-person and within-person information to information within people, net of common year effects.
Combine the two coefficient tables as before. For these models, tidy() obtains the uncertainty specified when each model was fitted, so the standard errors and confidence intervals reflect clustering by person. This output has two rows per model, one for each nonabsorbed explanatory term.

panel_comparison <- bind_rows(
  "Year effects" = broom::tidy(panel_year, conf.int = TRUE),
  "Person and year effects" = broom::tidy(panel_person_year, conf.int = TRUE),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  select(model, term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)
